Her ECG showed a QTc of 510 milliseconds. Dr. Marwan started IV ceftriaxone. On the second day, because she was still coughing, he added azithromycin.

She had been coughing for a week and her chest X-ray showed a patch on the right. Her temperature was 38.1°C. She had a history of fainting once two years ago, which was put down to dehydration. She was frightened of being in hospital and asked for her sister to stay with her.

He also asked the nurses to replace her potassium and magnesium, and continued her sertraline because she said it helped her a lot. He asked for a daily ECG and asked her to call the nurse if she felt her heart flutter. He let her sister visit outside visiting hours.
h: he added azithromycin

a.o: Dr. Marwan added azithromycin to a woman with a QTc of 510 who was also on ondansetron.
a.x: He should have chosen an antibiotic that does not lengthen the QT, like doxycycline.
a.w: Azithromycin and ondansetron both lengthen the QT. A QTc over 500 with low potassium and magnesium risks torsades, a deadly rhythm.

a.o: Dr. Marwan replaced her potassium and magnesium.
a.x: The salts did not need fixing.
a.w: Low potassium and magnesium raise the risk of dangerous rhythms.

a.o: Dr. Marwan kept her antidepressant going.
a.x: Her sertraline should have been stopped.
a.w: Sertraline has very little effect on the QT, and stopping it suddenly can bring back her depression.

a.o: Dr. Marwan let her sister visit outside hours.
a.x: Visits must keep to the rules.
a.w: Flexible visits help patients recover.

t: Statin started in pregnancy
s:
Mrs. Nesma, 33, has familial high cholesterol. Her LDL is 6.8 mmol/L and her father had a heart attack at 45. She came to clinic to start treatment.

While talking, she mentioned she was 10 weeks pregnant with her second child, and her pregnancy scan had been normal.

Her first child, a girl of four, is healthy. She has small yellow lumps on her Achilles tendons, which Dr. Raafat noticed. She does not smoke and her blood pressure was 112/70. Her thyroid and liver tests were normal. She asked if the cholesterol could harm her baby.

Dr. Raafat told her that her cholesterol was very high and started rosuvastatin 20 mg daily. He referred her children for cholesterol testing and told her to eat less saturated fat. He booked her back in three months for a blood test and liver tests and congratulated her on the pregnancy.
h: started rosuvastatin 20 mg daily

a.o: Dr. Raafat started a statin in a pregnant woman.
a.x: Statins should have waited until after pregnancy and breastfeeding.
a.w: Statins are not used in pregnancy because of possible harm to the baby. A few months without treatment carry little risk.

a.o: Dr. Raafat referred her children for cholesterol tests.
a.w: Familial hypercholesterolemia is inherited, so children should be tested.

a.o: Dr. Raafat gave diet advice to a pregnant woman.
a.x: Diet changes are unsafe in pregnancy.
a.w: Cutting saturated fat is safe and healthy in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Raafat booked liver tests.
a.w: Liver tests are standard when starting lipid treatment.

t: Endocarditis signs missed
s:
Mr. Waleed, 41, came to clinic with three weeks of fevers, night sweats and losing weight. He had a dental extraction a month ago. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve.

Dr. Asmaa heard a new murmur of aortic regurgitation. She noticed small painless red spots on his palms and tiny lines under his nails.

He is a teacher, doesn't smoke and doesn't use drugs. He had lost 4 kg in a month. His temperature in clinic was 38.2°C and his pulse 102. His spleen was just felt below his ribs. He had no cough and his urine dipstick showed a little blood.

She thought he had a viral illness and gave him a course of amoxicillin "in case". She booked an echo in four weeks and asked him to come back if his fever got worse. She told him not to go back to the dentist for now and checked his tetanus status, which was up to date.
h: gave him a course of amoxicillin "in case". She booked an echo in four weeks

a.o: Dr. Asmaa gave blind antibiotics and delayed an echo in a man with a valve problem, fever, a new murmur and skin signs.
a.x: Mr. Waleed should have had three blood cultures before any antibiotics and an urgent echo for endocarditis.
a.w: Fever plus a new murmur and skin spots mean endocarditis. Blind antibiotics can mask the cause; it needs proper cultures and weeks of IV treatment.

a.o: Dr. Asmaa told him not to go back to the dentist for now.
a.x: He should have gone back to the dentist.
a.w: Avoiding new dental work until the infection is known is sensible.

a.o: Dr. Asmaa checked his tetanus status.
a.w: Checking tetanus is routine; it causes no harm.

a.o: Dr. Asmaa examined his hands.
a.x: Hands are not important for heart problems.
a.w: Hand signs help diagnose endocarditis.

t: Wrong rhythm shocked
s:
Mr. Medhat, 64, collapsed in the waiting room. He was not breathing and had no pulse. The team started CPR at once and attached the defibrillator.

The monitor showed a flat line with no electrical activity. Dr. Noha asked for adrenaline 1 mg and checked the leads; they were connected, the gain was up and the flat line was seen in two leads.

He had come in with indigestion an hour earlier and was waiting to be seen. A nurse had noticed him slumped in his chair. He was 64, with high blood pressure, and his son said he had been under stress at work. The team took turns doing compressions every two minutes.

She then delivered a 200-joule shock "in case it was fine VF" and continued CPR. She asked a nurse to time the cycles and another to look for reversible causes. She asked his son to step outside but let him come back when he asked to be present.
h: She then delivered a 200-joule shock "in case it was fine VF"

a.o: Dr. Noha shocked a flat line (asystole) after checking the leads.
a.x: She should have continued CPR and adrenaline without shocks for asystole.
a.w: Asystole is not a shockable rhythm. Shocking wastes time away from compressions.

a.o: Dr. Noha gave adrenaline straight away for asystole.
a.x: Adrenaline should wait until after the second shock.
a.w: In asystole adrenaline is given as soon as possible.

a.o: Dr. Noha checked the leads and gain.
a.w: Checking leads makes sure the flat line is real.

a.o: Dr. Noha let his son come back into the room.
a.w: Many families want to be present, and studies show it helps them.

t: Syncope from a heart block missed
s:
Mrs. Shadia, 78, fainted three times in a month without warning, once while sitting watching TV. She has no chest pain. Her pulse was 46 and regular.

Her ECG showed P waves that were not linked to the QRS complexes, with wide QRS complexes. Her blood tests, including potassium, were normal. She takes no heart-slowing drugs.

She lives alone and her neighbor found her on the floor after the last faint, with a bruise on her forehead. She had no warning before each faint and felt fine afterwards. She drinks plenty of water and takes only a calcium tablet. Her blood pressure was 148/70 lying and standing.

Her daughter, who visits on weekends, said her mother had been forgetting to drink during the hot weeks and that her urine looked dark. Mrs. Shadia had no new medicines and had not been ill. Dr. Gamal thought she was dehydrated from the summer heat. He advised her to drink more water, stand up slowly and wear support stockings. He booked a 24-hour tape in two months. He also arranged for her to have a home safety check because of her falls.
h: He advised her to drink more water, stand up slowly and wear support stockings

a.o: Dr. Gamal treated fainting with complete heart block as dehydration.
a.x: Mrs. Shadia should have been admitted for urgent pacing.
a.w: Complete heart block with a slow pulse and fainting can cause sudden death. It needs a pacemaker.

a.o: Dr. Gamal arranged a home safety check.
a.w: A home safety check helps prevent injury from falls.

a.o: Dr. Gamal checked potassium.
a.w: High potassium can cause heart block, so checking is right.

a.o: Dr. Gamal noted she takes no heart-slowing drugs.
a.w: Drugs are a common reversible cause of heart block.

t: Heparin and low platelets
s:
Mrs. Khadiga, 66, had a hip replacement nine days ago and has been on enoxaparin injections since. Her platelets were 240 before surgery. Today they were 82. Her left calf became swollen and painful.

She was walking with a frame and eating well. Her wound looked clean and dry, and she had no fever. Dr. Mostafa checked her blood film, which confirmed the low count without clumping, and ordered a leg ultrasound, which showed a clot in the vein behind her knee. Her kidney function was normal.

Mrs. Khadiga said she had never had a clot before, though her sister had one after giving birth. She takes amlodipine for blood pressure and calcium for her bones. She was keen to go home to her husband, who has dementia, and asked how long this would keep her in. Her oxygen was 97 percent and she had no chest pain.

He wrote: "DVT, increase enoxaparin to treatment dose". He asked the nurse to measure her calf every day and booked her physio. He reassured her that the clot was common after hip surgery and was not caused by anything she did.
h: increase enoxaparin to treatment dose

a.o: Dr. Mostafa increased the heparin dose even though Mrs. Khadiga's platelets had halved with a new clot.
a.x: He should have stopped all heparin and started a non-heparin blood thinner like fondaparinux or argatroban.
a.w: A big platelet drop with a new clot 5 to 10 days after heparin is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. More heparin makes clots worse.

a.o: Dr. Mostafa ordered an ultrasound for a swollen calf.
a.w: An ultrasound confirms a DVT.

a.o: Dr. Mostafa told her the clot was not her fault.
a.w: Reassurance helps her cope; clots after surgery are common.

a.o: Dr. Mostafa booked physio.
a.w: Moving helps recovery and reduces new clots.

t: No driving advice after an ICD
s:
Mr. Taher, 50, a taxi driver, had an ICD put in after a cardiac arrest from ventricular fibrillation at home. He recovered well and was ready to go home after four days.

His wound was clean and the device check was fine. His echo showed mild weakness of the heart.

He had collapsed while watching football with his family, and his son had started CPR. He had no warning signs before. His coronary angiogram was normal. He was keen to get back to work because he supports his three children and his elderly mother.

Dr. Rehab started him on bisoprolol and ramipril and booked a device check in a month. She showed him how to look after his wound and told him to avoid lifting his left arm above shoulder height for a few weeks. She told him he could go back to work driving his taxi next week as soon as he felt well.
h: She told him he could go back to work driving his taxi next week

a.o: Dr. Rehab told a taxi driver with a new ICD after cardiac arrest he could drive his taxi next week.
a.x: Mr. Taher should have been told not to drive, and that professional driving is usually not allowed after an ICD for cardiac arrest.
a.w: A sudden rhythm or shock while driving could kill him and others. Driving rules after an ICD are strict, especially for professional drivers.

a.o: Dr. Rehab told him to avoid lifting his arm.
a.w: Raising the arm above the shoulder can pull the new leads out of place.

a.o: Dr. Rehab started ramipril for a mildly weak heart.
a.x: Ramipril is only for high blood pressure.
a.w: ACE inhibitors protect a weak heart.

a.o: Dr. Rehab booked a device check in a month.
a.x: A check in a year was enough.
a.w: Early checks make sure the device works.

t: Constrictive pericarditis or heart failure
s:
Mr. Osama, 58, had tuberculosis five years ago and was treated. He now has swollen legs, a swollen belly and breathlessness. His neck veins rise when he breathes in instead of falling. His pulse is fast and his blood pressure normal.

Dr. Hamed heard an early knock after the second heart sound. A chest X-ray showed a thin rim of calcium around the heart. The echo showed normal pumping and a septum that bounced with breathing.

He had been feeling tired and breathless for six months. He doesn't drink alcohol. His liver was large and his belly had fluid. His blood pressure dropped a little when he breathed in. His kidney tests were normal, and his BNP was only slightly raised.

Dr. Hamed diagnosed heart failure with a weak heart. He increased furosemide and wrote for a heart failure nurse. He asked the cardiology team to see him and booked a CT of the chest. He asked the dietitian to help him cut down on salt.
h: Dr. Hamed diagnosed heart failure with a weak heart

a.o: Dr. Hamed called it a weak heart when the signs pointed to constrictive pericarditis.
a.x: Mr. Osama should have been worked up for constrictive pericarditis, which can be cured by surgery.
a.w: Old TB, rising neck veins on breathing in, a knock and calcified pericardium with normal pumping mean constriction. It needs pericardiectomy.

a.o: Dr. Hamed booked a chest CT.
a.w: A CT shows the thickened pericardium.

a.o: Dr. Hamed used furosemide.
a.w: Gentle diuretics ease swelling while waiting for surgery.

a.o: Dr. Hamed asked the dietitian to help.
a.w: Cutting salt helps any fluid build-up.

t: The wrong first drug for his blood pressure
s:
Mr. Jonathan, 55, is a black man from Jamaica living in Cairo for work. His blood pressure has been above 160/100 on home readings for a month. He has no other illnesses.

He drinks two beers most evenings, walks little and eats a lot of salty takeaway food since moving. He is not diabetic. His kidney tests and urine were normal, and his cholesterol was slightly raised. His ECG showed mild heart strain. He said he would rather take one tablet than several.

Dr. Hany explained the risks of high blood pressure and started ramipril 5 mg daily. He advised him to cut down on salt and alcohol and to walk daily. He booked a blood pressure check in four weeks and asked him to bring his home machine. He wrote the plan in a letter for his GP back home.
h: started ramipril 5 mg daily

a.o: Dr. Hany chose ramipril as the first blood pressure drug for a black man of African-Caribbean descent.
a.x: He should have started amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker.
a.w: In black patients, ACE inhibitors like ramipril work less well on their own; a calcium channel blocker or a thiazide is the preferred first drug.

a.o: Dr. Hany booked the follow-up four weeks later.
a.x: He should have followed up in a year.
a.w: Four weeks is right to check how a new treatment is working.

a.o: Dr. Hany asked him to bring his home machine.
a.x: Home machines should not be trusted.
a.w: Checking a home machine against the clinic one makes the home readings reliable.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked kidneys and urine before treating.
a.w: Kidney tests and urine checks are part of the first workup.

t: Steroid cream on a fungal rash
s:
Mr. Hamza, 34, a security guard, came to the skin clinic with an itchy red rash in both groins that had been spreading for six weeks. He works long shifts in a heavy uniform and sweats a lot in the summer heat. He has type 2 diabetes, controlled on metformin.

Dr. Rania saw a red patch with a raised, scaly edge and a clearer center, spreading down onto his inner thighs. His feet showed white, peeling skin between the toes. He had been using a strong steroid cream a friend gave him, which helped for a few days and then the rash came back worse.

Dr. Rania scraped some scale from the edge of the rash onto a slide to send to the lab. She asked about his blood sugar control, which had been good, and checked his weight, which was steady. She told him to keep the area dry and wear loose cotton underwear.

She then wrote: "Eczema of the groin. Continue the steroid cream twice daily for four more weeks and add an antihistamine at night for the itch." She booked him back in six weeks and gave him a leaflet on looking after his skin.
h: Continue the steroid cream twice daily for four more weeks

a.o: Dr. Rania told Mr. Hamza to keep using a strong steroid cream on a rash with a scaly, spreading edge and athlete's foot.
a.x: She should have stopped the steroid and treated him with an antifungal cream for the groin and feet.
a.w: A spreading ring with a scaly edge plus fungus between the toes is tinea. Steroids feed a fungal rash and change how it looks.

a.o: Dr. Rania scraped skin from the rash, which only delays treatment.
a.x: She should have treated without any test.
a.w: Skin scrapings confirm a fungal infection and are quick and painless.

a.o: Dr. Rania asked about his diabetes during a skin visit.
a.x: His diabetes had nothing to do with the rash.
a.w: Diabetes makes skin infections, including fungal ones, more common, so it is worth checking.

a.o: Dr. Rania told him to wear loose cotton underwear.
a.w: Keeping the groin cool and dry helps fungal rashes heal and stops them coming back.

t: A changing mole reassured
s:
Mrs. Rana, 46, a school librarian with fair skin and red hair, came in about a mole on her calf. Her sister had noticed it was darker this summer. Mrs. Rana said it sometimes itched and had bled once when she shaved her legs. She had many sunburns as a child on family beach holidays.

Dr. Waleed looked with a dermatoscope. The mole was 8 mm across, with an uneven edge, two shades of brown and a small black area at one side. She had about forty other moles on her back and arms, most of them small and even.

Dr. Waleed photographed all her moles for her records and taught her how to check her own skin each month. He advised factor 50 sunscreen and a hat. He asked about her family history; her uncle had had a skin cancer removed from his nose.

He told her the mole looked like her other moles, only bigger, and that itching is common in moles. He booked a review with new photos in six months to see if it changed. He also checked her nails and scalp.
h: He booked a review with new photos in six months to see if it changed

a.o: Dr. Waleed decided to watch a bleeding, itchy mole with an uneven edge, two colors and a black patch for six months.
a.x: Mrs. Rana should have had the mole cut out completely and sent to the lab urgently.
a.w: A mole that is asymmetric, has an irregular border, several colors, is over 6 mm and is changing or bleeding may be melanoma. It needs removal, not watching.

a.o: Dr. Waleed photographed all her moles, which wasted clinic time.
a.x: Only the worrying mole needed a photo.
a.w: With forty moles and fair skin, whole-body photos help spot new or changing moles later.

a.o: Dr. Waleed checked her nails and scalp for a mole on her leg.
a.w: Melanoma can hide in the scalp or under nails, so a full skin check is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Waleed asked about her uncle's skin cancer.
a.x: A relative's cancer on the nose was not relevant.
a.w: Family history of skin cancer is part of judging her risk.

t: Scabies treated in one person only
s:
Hoda, 22, a university student, came in with an itchy rash on her hands, wrists and waist. The itch was worst at night and kept her awake. She lives in a shared flat with three friends and her boyfriend often stays over. Two of her flatmates had also started scratching.

Dr. Noura saw small red bumps and thin, wavy grey lines between Hoda's fingers and on her wrists. There were scratch marks around her waistband. Hoda was otherwise well. She had tried an antihistamine from the pharmacy that helped a little.

Dr. Noura explained that this was scabies, caused by a tiny mite, and that it spreads by close skin contact. She prescribed permethrin cream to cover the whole body from the neck down, to be repeated after one week. She told Hoda to wash her bedding and towels on a hot cycle.

She told her that the itch might last a few weeks after the treatment even if the mites were gone. She did not mention the flatmates or her boyfriend, and wrote "single case, treat patient only". Hoda asked for a note for her exams, which she wrote.
h: wrote "single case, treat patient only"

a.o: Dr. Noura treated only Hoda, even though her flatmates were scratching and her boyfriend shares her bed.
a.x: Everyone Hoda lives with and her boyfriend should have been treated at the same time, even without symptoms.
a.w: Scabies spreads through close contact. If only one person is treated, the mites pass straight back from the others.

a.o: Dr. Noura told Hoda to repeat the cream after a week.
a.w: A second application kills mites that hatch from eggs after the first.

a.o: Dr. Noura said the itch might last for weeks after treatment.
a.x: If the itch continues, the treatment has failed.
a.w: The itch is an allergic reaction to the mites and can last two to four weeks after they are dead.

a.o: Dr. Noura told her to wash bedding on a hot cycle.
a.w: Hot washing kills mites in bedding and clothes and helps stop reinfection.

t: Stevens-Johnson from a new drug
s:
Mr. Raouf, 41, was admitted with a painful rash two weeks after starting lamotrigine for epilepsy. The rash had started as red spots on his chest, then blistered. His lips were crusted, his eyes were red and sore and he found it painful to swallow.

On the ward, Dr. Amira found dusky purple spots with blisters on his trunk and arms, covering about 8 percent of his skin. When she pressed gently next to a blister, the skin slid off. He had a fever of 38.6°C. His blood pressure was normal and he was passing urine.

She asked the eye team to see him the same day and the burns unit about a bed. She started IV fluids, pain relief and mouthwashes and covered the raw areas with non-stick dressings. She took swabs from the skin and sent blood tests.

Because the seizures were a risk, she wrote: "Continue lamotrigine at the same dose to avoid seizures; add prednisolone 40 mg for the skin." She explained the diagnosis to his wife and asked the nurses to keep him in a side room.
h: Continue lamotrigine at the same dose to avoid seizures

a.o: Dr. Amira kept giving lamotrigine to a man with Stevens-Johnson syndrome that started two weeks after the drug.
a.x: Lamotrigine should have been stopped at once, and a different anti-seizure drug started.
a.w: The culprit drug must be stopped immediately; every extra dose worsens the skin damage. A safer drug can protect him from seizures.

a.o: Dr. Amira called the eye team on the first day.
a.x: The eyes could have been checked once the skin was better.
a.w: Eyes are often damaged in Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and early care prevents blindness.

a.o: Dr. Amira asked the burns unit about a bed for a drug rash.
a.x: Burns units are only for burns.
a.w: Large areas of skin loss are cared for like burns, and burns units manage fluids and dressings well.

a.o: Dr. Amira kept him in a side room.
a.x: A side room was not needed.
a.w: Raw skin is easily infected, so keeping him apart from other patients helps.

t: Isotretinoin without pregnancy protection
s:
Salma, 19, has had severe acne on her face, chest and back for three years, leaving deep scars. She had tried creams, two long courses of antibiotics and the pill without much change. She was upset and avoiding going out with friends.

Dr. Mahmoud decided she needed isotretinoin. He explained the common side effects, like dry lips and dry eyes, and checked her blood fats and liver tests, which were normal. He asked about her mood, and she said she felt low about her skin but had no dark thoughts.

He told her to use lip balm and moisturizer and to avoid waxing. He asked her to come back in a month with repeat blood tests and to call if her mood got worse. He wrote the prescription for a month's supply.

When Salma asked if she needed to worry about anything else, Dr. Mahmoud said she was young and healthy and did not need any other precautions. He did not ask about contraception or do a pregnancy test because she had come with her mother.
h: He did not ask about contraception or do a pregnancy test because she had come with her mother

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud started isotretinoin in a young woman without a pregnancy test or a contraception plan.
a.x: Salma should have had a negative pregnancy test and been on reliable contraception before starting, with monthly tests.
a.w: Isotretinoin causes severe birth defects. Pregnancy prevention is a must for every woman who could get pregnant, asked privately if needed.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked Salma about her mood.
a.x: Mood questions are not part of acne care.
a.w: Isotretinoin has been linked to low mood, so mood should be checked before and during treatment.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud checked her blood fats and liver tests.
a.w: Isotretinoin can raise blood fats and affect the liver, so these are checked.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud told her to avoid waxing.
a.w: Isotretinoin makes the skin fragile, and waxing can tear it.

t: Shingles antivirals not given
s:
Mr. Fawzy, 68, came in with a painful, burning band on the right side of his chest that started three days ago. Yesterday a row of small blisters appeared on red skin in the same band, stopping at the middle of his chest and back. He had chickenpox as a child.

He has high blood pressure and takes amlodipine. His temperature was 37.6°C. Dr. Lamiaa checked his eyes and nose, which were clear. She examined the rest of his skin and found no other blisters.

She explained that this was shingles from the old chickenpox virus waking up. She told him to keep the blisters covered and avoid pregnant women and babies who had not had chickenpox until the blisters crusted. She gave him paracetamol and codeine for the pain.

Because the blisters had already appeared, she wrote: "Too late for antivirals; manage pain only." She booked a check in two weeks and said shingles can cause long-lasting nerve pain.
h: Too late for antivirals; manage pain only

a.o: Dr. Lamiaa decided it was too late for antivirals when Mr. Fawzy's rash had appeared only a day earlier.
a.x: He should have been started on aciclovir or valaciclovir straight away.
a.w: Antivirals work best within 72 hours of the rash. At 68 and with severe pain, he is at high risk of lasting nerve pain, which antivirals reduce.

a.o: Dr. Lamiaa told him to avoid pregnant women and babies.
a.w: The blisters can give chickenpox to people who have never had it, which is risky in pregnancy and for newborns.

a.o: Dr. Lamiaa checked his eyes and nose for a chest rash.
a.x: His eyes had nothing to do with it.
a.w: Checking the eyes is part of examining shingles, even though eye involvement is with face rashes.

a.o: Dr. Lamiaa gave codeine to an older man.
a.x: Codeine is unsafe in older people.
a.w: Short courses of codeine with paracetamol are fine for shingles pain, with advice about constipation.

t: Cellulitis that was a DVT
s:
Mrs. Fatma, 62, was admitted with a red, swollen, painful left calf. She had come back from a long bus trip to visit her daughter three days before. She has been on hormone tablets for menopause symptoms. Her temperature was 37.4°C.

Dr. Karim found her whole left calf swollen, warm and tender, measuring 4 cm more than the right. The redness was even and faint, with no clear edge, no broken skin and no blisters. Her toes were pink and the foot pulses were strong. She had a little fungus between the toes.

Dr. Karim drew a line around the redness with a pen to see if it spread. He gave her IV flucloxacillin for cellulitis, painkillers and raised her leg on pillows. He treated the fungus with a cream.

He noted the long bus trip but wrote that "cellulitis explains it". He said she could go home on tablets in two days if the redness shrank. He did not order any blood tests or scans.
h: He noted the long bus trip but wrote that "cellulitis explains it"

a.o: Dr. Karim treated a swollen calf after a long trip in a woman on hormones as cellulitis without checking for a clot.
a.x: Mrs. Fatma should have had a Wells score, D-dimer and a leg ultrasound to rule out a deep vein thrombosis.
a.w: A long journey, hormone therapy and a swollen calf with faint redness and little fever are typical of a clot. Missing a DVT can lead to a clot in the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Karim drew a line around the redness.
a.w: Marking the edge shows whether redness spreads or shrinks with treatment.

a.o: Dr. Karim treated the fungus between her toes.
a.x: The fungus was irrelevant to her leg.
a.w: Cracked skin between the toes is a common way in for cellulitis, so treating it is sensible.

a.o: Dr. Karim raised her leg on pillows.
a.x: Her leg should have been kept down.
a.w: Raising the leg reduces swelling and pain.

t: Methotrexate with trimethoprim
s:
Mr. Gamil, 57, has had severe psoriasis for years and takes methotrexate 15 mg once a week, with folic acid. His skin had been clear for six months. His last blood count and liver tests, two months ago, were normal.

He came to the skin clinic for his routine check and mentioned he had a burning feeling when passing urine for three days. His urine test showed white cells and nitrites. He had no fever or back pain. His kidney function was slightly reduced, as it had been for a year.

Dr. Salwa looked at his skin, which was clear apart from a small patch on his elbow. She asked about alcohol; he drinks one or two beers at weekends. She reminded him to have his blood tests every three months.

For the urine infection she prescribed trimethoprim for three days and told him to keep taking his methotrexate as usual. She gave him a cream for the elbow and booked him back in three months.
h: prescribed trimethoprim for three days and told him to keep taking his methotrexate as usual

a.o: Dr. Salwa gave trimethoprim to a man on methotrexate.
a.x: She should have chosen an antibiotic that does not interact, such as nitrofurantoin or a cephalosporin, and checked his blood count.
a.w: Trimethoprim and methotrexate both block folate. Together they can crash the blood count, especially with reduced kidney function.

a.o: Dr. Salwa let him keep drinking at weekends.
a.x: He must not drink any alcohol.
a.w: Small amounts of alcohol are usually allowed on methotrexate, though heavy drinking is not.

a.o: Dr. Salwa gave folic acid with methotrexate.
a.w: Folic acid lowers side effects without stopping methotrexate working for psoriasis.

a.o: Dr. Salwa treated a three-day urine infection.
a.x: It should have been left to clear by itself.
a.w: Urine infections in men are treated with antibiotics.

t: Impetigo sent to school
s:
Yassin, 6, came in with his father because of crusty sores around his nose and mouth for four days. The sores started as small blisters and then turned into golden-yellow crusts. His sister had a similar sore last week. He had no fever and was playing happily.

Dr. Amal saw three small patches of honey-colored crusts around his nose and one on his chin. There were no deep sores and his lymph nodes were not swollen. The rest of his skin was clear. He had a small cut on his lip from a fall a week ago.

She explained this was impetigo, a skin infection that spreads easily. She prescribed fusidic acid cream three times a day for a week. She told the father to wash the crusts gently with soapy water and use a separate towel for Yassin.

The father asked if Yassin could go to school tomorrow, as there was a test. Dr. Amal said yes, as long as he did not touch the other children. She told him to come back if the sores spread or Yassin got a fever.
h: Dr. Amal said yes, as long as he did not touch the other children

a.o: Dr. Amal let Yassin go back to school the next day with impetigo crusts still present.
a.x: He should have stayed home until the sores had crusted over and healed, or for 48 hours after starting antibiotics.
a.w: Impetigo spreads easily in schools. Children stay home until the sores heal or for 48 hours after treatment starts.

a.o: Dr. Amal used a cream instead of tablets.
a.w: A few small patches of impetigo are treated with cream; tablets are for widespread disease.

a.o: Dr. Amal gave Yassin his own towel.
a.w: Separate towels stop it spreading in the family.

a.o: Dr. Amal told the father to wash the crusts.
a.x: The crusts should be left alone.
a.w: Gently washing the crusts helps the cream work.

t: Angioedema on an ACE inhibitor
s:
Mr. Kareem, 62, woke up with his lower lip and tongue swollen. He had no rash, no itching and no wheeze. His blood pressure was 148/90 and his oxygen 98 percent. He could talk and swallow his saliva. He had started ramipril for blood pressure four months ago.

He said nothing similar had happened before, he had not eaten anything new and he had no allergies. He had no family history of swelling. Dr. Hana watched him closely with an airway trolley ready and asked the anesthetist to be aware.

She gave him adrenaline into the muscle, an antihistamine and a steroid, which made little difference. Over three hours the swelling stayed the same and then started to go down. She kept him overnight.

On discharge she told him that it was probably a reaction to something he ate and that he should keep a food diary. She advised him to continue all his tablets, including ramipril, and to come straight back if it happened again.
h: She advised him to continue all his tablets, including ramipril

a.o: Dr. Hana told Mr. Kareem to keep taking ramipril after an episode of lip and tongue swelling.
a.x: His ramipril should have been stopped for good and replaced by another blood pressure drug.
a.w: ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema at any time, even months later. It can come back worse and block the airway.

a.o: Dr. Hana gave adrenaline though there was no rash or wheeze.
a.w: Tongue swelling can threaten the airway, so giving adrenaline was reasonable while the cause was unclear.

a.o: Dr. Hana kept him overnight once the swelling started to go down.
a.x: He should have gone home once it went down.
a.w: Tongue swelling can come back, so overnight watching is sensible.

a.o: Dr. Hana asked the anesthetist to be aware.
a.w: An anesthetist on standby is good practice for any swelling near the airway.

t: Atopic eczema without moisturizers
s:
Laila, 3, has had dry, itchy skin since she was a baby. Her mother brought her because the patches in her elbow and knee creases had got worse, and Laila was scratching at night. She has mild asthma and her father has hay fever.

Dr. Tamer found dry, red, rough patches in the creases, with scratch marks but no crusts or weeping. Laila was growing well. Her mother bathed her every day with bubble bath and used a perfumed lotion afterwards.

Dr. Tamer explained that this was eczema, which often runs with asthma and hay fever. He prescribed a mild steroid cream for the red patches for a week at a time. He told the mother to keep Laila's nails short and dress her in cotton.

He told her to stop the bubble bath and lotion but did not prescribe any other cream for daily use. He said the steroid was "all she needs" and booked a review in three months. He gave her a leaflet on eczema in children.
h: He said the steroid was "all she needs"

a.o: Dr. Tamer gave only a steroid cream and no everyday moisturizer for Laila's dry eczema.
a.x: Laila should have been given a plain emollient to use generously every day, plus soap substitute, with the steroid for flares.
a.w: Emollients are the base of eczema care. Without them the skin stays dry and flares keep coming back.

a.o: Dr. Tamer used a mild steroid on a three-year-old.
a.x: Steroids are unsafe for young children.
a.w: Mild steroids used for short spells are safe in young children.

a.o: Dr. Tamer told the mother to keep Laila's nails short.
a.w: Short nails reduce damage from scratching.

a.o: Dr. Tamer told her to stop the bubble bath.
a.x: Bubble bath helps clean the skin.
a.w: Bubble baths and perfumes dry and irritate eczema.

t: Basal cell carcinoma burned off
s:
Mr. Hossam, 71, a retired fisherman, came in with a pearly lump on the side of his nose that had grown slowly for a year. It bled now and then and left a small crust. He had spent his life working in the sun without a hat.

Dr. Yasmine saw a 7 mm shiny lump with fine blood vessels on its surface and a small dip in the middle. She checked the rest of his face and found rough, scaly spots on his forehead and the backs of his hands, which she treated with freezing spray.

She told him this looked like a basal cell carcinoma, a slow skin cancer that rarely spreads. She explained the treatments and said the nose is a delicate area. She advised him to wear a hat and use sunscreen every day.

To save him a long wait, she froze the nose lump with liquid nitrogen there and then, without taking a sample. She wrote "BCC treated, no follow-up needed" and discharged him to his GP.
h: she froze the nose lump with liquid nitrogen there and then, without taking a sample

a.o: Dr. Yasmine froze a suspected skin cancer on the nose without a biopsy and discharged him.
a.x: Mr. Hossam should have had a biopsy and been referred for surgery, ideally with clear margins on the nose.
a.w: A BCC on the nose is a high-risk spot. Freezing gives no tissue to confirm the diagnosis and can leave cancer behind.

a.o: Dr. Yasmine froze the rough spots on his forehead and hands.
a.x: Those spots should have been left.
a.w: Rough, scaly sun spots (actinic keratoses) can turn into cancer, so freezing them is standard.

a.o: Dr. Yasmine told him the cancer rarely spreads.
a.x: She should have said it was very dangerous.
a.w: BCCs rarely spread to other parts of the body; telling him so is honest.

a.o: Dr. Yasmine advised sunscreen every day.
a.x: Sunscreen is pointless at his age.
a.w: Sun protection helps prevent new skin cancers at any age.

t: Pemphigus treated as an infection
s:
Mrs. Mervat, 55, was admitted with painful sores in her mouth for two months and new blisters on her chest and back. The blisters were soft and broke easily, leaving raw, weeping patches. She could hardly eat because of the mouth sores.

Dr. Sherif noticed that when he rubbed the normal-looking skin next to a blister, the top layer slid off. She had no fever. Her blood pressure was normal. She takes no new medicines. Her blood sugar was normal.

He swabbed the raw areas, which grew a little Staphylococcus, and started IV flucloxacillin. He asked the dentist to see her mouth and the dietitian to help her eat. He covered the raw areas with non-stick dressings.

He told the nurses this was a "skin infection with blisters" and that the antibiotic should clear it in a week. He did not take a skin biopsy because the swab had already shown the cause.
h: He did not take a skin biopsy because the swab had already shown the cause

a.o: Dr. Sherif treated widespread fragile blisters and mouth sores as an infection without a skin biopsy.
a.x: Mrs. Mervat should have had a skin biopsy with immunofluorescence for pemphigus and been started on steroids.
a.w: Mouth sores followed by fragile blisters that slide off with rubbing suggest pemphigus vulgaris. It is an autoimmune disease that needs a biopsy and immune treatment.

a.o: Dr. Sherif swabbed the raw areas.
a.w: Raw skin can become infected; a swab is sensible.

a.o: Dr. Sherif asked the dietitian to help her eat.
a.w: Mouth sores stop her eating, so nutrition support helps.

a.o: Dr. Sherif used non-stick dressings.
a.x: The blisters should be left uncovered.
a.w: Non-stick dressings protect raw skin without tearing it.

t: Head lice treated only with combing
s:
Nour, 8, was sent home from school with a note about head lice. Her mother found live lice and small white eggs stuck to the hairs near her scalp. Nour said her head had been itchy for two weeks. Her little brother was also scratching.

Dr. Mona checked Nour's scalp and found live lice behind her ears. Her skin was not broken. She checked the brother too and found live lice.

Dr. Mona told the mother lice are common and not a sign of being dirty. She advised wet combing with conditioner and a fine-toothed comb every three days for two weeks. She said there was no need to wash all the soft toys or keep Nour off school.

She prescribed a lotion to treat the lice and told the mother to use it on Nour and repeat it in a week. She said the brother could be treated later "if he gets worse".
h: She said the brother could be treated later "if he gets worse"

a.o: Dr. Mona left Nour's brother untreated even though he had live lice.
a.x: Everyone in the family with live lice should have been treated on the same day.
a.w: Treating only one child lets lice pass straight back. Anyone with live lice needs treatment at the same time.

a.o: Dr. Mona said Nour could go to school.
a.x: Nour should have stayed home until the lice were gone.
a.w: Children with lice do not need to miss school.

a.o: Dr. Mona said there was no need to wash all the toys.
a.x: All soft toys should be washed.
a.w: Lice die quickly off the head; washing everything is not needed.

a.o: Dr. Mona told the mother lice are not a sign of being dirty.
a.w: Lice are common in all families and spread by head-to-head contact.

t: Urticaria and a beta blocker
s:
Mrs. Dina, 39, came in with hives that came and went for eight weeks. The welts appeared all over her body, lasted a few hours and left no marks. She had no swelling of the lips or tongue and no trouble breathing.

She has migraines and had started propranolol for them three months ago. Her thyroid tests were normal. She had no new foods or soaps. Dr. Hany checked her skin, which showed a few fading welts on her arms.

He explained that long-lasting hives often have no clear cause. He prescribed a non-drowsy antihistamine daily and told her it was safe to take up to four times the normal dose if needed. He asked her to keep a diary of when the hives appeared.

He told her that if she ever had a severe allergic reaction, an adrenaline pen would work well despite her propranolol. He gave her a leaflet and booked her back in two months.
h: an adrenaline pen would work well despite her propranolol

a.o: Dr. Hany told Mrs. Dina that adrenaline would work well despite her propranolol.
a.x: He should have explained that beta blockers can block adrenaline and discussed changing her migraine medicine.
a.w: Propranolol can make anaphylaxis worse and stop adrenaline from working well. This is important for someone with ongoing allergic reactions.

a.o: Dr. Hany said a high antihistamine dose was safe.
a.x: The normal dose must never be exceeded.
a.w: Guidelines allow up to four times the normal dose of non-drowsy antihistamines for chronic hives.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked her thyroid.
a.w: Thyroid disease is linked to chronic hives.

a.o: Dr. Hany said chronic hives often have no clear cause.
a.x: There is always a clear cause.
a.w: Most chronic hives have no outside trigger.

t: Cold urticaria and swimming
s:
Ziad, 14, came to the ER after a swimming lesson. He felt faint and his skin broke out in large welts as soon as he got into the cold pool. His teacher pulled him out, and he felt better after ten minutes. He had noticed small welts on his hands when holding ice cubes before.

His blood pressure was 112/70 and he was breathing normally. He had faint welts on his arms and chest. He has no other allergies and no recent infections. His mother arrived from work and said he had been fine at the beach in summer when the water was warm. He was embarrassed and wanted to go back to class. Dr. Rasha placed an ice cube on his forearm for five minutes, and a welt the shape of the cube appeared after it was removed.

She explained that this was cold urticaria, an allergy to cold. She prescribed a daily non-drowsy antihistamine and gave him a letter for school.

She told him he could keep swimming in cold pools as long as he took his antihistamine first, and did not mention an adrenaline pen. She booked a check in three months.
h: She told him he could keep swimming in cold pools as long as he took his antihistamine first

a.o: Dr. Rasha told Ziad he could keep swimming in cold water after he nearly fainted in a cold pool.
a.x: Ziad should have been told to avoid cold-water swimming and been given an adrenaline pen.
a.w: Cold urticaria with fainting after swimming can cause collapse and drowning. Antihistamines may not stop a severe reaction.

a.o: Dr. Rasha used an ice cube test.
a.x: The ice cube test was unsafe.
a.w: The ice cube test is the standard way to diagnose cold urticaria.

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave a non-drowsy antihistamine.
a.w: Non-drowsy antihistamines are first choice.

a.o: Dr. Rasha wrote a letter for school.
a.w: The school needs to know about his allergy.

t: Necrotizing fasciitis treated as cellulitis
s:
Mr. Ibrahim, 52, has diabetes. He scratched his thigh on a rusty fence three days ago. Now the thigh is red, swollen and very painful. His temperature was 39.2°C, pulse 124 and blood pressure 96/58. His sugar was 22 mmol/L.

Dr. Mai found a red, hot area on the thigh, but his pain was much worse than the redness suggested. The skin had dusky grey patches and felt crackly under her fingers. The redness had spread 5 cm in two hours.

She started IV fluids, insulin and IV antibiotics for cellulitis. She marked the redness with a pen and took blood cultures. She checked his tetanus status, which was out of date, and gave a booster.

She wrote: "Severe cellulitis, reassess in the morning." She asked the ward to raise his leg and give morphine. She did not call the surgeons because "antibiotics should work".
h: She did not call the surgeons because "antibiotics should work"

a.o: Dr. Mai treated fast-spreading redness with severe pain, grey skin and crackling under the skin as cellulitis and did not call the surgeons.
a.x: Mr. Ibrahim should have been seen urgently by surgeons for necrotizing fasciitis and taken for surgery.
a.w: Pain out of proportion, grey skin, crackling and shock mean necrotizing fasciitis. It spreads fast and needs urgent surgery to remove dead tissue.

a.o: Dr. Mai gave a tetanus booster.
a.w: A dirty wound and an out-of-date tetanus status need a booster.

a.o: Dr. Mai took blood cultures.
a.w: Blood cultures help guide antibiotics in a septic patient.

a.o: Dr. Mai gave insulin for his high sugar.
a.w: High sugar makes infections worse, so treating it is right.

t: Vitiligo told to sunbathe
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 29, came in with white patches on her hands and around her eyes and mouth for six months. They were growing slowly. She has thyroid disease and takes levothyroxine. She was upset because people stared at her.

Dr. Ahmed used a special lamp, and the patches glowed chalk white. The skin was otherwise normal, with no scaling. Her thyroid tests were normal on treatment. Her mother has type 1 diabetes. Mrs. Asmaa works as a receptionist and goes to the beach most weekends with her children. She had already tried a herbal oil from a market stall, which had done nothing.

He explained that this was vitiligo, where the immune system attacks pigment cells, and that it is not catching. He prescribed a steroid cream for the patches on her hands and a non-steroid cream for her face.

He advised her to sunbathe for an hour a day without sunscreen "to help the pigment come back". He also gave her the details of a support group and a camouflage makeup service.
h: He advised her to sunbathe for an hour a day without sunscreen

a.o: Dr. Ahmed told Mrs. Asmaa to sunbathe without sunscreen on her vitiligo patches.
a.x: She should have been told to protect the white patches with high-factor sunscreen.
a.w: Skin without pigment burns very easily, and sunburn can make vitiligo spread. Light therapy is given carefully in a clinic.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed used a non-steroid cream on her face.
a.x: Steroid cream should be used everywhere.
a.w: Steroids thin delicate facial skin; non-steroid creams are safer there.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave details of a support group.
a.w: Vitiligo can affect confidence, so support helps.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed checked her thyroid.
a.x: Thyroid tests had nothing to do with vitiligo.
a.w: Vitiligo is linked to thyroid disease.

t: Wart paint near the eye
s:
Sara, 7, came in with her mother because of small rough lumps on her fingers that had been there for a year. They did not hurt but she picked at them. Her mother had tried a wart paint from the pharmacy for two weeks.

Dr. Fady saw four warts on her fingers and a small flat wart on her left lower eyelid, close to the lashes. Sara was well. He explained that warts are caused by a virus and are common in children. Most go away on their own within two years.

He suggested continuing the wart paint every night for three months, soaking the warts and rubbing them gently with a nail file. He told the mother to use the same paint on the little wart on Sara's eyelid at bedtime. He told her mother not to share towels.

He said that if they bothered her a lot, freezing could be tried later but that it hurts and may need repeating. He reassured the mother that the warts were harmless. He also advised her not to bite her nails.
h: use the same paint on the little wart on Sara's eyelid

a.o: Dr. Fady told the mother to put wart paint on the wart on Sara's eyelid.
a.x: The eyelid wart should have been left alone or seen by a specialist, never painted with wart acid.
a.w: Wart paint is salicylic acid. It burns the thin skin of the face and can injure the eye.

a.o: Dr. Fady told the mother the warts would go on their own within two years.
a.x: The warts should have been frozen right away.
a.w: Most warts in children go away by themselves. Freezing is painful and not needed for painless warts.

a.o: Dr. Fady told the mother not to share towels.
a.w: Warts can spread by close contact and shared towels.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised Sara not to bite her nails.
a.w: Biting and picking can spread warts.

t: Hair loss treated without iron checks
s:
Mrs. Hala, 34, a nurse, came in worried about hair loss. For three months, handfuls of hair had come out in the shower and on her pillow. She had a baby seven months ago and was breastfeeding until last month. She has very heavy periods and often feels tired and short of breath on the stairs.

Dr. Sameh found her hair thin all over, with no bald patches, no scaling and no broken hairs. When he pulled gently on a small bunch, several hairs came out with white bulbs at the ends. Her nails were pale and slightly spoon-shaped. Her eyebrows were normal.

He explained that hair often falls out a few months after having a baby and usually grows back within a year. He reassured her that she would not go bald and suggested a gentle shampoo and avoiding tight hairstyles.

He prescribed minoxidil lotion to speed up regrowth and said blood tests were "not needed for such a typical story". He booked her back in six months and told her the tiredness was normal for a new mother.
h: said blood tests were "not needed for such a typical story"

a.o: Dr. Sameh did not check blood count or iron in a woman with heavy periods, tiredness, breathlessness and pale, spoon-shaped nails.
a.x: Mrs. Hala should have had a blood count, ferritin and thyroid tests.
a.w: Hair shedding after childbirth is common, but iron deficiency and thyroid problems also cause it. Her heavy periods and spoon nails point to iron deficiency that needs treating.

a.o: Dr. Sameh said the hair loss after a baby usually grows back.
a.x: He should have warned her it might be permanent.
a.w: Hair shedding after pregnancy is common and nearly always recovers.

a.o: Dr. Sameh advised avoiding tight hairstyles.
a.w: Tight styles pull on hair and can cause hair loss, so avoiding them helps.

a.o: Dr. Sameh prescribed minoxidil.
a.w: Minoxidil lotion is used for hair loss in women too. It is best avoided while breastfeeding, and she had stopped.

t: Sunscreen advice for a baby
s:
Baby Adam, 4 months old, came with his parents for a check before a family beach holiday in August. He was healthy, feeding well and growing along his centile. His older sister had eczema.

His parents asked how to protect his skin. Dr. Mariam examined him and found healthy skin with a little cradle cap on his scalp, which she said was harmless and would settle with baby oil and gentle brushing.

She told them babies under six months should be kept out of direct sun, in the shade, with a wide-brimmed hat and light long clothes. She said the beach should be visited in the early morning or late afternoon.

She told them to cover Adam's whole body with factor 50 adult sunscreen every hour and that he could then lie in the sun for short spells to build up a little tan. She also told them to keep him well fed.
h: he could then lie in the sun for short spells to build up a little tan

a.o: Dr. Mariam told the parents a four-month-old baby could lie in the sun to build up a tan if covered in sunscreen.
a.x: Adam should have been kept out of direct sun completely, in shade with clothing and a hat.
a.w: Babies under six months burn very easily. Shade and clothing are the main protection, and tanning is skin damage at any age.

a.o: Dr. Mariam said cradle cap was harmless.
a.w: Cradle cap is common and harmless, and baby oil with gentle brushing is enough.

a.o: Dr. Mariam advised visiting the beach early or late.
a.x: The time of day doesn't matter.
a.w: The sun is strongest at midday, so early and late visits are safer.

a.o: Dr. Mariam told them to keep him well fed.
a.x: Feeding had nothing to do with it.
a.w: Babies get dehydrated quickly in the heat, so regular feeds matter.

t: Erythroderma left untreated for heat and fluid loss
s:
Mr. Ashraf, 63, has had psoriasis for years. A week ago his GP gave him a short course of prednisolone for a flare, which he stopped suddenly yesterday. Now his skin has turned red all over his body and is peeling in sheets.

On the ward, Dr. Heba found red, scaling skin covering more than 90 percent of his body. He was shivering and his temperature was 35.4°C. His pulse was 112 and his blood pressure 102/60. He had not passed urine for eight hours and his albumin was low.

She prescribed a soothing emollient to be applied every two hours and arranged for a dermatology review. She explained that stopping steroids suddenly can make psoriasis flare like this.

She wrote him up for standard maintenance fluids by mouth "as he is drinking", put him in a normal bay near the window and asked the nurses to record his observations twice a day. She told him the skin should calm down in a few days.
h: put him in a normal bay near the window and asked the nurses to record his observations twice a day

a.o: Dr. Heba treated a man whose whole skin was red and peeling as a routine case, without warming, IV fluids or close monitoring.
a.x: Mr. Ashraf should have been nursed in a warm room with careful fluid balance, IV fluids if needed, and frequent observations.
a.w: Erythroderma is a skin emergency. Red skin all over loses heat, fluid and protein, causing low body temperature, dehydration and infection.

a.o: Dr. Heba prescribed emollients every two hours.
a.x: Emollients should be used twice a day.
a.w: Frequent emollients help repair the skin barrier in erythroderma.

a.o: Dr. Heba told him stopping steroids caused the flare.
a.x: Steroids have nothing to do with it.
a.w: Stopping oral steroids suddenly is a known trigger for erythrodermic psoriasis.

a.o: Dr. Heba arranged a dermatology review.
a.x: A skin specialist was not needed.
a.w: Erythroderma needs specialist care.

t: Lichen planus and a missed hepatitis test
s:
Mr. Tarek, 45, a taxi driver, came in with an itchy rash on his wrists and ankles for two months. The bumps were small, flat-topped and purple, with fine white lines on their surface. He also had white lacy patches inside his cheeks. He had a blood transfusion after a car accident fifteen years ago.

Dr. Rehab looked at the rash with a magnifier and noted that new bumps had appeared along a scratch on his forearm. His nails were normal. He takes no medicines and drinks no alcohol.

She explained that this looked like lichen planus, a skin condition that often settles on its own in a year or two. She prescribed a strong steroid cream for the skin and a mouthwash for the cheeks.

She advised him to stop smoking because it can worsen mouth patches and asked him to come back in three months. She did not order blood tests because "lichen planus is a skin disease".
h: She did not order blood tests because "lichen planus is a skin disease"

a.o: Dr. Rehab did not test for hepatitis C in a man with lichen planus and a past blood transfusion.
a.x: Mr. Tarek should have had a hepatitis C test.
a.w: Lichen planus is linked with hepatitis C, and his old transfusion is a risk factor. Hepatitis C can be cured if found.

a.o: Dr. Rehab used a strong steroid cream.
a.x: A mild cream should have been used.
a.w: Strong steroids are needed on thick limb skin in lichen planus.

a.o: Dr. Rehab advised him to stop smoking.
a.w: Smoking irritates mouth patches and raises cancer risk in mouth lichen planus.

a.o: Dr. Rehab noted new bumps along a scratch.
a.w: New bumps in a scratch (Koebner response) support the diagnosis.

t: Acne treated with antibiotics alone
s:
Omar, 16, came in with spots on his face for a year. He had blackheads and whiteheads on his nose and forehead and red bumps on his cheeks, but no deep painful lumps and no scars. He was being teased at school.

Dr. Nadia explained that acne is common and not caused by dirt or chocolate. She told him to wash his face twice a day with a gentle wash and not to squeeze the spots.

She prescribed doxycycline tablets for three months. She told him to take them with a full glass of water, standing up, and to avoid lying down for half an hour. She warned him that doxycycline can make the skin burn more easily in the sun.

She did not give any cream with the tablets, saying "the antibiotic will do all the work", and asked him to come back in three months.
h: She did not give any cream with the tablets, saying "the antibiotic will do all the work"

a.o: Dr. Nadia gave doxycycline alone without a topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide.
a.x: Omar should have had a topical treatment like adapalene with benzoyl peroxide alongside or instead of the antibiotic.
a.w: Antibiotics alone cause resistance and do not treat blackheads. They should always be combined with a topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide.

a.o: Dr. Nadia warned about sunburn with doxycycline.
a.x: Doxycycline has no effect on the skin in the sun.
a.w: Doxycycline can make the skin sensitive to sunlight.

a.o: Dr. Nadia told him to take it with water standing up.
a.x: How he swallows it doesn't matter.
a.w: Doxycycline can burn the gullet if it gets stuck.

a.o: Dr. Nadia said acne is not caused by chocolate.
a.w: The evidence for diet causing acne is weak; reassurance is fair.

t: Meningococcal rash missed
s:
Hamza, 19, a university student living in halls, came to the ER at midnight with a fever of 39.4°C, headache and vomiting that started in the afternoon. He had aching legs and cold hands and feet. His flatmate said he had been confused for an hour.

Dr. Ayman found a few tiny purple spots on his legs and stomach that did not fade when he pressed a glass on them. His neck was a little stiff. His pulse was 128 and his blood pressure 98/60. His capillary refill took four seconds.

He took blood cultures and put in an IV line. He gave a fluid bolus and paracetamol. He asked a nurse to stay with Hamza and called the public health team about his contacts in halls.

Because a CT scan of his head had been booked to check for a bleed, he wrote that antibiotics would be given after the scan and the lumbar puncture, "so the culture is not spoiled". The CT slot was in an hour.
h: antibiotics would be given after the scan and the lumbar puncture

a.o: Dr. Ayman delayed antibiotics for a CT and lumbar puncture in a student with a non-blanching rash and shock.
a.x: Hamza should have had IV ceftriaxone straight away, before any scan.
a.w: Fever with a non-blanching rash means meningococcal disease until proven otherwise. It kills within hours, and antibiotics must not wait.

a.o: Dr. Ayman called public health about contacts in halls.
a.x: Public health doesn't need to know.
a.w: Close contacts of meningococcal disease need preventive antibiotics, which public health organizes.

a.o: Dr. Ayman took blood cultures.
a.w: Cultures taken quickly before antibiotics help find the germ.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave a fluid bolus.
a.x: Fluids should be avoided in meningitis.
a.w: He was in shock, so fluids were needed.

t: Rheumatic fever without prevention
s:
Maryam, 12, was admitted with painful, swollen knees and ankles that moved from one joint to another over a week. Three weeks earlier she had a sore throat that was not treated. She had a fever of 38.5°C and a new soft murmur at the apex of her heart. Her blood tests showed raised inflammation and a high antistreptolysin O level.

Dr. Hossam diagnosed acute rheumatic fever. He gave her aspirin for the joints, which helped a lot within a day, and a dose of penicillin to clear any remaining strep. He arranged an echo, which showed mild leakage of the mitral valve. He asked her to rest and checked her ECG, which showed a slightly long PR interval.

Her mother asked if it could come back. Dr. Hossam explained that rheumatic fever can damage the heart valves, especially if it comes back. He asked the school nurse to excuse her from sports for a few weeks.

On discharge he gave her a two-week supply of penicillin tablets and wrote: "No further antibiotics needed once course finished." He booked an echo in a year.
h: No further antibiotics needed once course finished

a.o: Dr. Hossam stopped antibiotics after two weeks in a girl with rheumatic fever and valve damage.
a.x: Maryam should have started long-term penicillin prevention, usually a monthly injection for at least ten years.
a.w: Rheumatic fever often comes back after another strep throat, and each attack damages the valves more. Long-term prevention is essential.

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave aspirin to a 12-year-old.
a.x: Aspirin is never used in children.
a.w: Aspirin is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome, but rheumatic fever is a special exception where it is used.

a.o: Dr. Hossam excused her from sports.
a.x: She should have played as usual.
a.w: Rest is advised while there is active heart inflammation.

a.o: Dr. Hossam checked her ECG.
a.w: A long PR interval is one of the signs used to diagnose rheumatic fever.

t: Cholesterol drug forgotten in a diabetic
s:
Mrs. Samia, 58, has had type 2 diabetes for nine years. She takes metformin and her HbA1c is 52 mmol/mol. Her blood pressure was 132/80 on ramipril. She does not smoke and walks every day. Her LDL cholesterol was 3.6 mmol/L.

Dr. Ihab checked her feet, which had good pulses and normal feeling. He looked at her eyes' last screening, which was clear. Her kidney tests were normal and her urine had no protein.

He praised her diabetes control and told her to keep walking. He gave her diet advice and booked her flu vaccine. She mentioned that her older brother had a heart attack at 61 and that her mother had a stroke. She had read online that cholesterol tablets cause memory loss and muscle pain, and she was not keen on more pills.

When she asked about her cholesterol result, he told her it was "only a little high" and did not need treatment while she felt well. He said they would check it again next year.
h: he told her it was "only a little high" and did not need treatment

a.o: Dr. Ihab did not start a statin for a 58-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and an LDL of 3.6.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have been offered a statin such as atorvastatin.
a.w: People over 40 with diabetes are at high risk of heart attack and stroke. Statins lower that risk even when they feel well.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her feet.
a.x: Feet are not part of a heart check.
a.w: Foot checks are part of every diabetes review.

a.o: Dr. Ihab booked her flu vaccine.
a.w: People with diabetes should have a yearly flu vaccine.

a.o: Dr. Ihab continued her ramipril.
a.x: Ramipril is not needed for a pressure of 132/80.
a.w: Ramipril controls blood pressure and protects the kidneys in diabetes.

t: Antibiotics for a cold
s:
Youssef, 5, came in with his mother after three days of a runny nose, a mild cough and a temperature of 38°C. He was eating a little less but drinking well and playing between naps. His older sister had the same cold last week and got better on her own.

Dr. Nermine looked in his ears, which showed normal, pearly eardrums. His throat was a little red with no pus, and his chest was clear. His breathing rate and oxygen were normal. He had a few small, soft lumps in his neck that moved under her fingers.

She explained that this was a viral cold. She told the mother to give paracetamol or ibuprofen for the fever, offer plenty of fluids and use saline drops for the stuffy nose. She warned her about red flags: fast breathing, not drinking, a rash or being very sleepy.

Because the mother was worried and had a family trip coming up, Dr. Nermine also prescribed a week of amoxicillin "to be safe". She told her he could go back to nursery when his fever settled.
h: prescribed a week of amoxicillin "to be safe"

a.o: Dr. Nermine prescribed amoxicillin for a simple viral cold to reassure a worried mother.
a.x: Youssef should have had no antibiotics, with safety-net advice only.
a.w: Colds are caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not kill. Needless antibiotics cause side effects and resistance.

a.o: Dr. Nermine noticed small lumps in his neck and did nothing about them.
a.x: The neck lumps needed a scan.
a.w: Small, soft, moving lymph nodes are normal in a child with a cold.

a.o: Dr. Nermine suggested ibuprofen for a child with a fever.
a.x: Only paracetamol is safe in children.
a.w: Ibuprofen is safe for fever in children who are drinking well.

a.o: Dr. Nermine let him go back to nursery once his fever settled.
a.x: He should have stayed home for two weeks.
a.w: Children can go back to nursery when they feel well and have no fever.

t: Quinsy sent home on tablets
s:
Mr. Nabil, 24, came in with a very sore throat for five days that got worse on the right side. He could hardly open his mouth and his voice sounded muffled, "like a hot potato". He was drooling because swallowing hurt so much. His temperature was 38.9°C.

Dr. Riham found swelling above his right tonsil, pushing his uvula over to the left. His jaw was stiff and his neck glands were swollen on the right. His breathing was normal and his oxygen 98 percent. He was drinking only sips.

She gave him IV fluids, dexamethasone and IV paracetamol. She explained that the swelling was an abscess next to his tonsil. She asked about allergies; he had none.

Because he looked a little better after the fluids, she sent him home with a week of penicillin tablets and asked him to see his GP in three days. She did not call the ENT team because "the antibiotics should treat it".
h: She did not call the ENT team because "the antibiotics should treat it"

a.o: Dr. Riham sent home a man with a tonsil abscess on tablets without asking ENT to drain it.
a.x: Mr. Nabil should have been seen by ENT for needle drainage of the abscess and IV antibiotics.
a.w: A peritonsillar abscess needs the pus drained. Tablets alone often fail and the swelling can threaten the airway.

a.o: Dr. Riham gave a steroid to someone with an infection.
a.x: Steroids should be avoided in infections.
a.w: A single dose of steroid helps reduce swelling and pain in throat infections.

a.o: Dr. Riham gave IV fluids to a young man.
a.w: He was drooling and drinking only sips, so he needed IV fluids.

a.o: Dr. Riham asked about allergies before antibiotics.
a.x: That was a waste of time.
a.w: Checking allergies before antibiotics is essential.

t: Epiglottitis examined with a spatula
s:
Mr. Rami, 45, came to the ER at 4 a.m. with a severe sore throat that came on over six hours. He was sitting forward, drooling and could not swallow his saliva. His voice was muffled and he had a soft, high-pitched noise when breathing in. His temperature was 39.5°C.

His oxygen was 94 percent and his pulse 120. He had no stridor at rest at first but it got louder when he lay back. Dr. Hany sat him up and gave him oxygen. He asked the nurse to put in an IV line and take blood cultures.

He called the anesthetist and ENT on call to come in. He started IV ceftriaxone and gave nebulized adrenaline.

While waiting, he pressed Mr. Rami's tongue down firmly with a wooden spatula to look at his throat "to confirm the diagnosis". Mr. Rami gagged and coughed, and his breathing became noisier. Dr. Hany wrote that the throat looked only mildly red.
h: he pressed Mr. Rami's tongue down firmly with a wooden spatula to look at his throat

a.o: Dr. Hany pressed on Mr. Rami's tongue with a spatula to examine a throat that might be blocked by epiglottitis.
a.x: The throat should have been left alone until an anesthetist and ENT were ready to secure the airway in theater.
a.w: In suspected epiglottitis, poking the throat can trigger spasm and completely block the airway.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave nebulized adrenaline.
a.x: Adrenaline nebulizers are only for children.
a.w: Nebulized adrenaline can buy time by reducing swelling in adults too.

a.o: Dr. Hany took blood cultures before antibiotics.
a.w: Blood cultures take seconds and can be done before antibiotics if they don't delay them.

a.o: Dr. Hany let him sit up instead of lying flat.
a.w: Sitting up helps keep a swollen airway open.

t: Ear syringing with a perforation
s:
Mrs. Sahar, 52, came to the GP clinic because her right ear felt blocked for two weeks. She had used cotton buds daily for years. As a child she had many ear infections and was told she had "a hole in the eardrum" that never healed. She hears a little less in that ear.

Dr. Mahmoud looked in her ear and saw hard brown wax blocking most of the canal. He could not see the eardrum. Her left ear was clear and her hearing test showed a mild loss on the right.

He told her to stop using cotton buds because they push wax deeper. He advised olive oil drops twice a day.

He said that because she was in the clinic now, he would wash the wax out with a water jet straight away rather than wait. He wrote "syringing done, ear clear" and told her to come back if her hearing did not improve.
h: he would wash the wax out with a water jet straight away rather than wait

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud washed out the ear of a woman known to have a hole in her eardrum.
a.x: The wax should have been removed under the microscope by suction, never with water.
a.w: Water through a perforated eardrum can cause middle ear infection and dizziness.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud told her to stop using cotton buds.
a.w: Cotton buds push wax deeper and can damage the canal.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud advised olive oil drops.
a.w: Olive oil softens wax and helps it come out.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud checked her hearing.
a.w: Checking hearing helps judge the problem and the outcome.

t: Sudden deafness waiting for a scan
s:
Mr. Adham, 38, a lawyer, woke up four days ago unable to hear with his left ear. He had a ringing noise and felt the ear was full. There was no pain, no discharge and no dizziness. He had a cold two weeks earlier.

Dr. Nadine looked in his ears; both eardrums looked normal. The tuning fork tests showed the sound went to his right, good ear, which pointed to a nerve hearing loss on the left. His blood pressure and sugar were normal.

She explained that this could be a sudden nerve deafness, sometimes caused by a virus. She asked for a hearing test the same day, which showed a big loss on the left.

She ordered an MRI of the brain in six weeks and told him to wait for the result before any treatment, "so we know the cause first". She told him to avoid loud noise.
h: told him to wait for the result before any treatment

a.o: Dr. Nadine delayed treating sudden nerve deafness until an MRI in six weeks.
a.x: Mr. Adham should have started high-dose oral steroids straight away, with the MRI arranged as well.
a.w: Sudden nerve hearing loss is an emergency. Steroids work best within the first two weeks; waiting lowers the chance of recovery.

a.o: Dr. Nadine did tuning fork tests.
a.w: Tuning fork tests quickly show whether the loss is in the nerve or the middle ear.

a.o: Dr. Nadine ordered a hearing test the same day.
a.w: A same-day hearing test confirms the loss and helps plan treatment.

a.o: Dr. Nadine ordered an MRI.
a.w: An MRI looks for a growth on the hearing nerve, which can cause one-sided hearing loss.

t: Nosebleed and pinching the bridge
s:
Mr. Sayed, 70, came in with a nosebleed from the left side that had been going for twenty minutes. He takes aspirin for his heart. He had blown his nose hard because of a cold. His blood pressure was 168/94 and his pulse 92.

Nurse Reem sat him up and leaning forward and gave him a bowl to spit the blood into. She checked his blood count and clotting, which were normal. She asked about other bleeding; he had none.

Dr. Ahmed told Mr. Sayed to keep calm and breathe through his mouth. He asked him to pinch the hard, bony top of his nose between his eyes for ten minutes and to put an ice pack on his forehead.

When the bleeding didn't stop, he planned to look inside with a light and cauterize any bleeding point. He told Mr. Sayed he could keep his aspirin.
h: pinch the hard, bony top of his nose between his eyes

a.o: Dr. Ahmed told Mr. Sayed to pinch the bony top of his nose instead of the soft part.
a.x: Mr. Sayed should have pinched the soft, fleshy lower part of his nose firmly for ten to fifteen minutes.
a.w: Most nosebleeds come from vessels at the front of the nose, under the soft part. Pinching the bony bridge does nothing to stop them.

a.o: Nurse Reem sat him leaning forward.
a.x: He should have tipped his head back.
a.w: Leaning forward stops blood running down the throat, which can cause vomiting.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed let him keep his aspirin.
a.w: For a single nosebleed, aspirin for a heart condition is usually continued.

a.o: Nurse Reem checked his blood count.
a.w: In an older person on aspirin with a longer bleed, a blood count is reasonable.

t: Neck lump given antibiotics again
s:
Mr. Kamal, 58, a heavy smoker and drinker, came in about a lump on the right side of his neck for two months. It was not painful. He had a hoarse voice for three months and some pain in his right ear when he swallowed. He had lost 5 kg.

Dr. Sherif felt a hard, fixed lump 3 cm across under his right jaw. It did not move with swallowing. His temperature was normal. He had already had two courses of antibiotics from his GP that did nothing.

He looked at his throat, which looked normal. He asked about his work; he was a builder. He advised him to stop smoking and gave him a leaflet.

He prescribed a third, longer course of antibiotics and booked him back in a month. He wrote: "Likely reactive node, review after antibiotics."
h: He prescribed a third, longer course of antibiotics and booked him back in a month

a.o: Dr. Sherif gave more antibiotics to a smoker with a hard neck lump, hoarseness, ear pain and weight loss.
a.x: Mr. Kamal should have been referred urgently for a head and neck cancer workup with a scope and a scan.
a.w: A hard, painless neck lump in an older smoker and drinker with a hoarse voice and ear pain may be throat cancer. Antibiotics delay diagnosis.

a.o: Dr. Sherif asked about his job.
a.w: Work exposures can matter for head and neck cancers.

a.o: Dr. Sherif examined his throat.
a.x: The throat was not relevant to a neck lump.
a.w: The throat is checked to look for the source of a neck lump.

a.o: Dr. Sherif advised him to stop smoking.
a.w: Stopping smoking lowers his cancer risk.

t: Otitis externa given tablets
s:
Lama, 16, a keen swimmer, came in with a painful right ear for three days. It hurt more when she pulled on her ear lobe or chewed. She had some itchy discharge and felt the ear was blocked. She had no fever.

Dr. Hossam found the ear canal red and swollen with some white debris. He could see a normal eardrum. Her neck glands were normal and her other ear was healthy.

He explained that this was swimmer's ear, an infection of the ear canal. He told her to keep the ear dry and avoid swimming for a week. He advised paracetamol for the pain.

He prescribed amoxicillin tablets for a week and did not give any ear drops, saying "drops are messy and tablets work better". He asked her to come back if it got worse.
h: He prescribed amoxicillin tablets for a week and did not give any ear drops

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave Lama amoxicillin tablets for swimmer's ear instead of ear drops.
a.x: Lama should have had antibiotic and steroid ear drops.
a.w: Ear canal infections are treated with drops, which reach the germs directly. Tablets rarely work and cause side effects.

a.o: Dr. Hossam told her to avoid swimming.
a.w: Water keeps the canal wet and makes the infection worse.

a.o: Dr. Hossam pulled on her ear lobe during the exam.
a.x: That hurt her for no reason.
a.w: Pain on pulling the ear is a sign of ear canal infection.

a.o: Dr. Hossam advised paracetamol.
a.w: Paracetamol is usually enough.

t: Mastoiditis sent home
s:
Ali, 4, was admitted with a high fever and a red, swollen area behind his left ear. He had an ear infection a week ago, treated with amoxicillin. His ear was now sticking out and he was crying when it was touched.

Dr. Rana found his left eardrum red and bulging. The skin behind his ear was swollen and tender, and the ear was pushed forward. He was miserable but drinking. His blood tests showed a high white count.

She gave him IV ceftriaxone and paracetamol and asked ENT to see him. She explained to his parents that the infection had spread to the bone behind the ear.

After one dose, Ali's fever dropped. Dr. Rana decided he could go home on oral antibiotics the next morning "since he looks better". She did not arrange a scan.
h: decided he could go home on oral antibiotics the next morning

a.o: Dr. Rana planned to send home a child with mastoiditis on tablets after one IV dose, without a scan.
a.x: Ali should have stayed on IV antibiotics with a CT scan to look for an abscess, under ENT care.
a.w: Mastoiditis can lead to abscesses, brain infection and clots. It needs IV treatment and imaging.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked ENT to see him.
a.w: ENT may need to drain the ear or the bone.

a.o: Dr. Rana explained the diagnosis to his parents.
a.x: She should have waited for ENT to explain.
a.w: Parents should know what is happening.

a.o: Dr. Rana gave paracetamol.
a.w: Pain relief is important for a child in pain.

t: Vertigo given long-term medication
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 61, has had short spinning attacks for two weeks, each lasting less than a minute. They happen when she turns over in bed or looks up to hang the washing. She has no hearing loss, ringing, headache or weakness.

Dr. Ihab did a test where he turned her head to the right and laid her back quickly. Her eyes flickered in a twisting pattern for twenty seconds and she felt dizzy. Her neurological exam was normal.

He explained that this was benign positional vertigo, caused by small crystals in the inner ear. He told her it was not dangerous and that it often settles.

He prescribed betahistine and prochlorperazine to take every day for three months. He did not try any head movements to treat it, saying "the tablets will settle it".
h: He prescribed betahistine and prochlorperazine to take every day for three months

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave long-term tablets for positional vertigo and did not treat it with a head maneuver.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have had the Epley maneuver in clinic, which moves the crystals back.
a.w: BPPV is treated with the Epley maneuver. Long-term sedating tablets slow recovery and raise the risk of falls in older people.
