He explained that pregnancy stretches the ligaments and that the baby was pushing on her organs. He gave her paracetamol, which helped a little. Her husband asked whether she could eat something before going home.

He sent her home with paracetamol and told her to come back if it got worse. He did not arrange a scan or ask the surgeons to see her.
h: He sent her home with paracetamol and told her to come back if it got worse

a.o: Dr. Hamed sent Mrs. Heba home without looking for appendicitis.
a.x: Mrs. Heba should have had an ultrasound or MRI and a surgical review the same day.
a.w: The appendix moves up in pregnancy, so the pain is higher. Fever, nausea and a high white count point to appendicitis, and a burst appendix can cost the baby's life.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked the baby's heartbeat.
a.x: That was unnecessary for belly pain.
a.w: The baby must be checked in any pregnant woman with pain.

a.o: Dr. Hamed gave Mrs. Heba paracetamol.
a.w: Paracetamol is safe in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked Mrs. Heba's urine.
a.w: A kidney infection can cause similar pain and fever.

t: Crohn's patient told to keep smoking
s:
Ahmed, 26, has Crohn's disease of the last part of his small bowel. He came for review after his second flare this year. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and said smoking was the only thing that helped him relax at work.

Dr. Sherine checked his weight and blood count and arranged a scan of the bowel. She planned to start azathioprine and checked his TPMT enzyme level first, which was normal. She asked for blood tests every week for the first month.

She advised him to have the flu and pneumonia vaccines and to avoid live vaccines once on treatment. She also checked his vitamin B12, which was low, and started injections.

When he asked about smoking, she said he could carry on because "smoking calms bowel inflammation", and booked him back in three months.
h: she said he could carry on because "smoking calms bowel inflammation"

a.o: Dr. Sherine told Ahmed that smoking was fine for his Crohn's disease.
a.x: Ahmed should have been told that smoking makes Crohn's worse and offered help to stop.
a.w: Smoking may ease ulcerative colitis, but it makes Crohn's worse, with more flares and more surgery.

a.o: Dr. Sherine checked Ahmed's TPMT level.
a.w: Low TPMT means azathioprine can wipe out the blood count.

a.o: Dr. Sherine checked Ahmed's vitamin B12.
a.x: B12 has nothing to do with Crohn's.
a.w: Crohn's in the last part of the small bowel stops B12 being absorbed.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked for weekly blood tests.
a.w: Azathioprine can lower the blood count and harm the liver early on.

t: IBS label in an older woman
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 61, came in with bloating almost every day for three months. She also felt full after a few mouthfuls, had lost her appetite, and needed to pass urine more often. She had no diarrhea. She had never had bowel problems before.

Dr. Ihab examined her and found a soft belly that looked slightly swollen. Her blood count and kidney tests were normal. She said her friend had IBS and had been helped by peppermint oil.

He told her she had irritable bowel syndrome, which is common and not dangerous. He advised a low FODMAP diet and peppermint oil capsules, and told her stress could make it worse.

He booked a review in three months to see whether the diet had helped, and did not arrange any other tests. She was relieved and thanked him.
h: He told her she had irritable bowel syndrome, which is common and not dangerous

a.o: Dr. Ihab diagnosed IBS in Mrs. Fawzia, who is over 60 with new bloating.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have had a CA125 blood test and a pelvic ultrasound to look for ovarian cancer.
a.w: New, constant bloating and early fullness in a woman over 50 can be ovarian cancer. IBS rarely starts after 50.

a.o: Dr. Ihab suggested peppermint oil capsules.
a.w: Peppermint oil can ease IBS-type cramps and bloating.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Fawzia's blood count.
a.w: Blood tests help look for other causes.

a.o: Dr. Ihab mentioned that stress can make bowel symptoms worse.
a.w: Stress does worsen gut symptoms in many people.

t: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis missed
s:
Mr. Saad, 60, has cirrhosis with fluid in his belly. His wife brought him in because he had become slow and muddled over two days. He had a temperature of 37.9°C. His belly was swollen but only mildly tender, and his creatinine had risen from 90 to 150.

Dr. Mona checked his urine and chest X-ray, both clear, and sent blood cultures. She started lactulose for the confusion and stopped his water tablets because of his kidneys.

She thought the fever was from a virus going round the family. She did not tap his belly fluid, writing "no peritonitis signs, only mildly tender".

She gave him paracetamol 500 mg for the fever and asked the nurses to watch his urine output. She planned to see him again on the morning round.
h: She did not tap his belly fluid

a.o: Dr. Mona skipped a tap of Mr. Saad's belly fluid.
a.x: Mr. Saad should have had a diagnostic tap at once and IV antibiotics plus albumin if the white cells were high.
a.w: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis often has few belly signs. With fever, confusion and worse kidneys in cirrhosis it is common and deadly if missed.

a.o: Dr. Mona stopped Mr. Saad's water tablets.
a.x: The diuretics should have carried on.
a.w: Diuretics worsen kidney injury and must stop when kidneys fail.

a.o: Dr. Mona sent blood cultures from Mr. Saad.
a.w: Blood cultures help find the infection and guide antibiotics.

a.o: Dr. Mona gave Mr. Saad paracetamol.
a.x: Paracetamol is banned in liver disease.
a.w: Small doses of paracetamol are the safest painkiller in cirrhosis.

t: Gallstone pancreatitis without cholecystectomy
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 46, was admitted with mild pancreatitis caused by gallstones. An ultrasound showed stones in her gallbladder and a normal bile duct. She improved over four days with fluids, pain relief and early eating. Her blood tests were back to normal.

Dr. Waleed explained that a small stone had passed through and irritated the pancreas. He checked that she was eating a normal meal without pain and stopped her drip.

He advised her to cut down on fatty food while she waited, and prescribed paracetamol. He did not book an ERCP, as her bile duct and liver tests were normal.

He discharged her and told her the surgeons would see her in clinic in three months to discuss removing her gallbladder. Her husband asked whether it could happen again.
h: told her the surgeons would see her in clinic in three months to discuss removing her gallbladder

a.o: Dr. Waleed left Mrs. Nadia's gallbladder surgery for three months.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have had her gallbladder removed during this admission or within two weeks.
a.w: After mild gallstone pancreatitis, the risk of another attack is high while waiting, and some attacks are severe.

a.o: Dr. Waleed decided Mrs. Nadia didn't need an ERCP.
a.x: Every gallstone pancreatitis needs an ERCP.
a.w: ERCP is only for a blocked duct or cholangitis; her duct and liver tests were normal.

a.o: Dr. Waleed told Mrs. Nadia to cut down on fatty food.
a.x: Food has nothing to do with gallstones.
a.w: Fatty meals can bring on gallstone pain while waiting.

a.o: Dr. Waleed let Mrs. Nadia eat early.
a.x: She should have fasted until discharge.
a.w: Early eating is safe and helps in mild pancreatitis.

t: Rectal bleeding blamed on piles
s:
Mr. Hany, 62, came in for a blood pressure check. At the end he mentioned dark red blood mixed in with his stool a few times over the last month, and that he had been more tired than usual. His father had bowel cancer at 70.

Dr. Abeer checked his blood pressure, which was well controlled, and renewed his tablets. A blood count she had taken last week showed anemia with low iron. He had no belly pain and his weight was steady.

She said the blood was probably from piles because he had been constipated, gave him a soothing cream and advised more fiber and water. She gave him iron tablets for the anemia.

She did not examine his back passage or refer him, writing "likely hemorrhoids", and booked a review in three months.
h: She did not examine his back passage or refer him, writing "likely hemorrhoids"

a.o: Dr. Abeer blamed piles for Mr. Hany's bleeding with anemia.
a.x: Mr. Hany should have had a rectal exam and an urgent referral for a colonoscopy.
a.w: Rectal bleeding with iron-deficiency anemia over 60, and a father with bowel cancer, can be bowel cancer.

a.o: Dr. Abeer gave Mr. Hany iron tablets.
a.x: Iron should wait until the cause is found.
a.w: Iron can start while tests are arranged.

a.o: Dr. Abeer asked about Mr. Hany's father.
a.w: Bowel cancer in a parent raises his risk.

a.o: Dr. Abeer advised more fiber and water.
a.w: Fiber eases constipation and straining.

t: Hepatitis B reactivation forgotten
s:
Mr. Hassan, 55, has lymphoma and is due to start chemotherapy with rituximab. His screening blood tests showed he had hepatitis B in the past: core antibody positive, surface antigen negative. His liver tests were normal. He remembered being yellow as a young man in the army.

Dr. Nermine explained the treatment and its side effects. She checked his HIV and hepatitis C tests, which were negative, and asked for a heart scan before the chemotherapy.

She told him to avoid people with chickenpox and to call the ward at once if he had a fever. She gave him written information for his family.

She said that because his surface antigen was negative, the hepatitis B had cleared and nothing else was needed. She did not start an antiviral medicine.
h: She did not start an antiviral medicine

a.o: Dr. Nermine gave Mr. Hassan rituximab with no hepatitis B protection.
a.x: Mr. Hassan should have had an antiviral such as entecavir during rituximab and for at least a year after.
a.w: Rituximab can wake up hidden hepatitis B, even with a negative surface antigen, and cause liver failure.

a.o: Dr. Nermine checked Mr. Hassan for HIV and hepatitis C.
a.w: Hidden viral infections must be found before chemotherapy.

a.o: Dr. Nermine asked for a heart scan.
a.x: His heart had nothing to do with lymphoma.
a.w: Some lymphoma drugs can harm the heart.

a.o: Dr. Nermine told Mr. Hassan to call with any fever.
a.x: A fever can wait for clinic.
a.w: Fever on chemotherapy can be life-threatening sepsis.

t: Constipation in a child given an enema
s:
Laila, 5, came in with her mother because of belly pain and hard, large stools every five days for three months. She cries on the toilet and hides to hold it in. Her belly was soft with a firm stool mass on the left side. She was growing normally and had no vomiting.

Dr. Rana asked about her diet, which had little fruit or vegetables, and about her back and legs, which were normal. She checked the skin over her lower back for any dimple, and there was none.

She explained that Laila had constipation and that holding in stool makes it harder and more painful. She advised more water and fruit and a reward chart for sitting on the toilet after meals.

She gave Laila a phosphate enema in the ER and sent her home with no medicine, saying "the enema will fix it".
h: She gave Laila a phosphate enema in the ER and sent her home with no medicine

a.o: Dr. Rana treated Laila's long-term constipation with only an enema.
a.x: Laila should have had oral macrogol to clear the stool and then keep it soft for months.
a.w: Enemas frighten children and don't stop the cycle. Macrogol by mouth for months is first-line.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Laila's lower back.
a.w: A spinal problem can cause constipation, so checking the back is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Rana suggested a reward chart.
a.w: Toilet routines and rewards help children with constipation.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about Laila's diet.
a.w: A diet low in fiber can cause constipation.

t: Acute liver failure transferred late
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 34, was admitted three days ago after taking a large paracetamol overdose. She has been on acetylcysteine since she arrived. Today her INR has risen from 2.5 to 4.8, her pH is 7.24 and her creatinine 260. She has become more confused.

Dr. Ahmed continued the acetylcysteine and gave IV fluids. He checked her sugar every hour because it had been low, and started a glucose drip.

He asked the psychiatrists to see her when she was well enough. He spoke honestly to her family, telling them she was very ill.

He decided to wait until the next morning to call the liver transplant center, "to see if she improves overnight".
h: He decided to wait until the next morning to call the liver transplant center

a.o: Dr. Ahmed waited until morning to call the liver unit for Mrs. Asmaa.
a.x: Mrs. Asmaa should have been discussed with the liver transplant center at once.
a.w: A pH below 7.3 after paracetamol, with a rising INR and confusion, meets transplant criteria. Hours matter.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed kept acetylcysteine going.
a.x: It should stop after the usual course.
a.w: Acetylcysteine continues while the liver is failing.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed checked Mrs. Asmaa's sugar every hour.
a.w: A failing liver cannot make sugar, so low sugar is common.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed told the family she was very ill.
a.w: Families need honest information.

t: H. pylori tested on omeprazole
s:
Mr. Ibrahim, 39, had burning upper belly pain for three months, worse at night. He had no weight loss, no trouble swallowing and no black stools. He started omeprazole from the pharmacy a week ago, which helped.

Dr. Ghada thought he might have the stomach bug H. pylori. She asked about painkillers, and he said he took no ibuprofen or aspirin. She sent a stool test for the bacterium that same day.

The test came back negative, so she told him he did not have H. pylori. She did not refer him for a camera test, as he was young with no warning signs.

She advised him to keep taking omeprazole for a month and to cut down on coffee and late meals. He asked whether his brother, who had an ulcer, should be tested too.
h: She sent a stool test for the bacterium that same day

a.o: Dr. Ghada tested Mr. Ibrahim for H. pylori while he was on omeprazole.
a.x: He should have stopped omeprazole for two weeks before the test.
a.w: Proton pump inhibitors can make H. pylori tests falsely negative.

a.o: Dr. Ghada did not send Mr. Ibrahim for a camera test.
a.x: Everyone with stomach pain needs a scope.
a.w: Young people with no warning signs can be tested and treated without a scope.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Ibrahim about painkillers.
a.w: NSAIDs are a common cause of ulcers.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised cutting down on late meals.
a.w: Late meals can worsen night-time symptoms.

t: Hepatitis A vaccine not offered
s:
Mr. Sami, 45, has hepatitis C with early liver scarring and is on tablets that should cure it. He came to clinic before a three-month work trip to a country where hepatitis A is common. He was excited about the job and asked what he should watch for.

Dr. Nadia checked his liver blood tests, which were stable, and asked about alcohol; he drinks very little. She checked that he had enough tablets for the trip and gave him a letter for airport security.

She checked his hepatitis B blood test, which showed he was already immune from a vaccine years ago, and told him so.

She gave him advice about clean food and bottled water. She did not offer a hepatitis A vaccine, saying "you already have hepatitis".
h: She did not offer a hepatitis A vaccine, saying "you already have hepatitis"

a.o: Dr. Nadia didn't offer Mr. Sami a hepatitis A vaccine.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have been vaccinated against hepatitis A before his trip.
a.w: Hepatitis A on top of liver disease can cause liver failure. Having one hepatitis virus doesn't protect against another.

a.o: Dr. Nadia checked Mr. Sami's hepatitis B immunity.
a.w: If he were not immune, he would need a hepatitis B vaccine too.

a.o: Dr. Nadia gave Mr. Sami a letter for his tablets.
a.w: Carrying a letter avoids trouble with medicines at airports.

a.o: Dr. Nadia asked Mr. Sami about alcohol.
a.w: Alcohol speeds liver damage in hepatitis C.

t: Ulcerative colitis flare given loperamide
s:
Mrs. Rana, 33, has ulcerative colitis. She was admitted with bloody diarrhea ten times a day, a pulse of 104 and a temperature of 37.9°C. Her CRP was high and her albumin low. An X-ray of her belly showed no swelling of the colon.

Dr. Hossam started IV hydrocortisone and a daily blood thinner injection to prevent clots. He sent stool tests for infection, including C. difficile.

He asked the surgeons to see her on the first day in case she did not improve, and planned to review her on day three to decide on rescue treatment.

To slow the diarrhea and help her sleep, he also gave her loperamide and codeine. Her mother was worried about the blood thinner and asked if it would make the bleeding worse.
h: To slow the diarrhea and help her sleep, he also gave her loperamide and codeine

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave Mrs. Rana loperamide and codeine in a severe colitis flare.
a.x: Mrs. Rana should not have had anti-diarrhea drugs or opioids.
a.w: In severe colitis these drugs can cause toxic megacolon, where the colon swells and can burst.

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave Mrs. Rana a blood thinner while she was bleeding.
a.x: Blood thinners are dangerous with bloody diarrhea.
a.w: Severe colitis raises clot risk, and preventive blood thinners are standard.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked the surgeons to see her on day one.
a.x: Surgeons should only come if she gets worse.
a.w: Early surgical review is advised in severe colitis.

a.o: Dr. Hossam tested Mrs. Rana's stool for C. difficile.
a.x: Tests were unnecessary in a known colitis patient.
a.w: Infection can mimic or worsen a flare.

t: Variceal bleed without antibiotics
s:
Mr. Atef, 59, has cirrhosis and was admitted vomiting blood. His blood pressure was 92/60 and his hemoglobin 7.2. He was given blood to bring his hemoglobin up to about 8, and terlipressin. A camera test showed bleeding varices, which were banded.

Dr. Mai wrote him up for lactulose because blood in the gut can bring on confusion. She held his propranolol while his blood pressure was low.

She asked for him to be watched closely for more bleeding, with the camera team ready to repeat the scope. She spoke to his son, who asked if his father would bleed again.

She did not start any antibiotics, writing "no signs of infection, no fever".
h: She did not start any antibiotics, writing "no signs of infection, no fever"

a.o: Dr. Mai gave Mr. Atef no antibiotics after his variceal bleed.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have had IV antibiotics such as ceftriaxone from admission.
a.w: In cirrhosis with a gut bleed, antibiotics lower infection, rebleeding and death, even without fever.

a.o: Dr. Mai stopped the blood at a hemoglobin of about 8.
a.x: She should have given blood until it was normal.
a.w: Overfilling raises the pressure in the varices and causes rebleeding.

a.o: Dr. Mai held Mr. Atef's propranolol.
a.x: His beta blocker should have carried on.
a.w: Beta blockers are paused while the blood pressure is low from bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Mai gave Mr. Atef lactulose.
a.w: Blood in the gut can trigger encephalopathy.

t: Bowel obstruction given laxatives
s:
Mr. Sabri, 70, had an operation on his bowel two years ago. He came in with cramping belly pain, green vomiting and no stool or wind for two days. His belly was swollen and his bowel sounds were high-pitched and tinkling. His hernia sites were normal.

Dr. Inas sent bloods, which showed he was dry, and started a drip. She did an X-ray, which showed dilated loops of small bowel in the middle of the belly.

She asked about his medicines: he takes codeine for his back. She gave him an anti-sickness injection and checked his potassium, which was low, and added it to the drip.

She diagnosed constipation from codeine, gave him a strong laxative to drink, and asked the nurses to let him eat and drink normally.
h: She diagnosed constipation from codeine, gave him a strong laxative to drink

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Sabri laxatives for small bowel obstruction.
a.x: Mr. Sabri should have been nil by mouth, with a drip, a nasogastric tube, a CT scan and a surgical review.
a.w: Vomiting, no wind, a swollen belly and dilated loops after old surgery mean adhesions blocking the bowel. Laxatives can make it burst.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked Mr. Sabri's hernia sites.
a.w: A trapped hernia is a common cause of obstruction.

a.o: Dr. Inas replaced Mr. Sabri's potassium.
a.w: Low potassium slows the bowel and needs replacing.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about Mr. Sabri's codeine.
a.x: His medicines had nothing to do with it.
a.w: Codeine causes constipation and is worth knowing.

t: Refeeding syndrome after starvation
s:
Mr. Yasser, 44, was found at home after a long depression. He had barely eaten for three weeks and drank only tea. He weighs 41 kg, with a BMI of 14. His potassium was 3.4, his phosphate 0.7 and his magnesium low-normal. He was alert and his heart tracing was normal.

Dr. Hala gave him thiamine and a multivitamin before any feeding, and asked the dietitian to see him the same day. She asked the psychiatry team to assess his mood and his safety.

She checked his weight on the ward scale herself, and asked for a heart monitor overnight. His sister brought food from home and asked whether he could eat it.

Keen to build him up fast, she started full feeds of 2,500 kcal a day from the first day, with no extra phosphate or potassium, and asked for his salts to be checked "in a week".
h: she started full feeds of 2,500 kcal a day from the first day, with no extra phosphate or potassium

a.o: Dr. Hala fed Mr. Yasser full calories from day one with low salts and no checks.
a.x: Mr. Yasser should have started on about 10 kcal/kg a day, rising slowly, with phosphate, potassium and magnesium replaced and checked every day.
a.w: After starvation, sudden feeding drives phosphate and potassium into cells. Refeeding syndrome can cause heart failure, fits and death.

a.o: Dr. Hala gave Mr. Yasser thiamine before feeding.
a.w: Thiamine protects the brain and heart when feeding restarts.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked psychiatry to see Mr. Yasser.
a.x: His mood could wait until he was fed.
a.w: Severe self-neglect from depression needs a risk assessment.

a.o: Dr. Hala put Mr. Yasser on a heart monitor.
a.x: A monitor was unnecessary with a normal tracing.
a.w: Low salts during feeding can cause sudden heart rhythm problems.

t: Liver cancer screening skipped in cirrhosis
s:
Mr. Kareem, 61, has cirrhosis from hepatitis C, which was cured with tablets three years ago. He came for his yearly review feeling well. He has no fluid in his belly and no confusion, and he stopped drinking ten years ago.

Dr. Nesma checked his blood count, liver tests and INR, which were stable. A camera test two years ago showed small varices, and he takes carvedilol.

She praised him for staying off alcohol, checked that his flu and pneumonia vaccines were up to date, and advised him to keep his weight down because he had gained 5 kg.

She told him that because the virus was cured he no longer needed six-monthly liver scans, and discharged him to his GP. He was pleased to have one less appointment.
h: She told him that because the virus was cured he no longer needed six-monthly liver scans

a.o: Dr. Nesma stopped Mr. Kareem's six-monthly liver scans after his cure.
a.x: Mr. Kareem should have kept having a liver ultrasound, with or without an AFP test, every six months for life.
a.w: Curing hepatitis C lowers but does not remove the cancer risk once cirrhosis is present.

a.o: Dr. Nesma kept Mr. Kareem on carvedilol.
a.x: Beta blockers should stop once the virus is cured.
a.w: Carvedilol protects against bleeding from varices, which remain.

a.o: Dr. Nesma checked Mr. Kareem's vaccines.
a.w: People with cirrhosis are at high risk from flu and pneumonia.

a.o: Dr. Nesma warned Mr. Kareem about weight gain.
a.x: Weight doesn't matter after a cure.
a.w: Fatty liver from weight gain can worsen cirrhosis.

t: Down syndrome screen called a diagnosis
s:
Mrs. Yasmin, 38, is 13 weeks pregnant with her second baby. Her combined screening test, using a scan of the baby's neck and two blood tests, gave a chance of Down syndrome of 1 in 40. Her first child is well.

Dr. Soha saw her with her husband. She explained the scan findings clearly and checked that the dates of the pregnancy were right. She offered them time to talk and a quiet room.

She asked about any family history of genetic conditions; there was none. She gave them a leaflet and the number of a support charity.

She told them that the baby "has Down syndrome" and booked them to discuss ending the pregnancy next week. She did not offer any further test.
h: She told them that the baby "has Down syndrome" and booked them to discuss ending the pregnancy next week

a.o: Dr. Soha told Mrs. Yasmin a screening result was a diagnosis.
a.x: Mrs. Yasmin should have been told it was a higher chance, not a diagnosis, and offered NIPT or a CVS or amniocentesis to find out for sure.
a.w: A 1 in 40 chance means 39 in 40 such babies do not have Down syndrome. Only a diagnostic test can confirm it.

a.o: Dr. Soha gave Mrs. Yasmin and her husband a quiet room and time.
a.x: Bad news should be given quickly and moved on.
a.w: Unhurried, private counseling is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked the pregnancy dates.
a.w: Wrong dates can change the screening result.

a.o: Dr. Soha gave them a support charity's number.
a.x: That pushes them to keep the baby.
a.w: Balanced information includes support for either choice.

t: BRCA test for a child
s:
Mrs. Lobna, 42, carries a BRCA1 gene change. She found out after her own breast cancer, which was treated last year. She came to the genetics clinic with her two daughters, aged 19 and 12, to talk about testing.

Dr. Tamer explained what the gene means and drew a family tree going back three generations. He discussed screening with yearly MRI from age 30 and surgery to lower risk for carriers.

The 19-year-old said she wanted time to think, and he booked her a second talk in a month. He gave the family written information and the number of the genetics nurse.

At Mrs. Lobna's request, he also took blood from the 12-year-old for a BRCA1 test that day, "so the family knows where everyone stands".
h: he also took blood from the 12-year-old for a BRCA1 test that day

a.o: Dr. Tamer tested Mrs. Lobna's 12-year-old for BRCA1.
a.x: The 12-year-old should not have been tested until she could choose for herself as an adult.
a.w: BRCA risks start in adulthood and nothing changes for her in childhood, so testing takes away her own right to decide.

a.o: Dr. Tamer gave the 19-year-old time to think.
a.x: She should have been tested that day.
a.w: Predictive testing needs time and a free choice.

a.o: Dr. Tamer drew a three-generation family tree.
a.x: A family tree was unnecessary with a known gene.
a.w: A family tree shows who else may be at risk.

a.o: Dr. Tamer discussed risk-lowering surgery.
a.x: Surgery is too extreme to mention.
a.w: Removing breasts and ovaries greatly lowers risk for carriers.

t: Huntington result shared with a sister
s:
Mr. Waleed, 34, had a predictive test for Huntington disease because his father has it. The test showed he carries the gene change. He came with his wife and had had three counseling sessions before the test.

Dr. Mervat gave the result in a quiet room and arranged a follow-up with the counselor the next week. She asked how he was feeling and whether he had thoughts of harming himself, and gave him a number to call.

He said he did not want anyone else told yet, including his sister. She agreed and noted this in his file.

Two days later his sister phoned, worried, and asked for his result. Dr. Mervat told her that her brother carried the gene, "because she is at risk too".
h: Dr. Mervat told her that her brother carried the gene

a.o: Dr. Mervat told Mr. Waleed's sister his result without his consent.
a.x: Dr. Mervat should have kept the result private and offered the sister her own counseling and testing.
a.w: Genetic results are confidential. The sister's risk comes from her father and is the same whatever her brother's result.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked Mr. Waleed about self-harm.
a.w: Suicide risk rises after a positive Huntington result.

a.o: Dr. Mervat insisted on counseling before the test.
a.w: Predictive testing for Huntington always needs counseling first.

a.o: Dr. Mervat booked a follow-up for Mr. Waleed.
a.w: Support after the result is part of the testing plan.

t: Familial hypercholesterolemia relatives not tested
s:
Mr. Hesham, 39, had a heart attack last month. His LDL cholesterol was 7.6 mmol/L. He had yellow lumps on his Achilles tendons. His father died of a heart attack at 46, and he has two children, aged 10 and 14, and a younger brother.

Dr. Rana diagnosed familial hypercholesterolemia. She started high-dose atorvastatin and added ezetimibe, and asked for his cholesterol to be checked in six weeks.

She checked his thyroid and kidney tests to rule out other causes of high cholesterol, and his liver tests before starting treatment. She referred him to cardiac rehab.

She told him his family had "bad luck with hearts" and to eat well. She did not mention testing his brother or his children.
h: She did not mention testing his brother or his children

a.o: Dr. Rana didn't offer testing to Mr. Hesham's brother and children.
a.x: His brother and children should have been offered cholesterol and genetic tests.
a.w: Familial hypercholesterolemia is passed on to half of children. Children can start statins from about 10 years old.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Mr. Hesham's thyroid.
a.w: An underactive thyroid can raise cholesterol.

a.o: Dr. Rana added ezetimibe to his statin.
a.x: A statin alone is always enough.
a.w: Very high LDL often needs more than one drug.

a.o: Dr. Rana referred him to cardiac rehab.
a.w: Cardiac rehab improves recovery after a heart attack.

t: Cystic fibrosis risk told wrongly
s:
Mr. and Mrs. Atia came to the genetics clinic. Their nephew has cystic fibrosis, and blood tests showed they are both carriers of a CF gene change. They are planning their first child and are cousins.

Dr. Ihab drew a family tree and explained that cystic fibrosis is recessive, so a child needs a changed gene from both parents. He spoke slowly and checked they understood.

He told them about testing in pregnancy and about IVF with testing of embryos, and gave them time to ask questions. He said they did not need to decide anything that day.

He told them each child would have a 50% chance of having cystic fibrosis. They left very upset, saying they might not have children at all.
h: He told them each child would have a 50% chance of having cystic fibrosis

a.o: Dr. Ihab told the Atias each child had a 50% chance of cystic fibrosis.
a.x: They should have been told the chance is 1 in 4 for each pregnancy, with a 1 in 2 chance of a carrier child.
a.w: When both parents carry a recessive gene, each child has a 25% chance of being affected.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told them about IVF with embryo testing.
a.x: That was too complex to mention.
a.w: Embryo testing is a real option for carrier couples.

a.o: Dr. Ihab drew a family tree.
a.w: A family tree helps explain inheritance.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told them they need not decide that day.
a.x: They should have decided before leaving.
a.w: Reproductive choices need time.

t: Fragile X tested by karyotype
s:
Omar, 6, has learning difficulties and speech delay. He avoids eye contact and flaps his hands when excited. He has a long face and large ears. His mother's brother has a learning disability, and his grandfather had a tremor.

Dr. Nada examined him and found soft, stretchy skin and flat feet. She checked his hearing, which was normal, and asked the school for a report.

She referred him to speech therapy and to the child development team for assessment of autism.

His mother said he was a happy boy but became upset with loud noises and new places. He had a lot of ear infections as a toddler. His older sister is doing well at school. His mother, who is 29, asked whether a future baby could have the same problem.

She sent a standard chromosome karyotype to look for fragile X. When it came back normal, she told his mother fragile X had been ruled out.
h: She sent a standard chromosome karyotype to look for fragile X

a.o: Dr. Nada used a karyotype to rule out fragile X for Omar.
a.x: Omar should have had a DNA test for the FMR1 repeat.
a.w: A karyotype misses fragile X. Only a DNA test measures the repeat in the FMR1 gene.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Omar's hearing.
a.w: Hearing loss can cause speech delay.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about the grandfather's tremor.
a.x: A tremor has nothing to do with Omar.
a.w: Fragile X carriers can get a tremor later in life.

a.o: Dr. Nada took Omar's mother's question about a future baby seriously.
a.x: A future baby could not be affected.
a.w: Fragile X passes through mothers, so she may be a carrier.

t: Hemochromatosis patient given an iron tonic
s:
Mr. Mostafa, 48, was found to have genetic hemochromatosis after a check for tiredness and sore joints. He has two copies of the C282Y gene change. His ferritin was 1,100 and his liver tests mildly raised.

Dr. Rasha arranged regular venesection, taking a unit of blood every week, at the hospital day unit. She arranged a liver scan to look for scarring.

She told him to cut down on alcohol and offered testing to his brothers and sister. He was surprised the illness ran in families and agreed to tell them.

Because the blood taking would make him tired, she prescribed an iron and vitamin C tonic, and advised him to eat more red meat.
h: she prescribed an iron and vitamin C tonic

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave Mr. Mostafa an iron and vitamin C tonic.
a.x: Mr. Mostafa should have avoided iron and vitamin C supplements.
a.w: In hemochromatosis the body already has too much iron, and vitamin C increases how much is absorbed.

a.o: Dr. Rasha arranged weekly venesection.
a.w: Removing blood is the main treatment to lower iron.

a.o: Dr. Rasha offered testing to Mr. Mostafa's siblings.
a.x: His siblings were not at risk.
a.w: Brothers and sisters have a 1 in 4 chance of carrying two copies.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked for a liver scan.
a.w: A ferritin over 1,000 raises the risk of liver scarring.

t: Marfan features with no heart scan
s:
Karim, 17, came in for a sports form for the national volleyball team. He is very tall, with long arms and fingers. He wears thick glasses and had an eye operation for a slipped lens. His mother said his uncle died suddenly at 30.

Dr. Fady noticed that Karim could wrap his thumb and finger around his wrist and that his chest bone was sunken. His blood pressure and heart sounds were normal.

He asked about chest pain or fainting, which Karim denied. He asked his mother about the uncle's death and wrote it in the notes.

He signed the form to say Karim was fit to compete and told him to "enjoy the tall genes". He did not arrange a heart scan.
h: He signed the form to say Karim was fit to compete

a.o: Dr. Fady cleared Karim for competitive sport with Marfan features.
a.x: Karim should have had a heart scan of the aorta and a genetics referral before being cleared for sport.
a.w: Marfan syndrome can widen and tear the aorta, especially with strenuous sport. Normal heart sounds don't rule it out.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about the uncle's sudden death.
a.w: A sudden early death in the family is a red flag.

a.o: Dr. Fady did the wrist sign.
a.w: The wrist sign is a classic feature of Marfan syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked Karim about chest pain or fainting.
a.w: These can be warning signs of heart disease.

t: Turner syndrome called a late bloomer
s:
Malak, 15, came in with her mother because she had not started her periods and had no breast development. She is the shortest girl in her class at 141 cm. She has a broad chest and a low hairline at the back of her neck.

Dr. Ayman plotted her height on a growth chart and found she was below the lowest line. He asked about her health, and she had had many ear infections as a child.

He checked her blood pressure in both arms, which was high in the right arm and lower in the legs.

He told her mother she was "a late bloomer like her aunt" and booked a review in a year. He did not order any tests.
h: He told her mother she was "a late bloomer like her aunt"

a.o: Dr. Ayman called Malak a late bloomer without any tests.
a.x: Malak should have had a karyotype, hormone tests and a heart scan, with referral to a specialist.
a.w: Short stature, no puberty, a broad chest and a narrowed aorta point to Turner syndrome, which needs hormones and heart care.

a.o: Dr. Ayman plotted Malak's height on a chart.
a.w: Growth charts show if a child is growing abnormally.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked blood pressure in her arms and legs.
a.x: That was unnecessary in a teenager.
a.w: A difference suggests coarctation of the aorta.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked about ear infections.
a.w: Ear infections are common in Turner syndrome.

t: Klinefelter missed in an infertile man
s:
Mr. Sherif, 31, came with his wife after two years of trying for a baby. He is tall with long legs, little body hair and some breast tissue. His testes were small and firm. His semen test showed no sperm at all.

Dr. Abeer checked his wife's tests, which were normal. She asked about mumps, injuries or drugs, and he had none.

She explained gently that the problem was with sperm, and he was upset. She asked about his mood and offered a counselor.

She told him he was probably "stressed" and asked him to repeat the semen test in six months. She did not order any hormone or chromosome tests.
h: She told him he was probably "stressed" and asked him to repeat the semen test in six months

a.o: Dr. Abeer blamed stress for Mr. Sherif's absent sperm.
a.x: Mr. Sherif should have had hormone tests and a karyotype.
a.w: Small firm testes, breast tissue and no sperm point to Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), which needs testosterone and specialist fertility care.

a.o: Dr. Abeer asked about mumps.
a.w: Mumps can damage the testes.

a.o: Dr. Abeer checked his wife's tests too.
a.w: Infertility needs both partners to be assessed.

a.o: Dr. Abeer offered Mr. Sherif a counselor.
a.w: Infertility news can be very distressing.

t: Nitrofurantoin for a girl with G6PD deficiency
s:
Sara, 18, came in with burning on passing urine for two days. She had no fever or back pain. She has G6PD deficiency, found when she became yellow and pale as a child after eating fava beans.

Dr. Mahmoud checked her urine with a dipstick, which showed nitrites and white cells. He asked whether she might be pregnant, and she said no.

He advised her to drink plenty of water and to come back if she got a fever or back pain. He sent a urine sample to the lab.

She is a first-year nursing student and lives in a shared flat. She had one urine infection last year that cleared with antibiotics. She is not allergic to penicillin. She said she had been drinking very little water because of long shifts on the wards and was embarrassed to ask for a toilet break.

He prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days. He did not check the antibiotic against her G6PD deficiency.
h: He prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud gave nitrofurantoin to Sara, who has G6PD deficiency.
a.x: Sara should have had a safer antibiotic, such as a short course of cefalexin.
a.w: Nitrofurantoin can break down red cells in G6PD deficiency and cause severe anemia.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked whether Sara might be pregnant.
a.w: Pregnancy changes antibiotic choice.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud sent a urine sample.
a.w: A culture guides treatment if the infection does not clear.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud advised Sara to drink more water.
a.w: Drinking more helps flush the bladder.

t: Lynch syndrome not considered
s:
Mr. Tarek, 38, had bowel cancer removed last month. His mother had cancer of the womb at 45, and his grandfather had bowel cancer at 52. His tumor was on the right side of his bowel.

Dr. Waleed went through the operation results and planned chemotherapy with the oncologist. He checked his CEA and arranged a CT scan.

He asked about his children, a girl of 8 and a boy of 5, and his sister, who is 35.

Mr. Tarek works as an accountant and had noticed blood in his stool and tiredness for months before he saw anyone. His wife came with him and took notes. He asked whether his sister should have a camera test too, and whether his children would need checks when they grew up.

He told Mr. Tarek his cancer was "just bad luck". He did not send the tumor for mismatch repair testing or refer him to genetics.
h: He told Mr. Tarek his cancer was "just bad luck"

a.o: Dr. Waleed called Mr. Tarek's cancer bad luck without testing for Lynch syndrome.
a.x: Mr. Tarek's tumor should have been tested for mismatch repair, and he should have been referred to genetics.
a.w: Bowel cancer before 50 with womb and bowel cancer in the family points to Lynch syndrome. Relatives need early screening.

a.o: Dr. Waleed asked about Mr. Tarek's children.
a.w: Children of a Lynch carrier have a 1 in 2 chance of carrying it.

a.o: Dr. Waleed checked Mr. Tarek's CEA.
a.w: CEA helps follow up bowel cancer.

a.o: Dr. Waleed noted Mr. Tarek's worry about his sister.
a.x: His sister was not at risk.
a.w: A sister of someone with possible Lynch syndrome may need early screening.

t: PKU result left until next month
s:
Baby Ali is 9 days old. His heel prick test showed a very high phenylalanine level, suggesting phenylketonuria. He was feeding well on breast milk and seemed healthy.

Dr. Mona called the parents and explained the result gently. She asked about the family; the parents are cousins.

She told them PKU is treatable and that he could live a normal life with the right diet. She gave them written information and a contact number.

This is the couple's first baby. The mother had a normal pregnancy and an easy delivery, and the baby passed his hearing test before going home. The father works away during the week and asked whether they could wait until he was back to discuss everything together. The midwife had already weighed the baby, who had regained his birth weight.

She booked them to see the metabolic team at the next clinic in a month, and told them to carry on breastfeeding as normal until then.
h: She booked them to see the metabolic team at the next clinic in a month

a.o: Dr. Mona left Baby Ali's PKU treatment for a month.
a.x: Baby Ali should have been seen by the metabolic team within days, with treatment started at once.
a.w: High phenylalanine damages the developing brain. Treatment should start within the first two weeks of life.

a.o: Dr. Mona told the parents PKU is treatable.
a.w: With treatment, people with PKU can live normal lives.

a.o: Dr. Mona asked if the parents were related.
a.w: Cousin marriage raises the chance of recessive conditions.

a.o: Dr. Mona phoned the parents quickly with the result.
a.x: She should have waited for the father to be home.
a.w: Urgent results must reach the family quickly.

t: Down syndrome baby without a heart scan
s:
Baby Mariam was born at term to Mrs. Huda, 41. She has features of Down syndrome, which was confirmed by a blood test. She is feeding slowly on breast milk and has low muscle tone.

Dr. Hamed examined her and found no heart murmur. Her oxygen levels were normal in her hand and foot.

He explained the diagnosis kindly to her parents and gave them the number of a support group. He asked the lactation nurse to help with feeding.

Her parents were shocked, as the screening test in pregnancy had shown a low chance. Her father asked whether they had done something wrong. Mrs. Huda wanted to keep breastfeeding and was tired after a long labor. The baby's breathing was comfortable and her color was pink.

He told them that because there was no murmur, a heart scan was not needed. He arranged hearing and thyroid tests.
h: He told them that because there was no murmur, a heart scan was not needed

a.o: Dr. Hamed skipped a heart scan for Baby Mariam with Down syndrome.
a.x: Baby Mariam should have had an echocardiogram in the first weeks of life.
a.w: Almost half of babies with Down syndrome have a heart defect, and many have no murmur at first.

a.o: Dr. Hamed asked the lactation nurse to help.
a.w: Babies with Down syndrome often feed slowly.

a.o: Dr. Hamed arranged a thyroid test.
a.w: Thyroid problems are common in Down syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Hamed told the father it was not his fault.
a.x: The cause should have been looked into.
a.w: Most Down syndrome happens by chance and is no one's fault.

t: Mitochondrial disease counseled as paternal
s:
Mr. Raafat, 30, has a mitochondrial disease called MELAS. He has had strokes and his hearing is poor. His mother has diabetes and deafness. He and his wife are planning a baby.

Dr. Rehab explained the disease clearly and drew a family tree. She checked his heart, which was normal, and his sugar.

She told him about a support group and booked his hearing aid review.

Mr. Raafat works as a school teacher and uses hearing aids in class. His wife is healthy, and her family has no illness of this kind. His sister has had seizures and also has poor hearing. He had read on the internet that the disease could pass to children and was worried.

She told him his children would each have a 50% chance of having MELAS, and advised them to think about IVF with embryo testing.
h: She told him his children would each have a 50% chance of having MELAS

a.o: Dr. Rehab told Mr. Raafat his children had a 50% chance of MELAS.
a.x: Mr. Raafat should have been told that mitochondrial disease passes from mothers, so his children are not at risk from him.
a.w: Mitochondria come from the egg, not the sperm.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mr. Raafat's heart.
a.w: MELAS can affect the heart.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked about his mother.
a.w: His mother passed on the mitochondria.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked about Mr. Raafat's sister's seizures.
a.w: Siblings who share the mother's mitochondria can be affected too.

t: Achondroplasia recurrence overstated
s:
Mr. and Mrs. Hassan, both of average height, have a baby boy with achondroplasia, a form of short stature. They came to the genetics clinic to understand why and to plan another pregnancy.

Dr. Ihab examined the baby, who had a large head and short arms and legs. He checked the baby's breathing and arranged a sleep study.

He explained that achondroplasia is caused by a change in one gene and that children with it can go to school and live full lives.

The pregnancy had been normal until a late scan showed short thigh bones. Mrs. Hassan is 27 and her husband 41. Neither family has anyone with short stature. Mrs. Hassan was breastfeeding and the baby was gaining weight well. The father asked whether something he had done at work could have caused it.

He told them that each future child would have a 50% chance of having achondroplasia.
h: He told them that each future child would have a 50% chance of having achondroplasia

a.o: Dr. Ihab told the Hassans each future child had a 50% chance of achondroplasia.
a.x: They should have been told that with two average-height parents, it is almost always a new change, and the chance again is very low.
a.w: Most achondroplasia is a new mutation. The 50% risk applies only when a parent has achondroplasia.

a.o: Dr. Ihab arranged a sleep study.
a.w: Children with achondroplasia can have breathing problems in sleep.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told them their son could live a full life.
a.w: Most people with achondroplasia have normal intelligence and life span.

a.o: Dr. Ihab took the father's work question seriously.
a.x: The father's age was off topic.
a.w: Older fathers have a slightly higher chance of new gene changes like this one.

t: Cousins told marriage is forbidden
s:
Ahmed and Nour, both 25, are first cousins. They plan to marry and came to ask about the health risks for their children. Neither family has any known genetic disease.

Dr. Sherine drew a family tree going back three generations and asked about any babies who died young. There were none.

She offered carrier tests for conditions common in their community, such as thalassemia.

Both families were keen on the marriage, but Nour's friend had warned her that cousins have sick babies. They are both healthy university graduates. Ahmed's younger brother has asthma, and Nour's grandmother had diabetes. They asked whether there was any test that could reassure them.

She told them their children would have "a very high risk" of serious illness and advised them not to marry.
h: She told them their children would have "a very high risk" of serious illness and advised them not to marry

a.o: Dr. Sherine told Ahmed and Nour their risk was very high and advised against marriage.
a.x: They should have been told the extra risk is about 2 to 3%, with carrier testing offered.
a.w: First cousins have about a 4 to 6% chance of a child with a serious problem, compared with about 3% in the general population.

a.o: Dr. Sherine offered thalassemia carrier tests.
a.w: Carrier tests find couples at higher risk.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked about babies who died young.
a.w: Early deaths can be a clue to recessive disease.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked about Nour's grandmother's diabetes.
a.w: A full family history includes common illnesses too.

t: Malignant hyperthermia history ignored
s:
Mr. Fouad, 35, is having a planned knee operation. In the clinic he said his cousin "had a reaction to anesthetic" and needed intensive care. His uncle died during an operation years ago. He has never had an anesthetic himself.

Dr. Hala checked his airway, heart and lungs, which were normal. She asked about allergies, and he has none.

She explained the operation and the anesthetic and gave him a leaflet. She checked that he would fast before surgery.

He works as a builder and hurt his knee playing football. He is otherwise fit, takes no medicines and drinks little. His cousin's hospital had sent a letter to the family years ago, but he did not have a copy. He said he would be happy to have a spinal injection instead of being put to sleep if that was safer.

On the day, she used sevoflurane gas and suxamethonium, the usual drugs, and noted "family history unclear".
h: she used sevoflurane gas and suxamethonium

a.o: Dr. Hala used trigger drugs in Mr. Fouad despite a family history of malignant hyperthermia.
a.x: Mr. Fouad should have had a trigger-free anesthetic, such as propofol and no suxamethonium, with dantrolene ready.
a.w: Malignant hyperthermia is inherited, and gases and suxamethonium can trigger a deadly reaction.

a.o: Dr. Hala considered a spinal anesthetic for Mr. Fouad.
a.x: A general anesthetic is always better for a knee.
a.w: A spinal avoids trigger drugs and is a safe choice for knee surgery.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked about allergies.
a.w: Allergies change drug choice.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked Mr. Fouad about his uncle's death.
a.x: Old family deaths were off topic.
a.w: A death during surgery in the family can be a clue to malignant hyperthermia.

t: Duchenne boy called lazy
s:
Yusuf, 4, came in because he falls often and struggles to climb stairs. His mother said he was slow to walk. He uses his hands to push up off his legs when getting up from the floor. His calves are big.

Dr. Rana watched him walk and noticed he waddled. His speech was a little delayed.

She asked about his mother's family. His mother's brother died young of a muscle disease.

Yusuf goes to a nursery, and his teacher noticed he could not keep up with the other children on the playground. He has a younger sister, aged 2, who is walking and running well. His mother was pregnant with her third child and worried the new baby might have the same problem.

She told his mother he was "a bit lazy" and that he would grow out of it. She did not do any blood tests.
h: She told his mother he was "a bit lazy" and that he would grow out of it

a.o: Dr. Rana called Yusuf lazy instead of testing for a muscle disease.
a.x: Yusuf should have had a CK blood test and a referral to a children's muscle specialist.
a.w: A boy who pushes up off his legs, with big calves and a family history on his mother's side, points to Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

a.o: Dr. Rana watched Yusuf walk.
a.w: A waddling walk is a clue to weak hip muscles.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about his mother's family.
a.w: Duchenne is passed down through mothers.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about Yusuf's nursery.
a.w: A teacher's view helps show if a child keeps up.

t: Abacavir without HLA testing
s:
Mr. Samir, 32, was newly diagnosed with HIV. His viral load was high and his CD4 count 410. He has no other illnesses. He has hepatitis B immunity from a vaccine.

Dr. Nadia explained the treatment and checked his kidney function and his hepatitis tests. She checked for any interactions with his other medicines.

She advised him to tell his partner and offered testing for the partner.

He found out he had HIV after a test at a blood donation. He works as a chef and was worried about telling his employer. He has no allergies. His hepatitis C test was negative. He asked whether he could take one tablet a day and whether he would be able to have children in future.

She started abacavir, lamivudine and dolutegravir that day, without an HLA-B*5701 test.
h: She started abacavir, lamivudine and dolutegravir that day, without an HLA-B*5701 test

a.o: Dr. Nadia started abacavir without an HLA-B*5701 test.
a.x: Mr. Samir should have had an HLA-B*5701 test before abacavir.
a.w: People with HLA-B*5701 can have a severe, sometimes deadly allergy to abacavir.

a.o: Dr. Nadia checked his kidney function.
a.w: Some HIV drugs affect the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Nadia offered testing to his partner.
a.w: Partners need testing and protection.

a.o: Dr. Nadia offered Mr. Samir one combined tablet a day.
a.x: One tablet a day is not strong enough.
a.w: Simple once-daily treatment helps people take it reliably.

t: Carbamazepine without HLA testing
s:
Mr. Lin, 28, is from Malaysia and of Han Chinese background. He came with stabbing pain in his face, triggered by brushing his teeth and the wind. His examination was normal.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed trigeminal neuralgia. She asked for an MRI because he was young, to look for causes such as multiple sclerosis.

She explained the condition and advised him to keep a pain diary.

He works as a software engineer and had stopped eating on one side because chewing set off the pain. Paracetamol and ibuprofen had not helped. He has no other illnesses and takes no other medicines. He said the pain felt like an electric shock and was making him dread meals.

She started carbamazepine 100 mg twice a day without an HLA-B*1502 test.
h: She started carbamazepine 100 mg twice a day without an HLA-B*1502 test

a.o: Dr. Ghada started carbamazepine without an HLA-B*1502 test.
a.x: Mr. Lin should have had an HLA-B*1502 test before starting carbamazepine.
a.w: People of Han Chinese or Southeast Asian background with HLA-B*1502 have a high risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked for an MRI.
a.w: Young people with facial pain need a scan to look for other causes.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised a pain diary.
a.w: A diary helps track triggers and treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped relying on ibuprofen for Mr. Lin's pain.
a.w: Ordinary painkillers rarely help trigeminal neuralgia; anticonvulsants are used.

t: Combined pill with factor V Leiden
s:
Rasha, 22, came in for contraception. She has factor V Leiden, found after her mother had a clot in her leg. She has never had a clot herself. She does not smoke.

Dr. Mahmoud checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her BMI, which was 23.

He asked about her periods, which are regular, and about migraine, which she does not have.

She is in her final year of law school and has a long-term partner. She wanted something easy to remember and said her friends all take the pill. She has no plans for children for some years. She asked whether the pill would make her gain weight.

He prescribed the combined pill, saying "you have never had a clot".
h: He prescribed the combined pill, saying "you have never had a clot"

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud gave the combined pill to Rasha, who has factor V Leiden.
a.x: Rasha should have been offered a method without estrogen, such as a coil or progestogen-only pill.
a.w: Estrogen with factor V Leiden greatly raises the risk of clots.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked about migraine.
a.w: Migraine with aura also rules out the combined pill.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud checked her BMI.
a.w: A high BMI raises clot risk.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked about Rasha's mother's clot.
a.x: Her mother's clot was off topic.
a.w: A clot in a close relative raises her own risk.

t: Wilson disease missed in a young man
s:
Mr. Adel, 19, came with a shaky hand and trouble writing. His liver tests were raised for a year. His mood had changed and he had dropped out of university. His brother died of liver failure at 16.

Dr. Mervat examined him and found a tremor in both hands and slurred speech. She asked about drugs and alcohol, and he took none.

She checked his hepatitis tests, which were negative, and arranged a liver ultrasound.

His parents are cousins. He had been a top student but his grades had fallen, and he had become irritable at home. His mother said he dropped cups and his writing had become messy. His blood count showed mild anemia, and his urine had protein in it.

She said the tremor was "anxiety" and prescribed propranolol. She did not check caeruloplasmin or look at his eyes for copper rings.
h: She said the tremor was "anxiety" and prescribed propranolol

a.o: Dr. Mervat called Mr. Adel's tremor anxiety without testing for Wilson disease.
a.x: Mr. Adel should have had a caeruloplasmin test, a 24-hour urine copper test and an eye check for copper rings.
a.w: A young man with liver disease, tremor, mood change and a brother who died of liver failure points to Wilson disease.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about drugs and alcohol.
a.w: Drugs and alcohol can cause tremor and liver disease.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked his hepatitis tests.
a.w: Viral hepatitis is a common cause of raised liver tests.

a.o: Dr. Mervat noted that Mr. Adel's parents were cousins.
a.w: Recessive conditions like Wilson disease are more common when parents are related.

t: Polyposis teenager left until fifty
s:
Ziad, 13, came to clinic with his mother. His father had bowel cancer at 36 and was found to have familial adenomatous polyposis, a gene change that causes hundreds of polyps in the bowel. Ziad has no symptoms and plays football for his school.

Dr. Tamer explained the condition carefully, using a drawing of the bowel, and checked that Ziad understood. He asked Ziad whether he wanted to be tested, and Ziad said yes after talking with his mother.

The blood test showed Ziad carries the same APC gene change. Dr. Tamer told them about the genetics nurse and gave them a support group number. Ziad's mother asked about his younger sister, aged 9, and he offered testing for her when the family was ready.

Ziad asked whether he would get cancer like his father. Dr. Tamer said the risk was high but could be managed with regular checks.

He booked Ziad's first colonoscopy for when he turns 50, "like the national screening program".
h: He booked Ziad's first colonoscopy for when he turns 50

a.o: Dr. Tamer left Ziad's first bowel check until age 50.
a.x: Ziad should have started colonoscopy every one to two years from about age 12 to 14, with surgery planned when polyps grow.
a.w: In FAP, polyps start in the teens and cancer is almost certain by 40 without surgery.

a.o: Dr. Tamer tested Ziad at 13.
a.x: Children should never have genetic tests.
a.w: FAP testing is offered in childhood because checks start in the early teens.

a.o: Dr. Tamer asked Ziad himself if he wanted the test.
a.x: Only his mother needed to agree.
a.w: Involving the child in the decision is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Tamer offered testing for Ziad's sister when the family was ready.
a.x: His sister was not at risk.
a.w: Each child of a parent with FAP has a 1 in 2 chance.

t: Neurofibromatosis child without eye checks
s:
Hana, 4, has many coffee-colored patches on her skin and freckles in her armpits. Her father has neurofibromatosis type 1, with soft lumps on his skin. Hana was diagnosed with NF1 last year and is otherwise well. She is learning her letters at nursery.

Dr. Nada measured her head, height and blood pressure, which were normal, and plotted them on her growth chart. She examined her spine for any curve, and it was straight.

She asked about Hana's learning and behavior, as children with NF1 can have learning problems, and asked the nursery for a report.

Her father asked whether she would get lumps like his. Dr. Nada said they usually appear in the teenage years and are mostly harmless.

She booked a review in two years and said Hana did not need eye checks "because she can see well".
h: said Hana did not need eye checks "because she can see well"

a.o: Dr. Nada skipped yearly eye checks for Hana.
a.x: Hana should have had a yearly eye exam by an eye doctor until at least age 8.
a.w: Children with NF1 can grow a tumor on the optic nerve, which often shows no signs until vision is damaged.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Hana's blood pressure.
a.x: Blood pressure is not checked in small children.
a.w: NF1 can cause high blood pressure from narrowed kidney arteries.

a.o: Dr. Nada examined Hana's spine.
a.w: Scoliosis is common in NF1.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked the nursery about Hana's learning.
a.x: School reports are not a doctor's job.
a.w: Learning difficulties are common in NF1 and help comes early.

t: High INR with warfarin carried on
s:
Mr. Fikry, 74, takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. His routine INR came back at 8.4; his target is 2 to 3. He had started a course of clarithromycin for a chest infection five days ago. He had no bleeding, no black stools and no blood in his urine.

Dr. Ghada phoned him to ask about bruising and nosebleeds, and he had none. She asked whether he had fallen recently or hit his head, and he had not.

She stopped the clarithromycin, as his chest was better, and noted to avoid it with warfarin in future. She told him to watch for bleeding and gave him the number of the anticoagulation clinic.

He asked whether he should stop his evening walk because of the bruising risk. She said walking was good for him and he should carry on, taking care on uneven ground.

She told him to carry on with his usual warfarin dose and to recheck his INR in two weeks.
h: She told him to carry on with his usual warfarin dose and to recheck his INR in two weeks

a.o: Dr. Ghada left Mr. Fikry on the same warfarin dose with an INR of 8.4.
a.x: Mr. Fikry should have stopped warfarin, had a small dose of oral vitamin K, and had his INR rechecked the next day.
a.w: An INR above 8 carries a high bleeding risk, even without bleeding. Oral vitamin K brings it down safely.

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped Mr. Fikry's clarithromycin.
a.x: The antibiotic course should have been finished.
a.w: Clarithromycin raises the INR, and his chest had already improved.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Fikry about falls and head injury.
a.w: A head injury with a high INR could cause a hidden brain bleed.

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mr. Fikry to keep up his evening walks.
a.x: He should have stayed at home until his INR settled.
a.w: Staying active is good, and he had no bleeding.

t: Warfarin bleed treated with vitamin K alone
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 79, takes warfarin for a metal heart valve. She fell at home and came in drowsy, with a headache and vomiting. Her CT scan showed a bleed inside the skull. Her INR was 3.8 and her blood pressure 172/96.

Dr. Hamed stopped her warfarin and gave 10 mg of IV vitamin K. He called the neurosurgeons, who agreed to see her, and asked for her to be nursed with her head raised.

He brought her blood pressure down carefully with an IV drip, aiming for a top number of about 140. He checked her blood sugar and her platelets, which were normal.

Her son was worried about her metal valve and asked whether stopping the warfarin was safe. Dr. Hamed explained that the bleed was the bigger danger for now.

He said the vitamin K would "bring the INR down by morning", and did not give any other clotting treatment.
h: He said the vitamin K would "bring the INR down by morning", and did not give any other clotting treatment

a.o: Dr. Hamed relied on vitamin K alone for Mrs. Nawal's brain bleed on warfarin.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should also have had prothrombin complex concentrate at once to reverse the warfarin within minutes.
a.w: IV vitamin K takes hours to work. In a brain bleed, every minute of bleeding matters.

a.o: Dr. Hamed stopped warfarin despite Mrs. Nawal's metal valve.
a.x: A metal valve means warfarin must never stop.
a.w: In a life-threatening bleed, the bleed comes first; the valve risk over a few days is lower.

a.o: Dr. Hamed lowered Mrs. Nawal's blood pressure.
a.w: Careful lowering helps stop the bleed growing.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked Mrs. Nawal's platelets.
a.w: Low platelets would add to the bleeding.

t: Sickle cell crisis given pethidine
s:
Omar, 19, has sickle cell disease. He came in with severe pain in his back and legs, which started after a cold swim. He rated it 9 out of 10. His temperature was 37.6°C and his oxygen 97% on air. His chest was clear.

Dr. Dina saw him within 20 minutes. She checked his blood count, which showed his usual hemoglobin of 8.4, and his reticulocytes, which were high. She asked how much pain relief he usually needed in a crisis.

She started IV fluids, kept him warm and asked the nurses to check his pain, breathing and oxygen every half hour. She gave him a breathing exerciser to use every hour.

He asked to be treated quickly because he knew this pain. She believed him and did not make him wait for blood results.

For the pain she gave him pethidine 100 mg by injection every three hours, writing "he asked for something strong".
h: For the pain she gave him pethidine 100 mg by injection every three hours

a.o: Dr. Dina used pethidine for Omar's sickle crisis.
a.x: Omar should have had morphine or another strong opioid, often through a pump he controls, with regular paracetamol and laxatives.
a.w: Pethidine builds up a toxic product that can cause fits, and is avoided in sickle cell pain.

a.o: Dr. Dina gave Omar a breathing exerciser.
a.x: That was unnecessary with a clear chest.
a.w: Deep breathing helps prevent acute chest syndrome in a crisis.

a.o: Dr. Dina gave pain relief before the blood results.
a.x: She should have waited for the results.
a.w: Pain relief in a crisis should come within 30 minutes.

a.o: Dr. Dina kept Omar warm.
a.w: Cold triggers crises; keeping warm helps.

t: Acute chest syndrome missed in sickle cell
s:
Laila, 16, has sickle cell disease and was admitted two days ago with pain in her ribs and back. Today she had a new cough, a temperature of 38.4°C and fast breathing. Her oxygen had fallen from 98% to 91% on air. She had crackles at the right base.

Dr. Fouad checked her blood count, which showed her hemoglobin had dropped from 8 to 6.6. He sent blood cultures and asked for her to be weighed and her fluids charted.

He increased her pain relief, as her rib pain was making it hard to breathe deeply, and asked the physiotherapist to help with breathing exercises.

Her mother was worried and asked whether her daughter had a chest infection. He said it was likely, and that it was common.

He started oral amoxicillin, gave her oxygen by mask, and did not order a chest X-ray or call the hematology team, writing "probable mild chest infection".
h: did not order a chest X-ray or call the hematology team

a.o: Dr. Fouad treated Laila's new chest signs as a mild infection.
a.x: Laila should have had a chest X-ray, IV antibiotics including one for atypical germs, and urgent hematology review for a blood transfusion.
a.w: Fever, low oxygen and a new chest finding in sickle cell disease mean acute chest syndrome, the most common cause of death.

a.o: Dr. Fouad increased Laila's pain relief.
a.x: Strong painkillers slow breathing and should be cut.
a.w: Rib pain stops deep breathing, so good pain relief helps the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked for Laila's fluids to be charted.
a.w: Too much or too little fluid can worsen sickle cell chest problems.

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent blood cultures.
a.w: Infection is a common trigger.

t: B12 deficiency treated with folic acid
s:
Mrs. Samia, 66, came in with tiredness and tingling in both feet for three months. She had become a little unsteady when walking in the dark. Her blood count showed large red cells and a hemoglobin of 9.8. Her B12 was very low and her folate low.

Dr. Ihab asked about her diet, which was normal, and about stomach operations, which she had never had. He sent a test for antibodies to intrinsic factor, which came back positive.

He explained that she had pernicious anemia, where the body cannot absorb B12 from food. She asked whether she needed to stop eating meat, and he said no.

He checked her thyroid, which was normal, as the two conditions often go together.

He started folic acid tablets and planned to start B12 injections "once her folate is back up".
h: He started folic acid tablets and planned to start B12 injections "once her folate is back up"

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mrs. Samia folic acid before her B12.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have started B12 injections at once, with folic acid added after or alongside.
a.w: Folic acid alone can make the B12 nerve damage worse and lead to permanent damage to the spinal cord.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Samia's thyroid.
a.w: Autoimmune thyroid disease often comes with pernicious anemia.

a.o: Dr. Ihab tested for intrinsic factor antibodies.
a.w: It confirms pernicious anemia and means lifelong injections.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mrs. Samia she could keep eating meat.
a.w: Her problem is absorbing B12, not her diet.

t: Blood given without bedside checks
s:
Mr. Raouf, 71, was in hospital after a hip operation. His hemoglobin was 6.9, and he felt dizzy and short of breath. Dr. Hala decided he needed one unit of blood, explained why, and he agreed.

She checked that his group and save sample was valid and prescribed one unit to run over three hours. She checked his kidney function and noted he had a weak heart, so she added a small dose of furosemide.

She asked the nurses to check his temperature, pulse and blood pressure before the blood, after 15 minutes and at the end.

The ward was very busy. The blood arrived while Mr. Raouf was asleep in a bay with another patient of the same surname.

To avoid waking him, Dr. Hala hung the unit after checking the bag against the notes at the desk, without checking his wristband at the bedside.
h: without checking his wristband at the bedside

a.o: Dr. Hala hung blood without checking Mr. Raouf's wristband at the bedside.
a.x: The bag should have been checked against Mr. Raouf's wristband, name, date of birth and hospital number at the bedside, with the patient awake if possible.
a.w: Most wrong-blood errors happen at the bedside. With two patients of the same surname, the risk was even higher.

a.o: Dr. Hala gave Mr. Raouf furosemide with the blood.
a.w: In a weak heart, a diuretic can help prevent fluid overload.

a.o: Dr. Hala ran the unit over three hours.
a.x: Blood should be given in 30 minutes.
a.w: A slower rate is safer for a weak heart.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked for observations at 15 minutes.
a.x: Checks at the end were enough.
a.w: Serious reactions often start in the first 15 minutes.

t: Transfusion reaction treated by slowing the blood
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 58, was having a unit of blood for anemia after chemotherapy. Twenty minutes in, she said her back hurt and felt hot and anxious. Her temperature was 39°C, her pulse 124 and her blood pressure had fallen from 128/76 to 88/50. Her urine in the catheter bag looked dark.

Dr. Ayman came at once. He checked her airway and breathing, which were fine, and listened to her chest, which was clear.

He gave paracetamol for the fever and started IV fluids. He asked the nurse to keep a close watch and to call him if she got worse.

Her husband was frightened and asked if she was allergic to the blood. Dr. Ayman said reactions do happen and that she was in good hands.

He slowed the transfusion to half the rate and let the unit finish, saying "she really needs the blood".
h: He slowed the transfusion to half the rate and let the unit finish

a.o: Dr. Ayman let Mrs. Nadia's blood keep running during a serious reaction.
a.x: The transfusion should have been stopped at once, the bag and patient identity checked, and the lab and blood bank told.
a.w: Fever, back pain, low blood pressure and dark urine suggest an acute hemolytic reaction, often from the wrong blood. Every extra drop makes it worse.

a.o: Dr. Ayman started IV fluids.
a.w: Fluids support blood pressure and protect the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Ayman listened to Mrs. Nadia's chest.
a.w: Fluid overload and lung injury can also follow a transfusion.

a.o: Dr. Ayman came to see Mrs. Nadia at once.
a.w: A sick patient with a reaction needs a doctor at the bedside.

t: Neutropenic sepsis waiting for counts
s:
Mr. Medhat, 52, had chemotherapy for lymphoma eight days ago. He came in with a temperature of 38.6°C and shivering. His pulse was 112 and his blood pressure 104/66. He had no cough, and his urine was clear. He has a central line in his chest.

Dr. Rasha took blood cultures from his line and from his arm, and sent his blood count and kidney tests. She started IV fluids and asked the nurses to keep him in a side room.

She checked his line site, which looked clean, and asked about mouth ulcers and diarrhea, which he did not have.

His wife said the chemotherapy nurses had told them to come straight in with any fever. She was glad they had.

She decided to wait for his blood count before starting antibiotics, writing "may not be neutropenic". The count came back two hours later.
h: She decided to wait for his blood count before starting antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Rasha held back antibiotics from Mr. Medhat until his blood count came back.
a.x: Mr. Medhat should have had IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as piperacillin-tazobactam, within an hour of arriving.
a.w: A fever after chemotherapy is treated as neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise. Delays raise the risk of death.

a.o: Dr. Rasha took cultures from both the line and the arm.
a.w: Comparing both helps tell if the line is infected.

a.o: Dr. Rasha kept Mr. Medhat in a side room.
a.w: Protecting a patient who may have low white cells is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked about mouth ulcers and diarrhea.
a.w: They are common sources of infection after chemotherapy.

t: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia missed
s:
Mr. Kamal, 64, had a heart bypass operation eight days ago and is on heparin injections to prevent clots. His platelets were 280 before surgery, 230 on day 3 and are now 96. Today his left calf is swollen and tender, and an ultrasound shows a clot.

Dr. Mervat checked that the blood count sample was not clotted, and repeated it, which showed the same result. She looked at his drug chart for other causes of low platelets.

She asked about bleeding, and he had none. She stopped his aspirin for a day while she sorted out the clot.

His daughter asked if the clot came from lying in bed. Dr. Mervat said that was likely.

She increased his heparin to a full treatment dose for the clot, and asked for a platelet transfusion to bring his platelets up.
h: She increased his heparin to a full treatment dose for the clot, and asked for a platelet transfusion

a.o: Dr. Mervat increased heparin and gave platelets to Mr. Kamal with a falling count and a new clot.
a.x: Mr. Kamal should have had all heparin stopped, an HIT antibody test, and a non-heparin blood thinner such as argatroban or fondaparinux, without platelet transfusion.
a.w: A 50% fall in platelets 5 to 10 days after heparin, with a new clot, points to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. More heparin or platelets can cause more clots.

a.o: Dr. Mervat repeated the blood count.
a.w: A clotted sample can give a falsely low count.

a.o: Dr. Mervat looked at his drug chart.
a.w: Many drugs can lower platelets.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about bleeding.
a.w: Low platelets can cause bleeding.

t: Warfarin for a clot in pregnancy
s:
Mrs. Heba, 31, is 10 weeks pregnant. She came in with a swollen, painful left leg for three days. An ultrasound showed a clot in the vein behind her knee. She had no chest pain or breathlessness, and her oxygen was normal.

Dr. Sherine checked her blood count, kidney and liver tests, and her weight to work out the dose. She asked about any family history of clots, which there was none.

She explained that clots are more common in pregnancy and gave her compression advice and a leaflet. She asked the obstetric team to see her the next day.

Mrs. Heba asked whether the treatment would hurt the baby. Dr. Sherine said she would choose the safest one.

She started warfarin, aiming for an INR of 2 to 3, and booked her into the anticoagulation clinic.
h: She started warfarin, aiming for an INR of 2 to 3

a.o: Dr. Sherine started warfarin for Mrs. Heba's clot in early pregnancy.
a.x: Mrs. Heba should have had low molecular weight heparin injections for the rest of the pregnancy and at least six weeks after birth.
a.w: Warfarin crosses the placenta and can cause birth defects, especially between 6 and 12 weeks, and bleeding in the baby.

a.o: Dr. Sherine weighed Mrs. Heba.
a.w: Heparin doses are worked out by weight.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked about family clots.
a.w: A family history can point to an inherited clotting problem.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked the obstetric team to see her.
a.w: The pregnancy and delivery need to be planned around her treatment.

t: ITP treated before a blood film
s:
Yara, 6, came in with bruises on her legs and tiny red spots on her chest that appeared over two days. She had a cold two weeks ago. She was otherwise well, with no bone pain, fever or tiredness. Her liver, spleen and glands were not enlarged.

Her platelets were 12, but her hemoglobin and white cells were normal. Dr. Rana asked about nosebleeds and blood in the urine, which she had not had.

She explained that the most likely cause was ITP, where the body attacks its own platelets after a virus, and that most children get better by themselves.

She told Yara's parents to avoid contact sports and ibuprofen for now, and gave them a card with the ward's number.

To bring the platelets up quickly, she started prednisolone that evening before a blood film was looked at.
h: she started prednisolone that evening before a blood film was looked at

a.o: Dr. Rana started steroids for Yara before her blood film was checked.
a.x: Yara's blood film should have been looked at by a hematologist first. Most children with ITP and no bleeding just need watching.
a.w: Steroids can hide leukemia, which can look like ITP, and delay the right diagnosis.

a.o: Dr. Rana told Yara to avoid ibuprofen.
a.w: NSAIDs affect platelets and raise bleeding risk.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Yara's spleen and glands.
a.w: Big glands or spleen point to leukemia, not ITP.

a.o: Dr. Rana told the parents most children get better by themselves.
a.w: Most childhood ITP settles within months.

t: TTP given platelets
s:
