Mrs. Asmaa, 36, came in with confusion, a headache and purple spots on her legs. Her platelets were 14 and her hemoglobin 8.1, with broken red cells on the blood film. Her LDH was very high and her creatinine was mildly raised. She had a low fever.

Dr. Ahmed recognized the signs of TTP. He sent an ADAMTS13 test and called the hematologist, who agreed to start plasma exchange within hours.

He asked for a CT head because of her confusion, which was normal. He started steroids.

Her husband asked whether it was leukemia. Dr. Ahmed explained it was a different blood condition that could be treated.

While waiting for the line for plasma exchange, he gave her two units of platelets "to make the line safer".
h: he gave her two units of platelets "to make the line safer"

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave platelets to Mrs. Asmaa with TTP.
a.x: Platelet transfusion should be avoided unless she had life-threatening bleeding.
a.w: In TTP, platelets feed the clots that block small vessels in the brain and heart.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed started steroids.
a.w: Steroids are part of standard treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed asked for a CT head.
a.w: Confusion can mean a bleed or stroke.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed called the hematologist at once.
a.x: The hematologist could see her in the morning.
a.w: TTP is an emergency, and plasma exchange is urgent.

t: Hemophilia boy sent home after a head bump
s:
Adam, 8, has severe hemophilia A. He hit his head on a door frame at home two hours ago. He cried but did not pass out. He now had a small bump on his forehead and was playing with his tablet. He had no vomiting or headache.

Dr. Hamed examined him and found no other injuries. His neurological examination was normal, and he was alert and chatty.

He asked his mother about his usual factor VIII and when he last had it; it was three days ago. She had his treatment card with her.

He explained the signs of a brain bleed to his mother: vomiting, headache, drowsiness or a fit.

He sent Adam home with a head injury leaflet, without giving any factor VIII or arranging a scan, because "he looks well".
h: He sent Adam home with a head injury leaflet, without giving any factor VIII or arranging a scan

a.o: Dr. Hamed sent Adam home after a head injury without factor VIII.
a.x: Adam should have had factor VIII at once, before any scan, a CT scan of the head and a hemophilia team review.
a.w: In severe hemophilia, even a small bump can cause a brain bleed that shows up hours later.

a.o: Dr. Hamed explained the signs of a brain bleed.
a.x: That was frightening for the mother.
a.w: Parents need to know warning signs.

a.o: Dr. Hamed asked when Adam last had factor VIII.
a.x: The last dose was off topic.
a.w: The time since the last dose shows his level of protection.

a.o: Dr. Hamed looked at Adam's treatment card.
a.w: The card gives his dose and plan.

t: Polycythemia left without venesection
s:
Mr. Samy, 58, came in with headaches, itching after hot showers and a red face. His hemoglobin was 196 and his hematocrit 0.58. He has a JAK2 gene change. He does not smoke and his oxygen is normal.

Dr. Nermine examined him and found a big spleen. She asked about clots and he had none. She checked his blood pressure, which was 152/90, and started treatment for it.

She started low-dose aspirin and told him to drink plenty of water. She advised him to stay active and to report any chest pain or leg swelling.

His wife asked if it was cancer. Dr. Nermine explained it was a slow blood condition that could be managed.

She did not arrange venesection, writing "aspirin will thin the blood".
h: She did not arrange venesection, writing "aspirin will thin the blood"

a.o: Dr. Nermine relied on aspirin alone for Mr. Samy's polycythemia.
a.x: Mr. Samy should have had regular venesection to bring his hematocrit below 0.45, as well as aspirin.
a.w: A high hematocrit raises the risk of stroke and heart attack. Aspirin does not lower the red cell count.

a.o: Dr. Nermine treated Mr. Samy's blood pressure.
a.w: High blood pressure adds to clot risk.

a.o: Dr. Nermine asked about clots.
a.w: Polycythemia causes clots.

a.o: Dr. Nermine told Mr. Samy to drink water.
a.w: Dehydration thickens the blood more.

t: Splenectomy without vaccines
s:
Mr. Karim, 28, had his spleen removed after a car crash two days ago. He was recovering well, eating and walking. His blood count showed high platelets, which can happen after the spleen is taken out.

Dr. Abeer checked his wound and his pain, and stopped his drip. She asked the physiotherapist to help him walk more.

She gave him blood-thinning injections while he was in hospital. She talked to him about returning to work and avoiding heavy lifting for six weeks.

He asked whether he would miss his spleen. She said he could live a normal life without it.

She sent him home without vaccines or antibiotics, telling him "the spleen isn't vital".
h: She sent him home without vaccines or antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mr. Karim home with no vaccines or antibiotics after his splenectomy.
a.x: Mr. Karim should have had pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib and flu vaccines, daily antibiotics and an alert card.
a.w: Without a spleen, infections can be overwhelming and fatal within hours.

a.o: Dr. Abeer gave blood-thinning injections.
a.w: They prevent clots, especially with high platelets.

a.o: Dr. Abeer advised against heavy lifting.
a.w: Heavy lifting can strain a healing wound.

a.o: Dr. Abeer said he could live normally.
a.w: People live normal lives without a spleen with proper protection.

t: Thalassemia trait given iron
s:
Mrs. Rana, 26, came for a check before planning a pregnancy. Her hemoglobin was 112, with very small red cells. Her ferritin was normal. She was not tired and had no heavy periods. Her family is from Cyprus.

Dr. Mahmoud asked about her diet and periods. He checked her folate and started folic acid for the planned pregnancy.

He asked about her husband's health and family. She said they are not related.

She asked whether she could have another test to know more. He said the blood count was enough.

She works as a nursery teacher and eats meat most days. She had been told at school that she was 'a bit anemic' and had taken iron on and off since then without any change in her blood count. Her husband's family is also from the Mediterranean.

He told her she had iron deficiency and started iron tablets for three months, without ordering a hemoglobin electrophoresis.
h: He told her she had iron deficiency and started iron tablets for three months

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud gave iron to Mrs. Rana with small red cells and normal ferritin.
a.x: Mrs. Rana should have had a hemoglobin electrophoresis to look for thalassemia trait, and her husband tested too.
a.w: Small red cells with normal iron points to thalassemia trait. Iron won't help and can build up; if both partners carry it, the baby could have thalassemia major.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud started folic acid.
a.w: Folic acid before pregnancy prevents spine defects.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked about her husband.
a.w: Both partners matter for inherited blood disorders.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked about her periods.
a.w: Heavy periods are a common cause of low iron.

t: Tumor lysis not prevented
s:
Mr. Ali, 23, was diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma, a fast-growing cancer. He has a large mass in his belly. His white count was 42, his uric acid high and his potassium at the top of normal. His kidney function was slightly raised.

Dr. Rehab explained the treatment and checked his heart and lungs. She asked for a heart tracing, which was normal, and a line for chemotherapy.

She asked about fertility and offered sperm banking before treatment, and he agreed.

He asked if the chemotherapy would make him lose his hair. She said yes, but it would grow back.

She started chemotherapy that evening with normal fluids, without extra IV fluids, allopurinol or rasburicase.
h: She started chemotherapy that evening with normal fluids, without extra IV fluids, allopurinol or rasburicase

a.o: Dr. Rehab started chemotherapy for Mr. Ali without preventing tumor lysis.
a.x: Mr. Ali should have had high-rate IV fluids and rasburicase before chemotherapy, with salts checked every few hours.
a.w: A fast-growing tumor that breaks down quickly floods the blood with potassium, phosphate and uric acid, which can cause kidney failure and heart arrest.

a.o: Dr. Rehab offered sperm banking.
a.w: Chemotherapy can cause infertility.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked for a heart tracing.
a.w: A tracing shows the effect of high potassium.

a.o: Dr. Rehab told him his hair would grow back.
a.w: Hair loss from chemotherapy is usually temporary.

t: Massive bleed given only red cells
s:
Mr. Sabri, 34, was brought in after a motorbike crash. He had a broken pelvis and was bleeding heavily. His blood pressure was 78/40 and his pulse 140. The team activated the major hemorrhage protocol.

Dr. Inas gave tranexamic acid within an hour of the injury, and the team put a pelvic binder on. She kept him warm with blankets and a warming device for the fluids.

She called the surgeons and the radiologists, who prepared to stop the bleeding.

Mr. Sabri's brother arrived and asked if he would live. She said the team was doing everything possible.

Over an hour she gave him eight units of red cells and no plasma, platelets or cryoprecipitate, saying "the red cells are what he needs".
h: Over an hour she gave him eight units of red cells and no plasma, platelets or cryoprecipitate

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Sabri only red cells in a massive bleed.
a.x: Mr. Sabri should have had plasma and platelets with the red cells, close to a 1 to 1 ratio, and cryoprecipitate if his fibrinogen fell.
a.w: Red cells alone dilute the clotting factors and cause more bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave tranexamic acid.
a.w: Tranexamic acid within three hours reduces death in bleeding trauma.

a.o: Dr. Inas kept Mr. Sabri warm.
a.w: Cold makes clotting worse.

a.o: Dr. Inas used a pelvic binder.
a.w: A binder reduces bleeding from a broken pelvis.

t: Apixaban for a metal valve
s:
Mr. Amr, 56, had a metal aortic valve put in last year. He takes warfarin, but he finds the INR checks tiring and his INR swings a lot. He came to ask about changing.

Dr. Hala checked his kidney function, which was normal, and his weight. She asked about bleeding, and he had none.

She looked at his INR record, which showed many low and high values. She asked about his diet and alcohol, which were steady.

He asked whether he could use a home INR machine instead. She said that was possible but she had a better plan.

She stopped his warfarin and switched him to apixaban 5 mg twice a day, saying "no more blood tests".
h: She stopped his warfarin and switched him to apixaban 5 mg twice a day

a.o: Dr. Hala switched Mr. Amr from warfarin to apixaban with a metal valve.
a.x: Mr. Amr should have stayed on warfarin, with a home INR machine or more support to keep his INR steady.
a.w: Newer blood thinners do not prevent clots on metal valves and can lead to valve clots and strokes.

a.o: Dr. Hala looked at Mr. Amr's INR record.
a.w: The record shows how stable his treatment is.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked his kidney function.
a.w: Kidney function guides blood thinner choice.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked about his diet.
a.w: Changes in vitamin K in food change the INR.

t: Myeloma back pain with weak legs
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 68, has multiple myeloma. She came in with back pain for two weeks that was worse at night. Today her legs felt weak and she had trouble passing urine. Her calcium was high.

Dr. Fady examined her and found weakness in both legs and reduced feeling below her belly button. Her back was tender in the middle.

He gave her IV fluids for the high calcium and pain relief. He asked for a bladder scan, which showed she was holding urine, and put in a catheter.

Her daughter asked whether the myeloma had spread. He said it was possible.

He booked an MRI of her spine for the next week and did not give any steroids.
h: He booked an MRI of her spine for the next week and did not give any steroids

a.o: Dr. Fady delayed an MRI and steroids for Mrs. Fawzia with spinal cord compression.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have had high-dose dexamethasone at once and an MRI of the whole spine within 24 hours.
a.w: Back pain with weak legs and trouble passing urine in cancer means spinal cord compression. Delay can cause permanent paralysis.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave IV fluids for the calcium.
a.w: Fluids are the first treatment for high calcium.

a.o: Dr. Fady put in a catheter.
a.w: She was holding urine.

a.o: Dr. Fady examined her legs.
a.w: Weak legs and reduced feeling show where the cord is pressed.

t: Swollen neck gland given more antibiotics
s:
Mr. Tamer, 29, came in with a lump in his neck for six weeks. It was painless and slowly growing. He had night sweats and had lost 4 kg. He had already had two courses of antibiotics, which did not help.

Dr. Rasha felt a firm, rubbery 3 cm lump on the right side of his neck. She found another smaller lump above his collarbone. His throat and teeth looked healthy.

She asked about recent infections, travel, cats and TB contacts, and he had none. She asked about itching, which he had noticed after hot showers.

He asked whether it could be a bad tooth. She said no.

He works as a delivery driver and said he had been more tired than usual, needing to nap after work. He drinks a little at weekends and noticed that the lump ached after a beer. He had no sore throat or dental pain.

She gave him a third course of antibiotics and booked a review in a month.
h: She gave him a third course of antibiotics and booked a review in a month

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave Mr. Tamer more antibiotics instead of referring him.
a.x: Mr. Tamer should have been referred urgently for a blood test, a scan and a biopsy of the lump.
a.w: A painless, growing neck lump for more than six weeks, with night sweats and weight loss, can be lymphoma.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked about cats.
a.w: Cat scratch disease can cause swollen glands.

a.o: Dr. Rasha examined Mr. Tamer's throat and teeth.
a.w: Infections in the mouth can cause swollen glands.

a.o: Dr. Rasha felt above Mr. Tamer's collarbone.
a.w: A lump above the collarbone is a warning sign.

t: DVT treatment stopped after two weeks
s:
Mr. Hesham, 45, had a clot in his calf vein after a long flight. He was started on rivaroxaban three weeks ago. He has no other illness and his leg swelling has gone.

Dr. Ihab checked his kidney function, which was normal. He asked about bleeding, which he had not had, and about leg pain, which was better.

He advised him to walk regularly and wear compression stockings if they helped with comfort.

Mr. Hesham said he had another long flight in a month. He asked if he should take an aspirin.

He works as a sales manager and flies often for work. He had no injury, surgery or illness before the flight. His father had a clot in his fifties. He was taking the tablets every day and said he found them easy to remember.

He told him to stop the rivaroxaban, as "the leg is better now".
h: He told him to stop the rivaroxaban, as "the leg is better now"

a.o: Dr. Ihab stopped Mr. Hesham's rivaroxaban after three weeks.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have continued for at least three months.
a.w: Stopping blood thinners early after a clot raises the risk of another clot.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked his kidney function.
a.w: Rivaroxaban is cleared by the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised walking.
a.w: Walking helps recovery after a clot.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about bleeding.
a.w: Bleeding is the main side effect of blood thinners.

t: B12 injections stopped when levels normal
s:
Mrs. Nabila, 72, has pernicious anemia and has had B12 injections every three months for two years. She came for a check. Her blood count and B12 level are now normal and she feels well.

Dr. Ghada checked her thyroid, which was normal, and her feet for feeling, which were fine.

She asked about her mood and memory, which were good. She talked to her about her diet.

Mrs. Nabila said she hated the injections. She asked if she could take tablets instead.

She lives with her husband and walks to the market every morning. Before her diagnosis she had felt pins and needles in her feet and was very tired. She also takes levothyroxine for an underactive thyroid. She said the practice nurse was always kind but the injection left a bruise.

Dr. Ghada stopped the injections, saying "your level is normal now, so you're cured".
h: Dr. Ghada stopped the injections, saying "your level is normal now, so you're cured"

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped Mrs. Nabila's B12 injections.
a.x: Mrs. Nabila should have continued B12 injections every three months for life.
a.w: Pernicious anemia never goes away. The level is normal only because of the injections.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Nabila's feet.
a.w: B12 deficiency can damage nerves in the feet.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked her thyroid.
a.w: Thyroid disease often comes with pernicious anemia.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about memory.
a.w: B12 deficiency can affect memory.

t: Sickle cell child taken off penicillin
s:
Malik, 3, has sickle cell disease and takes penicillin twice a day. His mother brought him for his yearly review. He had been well, with no crises this year and no hospital stays. He is growing well and loves his tricycle.

Dr. Rana checked his spleen, which she could not feel, and his blood count, which showed his usual hemoglobin of 8.2. She arranged his yearly brain artery scan (a transcranial Doppler), which was normal.

She checked that his vaccines were up to date, including the extra pneumococcal one, and advised his mother to give him plenty to drink and keep him warm in winter.

His mother said he hated the taste of the penicillin, spat it out and cried every time. His grandmother thought he no longer needed it because he was so well.

Dr. Rana agreed to stop the penicillin, writing "well, vaccinated, no infections", and booked a review in a year.
h: Dr. Rana agreed to stop the penicillin

a.o: Dr. Rana stopped Malik's daily penicillin at age 3.
a.x: Malik should have kept taking penicillin at least until age 5, and usually for life, perhaps with a different flavor or tablet form.
a.w: Children with sickle cell disease have a spleen that does not work, so infections like pneumococcus can kill within hours. Vaccines alone are not enough.

a.o: Dr. Rana arranged a brain artery scan for Malik.
a.x: The scan was unnecessary with no symptoms.
a.w: A yearly Doppler finds children at high risk of stroke before it happens.

a.o: Dr. Rana told Malik's mother to keep him warm.
a.x: Warmth doesn't matter in sickle cell.
a.w: Cold can trigger a sickle crisis.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked that Malik had the extra pneumococcal vaccine.
a.w: Children with sickle cell need extra protection against pneumococcus.

t: Transfused thalassemia without chelation
s:
Youssef, 12, has beta thalassemia major. He has had a blood transfusion every four weeks since he was a baby. His hemoglobin before each transfusion is kept around 95. His ferritin has risen to 3,200 over the last year.

Dr. Nermine checked his growth, which was a little slow, and his puberty, which had not started. She asked the hormone team to see him and checked his thyroid and sugar.

She asked for a heart scan and a special MRI to measure iron in his heart and liver, and checked his hepatitis and HIV tests, which were negative.

His father said Youssef used to take a chelation medicine but stopped it a year ago because it upset his stomach. Youssef said he did not want any more tablets.

Dr. Nermine agreed to leave the chelation for now "so he can enjoy being a child", and continued his monthly transfusions.
h: Dr. Nermine agreed to leave the chelation for now

a.o: Dr. Nermine left Youssef without iron chelation.
a.x: Youssef should have restarted chelation, such as deferasirox in a form he could manage, with support to take it.
a.w: Every transfusion adds iron. A ferritin of 3,200 means iron is building up in his heart, liver and glands, which can cause heart failure and early death.

a.o: Dr. Nermine asked for a heart MRI.
a.w: Iron in the heart is the main cause of death in thalassemia.

a.o: Dr. Nermine checked Youssef's puberty.
a.w: Iron overload damages the glands and delays puberty.

a.o: Dr. Nermine kept Youssef's hemoglobin around 95 before transfusions.
a.x: It should be allowed to fall lower.
a.w: Keeping the hemoglobin above 90 to 100 lets children grow and stops the bone marrow overgrowing.

t: Meningococcal rash sent to hospital without antibiotics
s:
Nour, 17, came to the GP with her mother. She had a fever, a headache and pain in her legs since the morning. Her hands and feet were cold. She now had a few purple spots on her legs that did not fade when pressed with a glass.

Dr. Ghada checked her pulse, which was 128, and her blood pressure, 96/58. Her neck was a little stiff. She asked about allergies, and Nour had none.

She called an ambulance at once and phoned the hospital to warn them. She put Nour on oxygen and asked her mother to stay with her.

The practice had benzylpenicillin in its emergency bag, but the nurse said she had never seen it used. Nour's younger brother was at home, and her mother asked if he was at risk.

Dr. Ghada decided not to give antibiotics, so the hospital could "take blood cultures first", and waited with Nour for the ambulance, which arrived 35 minutes later.
h: decided not to give antibiotics, so the hospital could "take blood cultures first"

a.o: Dr. Ghada held back antibiotics from Nour with a meningococcal rash.
a.x: Nour should have had IV or IM benzylpenicillin at once in the surgery, before the ambulance came.
a.w: Meningococcal sepsis can kill within hours. Giving antibiotics early saves lives, and blood cultures should never delay them.

a.o: Dr. Ghada called an ambulance at once.
a.x: Nour could have driven with her mother.
a.w: A sick, septic teenager needs an emergency ambulance.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about allergies.
a.x: Allergies don't matter in an emergency.
a.w: Checking allergies is quick and avoids harm.

a.o: Dr. Ghada thought about Nour's brother.
a.x: Family members are not at risk.
a.w: Close contacts need preventive antibiotics.

t: Meningitis antibiotics delayed for a scan
s:
Mr. Waleed, 24, came in with a severe headache, fever of 39.2°C and neck stiffness for a day. He was alert and talking normally. His pupils were equal, with no weakness or fits. He had no rash and his blood pressure was normal.

Dr. Hossam took blood cultures straight away and sent bloods. He gave IV fluids and pain relief.

He planned a lumbar puncture, and asked the nurses to dim the lights because Mr. Waleed was sensitive to light.

Mr. Waleed's roommate said they shared a flat with three other students. The CT scanner was busy and had a two-hour wait.

Dr. Hossam decided to wait for a CT scan and lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics, writing "don't want to spoil the LP".
h: Dr. Hossam decided to wait for a CT scan and lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Hossam waited for a scan and LP before giving Mr. Waleed antibiotics.
a.x: Mr. Waleed should have had IV ceftriaxone and dexamethasone at once after blood cultures, with the LP done after.
a.w: Every hour of delay in bacterial meningitis raises the risk of death and brain damage. Blood cultures and PCR can still find the germ.

a.o: Dr. Hossam took blood cultures first.
a.w: Cultures take minutes and help find the germ.

a.o: Dr. Hossam dimmed the lights.
a.w: Light sensitivity is common in meningitis.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked about his flatmates.
a.w: Close contacts may need preventive antibiotics.

t: Malaria in a traveler called flu
s:
Mr. Sherif, 38, came in with fever, chills, headache and aches all over for three days. He had come back from a business trip to Nigeria two weeks ago. He did not take malaria tablets because he "forgot". He had no cough or rash.

Dr. Nada found a temperature of 38.9°C and a pulse of 110. His blood count showed low platelets. His liver tests were mildly raised.

She gave him paracetamol and fluids, and asked if he had been bitten by mosquitoes, which he had. She asked about other travelers, and his colleague was also unwell.

He asked whether he could go back to work the next day because he had a big meeting. She said he needed rest.

She diagnosed flu and sent him home with paracetamol, without a malaria test.
h: She diagnosed flu and sent him home with paracetamol, without a malaria test

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Sherif home as flu without a malaria test.
a.x: Mr. Sherif should have had urgent malaria blood films or a rapid test, repeated if negative.
a.w: Any fever after travel to a malaria area is malaria until proven otherwise. Falciparum malaria can kill within days.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about mosquito bites.
a.w: Bites support the risk of malaria.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about his colleague.
a.w: A sick fellow traveler points to a shared infection.

a.o: Dr. Nada noticed his low platelets.
a.w: Low platelets are common in malaria.

t: Severe malaria given oral tablets
s:
Mrs. Amira, 30, came back from Uganda a week ago. She was admitted with fever, confusion and yellow eyes. Her blood film showed falciparum malaria with 8% of red cells infected. Her creatinine was raised and her sugar low.

Dr. Fouad gave her IV glucose for the low sugar and fluids carefully. He asked for her to be checked every hour.

He asked the intensive care team to see her and called the infectious diseases team for advice.

Her husband asked whether she would recover. He also asked if he should be tested, since he had been with her on the trip.

Dr. Fouad started oral chloroquine tablets, saying "she can swallow", and planned to repeat the blood film the next day.
h: Dr. Fouad started oral chloroquine tablets, saying "she can swallow"

a.o: Dr. Fouad treated Mrs. Amira's severe malaria with oral chloroquine.
a.x: Mrs. Amira should have had IV artesunate at once.
a.w: Confusion, jaundice, kidney injury and over 2% infected cells mean severe malaria. It needs IV treatment, and falciparum is often resistant to chloroquine.

a.o: Dr. Fouad gave IV glucose.
a.w: Low sugar is common and dangerous in severe malaria.

a.o: Dr. Fouad called intensive care.
a.w: Severe malaria can worsen quickly.

a.o: Dr. Fouad thought about testing her husband.
a.w: Her husband shared the same risk on the trip.

t: TB treatment without pill advice
s:
Miss Hana, 24, was diagnosed with lung TB. She had a cough for two months and lost weight. Her sputum showed TB, sensitive to all drugs. She takes the combined pill for contraception. She is not pregnant.

Dr. Rasha started the four standard TB drugs: rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, with vitamin B6. She checked her liver tests and her eyesight first.

She arranged contact tracing for her family and flatmates, and advised her to stay home from work for two weeks.

Miss Hana asked if her urine would change color. Dr. Rasha said it would turn orange.

She did not warn Miss Hana that rifampicin makes the pill not work, and did not suggest other contraception.
h: She did not warn Miss Hana that rifampicin makes the pill not work

a.o: Dr. Rasha didn't warn Miss Hana that rifampicin stops the pill from working.
a.x: Miss Hana should have been told to use a coil or injection for contraception during TB treatment.
a.w: Rifampicin speeds up the breakdown of hormones, so the combined pill can fail and she could get pregnant.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked her eyesight.
a.w: Ethambutol can damage the eyes.

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave vitamin B6.
a.w: Isoniazid can cause nerve damage, which B6 prevents.

a.o: Dr. Rasha told her about orange urine.
a.w: Rifampicin turns body fluids orange; warning prevents worry.

t: Needlestick nurse made to wait for PEP
s:
Nurse Mona, 29, pricked her finger with a used needle while taking blood from a man with known HIV who was not on treatment. She came straight to the emergency department two hours later.

Dr. Hamed washed the wound with soap and water and let it bleed. He asked about her vaccines; she had had hepatitis B vaccines and was immune.

He asked for blood tests from her and, with consent, from the patient. He reported the injury to occupational health.

Nurse Mona was very upset and asked whether she could still breastfeed her baby.

He told her to wait for the patient's viral load result in three days before deciding on HIV medicines.
h: He told her to wait for the patient's viral load result in three days before deciding on HIV medicines

a.o: Dr. Hamed made Nurse Mona wait three days for HIV PEP.
a.x: Nurse Mona should have started HIV post-exposure prevention at once, ideally within hours.
a.w: PEP works best within 72 hours, and its effect falls with every hour. A source with untreated HIV is high risk.

a.o: Dr. Hamed let the wound bleed and washed it.
a.w: Washing and gentle bleeding is the first step; squeezing is not advised.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked her hepatitis B immunity.
a.w: Needlesticks can spread hepatitis B.

a.o: Dr. Hamed reported the injury.
a.w: Needlesticks must be reported.

t: Necrotizing fasciitis sent home as cellulitis
s:
Mr. Ramy, 55, has diabetes. He came in with severe pain in his thigh after a small cut while gardening two days ago. His thigh was red and swollen. His pain was much worse than the redness looked. He had a fever of 38.8°C and a pulse of 118.

Dr. Dina marked the edge of the redness with a pen. She checked his sugar, which was 18, and his blood pressure, which was 102/64.

She found a dark patch and crackling under the skin near the cut. His CRP was very high.

He asked whether he could go home because his wife was alone.

She diagnosed cellulitis and sent him home with oral flucloxacillin, asking him to come back if it spread.
h: She diagnosed cellulitis and sent him home with oral flucloxacillin

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Mr. Ramy home with oral antibiotics for what looked like necrotizing fasciitis.
a.x: Mr. Ramy should have had IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and an emergency surgical review.
a.w: Pain out of proportion, fever, fast pulse, crackling and dark skin point to necrotizing fasciitis, which needs urgent surgery.

a.o: Dr. Dina marked the edge of the redness.
a.w: Marking shows if the infection spreads.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked his sugar.
a.w: Diabetes raises infection risk.

a.o: Dr. Dina felt for crackling.
a.w: Crackling means gas in the tissue, a sign of a deep infection.

t: Co-amoxiclav after penicillin anaphylaxis
s:
Mrs. Samia, 46, came in with a cough, fever and green phlegm for five days. Her chest had crackles on the right side and her oxygen was 96%. Her notes, flagged in red, said she had anaphylaxis to penicillin ten years ago, with a swollen throat and a night in hospital.

Dr. Ihab checked her pulse, breathing rate and blood pressure, which were normal, and worked out a CRB-65 score of 0. He asked about smoking; she had stopped five years ago.

He explained that she could be treated at home, advised rest and fluids, and told her to come back if she became breathless or confused. He planned a chest X-ray in six weeks to make sure the shadow had cleared.

She is a school secretary and was due to fly to her sister's wedding in a week. She asked for "the strongest antibiotic" so she would be well enough to travel.

He prescribed co-amoxiclav, saying "it isn't penicillin, it's a different antibiotic".
h: He prescribed co-amoxiclav, saying "it isn't penicillin, it's a different antibiotic"

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave co-amoxiclav to Mrs. Samia after her penicillin anaphylaxis.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have had a non-penicillin antibiotic, such as doxycycline or clarithromycin.
a.w: Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin, which is a penicillin, so it can cause another anaphylaxis.

a.o: Dr. Ihab treated Mrs. Samia's pneumonia at home.
a.x: Every pneumonia needs a hospital bed.
a.w: A CRB-65 of 0 means low risk and home treatment is safe.

a.o: Dr. Ihab planned a chest X-ray for Mrs. Samia in six weeks.
a.x: A repeat X-ray was a waste.
a.w: A follow-up X-ray checks that the shadow was not hiding something else.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mrs. Samia to come back if she became breathless.
a.x: Safety advice was not needed for a mild case.
a.w: Patients need to know the signs of getting worse.

t: Urine infection in a man treated for three days
s:
Mr. Hany, 45, came in with burning on passing urine and going often for two days. He had no fever, no back pain and no discharge. His urine dipstick was positive for nitrites and white cells. He has no other illnesses and has never had a urine infection.

Dr. Abeer checked his temperature, which was normal, and felt his belly, which was soft and not tender over the kidneys.

She sent his urine to the lab for culture, and asked about new partners and discharge, which he did not have. She asked about his prostate symptoms, such as a weak stream, and he had none.

He works as a taxi driver and said he often holds his urine for hours on long shifts and drinks little. He asked whether he could still go to the gym, and she said yes if he felt well.

She prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days, "the same as for women".
h: She prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days, "the same as for women"

a.o: Dr. Abeer gave Mr. Hany only three days of antibiotics.
a.x: Mr. Hany should have had seven days of antibiotics, with the culture result checked.
a.w: Urine infections in men are counted as complicated and can involve the prostate. Three days is only for women.

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mr. Hany's urine for culture.
a.w: Urine infections in men need a culture to guide treatment.

a.o: Dr. Abeer asked Mr. Hany about new partners.
a.w: A sexual infection can look like a urine infection.

a.o: Dr. Abeer let Mr. Hany keep going to the gym.
a.w: Exercise is fine if he feels well and has no fever.

t: Positive dipstick blamed for confusion
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 84, lives in a care home. She was admitted with confusion for two days. She had no fever, no burning and no new pain. Her urine dipstick showed white cells and nitrites. Her sodium was 126.

Dr. Mai checked her drug chart and found she had started a new water tablet a week ago. She stopped it.

She checked her chest and found it clear. She asked her daughter how she usually was, and she was normally chatty.

Her daughter said her mother had not been eating or drinking well since the new tablet.

Dr. Mai diagnosed a urine infection from the dipstick and started antibiotics, writing "UTI causing confusion".
h: Dr. Mai diagnosed a urine infection from the dipstick and started antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Mai blamed a urine infection on a dipstick in an older woman with no urine symptoms.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem's low sodium from the water tablet should have been treated, without antibiotics.
a.w: Dipsticks are often positive in older women without infection. Her confusion came from low sodium.

a.o: Dr. Mai stopped the water tablet.
a.w: Water tablets can cause low sodium.

a.o: Dr. Mai asked about her usual self.
a.w: Knowing her usual state helps judge confusion.

a.o: Dr. Mai checked her chest.
a.w: A chest infection can cause confusion.

t: Shingles on the nose tip not referred
s:
Mr. Atef, 72, came in with a painful blistering rash on the right side of his forehead for two days. He also had blisters on the tip of his nose. His right eye was red and watery and felt gritty.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed shingles. She checked his vision, which was a little blurred in the right eye.

She started aciclovir tablets and gave him pain relief. She told him to keep the blisters clean and covered.

He asked whether his grandchildren could catch it. She said they could catch chickenpox from the blisters.

She told him to come back in a week, and did not refer him to an eye doctor.
h: She told him to come back in a week, and did not refer him to an eye doctor

a.o: Dr. Ghada didn't refer Mr. Atef to an eye doctor for shingles on his forehead and nose.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have been seen by an eye doctor the same day.
a.w: Blisters on the nose tip mean the eye nerve is involved, which can damage sight.

a.o: Dr. Ghada started aciclovir.
a.w: Antivirals within three days shorten shingles.

a.o: Dr. Ghada warned about the grandchildren.
a.w: Blisters can spread chickenpox to people who haven't had it.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked his vision.
a.w: Blurred vision suggests eye involvement.

t: Chickenpox contact in a pregnant woman
s:
Mrs. Heba, 28, is 16 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her nephew had chickenpox, and she spent an afternoon playing with him three days ago before the spots appeared. She has never had chickenpox herself, as far as she knows. She feels well and has no rash.

Dr. Soha sent a blood test for chickenpox immunity the same day, which came back negative. She checked her blood pressure and listened to the baby's heartbeat, which was normal.

She told her to avoid other people with chickenpox and to stay away from the antenatal clinic waiting room until 21 days after contact, in case she became infectious.

Mrs. Heba works as a nursery teacher and was very worried. She asked whether the baby was at risk and whether she should stay off work.

Dr. Soha told her to come back only if she got a rash, and did not offer any preventive treatment.
h: told her to come back only if she got a rash, and did not offer any preventive treatment

a.o: Dr. Soha offered Mrs. Heba nothing after her chickenpox contact.
a.x: Mrs. Heba should have been offered aciclovir tablets from day 7 to 14 after contact, or immunoglobulin if aciclovir was not suitable.
a.w: Chickenpox in pregnancy can cause severe pneumonia in the mother, and before 20 weeks it can harm the baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Heba's immunity first.
a.x: A blood test was a waste of time.
a.w: Many adults are immune without knowing, and then need no treatment.

a.o: Dr. Soha kept Mrs. Heba out of the antenatal waiting room.
a.w: She could become infectious from day 8 to 21 and spread it to other pregnant women.

a.o: Dr. Soha told Mrs. Heba to avoid other cases.
a.x: One more contact makes no difference.
a.w: Avoiding further exposure is sensible.

t: Endocarditis antibiotics before cultures
s:
Mr. Sami, 40, injects drugs. He was admitted with fever for two weeks, night sweats and weight loss. He had a new heart murmur and small dark lines under his nails. He was alert, with a blood pressure of 124/78 and a pulse of 98. His chest was clear.

Dr. Nadia asked for an urgent heart scan and checked his HIV and hepatitis tests. She checked his urine, which showed blood.

She asked the addiction team to see him and offered him a substitute medicine so he would not go into withdrawal on the ward.

He was anxious and wanted to leave for a few hours to see his mother. Dr. Nadia talked with him calmly and he agreed to stay.

She started IV antibiotics at once, before taking any blood cultures, writing "start treatment early".
h: She started IV antibiotics at once, before taking any blood cultures

a.o: Dr. Nadia started Mr. Sami's antibiotics before taking blood cultures.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have had three sets of blood cultures from different sites before the antibiotics, as he was stable.
a.w: In stable endocarditis, finding the germ guides weeks of treatment. Antibiotics first can make the cultures negative.

a.o: Dr. Nadia asked for an urgent heart scan.
a.w: A heart scan shows growths on the valves.

a.o: Dr. Nadia gave Mr. Sami a substitute medicine.
a.w: Treating withdrawal helps him stay for treatment.

a.o: Dr. Nadia talked Mr. Sami into staying.
a.x: She should have let him go.
a.w: Leaving mid-treatment risks death from endocarditis.

t: Gentamicin without levels
s:
Mr. Kareem, 70, was admitted with a kidney infection and sepsis. He was started on IV gentamicin once a day with a second antibiotic. His creatinine was 160, higher than his usual 110. He weighs 68 kg.

Dr. Hala worked out the gentamicin dose by his weight and his kidney function. She asked for his urine output to be measured every hour and gave IV fluids.

She asked about ringing in his ears and dizziness, which he did not have, and noted his hearing was good.

He is a retired engineer and wanted to know exactly how long each drug would last. His wife asked if he would need long-term antibiotics; Dr. Hala said the course would switch to tablets once he was better.

She did not ask for any gentamicin blood levels, writing "dose checked by weight".
h: She did not ask for any gentamicin blood levels, writing "dose checked by weight"

a.o: Dr. Hala gave Mr. Kareem gentamicin without checking blood levels.
a.x: Mr. Kareem should have had gentamicin levels checked, with the dose changed or stopped if they were high.
a.w: Gentamicin can damage the kidneys and inner ear. Levels must be checked, especially with weak kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Hala measured Mr. Kareem's urine every hour.
a.x: Hourly urine was too much fuss.
a.w: Urine output shows how his kidneys cope with sepsis.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked Mr. Kareem about ringing ears and dizziness.
a.x: Ears were off topic in a kidney infection.
a.w: Gentamicin can damage hearing and balance.

a.o: Dr. Hala dosed gentamicin by Mr. Kareem's weight.
a.x: A fixed dose is better for everyone.
a.w: Dosing by weight is safer.

t: Measles child sent to the waiting room
s:
Ahmed, 3, came in with fever, a cough, runny nose and red eyes for four days. Today he had a red, blotchy rash starting behind his ears and on his face. He had not had his MMR vaccine because his parents were worried about side effects.

Dr. Rana looked inside his mouth and saw tiny white spots on the inside of his cheeks. His chest was clear and he was drinking.

She advised fluids and paracetamol and told his mother to watch for fast breathing, drowsiness or fewer wet nappies.

His mother said his 7-month-old sister was at home. She asked whether it was too late for the MMR vaccine for Ahmed, and Dr. Rana said they could talk about it once he was well.

While she wrote a letter, she asked them to wait in the busy waiting room, next to other children and a pregnant woman.
h: she asked them to wait in the busy waiting room, next to other children and a pregnant woman

a.o: Dr. Rana sent Ahmed, with likely measles, to the busy waiting room.
a.x: Ahmed should have been kept in a separate room, with public health told about the case.
a.w: Measles spreads through the air and is dangerous to babies, pregnant women and people with weak immunity.

a.o: Dr. Rana looked inside Ahmed's mouth.
a.w: White spots inside the cheeks are a sign of measles.

a.o: Dr. Rana raised the MMR vaccine with Ahmed's mother.
a.x: Talking about vaccines now was pushy.
a.w: A good moment to talk about vaccines protects him and his sister later.

a.o: Dr. Rana thought about Ahmed's baby sister.
a.x: His sister was not at risk.
a.w: Babies under one are at high risk of measles complications.

t: Dog bite without rabies vaccine
s:
Mr. Samir, 34, was bitten on his hand by a stray dog while jogging in a country where rabies is common. The dog ran away and could not be found. The bite broke the skin and bled.

Dr. Inas washed the wound for 15 minutes with soap and running water, and cleaned it with antiseptic. She checked his tetanus status, which was up to date.

She left the hand wound open rather than stitching it, gave him co-amoxiclav to prevent infection and checked that he could move all his fingers.

He is a teacher and was worried about missing work. He asked whether the dog might have been sick, because it had been foaming at the mouth.

She told him rabies was rare and did not give a rabies vaccine.
h: She told him rabies was rare and did not give a rabies vaccine

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Samir no rabies treatment after a stray dog bite.
a.x: Mr. Samir should have had a course of rabies vaccines and rabies immunoglobulin into the wound.
a.w: Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start. A stray dog bite where rabies is common needs treatment at once.

a.o: Dr. Inas washed Mr. Samir's wound for 15 minutes.
a.w: Long washing lowers the risk of rabies.

a.o: Dr. Inas left Mr. Samir's hand wound open.
a.w: Hand bites are often left open to lower the risk of infection.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked Mr. Samir's finger movement.
a.w: Bites can damage tendons.

t: Dirty wound without tetanus check
s:
Mr. Fathi, 60, a farmer, cut his shin deeply on a rusty plough this morning. The wound was full of soil and manure. He could not remember ever having a tetanus injection, and his records showed none.

Dr. Nada gave him local anesthetic and washed the wound well with lots of saline. She removed dirt and dead tissue, then closed it loosely with a few stitches.

Because the wound was dirty, she gave him co-amoxiclav for a week. She checked his sugar, which was normal, and his foot pulses, which were strong.

He asked when the stitches could come out, and she said in about ten days. His son asked whether he could keep working, and she said he could do light jobs if he kept it clean.

She sent him home with a dressing and advice, without any tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin.
h: She sent him home with a dressing and advice, without any tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Fathi home with a dirty wound and no tetanus protection.
a.x: Mr. Fathi should have had a tetanus vaccine and tetanus immunoglobulin, with the rest of the vaccine course after.
a.w: A soil-dirty wound in someone with no record of vaccines is high risk for tetanus, which can be deadly.

a.o: Dr. Nada removed dead tissue from Mr. Fathi's wound.
a.w: Removing dead tissue lowers infection risk.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Fathi antibiotics.
a.w: Dirty wounds can get infected.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Mr. Fathi's foot pulses.
a.w: Good blood supply helps a shin wound heal.

t: Syphilis in pregnancy treated with doxycycline
s:
Mrs. Reem, 25, is 14 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her routine booking blood test showed syphilis. She had no sores or rash. She is not allergic to penicillin and has had it before for a sore throat.

Dr. Soha explained the result kindly and in private, and said it could be treated. She asked about her husband and offered him a test and treatment.

She checked her HIV and hepatitis B tests, which were negative, and planned to repeat the syphilis blood test after treatment to check it had worked.

Mrs. Reem was very upset and asked whether her baby would be harmed. She also said she was scared of needles and asked if there was a tablet instead.

Because of the fear of needles, Dr. Soha prescribed doxycycline tablets for two weeks.
h: Dr. Soha prescribed doxycycline tablets for two weeks

a.o: Dr. Soha gave Mrs. Reem doxycycline for syphilis in pregnancy.
a.x: Mrs. Reem should have had a benzathine penicillin injection, with support for her fear of needles.
a.w: Doxycycline harms the baby's bones and teeth, and does not treat the baby. Penicillin treats both mother and baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha offered Mrs. Reem's husband a test.
a.w: Partners need testing and treatment, or she can be reinfected.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Reem's HIV test.
a.w: Syphilis and HIV often go together.

a.o: Dr. Soha planned a repeat blood test after treatment.
a.w: A repeat test shows the treatment worked.

t: Gonorrhea treated without partner notification
s:
Mr. Tarek, 22, came in with a yellow discharge from his penis and burning on passing urine for three days. His swab showed gonorrhea. He had two partners in the last month and did not always use condoms.

Dr. Ihab gave him a ceftriaxone injection the same day. He also tested him for HIV, syphilis and chlamydia, and offered a hepatitis B vaccine.

He advised him to avoid sex for a week after treatment and to use condoms in future. He booked a test of cure in two weeks.

Mr. Tarek is a university student and was embarrassed. He asked whether his partners needed to know, and said he did not want to tell them himself.

Dr. Ihab said it was up to him, and did not offer the clinic's partner notification service.
h: Dr. Ihab said it was up to him, and did not offer the clinic's partner notification service

a.o: Dr. Ihab left Mr. Tarek's partners untold.
a.x: Mr. Tarek should have been offered help to tell his partners, or the clinic could have told them without naming him.
a.w: Partners may have no symptoms but can spread the infection or get complications like infertility.

a.o: Dr. Ihab tested Mr. Tarek for other infections.
a.w: Sexual infections often go together.

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mr. Tarek a ceftriaxone injection.
a.w: Ceftriaxone is the treatment for gonorrhea.

a.o: Dr. Ihab booked a test of cure.
a.x: A test of cure was a waste.
a.w: Gonorrhea resistance is rising, so a test checks the treatment worked.

t: Dengue given ibuprofen
s:
Miss Nadine, 27, came back from Thailand five days ago. She had fever, severe aches in her muscles and bones, and pain behind her eyes. Her platelets were 62 and her white count was low. Her dengue test was positive.

Dr. Fady checked her blood pressure lying and standing, which was steady, and asked about bleeding gums, nosebleeds and belly pain, which she had none.

He advised her to drink plenty of fluids and rest. He asked her to come back the next day for a blood count, as platelets can fall further on days 4 to 6.

She works as a nurse and said the pain was the worst she had ever felt. She had paracetamol at home but said it did nothing.

He prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the pain.
h: He prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the pain

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Miss Nadine ibuprofen for dengue.
a.x: Miss Nadine should have had paracetamol only, with no NSAIDs or aspirin.
a.w: NSAIDs raise bleeding risk in dengue, where platelets are already low.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Miss Nadine's blood pressure lying and standing.
a.w: A fall on standing can show fluid loss in severe dengue.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked Miss Nadine to come back the next day.
a.x: She could be seen in a week.
a.w: Platelets can fall further on days 4 to 6.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about belly pain.
a.w: Belly pain is a warning sign of severe dengue.

t: Toxic shock without the tampon removed
s:
Miss Lina, 19, came in with high fever, vomiting, diarrhea and a red rash all over like sunburn. Her blood pressure was 82/50 and her pulse 132. She was on her period. She is a student and lives in a shared flat.

Dr. Inas gave her IV fluids quickly and started IV antibiotics, including clindamycin. She called the intensive care team, who came to see her.

She took blood cultures and checked her kidney and liver tests, which were both a little raised. Her platelets were low.

Her mother arrived and asked if it was food poisoning, since her flatmate had been sick too. Miss Lina was too drowsy to answer many questions.

Dr. Inas did not ask about tampons or do an examination, writing "sepsis, source unclear".
h: Dr. Inas did not ask about tampons or do an examination

a.o: Dr. Inas didn't check for a tampon in Miss Lina's toxic shock.
a.x: The tampon should have been looked for and removed at once.
a.w: A retained tampon is the source of the toxin. Leaving it in keeps the toxin flowing.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Miss Lina clindamycin.
a.w: Clindamycin stops toxin production.

a.o: Dr. Inas called intensive care.
a.w: Toxic shock can kill quickly.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked Miss Lina's platelets.
a.w: Low platelets are part of toxic shock.

t: Antibiotics for a viral sore throat
s:
Mr. Ibrahim, 30, came in with a sore throat, runny nose and cough for two days. He had no fever. His tonsils were red but had no pus. His neck glands were not swollen. His FeverPAIN score was 0.

Dr. Ghada explained that the illness was most likely a virus that would get better by itself in a week.

She advised paracetamol, salt-water gargles and fluids, and told him to come back if he could not swallow or had trouble breathing.

He is a wedding singer and had a big wedding at the weekend. He asked for antibiotics to be sure his voice would be ready.

She prescribed amoxicillin for a week, saying "just in case".
h: She prescribed amoxicillin for a week, saying "just in case"

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave Mr. Ibrahim antibiotics for a viral sore throat.
a.x: Mr. Ibrahim should have had no antibiotics, with pain relief and voice rest.
a.w: A FeverPAIN of 0 means a virus. Antibiotics don't help and cause side effects and resistance.

a.o: Dr. Ghada suggested salt-water gargles.
a.w: Gargles soothe the throat.

a.o: Dr. Ghada said it was likely a virus.
a.w: Cough and runny nose point to a virus.

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mr. Ibrahim to come back if he could not swallow.
a.w: Trouble swallowing can mean an abscess.

t: Pneumonia with a high CURB-65 sent home
s:
Mr. Medhat, 78, came in with a cough, fever and breathlessness for three days. He was confused and did not know the date. His urea was 9, his breathing rate 32 and his blood pressure 94/58.

Dr. Rehab checked his oxygen, which was 92% on air, and gave him oxygen. His chest X-ray showed pneumonia on the right.

She took blood cultures and gave him the first dose of antibiotics in the department. She asked about his home, and he lives alone in a third-floor flat.

His daughter said he hated hospitals and would be better at home. She offered to stay with him for a few days.

Dr. Rehab sent him home with oral antibiotics, with his daughter staying.
h: Dr. Rehab sent him home with oral antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Rehab sent Mr. Medhat home with a CURB-65 of 5.
a.x: Mr. Medhat should have been admitted for IV antibiotics and senior review.
a.w: Confusion, high urea, fast breathing, low blood pressure and age give a CURB-65 of 5, which means a high risk of death.

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Medhat oxygen.
a.w: 92% in an older man with pneumonia needs support.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked about Mr. Medhat's flat.
a.w: Living alone matters for safety at discharge.

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave the first dose in the department.
a.w: Early antibiotics save lives in pneumonia.

t: Hepatitis B baby without birth vaccine
s:
Baby Yousef was born this morning by normal delivery to Mrs. Amal, 27. Her booking blood test showed she carries hepatitis B, with a high viral load, and she took tenofovir in the last months of pregnancy. The baby weighed 3.3 kg and was feeding well.

Dr. Hamed examined the baby, who was pink and active, with a normal heart and hips. He helped Mrs. Amal with skin-to-skin contact and checked that the midwife had given vitamin K.

He told her that breastfeeding was safe with hepatitis B and that she should keep taking her tablets for a few weeks after the birth, as her liver doctor had planned.

Mrs. Amal was tired and tearful, and her husband asked whether their baby had caught the virus. Dr. Hamed said most babies are protected with the right care.

He wrote that the baby's hepatitis B vaccine would be given "with the routine vaccines at eight weeks", and did not give immunoglobulin.
h: He wrote that the baby's hepatitis B vaccine would be given "with the routine vaccines at eight weeks"

a.o: Dr. Hamed left Baby Yousef's hepatitis B vaccine until eight weeks.
a.x: Baby Yousef should have had the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin within 24 hours of birth, ideally within 12.
a.w: Without a birth dose, about 9 in 10 babies of mothers with a high viral load become lifelong carriers.

a.o: Dr. Hamed told Mrs. Amal that breastfeeding was safe.
a.w: Breastfeeding is safe once the baby is vaccinated.

a.o: Dr. Hamed kept Mrs. Amal on tenofovir after birth.
a.x: Her tablets should stop at delivery.
a.w: Stopping suddenly can cause a flare; her liver doctor plans when to stop.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked that Baby Yousef had vitamin K.
a.w: Vitamin K prevents bleeding in all newborns.

t: Scabies treated in one person only
s:
Mrs. Nermine, 35, came in with an itchy rash for three weeks that was worse at night. She had small lines and bumps between her fingers and on her wrists. Her husband and two children had also started scratching. She was embarrassed and said she kept a clean house.

Dr. Ghada explained it was scabies, a tiny mite caught by close skin contact, and that it has nothing to do with cleanliness. She checked the rash for infected sores, and there were none.

She prescribed permethrin cream for the whole body from the neck down, to be washed off after 8 to 12 hours and repeated after a week. She warned that the itch can last a few weeks even after the mites are gone.

She advised washing bedding, towels and clothes at 50°C on the day of treatment. Mrs. Nermine works at a care home and asked whether she should tell her manager.

She prescribed cream only for Mrs. Nermine, telling her to "see if the others still itch next week".
h: She prescribed cream only for Mrs. Nermine, telling her to "see if the others still itch next week"

a.o: Dr. Ghada treated Mrs. Nermine but not her family.
a.x: Everyone in the house should have been treated on the same day, even without symptoms.
a.w: Untreated family members pass the mites back, and the infestation keeps returning.

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mrs. Nermine the itch could last weeks.
a.x: The itch should stop the next day.
a.w: The itch is an allergy to the mites and fades over weeks.

a.o: Dr. Ghada repeated the cream after a week.
a.w: A second dose kills mites that hatch from eggs.

a.o: Dr. Ghada said scabies has nothing to do with cleanliness.
a.x: Scabies only spreads in dirty homes.
a.w: Scabies spreads by close contact in any home.

t: Ramipril and ibuprofen carried on in a dry patient
s:
Mr. Hesham, 66, came in after three days of vomiting and diarrhea from a stomach bug that went round his family. He takes ramipril and furosemide for heart failure and metformin for diabetes. He felt dizzy when he stood up.

Dr. Ihab found his blood pressure 102/64 and his mouth dry. His blood tests showed his creatinine had risen from 95 to 170. His potassium was 5.4.

He paused the metformin and the furosemide and advised him to sip oral rehydration fluids little and often. He arranged repeat blood tests in two days.

Mr. Hesham said he had also been taking ibuprofen from the pharmacy for stomach cramps and a headache. His wife asked whether he should eat bananas for his strength.

Dr. Ihab told him to carry on with the ramipril and ibuprofen "because the heart needs them", and said bananas were fine.
h: Dr. Ihab told him to carry on with the ramipril and ibuprofen "because the heart needs them"

a.o: Dr. Ihab kept Mr. Hesham on ramipril and ibuprofen while he was dry with kidney injury.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have paused ramipril and stopped ibuprofen until he was eating and drinking normally again.
a.w: When dehydrated, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys and make kidney injury and high potassium worse.

a.o: Dr. Ihab paused Mr. Hesham's metformin.
a.x: Metformin is fine in a stomach bug.
a.w: Metformin can build up and cause lactic acidosis when the kidneys fail.

a.o: Dr. Ihab paused Mr. Hesham's furosemide.
a.x: Water tablets must never stop in heart failure.
a.w: A short pause is right while he is dry.

a.o: Dr. Ihab arranged repeat blood tests in two days.
a.w: Kidney function and potassium must be rechecked soon.

t: High potassium without calcium
s:
Mr. Atef, 68, has chronic kidney disease and came in feeling weak and tired. His potassium was 7.2. His heart tracing showed tall, peaked T waves and wide QRS complexes. His pulse was 52.

Dr. Nada put him on a heart monitor and repeated the potassium from a fresh sample without a tourniquet, which confirmed 7.2.

She gave 10 units of insulin with glucose through a drip, and nebulized salbutamol. She checked his sugar every hour afterwards and called the kidney team about dialysis.

His wife said he had started a potassium-sparing water tablet a month ago. He had also been drinking a lot of orange juice to "help his kidneys".

She did not give any calcium gluconate, writing "insulin will bring the potassium down quickly".
h: She did not give any calcium gluconate

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Atef no calcium for high potassium with heart tracing changes.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have had IV calcium gluconate at once, before the insulin, to protect his heart.
a.w: Calcium does not lower potassium, but it steadies the heart within minutes and prevents a deadly rhythm.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Mr. Atef's sugar every hour.
a.w: Insulin can cause low sugar for hours afterwards.

a.o: Dr. Nada repeated the potassium.
a.w: A damaged sample can give a falsely high result.

a.o: Dr. Nada called the kidney team.
a.w: Dialysis may be needed if medicines don't work.

t: Nitrofurantoin with weak kidneys
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 79, came in with burning and going often to pass urine for two days. She had no fever or back pain. Her urine dipstick showed nitrites and white cells. Her kidney function, checked last month, showed an eGFR of 22.

Dr. Abeer sent her urine for culture, as she had had two infections this year. She checked her temperature and her belly, which were normal.

She asked about her fluid intake, and Mrs. Fawzia said she drank little to avoid going to the toilet at night. She advised her to drink more during the day.

Mrs. Fawzia lives with her daughter and takes amlodipine, a statin and a water tablet. Her daughter asked whether her mother should take cranberry juice.

Dr. Abeer prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days, the usual choice for a bladder infection.
h: Dr. Abeer prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days, the usual choice for a bladder infection

a.o: Dr. Abeer gave Mrs. Fawzia nitrofurantoin with an eGFR of 22.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have had a different antibiotic, such as cefalexin or pivmecillinam, chosen with her kidney function in mind.
a.w: Nitrofurantoin does not reach the bladder well when the eGFR is low and can build up and harm the nerves and lungs.

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mrs. Fawzia's urine for culture.
a.w: Repeated infections need a culture.

a.o: Dr. Abeer advised Mrs. Fawzia to drink more in the day.
a.w: Fluids help flush the bladder.

a.o: Dr. Abeer checked Mrs. Fawzia's temperature.
a.w: A fever suggests a kidney infection.

t: Live vaccine on high-dose steroids
s:
Adam, 4, has nephrotic syndrome and is in his first course of high-dose prednisolone, 60 mg/m² a day, which he started two weeks ago. His urine has cleared of protein and the swelling around his eyes has gone.

Dr. Rana checked his blood pressure, which was normal, and his weight, which had dropped back to normal. She asked his mother to test his urine every morning with a dipstick.

She explained that the steroids would be slowly reduced over the next weeks, and that relapses are common. She asked about chickenpox, which he had not had.

His mother said his nursery wanted his MMR booster and chickenpox vaccine up to date. Adam was proud of his star chart for taking his medicine.

Dr. Rana gave Adam his MMR booster and chickenpox vaccine in clinic, saying "nephrotic children need extra protection".
h: Dr. Rana gave Adam his MMR booster and chickenpox vaccine in clinic

a.o: Dr. Rana gave Adam live vaccines while he was on high-dose steroids.
a.x: Adam's live vaccines should have waited until at least three months after high-dose steroids stopped.
a.w: High-dose steroids weaken immunity, so live vaccines can cause the very infection they are meant to prevent.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about chickenpox.
a.w: Chickenpox can be dangerous in children on steroids.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked Adam's mother to dipstick his urine daily.
a.w: Home tests find relapses early.

a.o: Dr. Rana warned that relapses are common.
a.w: Most children with nephrotic syndrome relapse.

t: Infected blocked kidney sent home
s:
Mrs. Heba, 34, came in with severe pain in her right side going down to her groin. She had a fever of 38.9°C and shivers. Her pulse was 118 and her blood pressure 104/68. Her urine showed blood and white cells.

Dr. Fouad gave her IV fluids, pain relief and IV antibiotics after blood and urine cultures. A CT scan showed a 6 mm stone in her right ureter, with a swollen kidney above it.

He checked that she was not pregnant, and her test was negative. Her white count was 19 and her creatinine normal.

She has two young children and her husband was at work. She asked whether she could go home since the pain was better after the medicines.

He sent her home with oral antibiotics and painkillers, and booked a urology clinic appointment in two weeks.
h: He sent her home with oral antibiotics and painkillers, and booked a urology clinic appointment in two weeks

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent Mrs. Heba home with an infected, blocked kidney.
a.x: Mrs. Heba should have been admitted for urgent drainage of the kidney with a stent or tube, and IV antibiotics.
a.w: An infected kidney behind a stone is a urological emergency. Antibiotics alone cannot clear it, and sepsis can kill.

a.o: Dr. Fouad did a CT scan.
a.w: CT finds stones and blockage.

a.o: Dr. Fouad checked for pregnancy.
a.w: Pregnancy changes scans and treatment.

a.o: Dr. Fouad took cultures before antibiotics.
a.w: Cultures guide treatment.

t: Blood pressure cuff on a fistula arm
s:
Mr. Sabri, 62, has kidney failure and has dialysis three times a week through a fistula in his left arm. He was admitted with a chest infection. He was alert, his oxygen 95% and his potassium normal.

Dr. Inas checked his fistula, which had a strong buzz. She wrote "no blood or cuffs on left arm" on his chart and stuck a sign above his bed.

She started antibiotics, adjusted for his kidney function, and asked the dialysis unit to see him on his usual day.

Mr. Sabri said his fistula is "his lifeline" and that he guards it carefully. His son asked if the infection would affect his dialysis.

That night, the new nurse could not get a reading on his right arm, so Dr. Inas told her to "just use the left arm this once".
h: Dr. Inas told her to "just use the left arm this once"

a.o: Dr. Inas allowed a blood pressure cuff on Mr. Sabri's fistula arm.
a.x: The left arm should never have been used; a leg cuff or a different method should have been used.
a.w: A blood pressure cuff can block a fistula, and a clotted fistula can mean no dialysis access.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked the fistula buzz.
a.w: A buzz shows the fistula is working.

a.o: Dr. Inas adjusted the antibiotics for his kidneys.
a.w: Many antibiotics build up in kidney failure.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked the dialysis unit to see him.
a.w: Missing dialysis is dangerous.

t: Post-strep kidney problem called a urine infection
s:
Ali, 8, came in with his father because his urine had looked like cola for two days. His face looked puffy in the mornings. He had a sore throat two weeks ago. He had no burning or pain when passing urine.

Dr. Mahmoud found his blood pressure was 138/92, which is high for his age. His urine dipstick showed blood and protein but no nitrites.

He asked about rashes, joint pain and belly pain, which Ali did not have. He weighed him and found he had gained 2 kg since his last visit.

Ali's father is a taxi driver and said Ali had been passing less urine than usual. Ali was quiet and tired but playing with his father's phone.

Dr. Mahmoud diagnosed a urine infection, started antibiotics and booked a review in a week.
h: Dr. Mahmoud diagnosed a urine infection, started antibiotics and booked a review in a week

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud called Ali's cola urine and high blood pressure a urine infection.
a.x: Ali should have been sent to the children's hospital the same day for kidney tests, blood pressure control and fluid balance.
a.w: Cola urine, swelling and high blood pressure after a sore throat point to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which can cause kidney failure and fits.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud weighed Ali.
a.w: Weight gain shows fluid build-up.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked about rashes and joint pain.
a.w: They can point to other kidney diseases, like HSP.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked about urine output.
a.w: Less urine shows the kidneys are struggling.

t: Kidney injury without a bladder scan
s:
Mr. Kamel, 78, was admitted with confusion and belly pain. His creatinine had risen from 90 to 280. He takes oxybutynin for an overactive bladder, started a month ago. He has an enlarged prostate.

Dr. Ayman gave him IV fluids and stopped his ramipril. He checked his potassium, which was 5.6, and started a heart monitor.

He asked for a kidney ultrasound, which would be done the next day.

Mr. Kamel's wife said he had been going to the toilet often but passing only small amounts. His belly felt full above the pubic bone.

Dr. Ayman did not do a bladder scan or put in a catheter, writing "AKI, likely dehydration".
h: Dr. Ayman did not do a bladder scan or put in a catheter

a.o: Dr. Ayman missed urine retention as the cause of Mr. Kamel's kidney injury.
a.x: Mr. Kamel should have had a bladder scan and a catheter at once, and the oxybutynin stopped.
a.w: A big prostate and an anticholinergic drug can stop the bladder emptying. Retention backs up into the kidneys and causes kidney injury and confusion.

a.o: Dr. Ayman stopped ramipril.
a.w: ACE inhibitors worsen kidney injury.

a.o: Dr. Ayman put Mr. Kamel on a monitor.
a.w: High potassium can cause heart rhythm problems.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked for a kidney ultrasound.
a.w: An ultrasound shows a blockage.

t: Rhabdomyolysis given slow fluids
s:
Mr. Raafat, 70, was found on the floor at home after lying there for a day after a fall. His legs were sore and his urine was dark brown. His CK was 48,000 and his creatinine 190. His potassium was 5.3.

Dr. Rehab checked his hips with an X-ray, which showed no fracture. She checked his heart tracing, which was normal.

She asked for a catheter to measure his urine every hour. She checked his skin for pressure sores, and found a red patch on his hip.

He lives alone and had pressed his alarm, but it had not worked. His neighbor found him.

She started IV fluids at 80 mL an hour, writing "elderly, avoid overload".
h: She started IV fluids at 80 mL an hour, writing "elderly, avoid overload"

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Raafat slow fluids for rhabdomyolysis.
a.x: Mr. Raafat should have had rapid IV fluids aiming for a urine output of about 200 mL an hour, with close checks of his heart and lungs.
a.w: Muscle breakdown floods the kidneys with myoglobin. Fast fluids flush it through and prevent kidney failure.

a.o: Dr. Rehab X-rayed Mr. Raafat's hips.
a.w: A fall can break a hip.

a.o: Dr. Rehab put in a catheter.
a.w: Hourly urine guides fluids.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked his skin.
a.w: Long lies cause pressure sores.

t: Clarithromycin with tacrolimus
s:
Mrs. Samia, 45, had a kidney transplant three years ago from her brother. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and a low dose of prednisolone. Her kidney function has been stable, with a creatinine of 105. She came to the transplant clinic with a cough and fever for four days.

Dr. Nermine found crackles at the left base and an oxygen level of 95%. A chest X-ray showed a small patch of pneumonia. Her creatinine today was 110 and her last tacrolimus level was in range.

She checked that Mrs. Samia had taken every dose of her transplant medicines, and sent sputum and a viral swab, since transplant patients can catch unusual germs.

Mrs. Samia teaches primary school and said she catches everything from the children. She is allergic to penicillin, which gave her a rash as a child.

Dr. Nermine prescribed clarithromycin for a week, without changing the tacrolimus dose or planning a level check.
h: Dr. Nermine prescribed clarithromycin for a week, without changing the tacrolimus dose or planning a level check

a.o: Dr. Nermine gave Mrs. Samia clarithromycin on tacrolimus with no level check.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have had an antibiotic that does not interact, such as doxycycline, or a reduced tacrolimus dose with levels checked within days.
a.w: Clarithromycin blocks the breakdown of tacrolimus. Toxic levels can damage the new kidney and cause tremor and high potassium.

a.o: Dr. Nermine checked that Mrs. Samia never missed her transplant tablets.
a.x: Her tablets were off topic in a chest infection.
a.w: Missed doses can cause rejection, and illness is a common time to miss them.

a.o: Dr. Nermine sent a viral swab as well as sputum.
a.w: Transplant patients get viral and unusual infections that need different treatment.

a.o: Dr. Nermine avoided penicillin for Mrs. Samia.
a.w: A recorded penicillin allergy should be respected unless properly tested.

t: Polycystic kidneys and a sudden headache
s:
Mr. Waleed, 38, has polycystic kidney disease. His mother had the same condition and died of a brain bleed at 50. He came in with a sudden, severe headache that hit like a thunderclap while he was lifting weights at the gym. He said it was the worst headache of his life and he vomited once.

Dr. Hossam found his neck slightly stiff and his blood pressure 168/98. He was alert, with equal pupils and no weakness.

He gave him paracetamol, morphine and anti-sickness medicine. He asked about his usual headaches, and Mr. Waleed said he had migraines once or twice a year, which built up slowly with flashing lights.

His girlfriend said he had been under stress at work and had skipped meals. After an hour the headache had eased a little, and he wanted to go home to rest.

Dr. Hossam diagnosed a migraine brought on by exercise and sent him home without a CT scan.
h: Dr. Hossam diagnosed a migraine brought on by exercise and sent him home without a CT scan

a.o: Dr. Hossam sent Mr. Waleed home without a CT scan for a thunderclap headache.
a.x: Mr. Waleed should have had an urgent CT scan of the head and, if normal, a lumbar puncture or CT angiogram.
a.w: Polycystic kidney disease raises the risk of brain aneurysms. A sudden worst-ever headache can be a subarachnoid hemorrhage, and pain relief does not rule it out.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked how Mr. Waleed's usual migraines start.
a.x: His old headaches were off topic.
a.w: A headache that is different from usual is a warning sign.

a.o: Dr. Hossam checked Mr. Waleed's neck.
a.w: A stiff neck can mean blood around the brain.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked about Mr. Waleed's mother.
a.w: Brain aneurysms cluster in families with polycystic kidneys.

t: EPO started with low iron
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 60, has chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 18. Her hemoglobin has fallen to 92 over six months, and she is tired and breathless on the stairs. Her ferritin is 45 and her transferrin saturation 12%.

Dr. Mervat checked her B12 and folate, which were normal, and asked about black stools and heavy bleeding, which she had none. Her stool test for hidden blood was negative.

She explained that healthy kidneys make a hormone that tells the bone marrow to make blood, and that her kidneys were not making enough. She checked her blood pressure, which was well controlled.

Mrs. Asmaa said she had been eating less because of nausea. Her daughter asked whether her mother needed a blood transfusion, and Dr. Mervat said she would rather avoid one if possible, to keep her safe for a future transplant.

Dr. Mervat started erythropoietin injections every week, without giving any iron.
h: Dr. Mervat started erythropoietin injections every week, without giving any iron

a.o: Dr. Mervat started Mrs. Asmaa on EPO without treating her low iron.
a.x: Mrs. Asmaa should have had IV iron to fill her stores before or alongside the EPO.
a.w: EPO cannot make red cells without iron. Low iron is the most common reason EPO fails in kidney disease.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Asmaa's B12 and folate.
a.w: Other causes of anemia should be ruled out first.

a.o: Dr. Mervat tried to avoid a transfusion for Mrs. Asmaa.
a.x: A transfusion would be quicker and better.
a.w: Transfusions can make antibodies that make a kidney transplant harder.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Asmaa's blood pressure before EPO.
a.w: EPO can raise blood pressure, so it must be controlled first.

t: Diabetic kidney disease without ramipril
s:
Mr. Ibrahim, 55, has had type 2 diabetes for ten years. His yearly urine test showed protein, with an albumin-creatinine ratio of 45, confirmed on a second sample. His eGFR was 62 and his blood pressure 136/84.

Dr. Ghada checked his HbA1c, which was 58, and his cholesterol, which was high, and started atorvastatin. She checked his feet and arranged his eye screening.

She advised him to stop smoking and to cut down on salt, and offered him a place on a stop-smoking course.

He works as a builder and said he was too busy to come to the clinic often. He asked if the protein meant he would need dialysis.

She told him the protein was "small" and did not start an ACE inhibitor, because "his blood pressure is fine".
h: did not start an ACE inhibitor, because "his blood pressure is fine"

a.o: Dr. Ghada held back an ACE inhibitor from Mr. Ibrahim with protein in his urine.
a.x: Mr. Ibrahim should have started an ACE inhibitor or ARB, with an SGLT2 inhibitor, and a kidney check two weeks later.
a.w: These drugs protect the kidneys in diabetes with protein in the urine, whatever the blood pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ghada repeated Mr. Ibrahim's urine test.
a.w: A second sample confirms that the protein is real.

a.o: Dr. Ghada started Mr. Ibrahim on a statin.
a.w: Statins protect the heart, which is the main risk in kidney disease.

a.o: Dr. Ghada offered Mr. Ibrahim a stop-smoking course.
a.w: Smoking speeds up kidney damage.

t: Bloody diarrhea in a child given antibiotics
s:
Laila, 5, came in with bloody diarrhea for three days after a family barbecue with undercooked burgers. Today she was pale, sleepy and had passed little urine since yesterday. Her stool test showed E. coli O157. Her platelets were 60, her hemoglobin 84 and her creatinine raised.

Dr. Dina checked her blood pressure, which was high, and asked for a blood film, which showed broken red cells.

She gave IV fluids carefully, with a fluid chart and daily weights, and called the children's kidney team, who arranged a transfer.

Laila's cousin, who was at the same barbecue, also had diarrhea. Her mother asked if the meat was to blame and whether they should tell anyone.

To fight the germ and stop the diarrhea, Dr. Dina started IV antibiotics and loperamide.
h: Dr. Dina started IV antibiotics and loperamide

a.o: Dr. Dina gave Laila antibiotics and loperamide for E. coli O157.
a.x: Laila should have had no antibiotics or anti-diarrhea drugs, with careful fluids and kidney team care.
a.w: Antibiotics and loperamide can increase toxin release and worsen hemolytic uremic syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Dina called the children's kidney team.
a.x: The kidney team was not needed yet.
a.w: HUS often needs dialysis.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked for a blood film.
a.w: Broken red cells confirm HUS.

a.o: Dr. Dina thought about the cousin.
a.w: A shared food source must be reported to public health.

t: Ramipril continued after a big creatinine rise
s:
Mr. Sami, 72, has high blood pressure, a past heart attack and narrowed arteries in his legs. He smoked for 40 years. He started ramipril two weeks ago, and his creatinine has risen from 100 to 165. His potassium is 5.2.

Dr. Hala checked his blood pressure, which had fallen from 168/96 to 128/76. She asked about dizziness, which he did not have, and about how much he was drinking.

When she listened over his belly, she heard a whooshing sound to the left of his belly button.

Mr. Sami said he felt better on the new tablet and his headaches had gone. His wife asked whether the kidney result was serious.

She continued the ramipril, saying "a rise is expected", and booked the next test in three months.
h: She continued the ramipril, saying "a rise is expected"

a.o: Dr. Hala kept Mr. Sami on ramipril after a 65% creatinine rise.
