a.x: Mr. Sami should have had the ramipril stopped and a scan to look for narrowed kidney arteries.
a.w: A small rise is expected, but more than 30% suggests renal artery stenosis, and continuing can cause kidney failure.

a.o: Dr. Hala listened over Mr. Sami's belly.
a.w: A whooshing sound suggests a narrowed artery.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked how much Mr. Sami was drinking.
a.w: Dehydration can also raise creatinine on an ACE inhibitor.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked Mr. Sami's potassium.
a.w: ACE inhibitors can raise potassium.

t: Spironolactone added without a potassium check
s:
Mr. Tamer, 74, has heart failure and kidney disease with an eGFR of 35. He takes ramipril, bisoprolol and furosemide. His heart doctor wrote suggesting spironolactone to help his heart. His last potassium, three months ago, was 5.0.

Dr. Ihab checked his blood pressure, which was 118/70, and his weight, which was steady. His ankles were a little swollen.

He asked about breathlessness at night and how many pillows he used; Mr. Tamer used two, as usual.

Mr. Tamer said he eats a lot of bananas and oranges because he was told they were good for the heart. He also uses a salt substitute.

Dr. Ihab started spironolactone 25 mg without checking his potassium or arranging a follow-up test.
h: Dr. Ihab started spironolactone 25 mg without checking his potassium or arranging a follow-up test

a.o: Dr. Ihab started Mr. Tamer's spironolactone with no potassium checks.
a.x: Mr. Tamer should have had potassium and kidney tests before starting and within a week after, with advice about salt substitutes.
a.w: Spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor and weak kidneys can cause dangerous high potassium.

a.o: Dr. Ihab followed the heart doctor's advice to add spironolactone.
a.x: Spironolactone is never used in kidney disease.
a.w: It helps heart failure if potassium is watched.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about Mr. Tamer's pillows.
a.w: Needing more pillows means worse heart failure.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Tamer's weight.
a.w: Weight gain shows fluid build-up.

t: Missed dialysis sent home
s:
Mr. Fikry, 58, has kidney failure and has dialysis three times a week. He missed his last two sessions because he went to his village for a funeral. He came in feeling weak and a little breathless. His potassium was 6.8 and his heart tracing showed peaked T waves.

Dr. Nada gave him IV calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose and nebulized salbutamol. She put him on a monitor and gave him oxygen.

An hour later his potassium was 5.9. His chest X-ray showed some fluid in his lungs, and his weight was 4 kg above his usual dry weight.

He said he felt better and wanted to go home to rest. He promised to come to his next session in two days.

She sent him home and asked him to keep his next dialysis appointment, without calling the dialysis unit.
h: She sent him home and asked him to keep his next dialysis appointment, without calling the dialysis unit

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Fikry home after missed dialysis without arranging dialysis.
a.x: Mr. Fikry should have had urgent dialysis that day.
a.w: Insulin and salbutamol only move potassium into cells for a few hours. Only dialysis removes it and the extra fluid.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave calcium gluconate.
a.w: Calcium protects the heart.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked his weight.
a.w: Weight shows fluid gained.

a.o: Dr. Nada put him on a monitor.
a.w: High potassium can cause heart rhythm problems.

t: Cloudy dialysis fluid treated with tablets
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 62, does peritoneal dialysis at home. She came in because her dialysis fluid had turned cloudy that morning, and she had a mild belly ache. She had no fever. Her exit site looked clean.

Dr. Fouad examined her belly, which was mildly tender all over. He asked about her technique, and she said she had rushed an exchange two days ago when her grandson was visiting.

He asked the dialysis nurse to check her exit site and to review her technique with her.

She lives with her husband and is very independent. She asked if she could keep doing her dialysis at home.

Dr. Fouad prescribed oral ciprofloxacin, without sending the fluid for a cell count and culture.
h: Dr. Fouad prescribed oral ciprofloxacin, without sending the fluid for a cell count and culture

a.o: Dr. Fouad treated Mrs. Nawal's cloudy dialysis fluid with tablets and no fluid tests.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have had the fluid sent for cell count and culture, and antibiotics given into the dialysis fluid.
a.w: Cloudy fluid in peritoneal dialysis is peritonitis until proven otherwise. Antibiotics into the fluid treat it best.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked about her technique.
a.w: A break in technique is a common cause.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked the nurse to retrain Mrs. Nawal.
a.w: Retraining after a break in technique prevents more infections.

a.o: Dr. Fouad examined Mrs. Nawal's belly.
a.x: The fluid was enough without an exam.
a.w: Tenderness supports peritonitis.

t: Blood in the urine treated as an infection
s:
Mr. Hassan, 66, came in because he had seen bright red blood in his urine three times in the last week. It did not hurt. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 45 years and worked in a dye factory.

Dr. Abeer checked his blood pressure and his belly, which were normal. His urine dipstick showed blood but no nitrites or white cells.

She sent his urine to the lab and checked his kidney function.

He said his wife had urine infections and he thought he had caught one.

He had no fever, no burning and no pain in his back. He takes aspirin after a mini-stroke and had lost a little weight, which he put down to eating less since retiring. He was keen not to make a fuss and said the blood had nearly stopped.

She prescribed antibiotics for a urine infection and did not refer him to urology.
h: She prescribed antibiotics for a urine infection and did not refer him to urology

a.o: Dr. Abeer treated Mr. Hassan's painless blood in the urine as an infection.
a.x: Mr. Hassan should have been referred urgently to urology for a camera test of the bladder and a scan.
a.w: Painless visible blood in the urine in a smoker over 45 can be bladder cancer. Dye work adds to the risk.

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mr. Hassan's urine to the lab.
a.w: A lab test checks for infection and other causes.

a.o: Dr. Abeer checked Mr. Hassan's kidney function.
a.w: Kidney disease can also cause blood in the urine.

a.o: Dr. Abeer asked about his work.
a.w: Dye work raises the risk of bladder cancer.

t: Furosemide for a dry kidney injury
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 81, was admitted after a week of diarrhea and poor eating. Her creatinine had risen from 80 to 230. She had passed only 200 mL of urine in 12 hours. Her mouth was dry and her blood pressure 96/58.

Dr. Mai stopped her ramipril and her water tablet. She asked for a catheter and hourly urine measurements.

She checked her potassium, which was 5.1, and her chest, which was clear.

Her daughter said her mother had not been drinking much because she did not want to keep getting up.

She lives alone in a ground-floor flat and has mild memory problems. Her legs were not swollen and her chest X-ray showed no fluid. Her heart scan last year was normal. The nurse said she had drunk only a cup of tea since arriving.

To "get the kidneys going", Dr. Mai gave 80 mg of IV furosemide.
h: To "get the kidneys going", Dr. Mai gave 80 mg of IV furosemide

a.o: Dr. Mai gave furosemide to Mrs. Hanem, who was dry with kidney injury.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem should have had IV fluids to correct her dehydration.
a.w: Furosemide removes more fluid and worsens kidney injury in a dry patient. It does not improve kidney recovery.

a.o: Dr. Mai stopped ramipril.
a.w: ACE inhibitors worsen kidney injury.

a.o: Dr. Mai put in a catheter.
a.w: Hourly urine guides treatment.

a.o: Dr. Mai checked her chest.
a.w: Clear lungs show she is not overloaded.

t: Kidney biopsy on clopidogrel
s:
Mr. Kareem, 50, has protein and blood in his urine and a falling eGFR. The kidney team planned a kidney biopsy the next morning. He takes clopidogrel after a heart stent two years ago, and atorvastatin.

Dr. Ayman checked his blood pressure, which was 132/80, his platelets and his clotting tests, which were normal.

He explained the biopsy and the risk of bleeding, and Mr. Kareem signed the consent form.

He asked whether he could eat breakfast before the biopsy. Dr. Ayman told him to fast from midnight.

Mr. Kareem works as a bus driver and wanted to get the biopsy done before his annual leave ended. His heart doctor had said his stent was stable and he had had no chest pain since. He had a nosebleed last month that took a long time to stop.

He did not stop the clopidogrel, writing "clotting normal".
h: He did not stop the clopidogrel, writing "clotting normal"

a.o: Dr. Ayman left Mr. Kareem on clopidogrel before his kidney biopsy.
a.x: Mr. Kareem's clopidogrel should have been stopped seven days before, after checking with his heart doctor.
a.w: Clopidogrel affects platelets, which normal clotting tests do not show. It raises the risk of serious bleeding after a kidney biopsy.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked his blood pressure.
a.w: High blood pressure raises biopsy bleeding risk.

a.o: Dr. Ayman explained the bleeding risk.
a.w: Patients must know the risks before consent.

a.o: Dr. Ayman told him to fast.
a.w: Fasting is needed for a procedure.

t: Febrile baby sent home with oral antibiotics
s:
Baby Yara, 7 weeks old, was brought in with a fever of 38.4°C and poor feeding for a day. She was a little sleepy but woke when handled. Her urine sample, caught clean, showed nitrites and white cells.

Dr. Rana checked her heart rate, which was 172, and her capillary refill, which was 3 seconds. She checked her soft spot, which was not bulging.

She sent the urine for culture and checked her blood sugar.

Her mother said Yara was her first baby and she was frightened. She asked if she could take her home.

Yara was born at term after a normal pregnancy and had been feeding well until yesterday. She had fewer wet nappies today. Her mother had given her no medicines. The department was very busy, and the children's ward had only one bed left.

Dr. Rana diagnosed a urine infection and sent Yara home with oral antibiotics.
h: Dr. Rana diagnosed a urine infection and sent Yara home with oral antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Rana sent Baby Yara home with oral antibiotics.
a.x: Baby Yara should have been admitted for blood tests, IV antibiotics and a full sepsis check.
a.w: Babies under 3 months with a fever are high risk. A urine infection can spread to the blood or brain.

a.o: Dr. Rana felt Baby Yara's soft spot.
a.x: The soft spot was off topic.
a.w: A bulging soft spot can mean meningitis.

a.o: Dr. Rana sent Baby Yara's urine for culture.
a.w: Culture guides treatment in babies.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Baby Yara's sugar.
a.w: Sick babies can have low sugar.

t: Morphine for a dialysis patient
s:
Mr. Sabri, 70, has kidney failure and has dialysis three times a week. He was admitted with a broken hip after a fall. He was in a lot of pain.

Dr. Inas arranged surgery for the next day. She asked the dialysis unit to fit his session around the operation.

She checked his potassium, which was normal, and his blood count.

His wife said he was usually very alert and did crosswords every day.

Mr. Sabri lives with his wife in a flat with a lift and walks with a stick. He had dialysis the day before the fall. He takes a phosphate binder and a blood pressure tablet. His hip was shortened and turned out, and the X-ray showed a broken neck of femur. He was frightened of the operation.

She prescribed morphine 10 mg every four hours as needed.
h: She prescribed morphine 10 mg every four hours as needed

a.o: Dr. Inas gave regular morphine to Mr. Sabri with kidney failure.
a.x: Mr. Sabri should have had a safer painkiller, such as low-dose fentanyl or oxycodone, or a nerve block.
a.w: Morphine's breakdown products build up in kidney failure and cause drowsiness, confusion and slow breathing.

a.o: Dr. Inas arranged surgery quickly.
a.w: Early hip surgery improves recovery.

a.o: Dr. Inas planned dialysis around surgery.
a.w: Missing dialysis is dangerous.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked his potassium.
a.w: High potassium is dangerous during surgery.

t: Naproxen for gout with weak kidneys
s:
Mr. Raouf, 69, woke up with a hot, red, swollen big toe that was too painful to touch with a bedsheet. He has had gout twice before. He has chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 28, high blood pressure and heart failure, and takes furosemide and ramipril.

Dr. Ghada examined the toe and found it very tender, with no break in the skin. He had no fever. His uric acid was high. She checked his last kidney tests and his potassium, which were stable.

She advised him to rest the foot, keep it cool with an ice pack wrapped in a towel, and keep the bedsheets off it with a frame. She told him to keep drinking water.

Mr. Raouf loves seafood and red meat and had been to a family feast two days ago. His wife asked whether he should stop his water tablet, which she had heard can cause gout.

Dr. Ghada prescribed naproxen 500 mg twice a day for a week, "the quickest way to settle gout".
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed naproxen 500 mg twice a day for a week

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave naproxen to Mr. Raouf with an eGFR of 28 and heart failure.
a.x: Mr. Raouf should have had a short course of prednisolone, or low-dose colchicine adjusted for his kidneys.
a.w: NSAIDs can tip weak kidneys into failure and worsen heart failure, especially with ramipril and furosemide.

a.o: Dr. Ghada kept Mr. Raouf's furosemide going.
a.x: The water tablet should have stopped to help the gout.
a.w: His heart failure needs the diuretic; gout is treated in other ways.

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mr. Raouf to put ice on the toe.
a.w: Cooling the joint eases gout pain.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about the family feast.
a.w: Large meals of meat and seafood can trigger gout.

t: Dialysis line fever sent home
s:
Mrs. Inas, 58, has kidney failure and has dialysis through a tunneled line in her neck, while her fistula matures. She had shivers and a fever of 38.7°C during her dialysis session today, an hour after it started. Her blood pressure dropped to 98/60.

Dr. Fady examined the line, and the skin around it was a little red. Her chest was clear and her urine output tiny, as usual. She had no cough, no belly pain and no wounds.

He gave her paracetamol and a small IV fluid bolus, and her blood pressure came back to 118/72. Her shivers settled within an hour.

She lives with her husband, who drives her to dialysis. She said she felt much better and wanted to go home to cook for her grandchildren, who were visiting.

He sent her home with oral co-amoxiclav, without taking blood cultures from the line or a vein.
h: He sent her home with oral co-amoxiclav, without taking blood cultures from the line or a vein

a.o: Dr. Fady sent Mrs. Inas home with oral antibiotics and no cultures for a likely line infection.
a.x: Mrs. Inas should have had blood cultures from the line and a vein, and IV antibiotics covering staph, such as vancomycin, with the line team involved.
a.w: Shivers during dialysis with a tunneled line mean a line infection until proven otherwise, which can cause sepsis and endocarditis.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Inas a small fluid bolus.
a.x: Fluids are dangerous in dialysis patients.
a.w: A small bolus treats low blood pressure safely.

a.o: Dr. Fady examined the skin around the line.
a.x: The line site was off topic.
a.w: Redness can show where the infection starts.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Inas's chest.
a.w: A chest infection is another common cause of fever.

t: Aspirin before a stroke scan
s:
Mr. Fathi, 67, came in by ambulance 50 minutes after his wife saw his face droop and his speech slur at breakfast. His right arm was weak. His sugar was 7.2 and his blood pressure 176/94. He takes metformin and amlodipine.

Dr. Nada called the stroke team at once and worked out his NIHSS score, which was 9. She checked his last-known-well time with his wife and wrote it down.

She asked the nurses to keep him nil by mouth until a swallow screen, and checked his blood count and clotting.

His wife said he was due to fly to Mecca next week and asked whether he would still be able to go. Mr. Fathi was frightened and kept trying to speak.

While waiting for the CT scanner, she gave him 300 mg of aspirin through a drip "to start treatment early".
h: she gave him 300 mg of aspirin through a drip "to start treatment early"

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Fathi aspirin before his brain scan.
a.x: Mr. Fathi should have had an urgent CT scan first, with clot-busting treatment considered, and aspirin only once a bleed was ruled out.
a.w: One in five strokes is a bleed, and aspirin worsens it. Aspirin before scanning can also rule out thrombolysis.

a.o: Dr. Nada wrote down the time Mr. Fathi was last well.
a.w: Clot-busting drugs depend on the time since onset.

a.o: Dr. Nada kept Mr. Fathi nil by mouth.
a.w: Stroke can affect swallowing and food can go into the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Mr. Fathi's sugar.
a.w: Low sugar can look exactly like a stroke.

t: Warning stroke sent home without aspirin
s:
Mrs. Samira, 71, came in because her left hand went weak and numb for 20 minutes yesterday, and she could not hold her cup. It went back to normal by itself. She has high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation, which she was told about last year but chose not to treat.

Dr. Ihab examined her and found her strength and speech normal. Her pulse was irregular, at 88, and her blood pressure was 158/90.

He did a heart tracing, which confirmed atrial fibrillation. He asked about headaches and eye problems, which she did not have.

Mrs. Samira said she was too busy caring for her husband with dementia to go to the hospital. She wanted to wait and see if it happened again.

He booked her into the stroke clinic in six weeks and did not start any treatment.
h: He booked her into the stroke clinic in six weeks and did not start any treatment

a.o: Dr. Ihab sent Mrs. Samira away with no treatment and a clinic in six weeks after a TIA.
a.x: Mrs. Samira should have started aspirin at once and been seen by a stroke specialist within 24 hours, with a blood thinner planned for her AF.
a.w: The risk of a full stroke is highest in the days after a TIA. AF makes the risk even higher.

a.o: Dr. Ihab did a heart tracing.
a.w: AF is a common cause of stroke.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about Mrs. Samira's caring duties.
a.x: Her home life was off topic.
a.w: Understanding barriers helps plan safe care.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Samira's strength again.
a.x: The exam was pointless once she was better.
a.w: A normal exam helps confirm a TIA.

t: Fitting child left without a rescue drug
s:
Ahmed, 6, has epilepsy. He was brought in by ambulance having a seizure that started at home 8 minutes ago. His arms and legs were jerking and his lips were blue. His mother had not given his rescue medicine because she was too frightened.

Dr. Dina put him on his side, gave high-flow oxygen and checked his sugar, which was 5.4. She asked the nurse to time the seizure.

She put in a drip and took bloods, including his drug levels. She asked his mother about his usual medicines and allergies.

His mother said he had been ill with a cold and had missed his evening doses because he was vomiting.

Dr. Dina decided to wait another ten minutes "to see if it stops by itself" before giving any medicine.
h: Dr. Dina decided to wait another ten minutes "to see if it stops by itself"

a.o: Dr. Dina waited longer with Ahmed fitting for 8 minutes.
a.x: Ahmed should have had IV lorazepam or buccal midazolam at once, with a second dose and then a second-line drug if he kept fitting.
a.w: A seizure over 5 minutes is unlikely to stop alone. The longer it lasts, the harder it is to stop and the higher the risk of brain damage.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Ahmed's sugar.
a.w: Low sugar can cause fits.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked the nurse to time the seizure.
a.w: The length of the seizure guides treatment.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked about missed doses.
a.w: Missed doses are a common cause of fits.

t: Valproate for a young woman without a plan
s:
Miss Reem, 19, had her first two seizures this year. Her EEG showed generalized epilepsy. She has myoclonic jerks in the mornings. She is a university student and has a boyfriend. She is not on contraception.

Dr. Mervat explained the diagnosis clearly and gave her advice on sleep, alcohol and showering instead of bathing.

She told her she could not drive until she had been seizure-free for a year, and to tell the licensing authority.

Miss Reem asked whether she could still have children one day. Dr. Mervat said most women with epilepsy have healthy babies.

She started sodium valproate, "the best drug for her type", without discussing pregnancy or contraception.
h: She started sodium valproate, "the best drug for her type", without discussing pregnancy or contraception

a.o: Dr. Mervat started valproate in Miss Reem without discussing pregnancy.
a.x: Miss Reem should have been offered another drug, such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam. Valproate is only used if nothing else works, with a pregnancy prevention plan.
a.w: Valproate in pregnancy causes birth defects in 1 in 10 babies and learning problems in up to 4 in 10.

a.o: Dr. Mervat told Miss Reem not to drive.
a.w: Seizures while driving can kill.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised showers instead of baths.
a.w: People with epilepsy can drown in the bath during a seizure.

a.o: Dr. Mervat said most women with epilepsy have healthy babies.
a.w: With planning, most do.

t: Guillain-Barre watched with oxygen levels only
s:
Mr. Hossam, 35, was admitted with tingling in his feet and hands, then weakness climbing up his legs over three days. He had diarrhea two weeks ago. Today he could not stand. His reflexes were absent.

Dr. Ayman diagnosed Guillain-Barre syndrome and started IV immunoglobulin. He asked for a heart monitor because the illness can affect heart rhythm.

He gave blood thinner injections to prevent clots and asked the physiotherapist to see him.

Mr. Hossam's voice was a little weak and he coughed when drinking water. His wife asked if he would walk again.

Dr. Ayman asked the nurses to check his oxygen levels every four hours, saying "his sats are 98%, his breathing is fine".
h: asked the nurses to check his oxygen levels every four hours, saying "his sats are 98%, his breathing is fine"

a.o: Dr. Ayman relied on oxygen levels to watch Mr. Hossam's breathing.
a.x: Mr. Hossam should have had his forced vital capacity measured every few hours, with ICU review if it fell.
a.w: Oxygen stays normal until breathing muscles fail suddenly. FVC falls first and warns of the need for a ventilator.

a.o: Dr. Ayman started immunoglobulin.
a.w: IVIG speeds recovery in GBS.

a.o: Dr. Ayman put Mr. Hossam on a heart monitor.
a.w: GBS can cause dangerous heart rhythm changes.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave blood thinners.
a.w: Immobile patients are at high risk of clots.

t: Gentamicin in myasthenia
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 52, has myasthenia gravis and takes pyridostigmine four times a day and a low dose of prednisolone. She was admitted with a kidney infection, with a fever of 38.8°C, shivers and pain in her right side. Her blood pressure was 112/70 and her pulse 104.

Dr. Fouad sent blood and urine cultures and gave IV fluids. He checked her kidney function, which was normal, and did an ultrasound, which showed no blockage.

He asked about her myasthenia, which had been stable for a year, with no drooping eyelids, double vision or trouble swallowing. He measured her breathing strength at the bedside, which was normal.

She works as a librarian and said she gets weak and slurred if her tablets are late. She asked the nurses to give them exactly on time, and Dr. Fouad wrote this on her chart.

He started IV gentamicin, writing "the best cover for kidney infections".
h: He started IV gentamicin, writing "the best cover for kidney infections"

a.o: Dr. Fouad gave gentamicin to Mrs. Nadia with myasthenia gravis.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have had a safer antibiotic, such as IV ceftriaxone.
a.w: Gentamicin blocks the nerve-muscle junction and can cause a myasthenic crisis with breathing failure.

a.o: Dr. Fouad measured Mrs. Nadia's breathing strength.
a.x: Her breathing was fine, so the test was a waste.
a.w: Infection can bring on a crisis, and breathing strength shows it early.

a.o: Dr. Fouad wrote Mrs. Nadia's tablet times on her chart.
a.x: The timing of her tablets doesn't matter.
a.w: Late pyridostigmine can cause weakness within hours.

a.o: Dr. Fouad did a kidney ultrasound.
a.w: A blocked kidney with infection needs urgent drainage.

t: Facial weakness sparing the forehead
s:
Mr. Hany, 63, woke with the right side of his mouth drooping and dribbling when he drank tea. He could raise both eyebrows and wrinkle his forehead evenly. When asked, he said his right hand had felt clumsy doing up his buttons. He has high blood pressure and smokes 20 a day.

Dr. Abeer looked in his right ear for blisters of shingles and found none. His blood pressure was 178/96 and his sugar 6.1.

She asked about recent colds, ear pain and changes in taste, which he did not have. She noted when he was last seen well: at 11 the night before, when he went to bed.

His daughter said his speech sounded slightly slurred, but he insisted he felt fine and wanted to go back to his shop.

She diagnosed Bell's palsy, started prednisolone and eye drops, and sent him home.
h: She diagnosed Bell's palsy, started prednisolone and eye drops, and sent him home

a.o: Dr. Abeer called Mr. Hany's facial weakness Bell's palsy though his forehead was spared.
a.x: Mr. Hany should have been treated as a stroke, with an urgent brain scan and stroke team review.
a.w: Bell's palsy weakens the whole side of the face. Sparing the forehead, with a clumsy hand and slurred speech, points to a stroke.

a.o: Dr. Abeer looked in Mr. Hany's ear for blisters.
a.w: Shingles of the facial nerve shows blisters in the ear.

a.o: Dr. Abeer noted when Mr. Hany was last seen well.
a.x: The time didn't matter for a face droop.
a.w: Stroke treatment depends on the time since onset.

a.o: Dr. Abeer listened to the daughter about his speech.
a.w: Family often notice changes the patient misses.

t: Giant cell arteritis steroids delayed
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 74, came in with a new headache on her right temple for three weeks. Her scalp hurt when she combed her hair, and her jaw ached when she chewed bread. Yesterday her vision in the right eye went blurry for a few minutes. Her ESR was 88 and her CRP high.

Dr. Rehab felt a tender, thick, pulseless artery on her right temple. She checked her vision and eye movements, which were normal today.

She booked a temporal artery biopsy for the next week and an ultrasound of the temple arteries. She also asked about shoulder stiffness in the mornings, which Mrs. Fawzia had.

Mrs. Fawzia had lost 3 kg and felt tired. She lives alone and was frightened, asking whether she would go blind.

Dr. Rehab told her to wait for the biopsy before starting steroids, "so the result is clear".
h: Dr. Rehab told her to wait for the biopsy before starting steroids

a.o: Dr. Rehab held back steroids from Mrs. Fawzia until her biopsy.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have started high-dose prednisolone that day, with the biopsy done within two weeks.
a.w: With visual symptoms, giant cell arteritis can cause sudden, permanent blindness. The biopsy stays positive for weeks after steroids start.

a.o: Dr. Rehab felt Mrs. Fawzia's temple.
a.w: A thick, tender, pulseless artery supports the diagnosis.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked Mrs. Fawzia about morning shoulder stiffness.
a.w: Polymyalgia often comes with giant cell arteritis.

a.o: Dr. Rehab booked an ultrasound of the temple arteries.
a.w: Ultrasound can show swollen artery walls quickly.

t: Morning headache with blurred discs
s:
Miss Lina, 24, came in with headaches every morning for a month. They were worse when she bent over or coughed, and she sometimes vomited on waking. She had put on 8 kg this year. She takes the combined pill and had started doxycycline for acne two months ago.

Dr. Ghada looked in her eyes with an ophthalmoscope and saw swollen optic discs on both sides. Her blood pressure was normal, and her arms and legs were strong.

She asked about her vision, and Miss Lina said it went gray for a few seconds when she stood up quickly. She also heard a whooshing sound in her ears at night.

Miss Lina is a law student and was stressed about exams. She asked for stronger painkillers so she could study.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed tension headaches, advised her on stress and posture, and prescribed co-codamol.
h: Dr. Ghada diagnosed tension headaches, advised her on stress and posture, and prescribed co-codamol

a.o: Dr. Ghada called Miss Lina's headaches tension headaches despite swollen optic discs.
a.x: Miss Lina should have been sent for an urgent brain scan the same day, with an eye review.
a.w: Swollen discs with morning headaches mean raised pressure in the skull, from a tumor, a clot in a brain vein, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

a.o: Dr. Ghada looked in Miss Lina's eyes.
a.x: An eye check was unnecessary for headaches.
a.w: Swollen discs are the key sign of raised pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about the whooshing sound.
a.w: A pulsing sound is common with raised pressure in the skull.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about Miss Lina's medicines.
a.x: Her acne tablets were off topic.
a.w: Doxycycline and the pill can both play a part in raised pressure or vein clots.

t: Parkinson's tablets missed while nil by mouth
s:
Mr. Sami, 76, has had Parkinson's disease for nine years and takes co-careldopa four times a day at fixed times. He was admitted with a bowel blockage. The surgeons kept him nil by mouth and put a tube through his nose to drain his stomach.

Dr. Hala gave him IV fluids and checked his salts and kidney tests. She asked the surgeons to review him the same day, and they planned to wait 48 hours to see if the blockage cleared.

She asked the nurses for a falls risk check and a pressure mattress, as he was frail.

His wife said he gets very stiff, cannot swallow and becomes confused if he misses even one dose. She brought in his tablets and timetable.

Dr. Hala stopped all his tablets, writing "nil by mouth".
h: Dr. Hala stopped all his tablets, writing "nil by mouth"

a.o: Dr. Hala stopped Mr. Sami's Parkinson's medicine while he was nil by mouth.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have kept his levodopa, given through the nose tube with the tube clamped briefly, or a rotigotine skin patch.
a.w: Missing Parkinson's medicine can cause severe stiffness, swallowing problems, pneumonia and a dangerous reaction like neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked for a pressure mattress.
a.w: Frail, stiff patients get pressure sores quickly.

a.o: Dr. Hala let the surgeons wait 48 hours.
a.x: Every blockage needs surgery at once.
a.w: Many adhesion blockages settle with drip and suck.

a.o: Dr. Hala looked at the timetable Mr. Sami's wife brought.
a.x: A home timetable was off topic.
a.w: Parkinson's medicines must be given at the patient's own times.

t: Metoclopramide in Parkinson's disease
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 72, has Parkinson's disease and takes co-beneldopa. She was admitted after a fall with a broken wrist, which was set in plaster. After her pain medicines she felt very sick and vomited twice.

Dr. Mai checked her salts and sugar, which were normal, and listened to her belly, which was soft with normal sounds. She swapped her morphine for a smaller dose to ease the nausea.

She made sure Mrs. Hanem's Parkinson's tablets were given on time and asked the physiotherapist to check her walking before discharge.

Her son said his mother hates being sick and asked for "the strongest anti-sickness injection". Mrs. Hanem was trembling and anxious.

Dr. Mai prescribed metoclopramide 10 mg three times a day as needed.
h: Dr. Mai prescribed metoclopramide 10 mg three times a day as needed

a.o: Dr. Mai gave Mrs. Hanem metoclopramide for nausea in Parkinson's disease.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem should have had domperidone or ondansetron instead.
a.w: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine in the brain and can make Parkinson's much worse, with stiffness and falls.

a.o: Dr. Mai cut Mrs. Hanem's morphine dose.
a.x: The dose should have stayed the same.
a.w: Opioids often cause nausea in older people.

a.o: Dr. Mai gave Mrs. Hanem's Parkinson's tablets on time.
a.x: The timing doesn't matter in hospital.
a.w: Late doses cause stiffness and falls.

a.o: Dr. Mai asked the physiotherapist to check her walking.
a.x: Walking was off topic with a wrist fracture.
a.w: Falls in Parkinson's are common, and a plaster changes balance.

t: Glucose before thiamine in a heavy drinker
s:
Mr. Medhat, 55, was brought in by the police after being found confused in the street. He smelled of alcohol. He was unsteady and could not walk in a straight line, and his eyes flickered when he looked to the side. His sugar was 2.9.

Dr. Rehab checked his airway and breathing, which were fine, and looked for head injuries, finding only a graze. She asked for a CT scan of his head.

She sent blood tests, including his liver function, salts and alcohol level, and put him on a monitor.

His brother arrived and said Mr. Medhat drinks a bottle of spirits a day and hardly eats. He had been like this since his wife died last year.

To treat the low sugar, Dr. Rehab gave him a glucose drip first, and planned to give thiamine "once he's stable".
h: Dr. Rehab gave him a glucose drip first, and planned to give thiamine "once he's stable"

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Medhat glucose before thiamine.
a.x: Mr. Medhat should have had IV thiamine (Pabrinex) straight away, with or before the glucose.
a.w: Glucose without thiamine can bring on or worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy, causing permanent memory loss.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked for a CT head.
a.x: The scan was unnecessary in a drinker.
a.w: Drinkers often fall and can have a hidden brain bleed.

a.o: Dr. Rehab looked at Mr. Medhat's eye movements.
a.w: Flickering eyes, confusion and unsteadiness point to Wernicke's.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mr. Medhat's salts.
a.w: Low sodium and magnesium are common in heavy drinkers.

t: First seizure and told he can drive
s:
Mr. Tarek, 32, came in after a fit at work yesterday. His colleagues saw him stiffen and jerk for about a minute, and he bit his tongue. He was confused for 20 minutes after. He had been working night shifts and sleeping badly.

Dr. Ihab examined him and found nothing abnormal. His blood tests, including sugar and salts, were normal. He referred him to the first seizure clinic within two weeks.

He advised him not to swim alone, to shower instead of bath, and to avoid heights at work until he was seen.

Mr. Tarek works as a delivery driver and said he would lose his job if he could not drive. He asked whether one seizure really counted.

Dr. Ihab told him he could carry on driving "because it was probably caused by tiredness".
h: Dr. Ihab told him he could carry on driving "because it was probably caused by tiredness"

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mr. Tarek he could keep driving after a first seizure.
a.x: Mr. Tarek should have been told to stop driving and to tell the licensing authority, usually for six months after a first seizure.
a.w: A seizure at the wheel can kill the driver and others. Sleep loss can trigger seizures but doesn't remove the risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab referred Mr. Tarek to a seizure clinic.
a.x: One fit doesn't need a specialist.
a.w: A first seizure needs specialist review and tests.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mr. Tarek to shower instead of bath.
a.w: People can drown in a bath during a seizure.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about Mr. Tarek's sleep.
a.w: Lack of sleep can trigger seizures.

t: Head injury on warfarin sent home
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 80, tripped on a rug at home and hit her head on a table. She did not pass out. She has a small bump above her left eye and a mild headache. She takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation, and her INR last week was 2.6.

Dr. Hamed found her alert, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 and no weakness. Her pupils were equal. He cleaned the cut and closed it with glue.

He checked her eyesight and her neck, which were fine, and asked about the rug. He asked the falls team to visit her home.

Her daughter said her mother lives alone but she could stay with her tonight. Mrs. Nawal wanted to go home and was cross about the fuss.

Dr. Hamed sent her home with head injury advice, without a CT scan, because "her GCS is 15".
h: Dr. Hamed sent her home with head injury advice, without a CT scan, because "her GCS is 15"

a.o: Dr. Hamed sent Mrs. Nawal home on warfarin after a head injury without a CT scan.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have had a CT scan of the head within eight hours, with an INR check.
a.w: People on blood thinners can have a slow brain bleed even if they seem well at first.

a.o: Dr. Hamed asked the falls team to visit.
a.w: Preventing the next fall matters.

a.o: Dr. Hamed closed the cut with glue.
a.x: Glue is not safe on the face.
a.w: Glue is fine for small face cuts.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked Mrs. Nawal's neck.
a.w: Head injuries can come with neck injuries.

t: Migraine with aura on the combined pill
s:
Miss Sara, 23, came in with headaches. She described zigzag lines in her vision for 20 minutes, followed by a throbbing headache on one side with nausea. This happens twice a month. She has taken the combined pill for three years.

Dr. Ghada examined her and found nothing abnormal. She checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her eyes.

She prescribed sumatriptan and an anti-sickness tablet, and advised her to keep a headache diary and avoid skipping meals.

Miss Sara said she liked the pill because her periods were lighter and her skin was better. She did not want to change it.

Dr. Ghada continued the combined pill, saying "the migraines aren't caused by it".
h: Dr. Ghada continued the combined pill, saying "the migraines aren't caused by it"

a.o: Dr. Ghada kept Miss Sara on the combined pill with migraine with aura.
a.x: Miss Sara should have stopped the combined pill and been offered a method without estrogen, such as a progestogen-only pill or coil.
a.w: Estrogen with migraine with aura raises the risk of stroke.

a.o: Dr. Ghada prescribed sumatriptan.
a.x: Triptans are dangerous in young women.
a.w: Triptans are standard migraine treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised a headache diary.
a.w: A diary helps find triggers.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised not skipping meals.
a.w: Hunger is a common migraine trigger.

t: More codeine for daily headaches
s:
Mrs. Rasha, 41, came in with daily headaches for four months. She had had migraines for years, but now she had a dull headache almost every day. She takes co-codamol most days and ibuprofen when it is bad, about 20 days a month.

Dr. Ihab examined her and found nothing abnormal. Her blood pressure and eyes were normal.

He asked about stress, sleep and caffeine. She drinks five cups of coffee a day and sleeps badly.

Mrs. Rasha is a nurse on night shifts and said the headaches were stopping her working. She asked for something stronger.

Dr. Ihab increased her co-codamol to the higher strength and told her to take it whenever she needed.
h: Dr. Ihab increased her co-codamol to the higher strength and told her to take it whenever she needed

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mrs. Rasha stronger co-codamol for daily headaches.
a.x: Mrs. Rasha should have been told she had medication overuse headache and helped to stop the painkillers, with migraine prevention started.
a.w: Painkillers on 10 to 15 days a month or more can cause daily headaches. More painkillers make it worse.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about caffeine.
a.w: Too much caffeine can cause headaches.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her eyes.
a.w: Swollen discs would mean raised pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about sleep.
a.w: Poor sleep worsens headaches.

t: Confusion after a fall called dementia
s:
Mr. Kamal, 82, has mild dementia and lives in a care home. He fell three weeks ago and hit his head. Since then he has become more confused and sleepy, and his left leg is weaker. He takes aspirin and clopidogrel.

Dr. Mervat checked his urine and chest, which were clear. His blood tests were normal apart from a mild anemia.

She asked the care home staff, who said he used to walk to the dining room alone but now needs two people.

His son said his father had been "slipping away" and asked whether this was just the dementia getting worse.

Dr. Mervat said it was likely "progression of dementia" and did not arrange a scan.
h: Dr. Mervat said it was likely "progression of dementia" and did not arrange a scan

a.o: Dr. Mervat blamed Mr. Kamal's new confusion and weakness on dementia.
a.x: Mr. Kamal should have had a CT scan of the head.
a.w: A fall weeks before, new weakness and confusion on blood thinners point to a chronic subdural hematoma, which can be drained.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked his urine and chest.
a.w: Infections are common causes of confusion.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked the care home staff.
a.w: Staff know his usual abilities.

a.o: Dr. Mervat noticed his anemia.
a.w: Blood thinners can cause bleeding.

t: Tight carotid narrowing not referred
s:
Mr. Raouf, 66, had a TIA two weeks ago, with weakness in his right hand and trouble finding words for 30 minutes. A scan of his neck arteries showed 80% narrowing of his left carotid artery.

Dr. Fady started aspirin and clopidogrel, a high-dose statin, and treated his blood pressure. He advised him to stop smoking.

He told him not to drive for a month and checked his sugar, which was normal.

Mr. Raouf said he was afraid of operations and asked whether tablets would be enough.

He is a retired army officer and walks two miles every morning. His heart tracing showed a normal rhythm. He had had his hernia repaired under general anesthetic years ago without problems. His wife said she would rather he had whatever gave him the best chance of avoiding a big stroke.

Dr. Fady agreed tablets were enough and did not refer him to a vascular surgeon.
h: Dr. Fady agreed tablets were enough and did not refer him to a vascular surgeon

a.o: Dr. Fady didn't refer Mr. Raouf for carotid surgery after a TIA with 80% narrowing.
a.x: Mr. Raouf should have been referred to a vascular surgeon to consider surgery within two weeks.
a.w: Surgery on a tight, symptomatic carotid narrowing greatly lowers the risk of a major stroke.

a.o: Dr. Fady started a statin.
a.w: Statins lower stroke risk.

a.o: Dr. Fady told him not to drive.
a.w: Driving rules apply after a TIA.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised stopping smoking.
a.w: Smoking raises stroke risk.

t: Stroke patient fed without a swallow test
s:
Mrs. Amal, 75, was admitted with a stroke affecting her left side. She was drowsy but rousable. Her speech was slurred and she was dribbling. A CT showed a clot, not a bleed.

Dr. Ayman started aspirin through a nasogastric tube and asked the stroke nurses to check her blood pressure and sugar.

He asked the physiotherapist to see her and arranged a pressure mattress.

Her daughter brought her favorite soup and asked to feed her mother.

Mrs. Amal lives with her husband, who has heart failure, and she is usually his main carer. She was a keen cook and had made the same lentil soup for her family for fifty years. When the nurse gave her a sip of water earlier, she coughed and her voice sounded wet and gurgly afterwards.

Dr. Ayman said she could have the soup, without a swallow screen.
h: Dr. Ayman said she could have the soup, without a swallow screen

a.o: Dr. Ayman let Mrs. Amal eat before a swallow test.
a.x: Mrs. Amal should have stayed nil by mouth until a swallow screen.
a.w: Stroke can affect swallowing, and food or drink can go into the lungs, causing pneumonia.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave Mrs. Amal's aspirin through a nose tube.
a.x: Aspirin should wait until she can swallow.
a.w: Aspirin is given early once a bleed is ruled out, by tube or suppository if needed.

a.o: Dr. Ayman arranged a pressure mattress for Mrs. Amal.
a.x: The mattress could wait a week.
a.w: Weak, drowsy stroke patients get pressure sores quickly.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked the physiotherapist to see Mrs. Amal early.
a.x: Therapy should wait until she is stronger.
a.w: Early, gentle therapy helps stroke recovery.

t: Encephalitis treated without aciclovir
s:
Mrs. Nesma, 48, came in with fever, headache and strange behavior for two days. She was confused and had a fit in the ambulance. Her CT scan was normal. Her lumbar puncture showed raised white cells, mainly lymphocytes.

Dr. Dina gave her IV ceftriaxone and a seizure medicine. She asked for an MRI and an EEG.

She asked for the spinal fluid to be tested for viruses with PCR.

Her husband said she had been talking nonsense and smelling things that weren't there.

She works as an accountant and had no recent travel. She has no allergies and takes no regular medicines. Her kidney function was normal. Her blood pressure was 132/80 and her neck was only mildly stiff. The MRI had a waiting list until the next morning.

Dr. Dina did not start aciclovir, writing "await viral PCR".
h: Dr. Dina did not start aciclovir, writing "await viral PCR"

a.o: Dr. Dina held back aciclovir from Mrs. Nesma until the PCR came back.
a.x: Mrs. Nesma should have had IV aciclovir at once.
a.w: Fever, confusion, fits and smell changes suggest herpes encephalitis. Every hour without aciclovir raises the risk of death and brain damage.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked for an MRI.
a.w: MRI can show changes from encephalitis.

a.o: Dr. Dina gave a seizure medicine.
a.w: Seizures must be controlled.

a.o: Dr. Dina sent PCR.
a.w: PCR confirms the virus.

t: Brain bleed without nimodipine
s:
Mr. Waleed, 45, was admitted with a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a burst brain aneurysm. The aneurysm was coiled today. He is awake and talking.

Dr. Hossam asked for neurological checks every hour and kept his blood pressure steady.

He gave him IV fluids to keep him well hydrated and checked his sodium.

His wife asked whether he would have more bleeding.

Mr. Waleed is a bank manager and had a sudden thunderclap headache while playing tennis. He smokes and has high blood pressure, which he had not been treating. His blood pressure now was 138/82. His mother had died young of a stroke. He was alert and had no weakness, though his headache was still bad.

Dr. Hossam did not prescribe nimodipine, writing "aneurysm secured".
h: Dr. Hossam did not prescribe nimodipine, writing "aneurysm secured"

a.o: Dr. Hossam didn't give nimodipine after Mr. Waleed's subarachnoid hemorrhage.
a.x: Mr. Waleed should have had nimodipine for 21 days.
a.w: Nimodipine reduces brain damage from narrowing of the arteries after a bleed.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked for hourly neurological checks on Mr. Waleed.
a.x: Once the aneurysm is coiled, checks can stop.
a.w: A drop in alertness can mean artery spasm or fluid build-up.

a.o: Dr. Hossam kept Mr. Waleed well hydrated.
a.x: Fluids should be cut to protect the brain.
a.w: Dehydration worsens artery narrowing after a bleed.

a.o: Dr. Hossam checked Mr. Waleed's sodium.
a.w: Low sodium is common after a brain bleed.

t: Antipsychotic first for agitation in dementia
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 85, has Alzheimer's disease and was admitted with a urine infection. At night she became agitated, calling out and trying to get out of bed.

Dr. Rana treated the infection and checked her pain, which seemed to be from constipation. She gave her a laxative.

She asked the nurses to keep the lights low and to have a familiar person nearby.

Her daughter said her mother calms down with music and familiar photos.

Mrs. Fawzia was a retired music teacher and still hummed the songs she used to teach. At home she sleeps well with her own blanket and a night light. She had a small stroke two years ago and takes aspirin. The night nurses were busy and asked for something to calm her.

Dr. Rana prescribed regular haloperidol at night "to keep her settled".
h: Dr. Rana prescribed regular haloperidol at night "to keep her settled"

a.o: Dr. Rana started regular haloperidol for Mrs. Fawzia's agitation.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have had the causes treated and calming care, with antipsychotics only as a last resort, at the lowest dose and for a short time.
a.w: Antipsychotics in dementia raise the risk of stroke, falls and death.

a.o: Dr. Rana treated Mrs. Fawzia's constipation.
a.w: Pain and constipation often cause agitation in dementia.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked for someone familiar to sit with Mrs. Fawzia.
a.w: Familiar people calm patients with dementia.

a.o: Dr. Rana treated Mrs. Fawzia's urine infection.
a.x: The infection was not linked to her behavior.
a.w: Infection often causes sudden confusion in dementia.

t: Phenytoin pushed without a heart monitor
s:
Mr. Samy, 61, was admitted after a run of seizures. He had two doses of lorazepam in the ambulance and was now drowsy but not fitting. He has heart disease and takes bisoprolol. His sugar and salts were normal.

Dr. Ayman decided to load him with IV phenytoin to stop more seizures. He worked out the dose by his weight, 82 kg, and checked that he had no allergy.

He checked a heart tracing before starting, which showed a slow but normal rhythm of 56. He asked the nurses to check his breathing and oxygen every 15 minutes.

The ward was short of monitors, and the only one was in use for another patient. Mr. Samy's son asked whether his father would have more fits.

Dr. Ayman gave the phenytoin by a quick push over five minutes, without a heart monitor, "to get it in before the next fit".
h: Dr. Ayman gave the phenytoin by a quick push over five minutes, without a heart monitor

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave Mr. Samy IV phenytoin fast and without a heart monitor.
a.x: Mr. Samy should have had phenytoin given slowly, no faster than 50 mg a minute, with heart and blood pressure monitoring throughout, or a drug like levetiracetam instead.
a.w: Fast IV phenytoin can cause low blood pressure, slow heart rhythms and cardiac arrest, especially with heart disease and a beta blocker.

a.o: Dr. Ayman dosed phenytoin by Mr. Samy's weight.
a.w: Phenytoin loading doses are worked out by weight.

a.o: Dr. Ayman did a heart tracing first.
a.x: The tracing was a waste of time.
a.w: A baseline tracing shows heart block that makes phenytoin dangerous.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked for breathing checks every 15 minutes.
a.x: Checks were not needed once the fits stopped.
a.w: Lorazepam and fits can both slow breathing.

t: Lumbar puncture on rivaroxaban
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 57, was admitted with confusion and a low fever for a day. Her CT head was normal. The team planned a lumbar puncture to check for meningitis or encephalitis. She takes rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation, last taken this morning.

Dr. Mervat had already started IV ceftriaxone and aciclovir so treatment would not be delayed. She checked her platelets, which were normal, and her kidney function, which was mildly reduced.

She explained the procedure to Mrs. Asmaa's husband, as Mrs. Asmaa was too confused to consent, and wrote the decision down as being in her best interests.

Her husband said she had a heart stent five years ago but no recent clots. He asked whether the test was painful.

Dr. Mervat did the lumbar puncture that afternoon, six hours after the rivaroxaban dose, writing "clotting tests normal".
h: Dr. Mervat did the lumbar puncture that afternoon, six hours after the rivaroxaban dose

a.o: Dr. Mervat did Mrs. Asmaa's lumbar puncture six hours after rivaroxaban.
a.x: The lumbar puncture should have waited until about 48 hours after the last dose with weaker kidneys, while antibiotics and aciclovir continued.
a.w: A bleed around the spinal cord after a lumbar puncture on a blood thinner can cause paralysis. Normal clotting tests do not show rivaroxaban's effect.

a.o: Dr. Mervat started antibiotics and aciclovir before the lumbar puncture.
a.x: Treatment should wait for the spinal fluid.
a.w: Treatment should never be delayed for a lumbar puncture.

a.o: Dr. Mervat acted in Mrs. Asmaa's best interests.
a.x: She should have waited until Mrs. Asmaa could consent.
a.w: When a patient lacks capacity, urgent tests can be done in their best interests.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Asmaa's kidney function.
a.w: Rivaroxaban lasts longer when the kidneys are weak.

t: Spinal injury patient laid flat with a pounding headache
s:
Mr. Karim, 29, has a spinal cord injury at the level of his upper chest after a car crash two years ago. He was in hospital for a pressure sore. This afternoon he suddenly had a pounding headache, a blocked nose and sweating above his chest. His blood pressure was 210/120 and his pulse 52.

Dr. Hala recognized that his usual blood pressure was about 100/60. She checked his catheter bag, which was empty, and saw that the tube was kinked under his leg.

She asked the nurse to loosen his tight leg straps and checked his skin for any new pressure area.

Mr. Karim said this had happened once before when his bladder was full. He was frightened and his face was flushed.

Dr. Hala laid him flat to rest and gave him a pain-relief tablet for the headache, saying she would come back after the round.
h: Dr. Hala laid him flat to rest and gave him a pain-relief tablet for the headache

a.o: Dr. Hala laid Mr. Karim flat and left him with very high blood pressure.
a.x: Mr. Karim should have been sat upright with legs down, his catheter unkinked at once, and his blood pressure checked every few minutes, with a fast-acting medicine like nifedipine if it stayed high.
a.w: This is autonomic dysreflexia. The blood pressure can cause a stroke or fits within minutes unless the trigger, often a blocked bladder, is removed.

a.o: Dr. Hala compared Mr. Karim's blood pressure with his usual.
a.x: His usual reading was off topic.
a.w: People with high spinal injuries usually have low blood pressure, so 210 is a huge rise.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked the nurse to loosen Mr. Karim's leg straps.
a.w: Tight clothing below the injury can trigger dysreflexia.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked Mr. Karim's catheter.
a.w: A blocked bladder is the most common trigger.

t: Ectopic pregnancy called period pain
s:
Miss Nour, 26, came in with pain low on her left side for a day and some brown spotting. Her last period was six weeks ago, and she said her periods are often irregular. She had chlamydia two years ago. Her urine pregnancy test was positive.

Dr. Inas checked her pulse, which was 96, and her blood pressure, which was 112/70. Her belly was tender on the left, low down, and she felt pain at the tip of her shoulder when lying flat.

She gave her paracetamol and sent a blood test for hCG. She asked about her contraception, and Miss Nour said she had a coil fitted a year ago.

Miss Nour works in a call center and was worried about missing her shift. She said she had heavy period pains every month and this felt similar.

Dr. Inas told her it was likely period pain from an early miscarriage, and sent her home to wait for the hCG result the next day, without arranging a scan.
h: sent her home to wait for the hCG result the next day, without arranging a scan

a.o: Dr. Inas sent Miss Nour home with a positive test and one-sided pain without a scan.
a.x: Miss Nour should have had an urgent pelvic ultrasound the same day and stayed in until an ectopic pregnancy was ruled out.
a.w: One-sided pain, spotting, shoulder-tip pain and a past chlamydia infection point to an ectopic pregnancy, which can burst and bleed fatally.

a.o: Dr. Inas sent an hCG blood test.
a.w: A blood level helps judge the pregnancy with the scan.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about the coil.
a.x: A coil means she can't be pregnant.
a.w: Pregnancies with a coil are more likely to be ectopic.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about shoulder-tip pain.
a.w: Blood in the belly can cause shoulder-tip pain.

t: High blood pressure in pregnancy sent home
s:
Mrs. Yasmin, 32, is 35 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She came to the antenatal clinic with a headache for two days and flashing lights in her eyes. Her feet and face had swollen in the last week. Her blood pressure was 162/110 and her urine showed 2+ protein.

Dr. Soha checked the baby's heartbeat, which was normal, and felt her belly, which was tender just under the ribs on the right. Her reflexes were brisk.

She sent blood tests for her liver, kidneys and platelets, and gave her paracetamol for the headache.

Mrs. Yasmin is a pharmacist and had a busy week at work. Her husband was away, and she asked whether she could go home and rest instead of staying.

Dr. Soha started labetalol tablets and sent her home, asking her to come back in two days for a blood pressure check.
h: Dr. Soha started labetalol tablets and sent her home, asking her to come back in two days

a.o: Dr. Soha sent Mrs. Yasmin home with severe pre-eclampsia.
a.x: Mrs. Yasmin should have been admitted for blood pressure control, magnesium sulfate and planning for delivery.
a.w: A blood pressure of 160/110 with headache, visual signs, right upper belly pain and protein means severe pre-eclampsia, which can cause fits, strokes and liver rupture.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked the baby's heartbeat.
a.w: Pre-eclampsia can affect the baby's growth and well-being.

a.o: Dr. Soha started labetalol.
a.x: Blood pressure should not be lowered in pregnancy.
a.w: Labetalol is the first choice for high blood pressure in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Soha sent liver tests.
a.w: Pre-eclampsia can damage the liver and lower platelets.

t: Fit in pregnancy treated with diazepam only
s:
Mrs. Heba, 28, is 37 weeks pregnant. She had a fit in the antenatal ward. Her blood pressure was 168/112 and her urine had 3+ protein. She had complained of a headache all morning.

Dr. Soha turned her onto her left side, gave oxygen and called the senior obstetrician and anesthetist. The fit stopped after two minutes.

She gave labetalol through a drip to lower her blood pressure and checked the baby's heartbeat, which was slow during the fit but recovered.

Mrs. Heba's mother was waiting outside and was terrified. She asked whether her daughter had epilepsy.

Dr. Soha gave IV diazepam to stop more fits, and did not start magnesium sulfate.
h: Dr. Soha gave IV diazepam to stop more fits, and did not start magnesium sulfate

a.o: Dr. Soha used diazepam for Mrs. Heba's eclamptic fit and gave no magnesium.
a.x: Mrs. Heba should have had IV magnesium sulfate, a loading dose then a drip, with delivery planned once she was stable.
a.w: Magnesium is the drug that prevents and treats eclamptic fits. It works better than diazepam or phenytoin.

a.o: Dr. Soha turned Mrs. Heba onto her left side.
a.x: She should have been laid flat on her back.
a.w: Lying on the left side stops the womb pressing on the big vein.

a.o: Dr. Soha lowered Mrs. Heba's blood pressure.
a.x: Blood pressure is not urgent after a fit.
a.w: Very high blood pressure can cause a stroke.

a.o: Dr. Soha called the senior obstetrician.
a.x: The junior doctor could manage alone.
a.w: Eclampsia needs a team.

t: Postpartum bleed while waiting for blood
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 30, delivered her third baby an hour ago. She suddenly started bleeding heavily, and the midwife estimated 1,000 mL of blood loss. Her pulse was 118 and her blood pressure 98/60. Her uterus felt soft and boggy above her belly button.

Dr. Rana called for help and put in two large drips. She sent blood for crossmatch and a blood count.

She checked the placenta, which was complete, and looked for tears, finding only a small graze.

Mrs. Nadia's husband was holding the baby and asked why there was so much blood. He was pale himself.

Dr. Rana started IV fluids and waited for the blood to arrive, without rubbing the uterus or giving any drug to make it contract.
h: without rubbing the uterus or giving any drug to make it contract

a.o: Dr. Rana didn't massage Mrs. Nadia's uterus or give drugs to make it contract.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have had the uterus rubbed firmly and been given oxytocin, then ergometrine, carboprost or misoprostol if needed, plus tranexamic acid.
a.w: A soft uterus is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Making it contract stops the bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked the placenta was complete.
a.w: A piece left inside can cause bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Rana put in two large drips.
a.w: Heavy bleeding needs fast fluids and blood.

a.o: Dr. Rana looked for tears.
a.w: Tears are another cause of bleeding after birth.

t: Rhesus-negative bleed without anti-D
s:
Mrs. Rana, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant with her second baby. She came in with light bleeding after falling on the stairs. She has no pain. Her blood group is O negative, and her husband is A positive. The baby's heartbeat was normal on the scan.

Dr. Ihab examined her and found no tenderness. The scan showed the placenta was high and the baby was well.

He checked the size of the bleed and explained that light bleeding after a fall is often minor. He advised her to rest for a day.

Mrs. Rana said she had anti-D injections in her first pregnancy and did not like needles. She asked whether she needed one this time.

He told her the bleed was small and sent her home without anti-D.
h: He told her the bleed was small and sent her home without anti-D

a.o: Dr. Ihab sent Mrs. Rana home without anti-D after a bleed.
a.x: Mrs. Rana should have had anti-D within 72 hours, with a Kleihauer test to check how much of the baby's blood had crossed.
a.w: Any bleed or fall after 12 weeks in a rhesus-negative mother can let the baby's blood cross. Antibodies can harm this and future babies.

a.o: Dr. Ihab scanned to check the placenta.
a.w: A low placenta can cause bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked for tenderness.
a.w: Pain can mean the placenta is separating.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about her first pregnancy.
a.x: The first pregnancy was off topic.
a.w: She needs anti-D in each pregnancy.

t: Internal exam with a low placenta
s:
Mrs. Amal, 33, is 32 weeks pregnant with her third baby. She came in with painless bright red bleeding that soaked a pad. Her 20-week scan said the placenta was low-lying, but she missed her follow-up scan. Her blood pressure was 118/74.

Dr. Soha checked the baby's heartbeat, which was normal, and felt her belly, which was soft and not tender. She put in a drip and sent blood for crossmatch.

She gave steroid injections to help the baby's lungs in case of an early birth.

Mrs. Amal had two cesareans before. Her husband asked whether the baby would be all right.

To see whether the cervix was opening, Dr. Soha did an internal exam with her fingers before the scan.
h: Dr. Soha did an internal exam with her fingers before the scan

a.o: Dr. Soha did an internal exam before a scan in Mrs. Amal with a likely low placenta.
a.x: Mrs. Amal should have had an ultrasound first, with no finger exam until placenta previa was ruled out.
a.w: A finger exam can tear a low placenta and cause a massive bleed.

a.o: Dr. Soha gave steroid injections.
a.w: Steroids help the baby's lungs if born early.

a.o: Dr. Soha sent blood for crossmatch.
a.w: Heavy bleeding may need transfusion.

a.o: Dr. Soha asked about past cesareans.
a.w: Past cesareans raise the risk of a placenta growing into the scar.

t: Group B strep in labor without antibiotics
s:
Mrs. Sara, 29, is in labor at 39 weeks with her first baby. Her waters broke four hours ago and the fluid was clear. A swab taken at 36 weeks, because her sister's baby had been very ill with an infection, showed group B streptococcus. She has no allergies.

Dr. Ihab checked her temperature, which was 37.1°C, and the baby's heart tracing, which was normal. He examined her and found her cervix 4 cm open.

He offered her pain relief, and she chose an epidural. He also checked her blood pressure and asked the midwife to keep a fluid chart.

Mrs. Sara had planned a water birth and was disappointed about the epidural. Her husband asked whether the swab result meant the baby would be sick.

Dr. Ihab did not start IV antibiotics, writing "no fever, waters clear, baby well".
h: Dr. Ihab did not start IV antibiotics, writing "no fever, waters clear, baby well"

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mrs. Sara no antibiotics in labor despite group B strep.
a.x: Mrs. Sara should have had IV benzylpenicillin every four hours from the start of labor until the birth.
a.w: Group B strep can cause sepsis and meningitis in newborns. Antibiotics in labor greatly lower the risk, with or without fever.

a.o: Dr. Ihab took Mrs. Sara's temperature in labor.
a.x: Temperature checks were a waste of time.
a.w: A fever in labor can mean infection in the womb.

a.o: Dr. Ihab let Mrs. Sara choose an epidural.
a.w: Pain relief is her choice and is safe with group B strep.

a.o: Dr. Ihab kept watching the baby's heart tracing.
a.x: The tracing was not needed once it was normal.
a.w: Changes in the tracing can be the first sign of infection.

t: Hyperemesis sent home with ketones
s:
Mrs. Lobna, 24, is 9 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She has been vomiting about ten times a day for a week and can't keep even water down. She has lost 3 kg. Her urine showed 3+ ketones, her pulse was 108 and her mouth was dry.

Dr. Rasha checked her salts, which showed a low potassium of 3.1, and her thyroid tests, which were slightly overactive, as often happens in early pregnancy.

She arranged a scan, which showed a single baby with a normal heartbeat and no twins.

Mrs. Lobna works as a dental nurse and had been too sick to go to work. She felt dizzy when she stood up and asked whether the vomiting would harm the baby.

Dr. Rasha gave her anti-sickness tablets and sent her home, advising "small, dry meals".
h: Dr. Rasha gave her anti-sickness tablets and sent her home

a.o: Dr. Rasha sent Mrs. Lobna home with severe vomiting and ketones.
a.x: Mrs. Lobna should have been admitted for IV fluids with potassium, injected anti-sickness drugs, thiamine and clot-prevention injections.
a.w: Hyperemesis with weight loss, ketones and low potassium can cause kidney injury, Wernicke's encephalopathy and clots.

a.o: Dr. Rasha arranged a scan for Mrs. Lobna.
a.w: Twins or a molar pregnancy can cause severe vomiting.

a.o: Dr. Rasha did not treat Mrs. Lobna's slightly overactive thyroid test.
a.x: The thyroid needed tablets at once.
a.w: Pregnancy hormones often raise thyroid tests briefly in early pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Lobna's potassium.
a.w: Vomiting lowers potassium.

t: Low-dose folic acid for a woman with epilepsy
s:
Mrs. Dina, 30, came to plan her first pregnancy. She has epilepsy, well controlled on lamotrigine, and has not had a fit for three years. Her BMI is 33. She does not smoke or drink.

Dr. Rasha checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her rubella immunity, which was good. She sent a blood count and thyroid test.

She talked with her neurologist, who agreed to keep the lamotrigine and to check her levels during pregnancy, as they often fall.

Mrs. Dina works as a graphic designer and had read about pregnancy online. She asked about safe foods, and Dr. Rasha told her to avoid liver and unpasteurized cheese.

Dr. Rasha advised her to take the usual 400 microgram folic acid tablet from the pharmacy, starting now.
h: Dr. Rasha advised her to take the usual 400 microgram folic acid tablet from the pharmacy

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave Mrs. Dina the low dose of folic acid.
a.x: Mrs. Dina should have had 5 mg of folic acid a day, starting before conception and continuing to 12 weeks.
a.w: Epilepsy drugs and a BMI over 30 both raise the risk of spine defects, so the high dose is needed.

a.o: Dr. Rasha kept Mrs. Dina on lamotrigine.
a.x: All epilepsy drugs must stop before pregnancy.
a.w: Lamotrigine is one of the safer epilepsy drugs in pregnancy, and fits are dangerous.

a.o: Dr. Rasha planned lamotrigine level checks in pregnancy.
a.w: Pregnancy speeds up the breakdown of lamotrigine.

a.o: Dr. Rasha told Mrs. Dina to avoid liver.
a.x: Liver is a healthy food in pregnancy.
a.w: Liver is very high in vitamin A, which can harm the baby.

t: Ramipril carried on in pregnancy
s:
Mrs. Samar, 36, has type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. She came to clinic at 7 weeks pregnant, which was unplanned. She takes metformin, ramipril and atorvastatin. Her blood pressure was 138/86 and her HbA1c 52.

Dr. Mervat stopped the atorvastatin and started 5 mg of folic acid and low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks. She arranged an early scan, which showed a healthy heartbeat.

She referred her to the joint diabetes and pregnancy clinic and arranged eye screening.

Mrs. Samar works as a nurse and was worried that her tablets had already harmed the baby. Her husband asked whether she should stop all her medicines.

Dr. Mervat kept the metformin and continued the ramipril, saying "her blood pressure is well controlled".
h: continued the ramipril, saying "her blood pressure is well controlled"

a.o: Dr. Mervat kept Mrs. Samar on ramipril in pregnancy.
a.x: Mrs. Samar should have stopped ramipril and switched to labetalol or nifedipine.
a.w: ACE inhibitors harm the baby's kidneys and skull, especially later in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Mervat stopped the atorvastatin.
a.w: Statins are stopped in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Mervat kept the metformin.
a.w: Metformin is safe in pregnancy and helps sugar control.

a.o: Dr. Mervat arranged eye screening.
a.w: Diabetic eye disease can worsen in pregnancy.

t: Reduced baby movements told normal
s:
Mrs. Yara, 27, is 34 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She came in because the baby had been moving much less since yesterday. Usually the baby kicks a lot after dinner and when she lies down at night. Her pregnancy had been healthy so far.

Dr. Soha checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her urine, which was clear. She felt her belly, which was soft, and measured the bump, which matched her dates.

She listened with a handheld Doppler for a minute and heard a heartbeat of 140.

Mrs. Yara is a teacher and said she had been busy with exams at school and might not have noticed. She felt silly for coming in and apologized for wasting time.

Dr. Soha reassured her that the heartbeat was normal and sent her home without a CTG.
h: Dr. Soha reassured her that the heartbeat was normal and sent her home without a CTG

a.o: Dr. Soha sent Mrs. Yara home after reduced movements without a CTG.
a.x: Mrs. Yara should have had a CTG for at least 20 minutes, and a growth scan if there were other risks.
a.w: Reduced movements can be the first sign a baby is in trouble. A one-minute heartbeat check does not show the baby is well.

a.o: Dr. Soha measured Mrs. Yara's bump.
a.x: The bump size was off topic.
a.w: A small bump can mean the baby is not growing well.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Yara's blood pressure.
a.w: Pre-eclampsia can affect the baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha told Mrs. Yara she was right to come in.
a.x: She should not have come for that.
a.w: Women should always come in with reduced movements.

t: Bleeding after sex blamed on a normal smear
s:
Mrs. Hala, 38, came in with bleeding after sex for two months. She also had a watery, sometimes blood-stained discharge between periods. Her last smear test a year ago was normal. She has three children and smokes 10 cigarettes a day.

Dr. Ghada asked about pain, which she did not have, and sent swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhea. She checked a pregnancy test, which was negative.

She asked about her periods, which were regular, and her contraception, which was condoms. She advised her to stop smoking.

Mrs. Hala was embarrassed and said her husband was worried. She asked whether it could be cancer, because her aunt had died of it.

Dr. Ghada said cancer was unlikely because the smear was normal, and did not examine her cervix.
h: Dr. Ghada said cancer was unlikely because the smear was normal, and did not examine her cervix

a.o: Dr. Ghada relied on a normal smear for Mrs. Hala's bleeding after sex.
a.x: Mrs. Hala should have had her cervix looked at with a speculum, with an urgent referral if it looked abnormal.
a.w: A normal smear does not rule out cervical cancer. Bleeding after sex always needs the cervix to be seen.

a.o: Dr. Ghada sent swabs for infection.
a.w: Chlamydia can cause bleeding after sex.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised Mrs. Hala to stop smoking.
a.w: Smoking raises the risk of cervical cancer.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked a pregnancy test.
a.w: Pregnancy can cause bleeding.

t: Bleeding after menopause blamed on HRT
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 58, came in with vaginal bleeding for a week. She went through the menopause six years ago. She started continuous combined HRT tablets a year ago and had had no bleeding until now. Her BMI is 36 and she has type 2 diabetes.

Dr. Ihab checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and asked about her breasts. She had no lumps and her mammogram last year was clear.

He asked whether she had missed any doses or started other medicines, and she had not.

Mrs. Nawal said she felt much better on the HRT, with no more hot flushes or night sweats, and did not want to stop it.

He said the HRT caused the bleeding and told her to carry on, without arranging a scan.
h: He said the HRT caused the bleeding and told her to carry on, without arranging a scan

a.o: Dr. Ihab blamed Mrs. Nawal's new bleeding on HRT without a scan.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have had an urgent scan of the womb lining, with a biopsy if thickened.
a.w: New bleeding after the menopause, even on HRT, can be womb cancer. Obesity and diabetes raise the risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked whether Mrs. Nawal missed doses.
a.w: Missed doses can cause bleeding on HRT.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about Mrs. Nawal's mammogram.
a.w: HRT slightly raises breast cancer risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab noted that she had no bleeding for the first year.
a.w: New bleeding after a settled spell on HRT needs checking.

t: Breech at 37 weeks booked for cesarean
s:
Mrs. Amira, 31, is 37 weeks pregnant with her second baby. Her first baby was born normally three years ago. A scan showed the baby was breech, bottom first, with plenty of fluid around it. The baby was growing well and the placenta was high.

Dr. Soha explained what breech means and checked her blood pressure, which was normal. She checked her blood group, which was positive.

She asked about Mrs. Amira's wishes for the birth and her first labor, which was quick and easy.

Mrs. Amira said she wanted a normal birth if at all possible, because she has a toddler at home and wanted a fast recovery.

Dr. Soha booked a cesarean for 39 weeks, without offering an attempt to turn the baby.
h: Dr. Soha booked a cesarean for 39 weeks, without offering an attempt to turn the baby

a.o: Dr. Soha didn't offer Mrs. Amira an attempt to turn the breech baby.
a.x: Mrs. Amira should have been offered external cephalic version at 37 weeks.
a.w: Turning the baby works in about half of women, more after a previous birth, and can avoid a cesarean.

a.o: Dr. Soha asked about Mrs. Amira's wishes.
a.w: Women should share in birth decisions.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked the placenta position.
a.w: A low placenta rules out turning the baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Amira's blood group.
a.x: Her blood group was off topic.
a.w: Rhesus-negative women need anti-D after a turning attempt.

t: Shoulder dystocia with fundal pressure
s:
Mrs. Heba, 34, has gestational diabetes and was in labor with a baby estimated at 4.3 kg. The head was delivered, but then pulled back against her perineum. The next contraction did not deliver the shoulders.

Dr. Rana called for help, including the senior obstetrician and the newborn team. She noted the time the head was born.

She asked Mrs. Heba to stop pushing and laid the bed flat. She told her calmly what was happening.

Mrs. Heba's husband was frightened and asked why the baby was stuck. The midwife held Mrs. Heba's hand.

To push the baby out, Dr. Rana asked the midwife to press hard on the top of Mrs. Heba's belly.
h: Dr. Rana asked the midwife to press hard on the top of Mrs. Heba's belly

a.o: Dr. Rana used fundal pressure for Mrs. Heba's shoulder dystocia.
a.x: Mrs. Heba should have had McRoberts' position, with her legs pulled back to her chest, and pressure just above the pubic bone.
a.w: Pressing on the top of the womb pushes the shoulder harder against the bone and can tear the womb or damage the baby's nerves.

a.o: Dr. Rana called for help.
a.w: Shoulder dystocia needs a team.

a.o: Dr. Rana noted the time the head was born.
a.w: Time matters for the baby's oxygen.

a.o: Dr. Rana laid the bed flat.
a.w: Flat is needed for McRoberts' position.

t: Postnatal psychosis sent home
s:
Mrs. Rasha, 29, had her first baby five days ago. Her husband brought her back because she had not slept for three nights, was talking very fast and said the baby was "not hers". She had bipolar disorder as a teenager but stopped treatment years ago.

Dr. Fady checked her for infection, and her temperature, urine and blood tests were normal. He checked her thyroid.

He asked about thoughts of harming herself or the baby. She said she heard voices telling her the baby was evil.

Her husband was exhausted and frightened. Her mother offered to stay with them at home.

Dr. Fady diagnosed "baby blues", advised rest and sent her home with her mother.
h: Dr. Fady diagnosed "baby blues", advised rest and sent her home with her mother

a.o: Dr. Fady called Mrs. Rasha's symptoms baby blues and sent her home.
a.x: Mrs. Rasha should have had an urgent psychiatric assessment and admission, ideally to a mother and baby unit.
a.w: Hearing voices, no sleep and odd beliefs about the baby after birth, with past bipolar disorder, mean postpartum psychosis, an emergency that can lead to suicide or harm to the baby.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked for infection.
a.w: Infection can cause confusion after birth.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about harming the baby.
a.w: Asking about harm is vital for safety.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked her thyroid.
a.w: Thyroid problems after birth can affect mood.

t: Methotrexate for an ectopic with a heartbeat
s:
Mrs. Nermine, 31, came in with pain on her right side at 7 weeks of pregnancy. A scan showed an ectopic pregnancy in her right tube, 4 cm across, with a heartbeat. Her hCG was 8,200. She was stable, with a blood pressure of 118/76.

Dr. Soha explained the diagnosis gently. She checked her blood count, kidney and liver tests, which were normal.

She asked about her plans for future pregnancies, and Mrs. Nermine said she very much wanted children.

Mrs. Nermine was frightened of surgery and asked whether there was a tablet or injection instead.

Dr. Soha gave her methotrexate and planned to check her hCG on days 4 and 7.
h: Dr. Soha gave her methotrexate and planned to check her hCG on days 4 and 7

a.o: Dr. Soha gave methotrexate for Mrs. Nermine's large ectopic with a heartbeat.
a.x: Mrs. Nermine should have had keyhole surgery to remove the ectopic.
a.w: Methotrexate fails often when there is a heartbeat, the hCG is over 5,000 or the mass is large. A burst tube can bleed fatally.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked liver and kidney tests.
a.w: Methotrexate can harm the liver and kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Soha asked about future pregnancies.
a.w: Plans affect the type of surgery.

a.o: Dr. Soha explained Mrs. Nermine's diagnosis gently.
a.x: Kindness wastes time in an emergency.
a.w: Losing a pregnancy is distressing, and gentle news helps.

t: Magnesium drip without reflex checks
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 26, is on a magnesium sulfate drip after severe pre-eclampsia. She delivered by cesarean six hours ago. Her blood pressure was 148/94. Her urine output had fallen to 15 mL an hour for the last three hours.
