Dr. Rehab checked her blood tests, which showed a rising creatinine. She asked for her fluids to be measured carefully.

She checked her wound, which was clean, and her uterus, which was firm.

Mrs. Asmaa said she felt heavy and sleepy, and her speech was a little slurred. Her breathing rate was 11.

She is a primary school teacher and this was her first baby, a girl now in the newborn unit for warmth and feeding help. Her husband had gone to see the baby. The night midwife had written that she seemed more drowsy than an hour ago but put it down to tiredness after surgery.

Dr. Rehab continued the magnesium at the same rate, without checking her reflexes or her magnesium level.
h: Dr. Rehab continued the magnesium at the same rate, without checking her reflexes or her magnesium level

a.o: Dr. Rehab kept Mrs. Asmaa's magnesium running without checks.
a.x: Mrs. Asmaa should have had her reflexes and magnesium level checked, the drip stopped or reduced, and calcium gluconate ready.
a.w: Magnesium builds up when the kidneys slow down. Sleepiness, slurred speech and slow breathing are signs of toxicity.

a.o: Dr. Rehab measured Mrs. Asmaa's fluids carefully.
a.x: Fluid charts were unnecessary after delivery.
a.w: Low urine shows kidney problems, which make magnesium build up.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mrs. Asmaa's uterus.
a.w: A firm uterus shows she is not bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mrs. Asmaa's creatinine.
a.w: Magnesium is cleared by the kidneys.

t: Oxytocin increased after a previous cesarean
s:
Mrs. Samia, 33, had a cesarean three years ago. She is in labor at 40 weeks, planning a vaginal birth. Her labor was slow, so oxytocin was started.

Dr. Ihab checked the baby's heart tracing, which had started to show late dips. He checked her cervix, which had not changed for three hours.

He asked about her pain. She had a sharp, constant pain over her old scar, even between contractions.

Her husband said she had been coping well until now. The midwife said her contractions had become weaker.

Her first cesarean was for a breech baby, and the scar healed well. She had read a lot about vaginal birth after cesarean and was keen to try. Her pulse had risen to 112 in the last half hour, and the midwife noticed a little fresh bleeding.

Dr. Ihab increased the oxytocin "to get things moving".
h: Dr. Ihab increased the oxytocin "to get things moving"

a.o: Dr. Ihab increased oxytocin in Mrs. Samia with signs of a torn womb.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have had the oxytocin stopped and an urgent cesarean.
a.w: Constant scar pain, weaker contractions and a worsening heart tracing after a past cesarean point to uterine rupture, which can kill mother and baby.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked the heart tracing.
a.w: Tracing changes show the baby is in trouble.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about pain.
a.w: Scar pain is a warning sign.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her cervix.
a.w: Slow progress is a warning sign.

t: Cord prolapse left lying flat
s:
Mrs. Lina, 30, is in labor at 38 weeks with her second baby. Her waters broke suddenly. The midwife saw a loop of cord at the entrance of the vagina. The baby's heart rate dropped to 80.

Dr. Rana called for help and asked the team to prepare for an emergency cesarean.

She told Mrs. Lina calmly what was happening and asked the midwife to stop the oxytocin.

Mrs. Lina's husband asked whether the baby would be all right.

Her first baby was born quickly and easily. The baby's head had been high in the pelvis at her last check, and there was a lot of fluid around the baby. The theater team said they needed ten minutes to be ready.

While waiting, she left Mrs. Lina lying flat on her back and did not lift the baby's head off the cord.
h: she left Mrs. Lina lying flat on her back and did not lift the baby's head off the cord

a.o: Dr. Rana didn't take pressure off the cord while waiting.
a.x: Mrs. Lina should have been put on all fours or knees-to-chest, with a hand pushing the baby's head off the cord, or the bladder filled.
a.w: The baby's head presses on the cord and cuts off oxygen. Lifting it buys time.

a.o: Dr. Rana called for help at once.
a.w: Cord prolapse needs a whole team fast.

a.o: Dr. Rana stopped Mrs. Lina's oxytocin.
a.x: Oxytocin speeds the birth and should carry on.
a.w: Contractions press the baby onto the cord.

a.o: Dr. Rana got the team ready for a cesarean.
a.x: A normal birth should be tried first.
a.w: With the cervix not fully open, a fast cesarean is safest.

t: Preterm labor without steroids
s:
Mrs. Reem, 27, is 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She came in with tightenings every five minutes for three hours and a little blood-stained mucus. Her cervix was 3 cm open. Her waters had not broken, and she had no fever.

Dr. Soha checked the baby's heart tracing, which was normal, and confirmed the baby was head down. She started nifedipine to slow the contractions and arranged a bed in a hospital with a newborn intensive care unit.

She started magnesium sulfate to protect the baby's brain, as birth before 32 weeks looked likely. She sent a swab for group B strep and checked her urine for infection.

Mrs. Reem is a nurse and asked many questions about what the baby would face. Her husband was driving back from another city and would arrive in three hours.

Dr. Soha did not give steroid injections, writing "contractions may settle with nifedipine".
h: Dr. Soha did not give steroid injections, writing "contractions may settle with nifedipine"

a.o: Dr. Soha held back steroids from Mrs. Reem in preterm labor at 30 weeks.
a.x: Mrs. Reem should have had two steroid injections, 12 to 24 hours apart, straight away.
a.w: Steroids before an early birth help the baby's lungs and lower the risk of death, brain bleeds and bowel problems. They work best when given early.

a.o: Dr. Soha started magnesium sulfate for Mrs. Reem.
a.w: Magnesium before 32 weeks protects the baby's brain from cerebral palsy.

a.o: Dr. Soha moved Mrs. Reem to a hospital with a newborn intensive care unit.
a.x: A transfer was too risky in labor.
a.w: A very early baby does best when born where intensive care is ready.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Reem's urine.
a.x: Urine was off topic in labor.
a.w: Infection can trigger early labor.

t: Fever after a cesarean given tablets
s:
Mrs. Amal, 30, had an emergency cesarean four days ago after a long labor. She was sent home yesterday but came back with a fever of 38.9°C, shivers and lower belly pain. Her pulse was 122 and her blood pressure 98/60. Her vaginal loss smelled bad.

Dr. Rehab examined her and found her womb tender. Her wound was clean and dry. Her breasts were soft, with no red patches. Her calves were soft and not swollen.

She took blood cultures and a vaginal swab and measured her lactate, which was 3.4. She asked about breastfeeding, which was going well.

Mrs. Amal's mother was looking after the baby and asked whether her daughter could breastfeed while on antibiotics.

Dr. Rehab started oral co-amoxiclav and sent her home, with a review in two days.
h: Dr. Rehab started oral co-amoxiclav and sent her home, with a review in two days

a.o: Dr. Rehab sent Mrs. Amal home on tablets with sepsis after her cesarean.
a.x: Mrs. Amal should have been admitted for IV antibiotics and fluids within an hour, with close monitoring.
a.w: A fast pulse, low blood pressure and a high lactate mean sepsis from infection of the womb, which can kill quickly after birth.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mrs. Amal's calves.
a.w: Clots in the legs are common after a cesarean.

a.o: Dr. Rehab looked at Mrs. Amal's breasts.
a.w: Mastitis is another cause of fever after birth.

a.o: Dr. Rehab measured Mrs. Amal's lactate.
a.w: A high lactate shows how severe sepsis is.

t: Mastitis and told to stop breastfeeding
s:
Mrs. Hana, 28, had her baby three weeks ago. She came in with a red, hot, painful patch on her left breast for a day, a fever of 38.2°C and aches all over. She had no lump. Her baby had been feeding less often because he was sleeping longer at night.

Dr. Ghada examined her and found a red wedge on the upper part of the breast, with no swelling or fluid under the skin. Her nipple had a small crack.

She prescribed flucloxacillin for ten days and paracetamol. She advised warm packs before feeds and asked the health visitor to check the baby's latch.

Mrs. Hana was in pain and tearful, and said her mother-in-law thought her milk was "bad". She asked whether the antibiotics would harm the baby.

Dr. Ghada told her to stop feeding from the left breast until the infection cleared, and to give formula instead.
h: Dr. Ghada told her to stop feeding from the left breast until the infection cleared

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mrs. Hana to stop feeding from the infected breast.
a.x: Mrs. Hana should have kept breastfeeding from both breasts, starting on the sore side, or expressing.
a.w: Emptying the breast helps mastitis clear. Stopping can lead to an abscess, and the milk is safe for the baby.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked the health visitor to check the latch.
a.w: A poor latch causes cracked nipples and mastitis.

a.o: Dr. Ghada prescribed flucloxacillin.
a.w: Flucloxacillin is safe in breastfeeding.

a.o: Dr. Ghada suggested warm packs before feeds.
a.w: Warmth helps milk flow.

t: Morning-after pill on day five
s:
Miss Salma, 22, came in four and a half days after unprotected sex, when a condom split. She is not using other contraception. Her period is regular and she is mid-cycle. She has no medical problems and takes no medicines.

Dr. Ihab took a careful history and checked that she was not already pregnant from earlier sex. Her pregnancy test was negative.

He talked about future contraception and offered her chlamydia and gonorrhea tests, which she accepted.

Miss Salma is a university student and was anxious. She asked which option worked best and said she was willing to have a coil if needed.

He prescribed levonorgestrel 1.5 mg, saying "it works for up to five days".
h: He prescribed levonorgestrel 1.5 mg, saying "it works for up to five days"

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Miss Salma levonorgestrel at day four and a half.
a.x: Miss Salma should have been offered a copper coil, the most effective option, or ulipristal if she declined.
a.w: Levonorgestrel is licensed only up to 72 hours and works poorly after that. A copper coil works up to five days.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked for an earlier pregnancy.
a.w: Emergency contraception doesn't work on an existing pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Ihab offered infection tests.
a.w: Unprotected sex carries a risk of infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab talked about future contraception.
a.w: Planning ahead prevents more emergencies.

t: Molar pregnancy without hCG follow-up
s:
Mrs. Nermine, 35, had heavy bleeding at 10 weeks of pregnancy. A scan showed a "snowstorm" pattern, and her hCG was 180,000. She had a suction evacuation, and the lab confirmed a complete molar pregnancy.

Dr. Soha explained the diagnosis and checked her blood group, which was positive. She checked her thyroid, which was a little overactive, and her blood pressure.

She advised her to avoid getting pregnant for now and discussed contraception, starting the combined pill.

Mrs. Nermine was sad and asked whether she could try again soon. She said she lived far from the hospital.

Dr. Soha told her the evacuation had cured it and discharged her, without registering her for hCG follow-up.
h: Dr. Soha told her the evacuation had cured it and discharged her, without registering her for hCG follow-up

a.o: Dr. Soha discharged Mrs. Nermine without hCG follow-up.
a.x: Mrs. Nermine should have been registered with a specialist center for hCG checks until normal.
a.w: A molar pregnancy can turn into a cancer, choriocarcinoma. Rising hCG is the warning sign.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked her thyroid.
a.w: High hCG can overstimulate the thyroid.

a.o: Dr. Soha advised avoiding pregnancy for now.
a.w: A new pregnancy would hide a rising hCG.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked her blood group.
a.x: The blood group was off topic.
a.w: Rhesus-negative women may need anti-D.

t: Painful red eye given dilating drops
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 68, came in with severe pain in her right eye and a headache since watching TV in a dark room last night. She had vomited twice. She saw halos around lights and her vision was blurred. She is long-sighted and wears thick glasses.

Dr. Nada found her right eye red, with a hazy cornea and a mid-sized pupil that did not react to light. The eye felt hard as stone through the lid.

She gave her anti-sickness medicine and morphine for the pain, and asked her to lie flat on her back.

Mrs. Fawzia's son said his mother had never had eye problems before, apart from her glasses. He asked whether she was having a stroke.

To get a better look at the back of the eye, Dr. Nada put dilating drops in both eyes and planned for the eye team to see her in the morning.
h: Dr. Nada put dilating drops in both eyes and planned for the eye team to see her in the morning

a.o: Dr. Nada used dilating drops in Mrs. Fawzia's acute angle-closure glaucoma.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have had pressure-lowering drops, IV acetazolamide and pilocarpine, with an urgent same-night eye review.
a.w: Dilating the pupil closes the drainage angle further. Acute angle closure can blind the eye within hours.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mrs. Fawzia anti-sickness medicine.
a.w: High eye pressure causes vomiting.

a.o: Dr. Nada felt the eye through the lid.
a.w: A rock-hard eye shows very high pressure.

a.o: Dr. Nada noted that Mrs. Fawzia is long-sighted.
a.w: Long-sighted eyes have narrow angles.

t: Floaters and a shadow told to wait
s:
Mr. Hesham, 58, came in with a shower of new floaters in his left eye since yesterday, like a swarm of flies. This morning he noticed a gray shadow coming in from the top of his vision. He is very short-sighted and had cataract surgery on that eye last year.

Dr. Ghada checked his vision, which was 6/9 in the left eye, and his pupils, which reacted normally. She could not see the back of his eye well without dilating drops.

She asked about flashes of light, and he had seen them in the corner of his eye last night. She asked about any blow to the head, and there was none.

Mr. Hesham is a tailor and was worried about losing work. He said the floaters were annoying but did not hurt.

Dr. Ghada told him floaters are common with age and booked him into the routine eye clinic in six weeks.
h: Dr. Ghada told him floaters are common with age and booked him into the routine eye clinic in six weeks

a.o: Dr. Ghada booked Mr. Hesham's new floaters and shadow for six weeks.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have been sent to the eye emergency service the same day.
a.w: New floaters, flashes and a curtain-like shadow mean a retinal tear or detachment. Repair before the center is affected saves sight.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about flashes of light.
a.w: Flashes mean the retina is being pulled.

a.o: Dr. Ghada noted Mr. Hesham's short sight.
a.w: Short sight and past cataract surgery raise the risk of detachment.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked his pupils.
a.w: An abnormal pupil reaction can show a large detachment.

t: Sudden blindness in one eye sent to clinic
s:
Mr. Raouf, 72, suddenly lost almost all the sight in his right eye an hour ago, while reading the newspaper. It did not hurt. He has high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation and stopped his blood thinner a month ago because of bruising.

Dr. Fouad found he could only see hand movements with the right eye. The right pupil reacted poorly to light. Through the ophthalmoscope, the retina looked pale with a cherry-red spot in the center.

He checked his blood pressure, 168/94, and sent an ESR and CRP to rule out giant cell arteritis. Mr. Raouf had no headache or jaw pain.

His wife said this was the second time; three days ago his vision went dark for five minutes and came back. Mr. Raouf was frightened and asked if it would come back.

Dr. Fouad referred him to the eye clinic for the next morning and sent him home.
h: Dr. Fouad referred him to the eye clinic for the next morning and sent him home

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent Mr. Raouf home with a central retinal artery occlusion.
a.x: Mr. Raouf should have had urgent same-day eye and stroke team review, as this is a form of stroke.
a.w: A blocked retinal artery is an eye stroke. He is at high risk of a brain stroke, especially with untreated atrial fibrillation.

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent an ESR and CRP.
a.w: Giant cell arteritis can block the eye artery too.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked about headache and jaw pain.
a.w: Those point to giant cell arteritis.

a.o: Dr. Fouad took the earlier dark spell seriously.
a.x: The earlier spell had passed and didn't matter.
a.w: A brief loss of vision is a warning sign of a stroke.

t: Chemical splash examined before washing
s:
Mr. Atef, 40, splashed oven cleaner into his left eye while cleaning his restaurant kitchen ten minutes ago. He could not open the eye because of the pain. The bottle said it contained sodium hydroxide, an alkali.

Dr. Nada asked for the bottle and checked the label. She checked his right eye, which was fine.

She gave him anesthetic eye drops to ease the pain so he could open his eye.

His colleague had driven him in and said Mr. Atef had rinsed his eye for a few seconds under the tap.

Before washing the eye, Dr. Nada sent him to wait for the slit lamp to check the damage and his vision.
h: Before washing the eye, Dr. Nada sent him to wait for the slit lamp to check the damage and his vision

a.o: Dr. Nada delayed washing Mr. Atef's alkali-burned eye to examine it first.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have had his eye washed at once with at least a liter of saline, until the pH was normal, before any exam.
a.w: Alkali burns keep damaging the eye every second. Washing comes first, even before checking vision.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked for the bottle.
a.w: Alkali burns are worse than acid burns.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave anesthetic drops.
a.w: Numbing drops let the eye be opened and washed.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked his other eye.
a.x: The other eye was off topic.
a.w: Splashes often hit both eyes.

t: Contact lens ulcer patched
s:
Miss Rana, 23, came in with a painful red right eye for a day. She wears soft contact lenses, which she sometimes sleeps in. The eye was watering, she could not bear bright light, and her vision was blurred. She had removed the lens.

Dr. Inas stained the eye with fluorescein and saw a small white spot on the cornea with a stain around it. She checked her vision, which was reduced.

She advised her not to wear contact lenses until the eye was healed and to bring her lenses and case for testing.

Miss Rana works as a receptionist and said she sometimes rinsed her lenses with tap water.

Dr. Inas put on an eye patch and chloramphenicol ointment, and booked her into the eye clinic in a week.
h: Dr. Inas put on an eye patch and chloramphenicol ointment, and booked her into the eye clinic in a week

a.o: Dr. Inas patched Miss Rana's eye and booked her clinic in a week.
a.x: Miss Rana should have been sent for same-day eye review for scrapings, with strong antibiotic drops such as a quinolone every hour and no patch.
a.w: A white spot on the cornea in a lens wearer is a corneal ulcer, often from Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba. Patching can make it worse, and it can scar within days.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked for her lenses and case.
a.w: The lens case can grow the germ.

a.o: Dr. Inas told her to stop wearing lenses.
a.w: Lenses must stop while infected.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about tap water.
a.w: Tap water can carry Acanthamoeba.

t: Steroid drops for a branching ulcer
s:
Mr. Sami, 45, came in with a red, watery, gritty left eye for four days. He had a cold sore last week. His vision was a little blurred. He does not wear contact lenses.

Dr. Ghada stained his eye with fluorescein and saw a branching, tree-shaped ulcer on the cornea.

She checked his vision and asked about previous eye problems, and he had a similar one two years ago.

Mr. Sami is a teacher and wanted to be fit for school the next week. He asked for something to make the redness go away quickly.

He has mild asthma and uses an inhaler. The eye was not painful enough to stop him sleeping, and the pupil reacted normally. His wife had read that steroid drops calm red eyes fast and asked for them.

Dr. Ghada prescribed prednisolone eye drops four times a day to settle the inflammation.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed prednisolone eye drops four times a day to settle the inflammation

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave steroid drops for Mr. Sami's herpes ulcer.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have had antiviral treatment, such as aciclovir ointment, with an eye clinic review and no steroids.
a.w: A branching ulcer is herpes simplex. Steroid drops make it spread and can perforate the cornea.

a.o: Dr. Ghada stained the eye.
a.w: The stain shows the ulcer shape.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about cold sores.
a.w: The same virus causes cold sores and eye ulcers.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about past eye problems.
a.w: Herpes eye ulcers often come back.

t: Swollen eyelid in a child treated with tablets
s:
Yusuf, 7, came in with a swollen, red right eyelid for two days after a cold. Today the eye was bulging a little, it hurt to move, and he said he saw double. He had a fever of 38.9°C and was miserable.

Dr. Dina gently opened the lid and found the eye red, with reduced movement looking up and out. She checked his vision with a chart, which was a little reduced, and his pupils, which reacted normally.

She sent blood tests and asked about his vaccines, which were up to date. She gave him paracetamol and ibuprofen for the fever.

His mother said he had blocked sinuses all week. She works night shifts and asked whether they could go home and come back tomorrow if he was worse.

Dr. Dina diagnosed a lid infection and sent him home with oral co-amoxiclav, with a review in two days.
h: Dr. Dina diagnosed a lid infection and sent him home with oral co-amoxiclav

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Yusuf home on tablets with signs of orbital cellulitis.
a.x: Yusuf should have been admitted for IV antibiotics, an urgent CT scan and eye and ENT review.
a.w: Painful eye movement, double vision, bulging and reduced vision mean infection behind the eye. It can cause blindness, brain abscess or meningitis.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Yusuf's vision with a chart.
a.x: A chart is unreliable in a child.
a.w: Reduced vision is a red flag for orbital infection.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked about Yusuf's sinuses.
a.w: Orbital cellulitis often spreads from the sinuses.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Yusuf's pupils.
a.w: A poor pupil reaction can show pressure on the optic nerve.

t: Diabetes eye screening skipped
s:
Mr. Hamdy, 52, has had type 2 diabetes for eight years. He came for his yearly review. His HbA1c was 74 and his blood pressure 148/92. He said his vision was perfect and he only needed reading glasses.

Dr. Ihab checked his feet, which had good feeling and pulses, and his kidney tests, which showed a little protein. He started ramipril for his blood pressure and kidneys.

He talked about diet and offered a place on a diabetes education course, which Mr. Hamdy accepted.

Mr. Hamdy said he had missed his last two eye screening appointments because they made his eyes blurry for hours after the drops, and he had to work.

Dr. Ihab agreed that eye screening could stop "since his eyesight is fine".
h: Dr. Ihab agreed that eye screening could stop "since his eyesight is fine"

a.o: Dr. Ihab let Mr. Hamdy stop diabetic eye screening because his eyesight was fine.
a.x: Mr. Hamdy should have been encouraged back into yearly eye screening, with help to arrange a day off.
a.w: Diabetic eye disease causes no symptoms until it is advanced. Screening finds it early, when laser or injections can save sight.

a.o: Dr. Ihab started ramipril for Mr. Hamdy.
a.w: ACE inhibitors protect the kidneys in diabetes with protein in the urine.

a.o: Dr. Ihab offered a diabetes course.
a.x: Courses are a waste of time.
a.w: Education helps people control their sugar.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Hamdy's feet.
a.w: Diabetes damages nerves and blood flow in the feet.

t: Hydroxychloroquine without eye checks
s:
Mrs. Samia, 50, has lupus and has taken hydroxychloroquine 400 mg a day for seven years. She weighs 54 kg. Her lupus has been quiet, with only mild joint pain. Her kidney function has slowly fallen to an eGFR of 55.

Dr. Mervat checked her blood count, urine and complement levels, which were stable. She checked her blood pressure, which was normal.

She advised her to use sun cream and a hat, as sunlight can trigger lupus flares, and checked that she was up to date with her flu vaccine.

Mrs. Samia said she had noticed some trouble reading small print, but thought it was her age. She had never had an eye test since starting the tablets.

Dr. Mervat continued the same dose and told her to see an optician for reading glasses.
h: Dr. Mervat continued the same dose and told her to see an optician for reading glasses

a.o: Dr. Mervat ignored the eye risk of Mrs. Samia's long-term hydroxychloroquine.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have been referred for retinal screening, with a dose review, as it is over 5 mg/kg and her kidneys are weaker.
a.w: After five years, hydroxychloroquine can damage the retina, especially with high doses and poor kidney function. The damage is permanent.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised sun cream.
a.w: Sunlight can trigger lupus flares.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked her complement levels.
a.w: Complement levels help show lupus activity.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked her flu vaccine.
a.w: People on immune medicines need flu protection.

t: Eye injury with pressure on the eye
s:
Mr. Ali, 30, was hit in the left eye by a piece of glass when a window broke at work. His vision was very blurred. Dr. Fady saw a cut through the cornea, with dark tissue poking out and a peaked pupil.

He checked the vision in both eyes, and asked about his last meal and his tetanus status, which was up to date.

He gave him an anti-sickness injection, as vomiting could raise the eye pressure, and pain relief.

Mr. Ali was very anxious and kept trying to rub his eye. His manager said he had been wearing safety glasses but they slipped.

Dr. Fady put a pressure bandage on the eye and pressed it firmly to stop the bleeding, while waiting for the eye surgeon.
h: Dr. Fady put a pressure bandage on the eye and pressed it firmly to stop the bleeding

a.o: Dr. Fady put pressure on Mr. Ali's open eye injury.
a.x: Mr. Ali should have had a rigid shield taped over the eye, with no pressure, no drops, and urgent surgery.
a.w: Pressure on an open eye can push the contents out and destroy it.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave anti-sickness medicine.
a.w: Vomiting can raise pressure in the eye.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked Mr. Ali about his last meal.
a.x: Food has nothing to do with an eye injury.
a.w: Surgery under general anesthetic needs a known fasting time.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Ali's tetanus status.
a.x: Tetanus only matters in dirty skin wounds.
a.w: Penetrating eye injuries can also cause tetanus.

t: Numbing drops sent home for an abrasion
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 35, scratched her right eye with her baby's fingernail this morning. It was very painful and watering, and she could not open it in bright light. Her vision was a little blurred.

Dr. Inas put a numbing drop in the eye, which eased the pain at once. She stained the eye with fluorescein and saw a small scratch on the cornea, with no foreign body under the lid.

She prescribed chloramphenicol ointment to prevent infection and advised her to wear sunglasses.

Mrs. Nadia was relieved by the numbing drops and asked whether she could have some to take home, because she had to care for her baby.

Dr. Inas gave her a bottle of the numbing drops to use as needed for the pain.
h: Dr. Inas gave her a bottle of the numbing drops to use as needed for the pain

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mrs. Nadia numbing drops to take home.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have had paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain at home, with no numbing drops.
a.w: Repeated numbing drops slow healing and can damage the cornea, and she would not feel a new injury.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked under the lid.
a.w: A foreign body under the lid can scratch the eye.

a.o: Dr. Inas prescribed chloramphenicol.
a.w: Ointment helps prevent infection.

a.o: Dr. Inas advised sunglasses.
a.w: Light sensitivity is common with a scratched eye.

t: Sticky eyes in a newborn called blocked ducts
s:
Baby Malak, 4 days old, was brought in because both eyes had become swollen with thick yellow pus since yesterday. The pus came back within minutes of wiping. She was born by normal delivery and was feeding well. Her mother had no antenatal care.

Dr. Rana examined her and found both eyelids swollen and red. The baby had no fever and was alert.

She asked about the mother's health, and the mother said she had a discharge in late pregnancy but had not seen anyone.

The baby's grandmother said all her children had sticky eyes as babies and it went away with breast milk.

Dr. Rana said it was likely blocked tear ducts, advised cleaning with cooled boiled water, and sent them home.
h: Dr. Rana said it was likely blocked tear ducts, advised cleaning with cooled boiled water, and sent them home

a.o: Dr. Rana called Baby Malak's heavy pus blocked tear ducts.
a.x: Baby Malak should have had urgent swabs for gonorrhea and chlamydia, IV or IM antibiotics and an eye review, with the mother tested and treated.
a.w: Heavy pus in the first week, with a mother's untreated discharge, points to gonococcal infection, which can perforate the cornea within a day.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about the mother's discharge.
a.x: The mother's health was off topic.
a.w: Newborns catch eye infections from the birth canal.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Baby Malak's temperature.
a.w: Infection in a newborn can spread to the blood.

a.o: Dr. Rana noted that the pus returned within minutes.
a.x: How fast it came back was off topic.
a.w: Pus that comes back fast is a sign of a serious infection.

t: Child's squint told to wait
s:
Laila, 3, was brought in because her mother noticed her left eye turning in, especially when she was tired. It had been happening for two months. Her father had a lazy eye as a child.

Dr. Ghada looked at her eyes with a light and saw that the reflection was not in the same place in both eyes. She covered each eye in turn and the left eye moved.

She checked for a red reflex in both eyes, which was present and equal.

Laila's mother said Laila was clumsy and sometimes tilted her head to watch TV.

Dr. Ghada told her mother that children often grow out of a squint and booked a review in a year.
h: Dr. Ghada told her mother that children often grow out of a squint and booked a review in a year

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Laila's mother the squint would go by itself.
a.x: Laila should have been referred to the children's eye clinic for glasses and treatment.
a.w: A squint that lasts past a few months of age can cause a lazy eye. Treatment works best when started early.

a.o: Dr. Ghada did the cover test.
a.w: The cover test confirms a squint.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked the red reflex.
a.w: A missing red reflex can mean cataract or a tumor.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about the father's lazy eye.
a.w: Squints run in families.

t: White pupil in a photo dismissed
s:
Adam, 18 months, came in because his mother saw a white glow in his right eye in a flash photo. It had happened in a few photos over the last month. He was well and walking normally.

Dr. Ihab looked at his eyes and could not see a clear red reflex in the right eye with the ophthalmoscope, though Adam was wriggling.

He asked about family history, and Adam's father had an eye removed as a baby.

Adam's mother showed him the photos. She said Adam sometimes bumped into things on his right side.

Dr. Ihab said the photo glow was a camera trick and booked a routine eye check in three months.
h: Dr. Ihab said the photo glow was a camera trick and booked a routine eye check in three months

a.o: Dr. Ihab dismissed Adam's white pupil as a camera trick.
a.x: Adam should have been referred urgently to the eye team within two weeks.
a.w: A white pupil can be retinoblastoma, an eye cancer in young children. A father who lost an eye as a baby makes it more likely.

a.o: Dr. Ihab looked for the red reflex.
a.w: A missing red reflex can mean a tumor.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about family history.
a.w: Retinoblastoma can be inherited.

a.o: Dr. Ihab looked at the photos.
a.w: Photos often show the white glow first.

t: Blood in the eye given aspirin
s:
Karim, 16, was hit in the right eye by a football. His vision was blurred and there was a layer of blood at the bottom of the iris, 2 mm high. The eye was not cut.

Dr. Fady checked his vision and the eye pressure, which was normal. He asked about any bleeding problems, and Karim had none.

He advised him to rest with his head up and avoid sports for two weeks.

Karim's father asked whether he should take anything for the pain.

Karim plays in the school team and had a match on Saturday. He has sickle cell trait, which his father mentioned when asked about family illnesses. The pain was a dull ache, worse when he looked at bright lights.

Dr. Fady prescribed aspirin for the pain and sent him home.
h: Dr. Fady prescribed aspirin for the pain and sent him home

a.o: Dr. Fady gave aspirin to Karim with a hyphema.
a.x: Karim should have had paracetamol for the pain, and an eye clinic review within a day.
a.w: Aspirin raises the risk of a second, bigger bleed in the eye.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Karim's eye pressure.
a.x: The pressure was off topic in a bruise.
a.w: Blood can block drainage and raise the pressure, especially with sickle trait.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about bleeding problems.
a.w: Bleeding disorders raise the risk of rebleeding.

a.o: Dr. Fady told Karim to sleep with his head raised.
a.w: Head up lets the blood settle away from the pupil.

t: Red eye in back pain called conjunctivitis
s:
Mr. Tarek, 32, came in with a painful red left eye for two days. Bright light hurt, and his vision was a little blurred. He had no discharge. He has ankylosing spondylitis, with back stiffness every morning.

Dr. Ihab found redness mostly around the edge of the cornea. The left pupil was small and slightly irregular. He checked his vision, which was 6/12 in the left eye.

He asked about contact lenses, which Mr. Tarek does not wear, and about previous red eyes; he had one last year that "went away with drops from the eye hospital".

Mr. Tarek is a software developer and works long hours at a screen. He thought the screen had strained his eye.

Dr. Ihab diagnosed conjunctivitis and prescribed chloramphenicol drops.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed conjunctivitis and prescribed chloramphenicol drops

a.o: Dr. Ihab called Mr. Tarek's painful red eye conjunctivitis.
a.x: Mr. Tarek should have been sent to the eye clinic the same day for anterior uveitis.
a.w: Pain, light sensitivity, a small irregular pupil and redness around the cornea, with ankylosing spondylitis, point to uveitis, which needs steroid drops and can harm sight.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Tarek's vision.
a.x: Vision was off topic in a red eye.
a.w: Reduced vision is a warning sign in a red eye.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about previous red eyes.
a.w: Uveitis often comes back.

a.o: Dr. Ihab looked at the pupil.
a.w: A small irregular pupil is a sign of uveitis.

t: Sudden wavy vision told to wait for clinic
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 76, came in because straight lines had looked wavy in her right eye for a week. Door frames looked bent and there was a blurry patch in the middle of her vision. She has dry macular degeneration in her left eye.

Dr. Ghada checked her vision, which was 6/24 in the right eye, down from 6/9 last year. She used an Amsler grid, and Mrs. Hanem saw the lines bent in the middle.

She asked about smoking, and Mrs. Hanem stopped ten years ago. She checked her blood pressure, which was normal.

Mrs. Hanem lives alone and reads the Quran every day. She was worried about losing her reading.

Dr. Ghada booked a routine eye clinic appointment in three months.
h: Dr. Ghada booked a routine eye clinic appointment in three months

a.o: Dr. Ghada booked Mrs. Hanem's sudden wavy vision for three months.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem should have been referred to the macular clinic within a few days for possible wet macular degeneration.
a.w: Sudden distortion can be wet AMD. Injections within weeks can save sight; waiting months can mean permanent loss.

a.o: Dr. Ghada used an Amsler grid.
a.x: The grid was a waste of time.
a.w: The grid shows distortion from macular disease.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about smoking.
a.w: Smoking raises the risk of macular degeneration.

a.o: Dr. Ghada compared her vision with last year.
a.w: A fall in vision shows a new problem.

t: Hammering metal fragment without an X-ray
s:
Mr. Hassan, 38, was hammering a metal chisel at work when he felt something hit his right eye. It hurt a little at first, but now felt fine. His vision was slightly blurred. He was not wearing safety glasses.

Dr. Nada stained the eye and saw a tiny mark on the cornea. She looked under the lids and found no foreign body.

She checked his vision and his pupil, which was a little irregular.

Mr. Hassan wanted to get back to work and said the pain had already gone.

His manager had driven him in and said the workshop had a rule about safety glasses that no one followed. Mr. Hassan's tetanus was up to date. His eye pressure could not be measured because the machine was broken.

Dr. Nada gave him antibiotic ointment and sent him home, without an X-ray or CT of the eye.
h: Dr. Nada gave him antibiotic ointment and sent him home, without an X-ray or CT of the eye

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Hassan home without imaging after a hammering injury.
a.x: Mr. Hassan should have had an X-ray or CT of the eye and urgent eye review.
a.w: Metal hitting metal can fire a tiny fragment into the eye at high speed. It can cause blindness if left inside.

a.o: Dr. Nada looked under the lids.
a.w: A foreign body can hide under the lid.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked his pupil.
a.w: An irregular pupil can mean the eye was pierced.

a.o: Dr. Nada stained the eye.
a.w: The stain shows the entry point.

t: Narrowing side vision given new glasses
s:
Mr. Sherif, 48, came in because he kept bumping into door frames and had scraped his car twice on the passenger side. He had headaches for months. He also said his shoe size had gone up and his wedding ring no longer fit.

Dr. Abeer checked his vision in each eye, which was good for reading. When she tested his side vision by moving her fingers from the sides, he could not see them on the outer side of either eye.

She checked his blood pressure, which was 156/94, and his sugar, which was high.

Mr. Sherif's wife said his face had changed and his voice had become deeper. He thought he just needed new glasses.

Dr. Abeer said his central vision was fine and sent him to an optician for new glasses.
h: Dr. Abeer said his central vision was fine and sent him to an optician for new glasses

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mr. Sherif for new glasses with loss of both outer fields.
a.x: Mr. Sherif should have had an urgent brain MRI and hormone tests.
a.w: Loss of the outer vision in both eyes means pressure on the optic chiasm, often from a pituitary tumor. Growing hands and feet point to acromegaly.

a.o: Dr. Abeer tested his side vision.
a.w: The finger test can pick up a field defect.

a.o: Dr. Abeer checked his sugar.
a.w: Acromegaly can cause diabetes.

a.o: Dr. Abeer listened to his wife about his face.
a.w: Slow face changes are often seen first by family.

t: Brief blindness in one eye not referred
s:
Mr. Medhat, 69, came in because yesterday the vision in his left eye went dark like a curtain coming down for five minutes, then came back fully. He has high blood pressure and high cholesterol and smokes. He had no headache or jaw pain.

Dr. Ihab checked his vision, which was normal now, and looked in his eyes, which looked normal. He listened to his neck and heard a whooshing sound on the left.

He checked his heart rhythm, which was regular, and his blood pressure, which was 162/94.

Mr. Medhat said he felt fine now and did not want a fuss. He was planning a fishing trip at the weekend.

Dr. Ihab said the vision had come back so it was nothing serious, and booked a routine review in a month.
h: Dr. Ihab said the vision had come back so it was nothing serious, and booked a routine review in a month

a.o: Dr. Ihab treated Mr. Medhat's brief blindness as nothing serious.
a.x: Mr. Medhat should have started aspirin and been seen in the TIA clinic within 24 hours, with a scan of his neck arteries.
a.w: Brief loss of vision in one eye is a TIA of the eye, often from a narrowed carotid artery. A stroke can follow within days.

a.o: Dr. Ihab listened over Mr. Medhat's neck.
a.x: A neck exam was pointless for an eye problem.
a.w: A whooshing sound suggests a narrowed carotid artery.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about jaw pain.
a.w: Jaw pain can point to giant cell arteritis.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked his heart rhythm.
a.w: Atrial fibrillation can cause clots that block eye arteries.

t: Long-term steroid drops without pressure checks
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 45, has had allergic eye disease for years. A pharmacist in another country sold her dexamethasone eye drops two years ago, and she has used them every day since because they stop the itch. She came for new glasses because her vision seemed dim.

Dr. Mervat checked her vision, which was 6/12 in both eyes, and noticed early clouding of both lenses. Her eyelids were a little puffy but the eyes were white.

She advised cold compresses and antihistamine drops for the itch, and checked her blood pressure and sugar, which were normal.

Mrs. Nawal works as a seamstress and said the drops were the only thing that let her work. She asked for a new prescription so she would not have to buy them abroad.

Dr. Mervat renewed the dexamethasone drops and sent her to an optician for glasses, without checking her eye pressure.
h: Dr. Mervat renewed the dexamethasone drops and sent her to an optician for glasses, without checking her eye pressure

a.o: Dr. Mervat renewed Mrs. Nawal's steroid drops without checking her eye pressure.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have had her eye pressure and optic nerves checked, and the steroid drops tapered and replaced with safer allergy drops.
a.w: Long-term steroid drops raise eye pressure, causing glaucoma, and speed up cataracts. Both cause silent sight loss.

a.o: Dr. Mervat suggested antihistamine drops.
a.w: They treat allergic eye itch without steroid side effects.

a.o: Dr. Mervat noticed early clouding of the lenses.
a.w: Steroid drops can cause cataracts.

a.o: Dr. Mervat suggested cold compresses.
a.w: Cold soothes itchy allergic eyes.

t: Tamsulosin not flagged before cataract surgery
s:
Mr. Kamal, 71, is booked for cataract surgery on his right eye next month. His vision is 6/36 and he can no longer read street signs. He takes tamsulosin for an enlarged prostate, started a year ago, and amlodipine.

Dr. Fady checked his eye pressure, which was normal, and measured his eye for the new lens. He checked that his blood pressure and sugar were controlled.

He explained the risks of surgery, including infection and the need for glasses after, and Mr. Kamal signed the consent form.

Mr. Kamal said he would stop his amlodipine before surgery "to be safe". Dr. Fady told him to keep taking all his tablets.

Dr. Fady did not record the tamsulosin on the surgery form or tell the surgeon, writing "no eye drugs".
h: Dr. Fady did not record the tamsulosin on the surgery form or tell the surgeon

a.o: Dr. Fady didn't flag Mr. Kamal's tamsulosin before cataract surgery.
a.x: The tamsulosin should have been clearly recorded and the surgeon told, so they could plan for a floppy iris.
a.w: Tamsulosin causes floppy iris syndrome even after it is stopped. The surgeon needs to prepare to avoid damage during surgery.

a.o: Dr. Fady told Mr. Kamal to keep taking his tablets.
a.x: All tablets should stop before surgery.
a.w: Stopping blood pressure tablets can make surgery less safe.

a.o: Dr. Fady measured the eye for the new lens.
a.w: Lens power must be worked out before surgery.

a.o: Dr. Fady explained the need for glasses after.
a.w: Most people still need reading glasses after surgery.

t: Painful eye after cataract surgery given drops only
s:
Mrs. Samira, 73, had cataract surgery on her left eye three days ago. Today the eye became very painful and red, and her vision dropped to counting fingers. She has diabetes. She was using her steroid and antibiotic drops as told.

Dr. Nada saw a layer of white pus at the bottom of the front chamber of the eye and swollen lids. Her temperature was normal.

She checked her sugar, which was 14, and her blood pressure.

Mrs. Samira's daughter said her mother had touched her eye with her fingers when it itched yesterday.

Dr. Nada increased her antibiotic drops to every hour and booked her into the eye clinic in two days.
h: Dr. Nada increased her antibiotic drops to every hour and booked her into the eye clinic in two days

a.o: Dr. Nada treated Mrs. Samira's likely endophthalmitis with drops and a clinic in two days.
a.x: Mrs. Samira should have been seen by the eye surgeon that day for a sample of fluid from the eye and antibiotics injected into the eye.
a.w: Pain, falling vision and pus after cataract surgery mean infection inside the eye. Drops don't reach it, and sight can be lost within hours.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Mrs. Samira's sugar.
a.w: Diabetes raises infection risk.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about touching the eye.
a.w: Touching the eye can bring in germs.

a.o: Dr. Nada noted the pus in the eye.
a.x: The pus was a normal finding after surgery.
a.w: Pus inside the eye is a sign of serious infection.

t: Glaucoma with field loss told to keep driving
s:
Mr. Waleed, 66, has glaucoma and uses eye drops every evening. His latest field test showed loss in both eyes that together left a large gap in his lower vision. His central vision was good.

Dr. Ihab checked that he was using his drops correctly, and he was. He asked about eye side effects, and Mr. Waleed said the drops sting a little.

He checked his blood pressure, which was normal, and his heart rate, which was 60.

Mr. Waleed drives his grandchildren to school every day. He said he had nearly hit a cyclist last week but thought it was the cyclist's fault.

Dr. Ihab told him he could keep driving because his central vision was good.
h: Dr. Ihab told him he could keep driving because his central vision was good

a.o: Dr. Ihab let Mr. Waleed keep driving with field loss in both eyes.
a.x: Mr. Waleed should have been told to stop driving and tell the licensing authority, who may arrange a formal field test.
a.w: Field loss in both eyes can stop drivers seeing hazards at the side and below. A near miss is a warning.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked his heart rate.
a.w: Beta-blocker eye drops can slow the heart.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked his drop technique.
a.w: Poor technique means the drops don't work.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about stinging.
a.w: Side effects stop people using their drops.

t: Baby with eye bleeds sent home
s:
Baby Omar, 4 months old, was brought in by his father because he was floppy and vomiting since the afternoon. His father said he had rolled off the sofa onto a carpet. He had no bruises. He had one fit in the department.

Dr. Rana checked his soft spot, which was full, and looked in his eyes, finding many bleeds in the retinas of both eyes. A CT showed a thin bleed over the brain.

She gave him medicine for the fit, put him on oxygen and called the children's intensive care team and the neurosurgeons.

His father seemed angry and kept asking to go home. The mother was at work and had not been told.

Dr. Rana wrote "accidental fall from sofa" and did not contact the child protection team.
h: Dr. Rana wrote "accidental fall from sofa" and did not contact the child protection team

a.o: Dr. Rana accepted a fall from a sofa without child protection review.
a.x: The child protection team and the police should have been told the same day, with a skeletal survey and other children in the home checked.
a.w: A short fall cannot explain retinal bleeds and a brain bleed in a baby. This pattern points to shaking injury.

a.o: Dr. Rana looked in Omar's eyes.
a.x: That was unnecessary in a fall.
a.w: Retinal bleeds are a key sign of shaking.

a.o: Dr. Rana called the neurosurgeons.
a.w: A brain bleed may need surgery.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked the soft spot.
a.w: A full soft spot shows raised pressure.

t: Back pain with numb saddle sent home
s:
Mr. Hossam, 44, came in with severe low back pain for three days after lifting boxes, now going down both legs. Today he had trouble passing urine and felt numb around his bottom when he wiped. He has no fever or cancer history.

Dr. Inas checked his legs, which had normal strength but reduced reflexes at the ankles. She did a bladder scan, which showed 600 mL of urine after he tried to pass it.

She gave him diazepam for muscle spasm and morphine for the pain.

Mr. Hossam works as a removals man and said he could not afford time off. He wanted to go home with painkillers.

Dr. Inas diagnosed a slipped disc and sent him home with painkillers and a physiotherapy referral.
h: Dr. Inas diagnosed a slipped disc and sent him home with painkillers and a physiotherapy referral

a.o: Dr. Inas sent Mr. Hossam home with signs of cauda equina syndrome.
a.x: Mr. Hossam should have had an emergency MRI of the spine and urgent spinal surgery review.
a.w: Pain in both legs, a numb saddle area and urine retention mean the nerves at the base of the spine are squashed. Delay can cause permanent loss of bladder, bowel and sexual function.

a.o: Dr. Inas did a bladder scan.
a.w: A full bladder after voiding shows retention.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked his reflexes.
a.w: Reduced reflexes show nerve compression.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave diazepam.
a.w: A short course can ease muscle spasm.

t: Leg pain in a cast given more morphine
s:
Mr. Sabri, 24, broke his shin bone playing football and had it fixed with a rod this morning. Tonight he had severe pain in his lower leg, much worse than expected. It was worse when the nurse gently moved his toes. His leg felt tight under the dressing.

Dr. Ayman checked his foot pulses, which were present, and his toes, which were pink and warm. Mr. Sabri said his foot felt tingly between the big toe and second toe.

He checked his blood pressure and pulse, which were normal, and loosened the bandage a little.

Mr. Sabri plays semi-professional football and was worried about his career. His girlfriend said he had already had two doses of morphine with little effect.

Dr. Ayman gave a higher dose of morphine and asked the nurses to check him in four hours, writing "pulses present, no compartment syndrome".
h: Dr. Ayman gave a higher dose of morphine and asked the nurses to check him in four hours

a.o: Dr. Ayman treated Mr. Sabri's escalating pain with more morphine.
a.x: Mr. Sabri should have had all dressings split to the skin and an urgent call to the orthopedic surgeon for a fasciotomy if pain stayed severe.
a.w: Pain out of proportion, worse on stretching the toes, with tingling, means compartment syndrome. Pulses stay normal until late, and muscles die within hours.

a.o: Dr. Ayman loosened the bandage.
a.w: Tight dressings raise pressure in the leg.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked about tingling.
a.w: Tingling shows the nerves are squeezed.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked the foot pulses.
a.w: Pulses help but don't rule out compartment syndrome.

t: Wrist sprain with a tender snuffbox
s:
Miss Nour, 19, fell on her outstretched hand while roller skating. Her wrist hurt on the thumb side. She was tender in the hollow at the base of her thumb, and it hurt when the doctor pushed her thumb towards the wrist.

Dr. Fady sent her for an X-ray of the wrist, which showed no fracture. He checked her fingers, which moved well, and her feeling, which was normal.

He gave her paracetamol and ibuprofen for the pain and advised ice and rest.

Miss Nour is a piano student and had an exam in a month. She asked whether she could keep practicing.

Dr. Fady told her it was a sprain, gave her a soft bandage and discharged her without follow-up.
h: Dr. Fady told her it was a sprain, gave her a soft bandage and discharged her without follow-up

a.o: Dr. Fady discharged Miss Nour with a likely scaphoid fracture.
a.x: Miss Nour should have had a thumb splint and a fracture clinic review within days, with an MRI or repeat X-ray.
a.w: Snuffbox tenderness after a fall means a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise. Early X-rays often miss it, and it can lose its blood supply.

a.o: Dr. Fady sent her for an X-ray.
a.w: An X-ray can show a fracture.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked her fingers.
a.w: Nerve or tendon damage can come with wrist injuries.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised ice.
a.w: Ice reduces swelling.

t: Hip pain after a fall with a normal X-ray
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 82, fell at home and now has pain in her left hip. She could not stand on her left leg. Her X-ray showed no fracture. She has osteoporosis and takes alendronic acid.

Dr. Nada examined her and found pain when the hip was turned. Her leg was not shortened or turned out.

She checked her blood count, kidney function and heart tracing, which were normal. She asked about the fall, which was a trip on a rug.

Mrs. Fawzia lives alone and her daughter lives in another city. She was keen to go home.

She had lain on the floor for an hour before her neighbor heard her calling. She takes no blood thinners. Her pain was worse when the nurse tried to help her walk to the toilet, and she needed two people to get back to bed.

Dr. Nada sent her home with painkillers, writing "X-ray normal, soft tissue injury".
h: Dr. Nada sent her home with painkillers, writing "X-ray normal, soft tissue injury"

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mrs. Fawzia home unable to bear weight after a normal X-ray.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have had an MRI or CT of the hip to look for a hidden fracture.
a.w: Up to 1 in 10 hip fractures don't show on the first X-ray. Not being able to stand after a fall needs more imaging.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about the fall.
a.w: Trips are different from faints.

a.o: Dr. Nada did a heart tracing.
a.w: A heart problem can cause falls.

a.o: Dr. Nada examined the hip.
a.w: Pain on turning suggests a hip problem.

t: Hot swollen knee called gout
s:
Mr. Atef, 66, came in with a hot, swollen, very painful right knee for a day. He could not bend it. He had a fever of 38.4°C. He has had gout in his big toe before. He had a steroid injection into the knee two weeks ago.

Dr. Inas checked his blood tests, which showed a high white count and CRP. His uric acid was high.

She X-rayed the knee, which showed swelling but no fracture.

Mr. Atef said this felt like his gout. He asked for colchicine, which had worked before.

He has type 2 diabetes and his sugar today was 16. He lives with his wife on the second floor of a building with no lift. The knee was warm all over, with a large swelling that moved when pressed.

Dr. Inas diagnosed gout, started colchicine and sent him home, without draining the joint.
h: Dr. Inas diagnosed gout, started colchicine and sent him home, without draining the joint

a.o: Dr. Inas called Mr. Atef's hot knee gout without draining it.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have had the knee drained for testing before any antibiotics, and been admitted if infected.
a.w: A hot, swollen joint with fever, after an injection, is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. It can destroy the joint in days. A high uric acid does not rule out infection.

a.o: Dr. Inas X-rayed the knee.
a.w: An X-ray rules out a fracture.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked his uric acid.
a.w: High uric acid supports gout, though it is not proof.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about past gout.
a.w: Past gout makes gout more likely.

t: Knee pain in a teenager with a limp
s:
Ahmed, 13, came in with pain in his left knee for three weeks and a limp. He is overweight. He had no injury. The pain was worse after football.

Dr. Ghada examined his knee, which was normal, with no swelling or tenderness. When she turned his hip, it turned outwards and hurt.

She checked his weight and height, and he was heavier than most boys his age.

Ahmed's mother said he had been walking with his foot turned out.

Ahmed plays goalkeeper for his school team and said the pain sometimes went up into his thigh. He had no fever and was otherwise well. His thyroid had been checked last year for tiredness and was normal.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed a knee strain and advised rest from football for two weeks.
h: Dr. Ghada diagnosed a knee strain and advised rest from football for two weeks

a.o: Dr. Ghada called Ahmed's knee pain a strain without checking his hip.
a.x: Ahmed should have had an urgent X-ray of both hips and orthopedic referral, with no weight on the leg.
a.w: Knee pain in an overweight teenager with a limp and painful hip turning is a slipped upper femoral epiphysis. It can get worse and damage the hip.

a.o: Dr. Ghada examined Ahmed's hip for knee pain.
a.w: Hip problems often cause pain felt in the knee.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Ahmed's weight.
a.w: Being overweight raises the risk of a slipped hip growth plate.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked how Ahmed was walking.
a.w: A turned-out foot is a sign of a slipped hip growth plate.

t: Open fracture without antibiotics
s:
Mr. Samir, 35, came off his motorbike on a country road. His right shin was bent, and a sharp end of bone had broken through the skin, with mud and grass in the wound. His foot was pink with a good pulse. He had no other injuries.

Dr. Fady gave him IV morphine and straightened the leg gently into a splint. He photographed the wound for the surgeons and covered it with a saline-soaked dressing.

He checked his tetanus status, which was up to date, and the feeling and movement in his foot, which were normal. He kept him nil by mouth for theater.

Mr. Samir is a farmer and asked whether he would keep his leg. His brother said the surgeon on call was busy and might not operate until the next day.

Dr. Fady referred him to orthopedics and wrote "antibiotics in theater".
h: Dr. Fady referred him to orthopedics and wrote "antibiotics in theater"

a.o: Dr. Fady left Mr. Samir's antibiotics for theater.
a.x: Mr. Samir should have had IV antibiotics, such as co-amoxiclav, within an hour of arrival.
a.w: Open fractures, especially with soil in them, get deep bone infections. Every hour of delay raises the risk.

a.o: Dr. Fady photographed the wound.
a.w: Photos stop the dressing being lifted again and again.

a.o: Dr. Fady straightened the leg into a splint.
a.x: The leg should be left as found.
a.w: Straightening restores blood flow and eases pain.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Samir's tetanus.
a.w: Dirty open wounds can cause tetanus.

t: Clicky hip in a baby told normal
s:
Baby Laila, 6 weeks old, came for her baby check. She was born breech by cesarean and is the first girl in her family. Her mother had a hip problem as a baby.

Dr. Ghada examined her hips and felt a clunk on the left when she moved the leg out. The thigh creases looked uneven.

She checked her weight, which was good, and her heart and eyes, which were normal.

Laila's mother said she liked to swaddle the baby tightly with her legs straight, as her grandmother did.

Laila was feeding well on breast milk and had gained weight steadily since birth. Her mother is a nurse and had read that clicks are usually harmless. Laila's older brother had normal hips.

Dr. Ghada said many baby hips click and that it would settle, without arranging a scan.
h: Dr. Ghada said many baby hips click and that it would settle, without arranging a scan

a.o: Dr. Ghada didn't arrange a hip scan for Baby Laila.
a.x: Baby Laila should have had an urgent hip ultrasound and orthopedic referral.
a.w: A clunk, uneven creases, breech birth, being a girl and a family history point to developmental dysplasia of the hip. Early harness treatment avoids surgery.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked the thigh creases.
a.w: Uneven creases can be a sign of hip problems.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about swaddling.
a.w: Tight swaddling with straight legs can harm hips.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about the mother's hip.
a.w: Hip dysplasia runs in families.

t: Spiral fracture in a baby not walking
s:
Baby Yusuf, 9 months old, was brought in by his mother because he cried when his right leg was moved. She said his leg got caught in the cot bars. He is not yet crawling. An X-ray showed a spiral fracture of the thigh bone.

Dr. Dina gave him pain relief and put his leg in traction. She called the orthopedic team.

She examined him fully and found small bruises on his upper arm and behind his ear. His growth was below average.

His mother said he was a clumsy baby. She said she was alone with three children and very tired.

Dr. Dina wrote "accidental injury" and did not contact the child protection team.
h: Dr. Dina wrote "accidental injury" and did not contact the child protection team

a.o: Dr. Dina accepted the cot story without child protection review for Baby Yusuf.
a.x: The child protection team should have been called the same day, with a skeletal survey and an eye check.
a.w: A thigh fracture in a baby who can't walk, with bruises behind the ear, points to abuse.

a.o: Dr. Dina examined Baby Yusuf from head to toe.
a.w: A full exam can find other injuries, like the bruises.

a.o: Dr. Dina noticed his growth.
a.w: Poor growth can be a sign of neglect.

a.o: Dr. Dina put Baby Yusuf's leg in traction.
a.x: A baby's leg doesn't need support.
a.w: Traction eases pain and holds the bone in place.

t: Elbow fracture without a pulse check
s:
Sara, 7, fell off the monkey bars onto her outstretched arm. Her right elbow was swollen and bent. An X-ray showed a displaced fracture above the elbow.

Dr. Inas gave her intranasal pain relief and a splint. She called the orthopedic team, who would operate that evening.

She kept her nil by mouth and asked her mother about her last meal.

Sara was crying and her hand looked pale. Her mother asked if she would need an operation.

The department was very busy, with two ambulances arriving at the same time. Sara's father was on his way from work and her little brother was with them. Her fingers were cold to touch when the nurse held her hand.

Dr. Inas did not check the pulse at the wrist or the feeling and movement in her hand.
h: Dr. Inas did not check the pulse at the wrist or the feeling and movement in her hand

a.o: Dr. Inas didn't check Sara's wrist pulse or hand nerves.
a.x: Sara should have had her pulse, color, feeling and finger movements checked and recorded, with urgent surgery if the pulse was absent.
a.w: Supracondylar fractures can damage the artery and nerves. A pale hand without a pulse needs surgery straight away.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Sara pain relief through her nose.
a.x: Pain relief could wait for theater.
a.w: Quick pain relief through the nose is kind and works fast.

a.o: Dr. Inas kept Sara nil by mouth.
a.x: Sara could eat since she was hungry.
a.w: She may need an operation under anesthetic.

a.o: Dr. Inas called the orthopedic team.
a.x: A cast in the department was enough.
a.w: Displaced elbow fractures need surgery.

t: Child's bone pain and fever called a sprain
s:
Omar, 8, came in with pain in his right shin for four days and a fever of 38.6°C. He was limping and did not want to walk. He had a cut on his knee from a fall a week ago.

Dr. Ihab found the shin very tender over one spot, warm and a little swollen. The cut had healed.

He checked his temperature and gave him ibuprofen.

Omar's father said he had been off his food and sleeping more than usual.

Omar plays football every afternoon and had been kicked on the same leg last week. He has had all his vaccines and no other illnesses. His mother had given him paracetamol, which brought the fever down for a few hours each time.

Dr. Ihab said it was a sprain and advised rest and ibuprofen.
h: Dr. Ihab said it was a sprain and advised rest and ibuprofen

a.o: Dr. Ihab called Omar's bone pain and fever a sprain.
a.x: Omar should have been sent to hospital the same day for blood tests, cultures, imaging and IV antibiotics.
a.w: Fever, a limp and pain over one spot of bone in a child mean osteomyelitis until proven otherwise. Delay can damage the bone and growth plate.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about the cut.
a.w: A skin break can let germs in.

a.o: Dr. Ihab felt Omar's shin for warmth.
a.w: A warm spot over the bone suggests infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab took Omar's temperature himself.
a.w: A measured fever is a key sign of bone infection.

t: Tight cast and swollen fingers sent home
s:
Mrs. Amal, 52, had a plaster cast put on yesterday for a broken wrist. She came back because her fingers were swollen, purple and throbbing all night. She could hardly move them, and they felt numb. The cast felt very tight.

Dr. Nada checked the fingers, which were cold and slow to turn pink after pressing. Moving the fingers caused a lot of pain.

She checked her pain relief and advised her to keep her arm raised on pillows. She asked about her other medicines, and she takes only a blood pressure tablet.

Mrs. Amal is a hairdresser and was worried about losing work. Her husband said she had not slept at all because of the pain, and that she had been told to come back if this happened.

Dr. Nada told her swelling was normal after a fracture, gave her stronger painkillers and sent her home with the cast as it was.
h: Dr. Nada told her swelling was normal after a fracture, gave her stronger painkillers and sent her home with the cast as it was

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mrs. Amal home in a tight cast with cold, numb fingers.
a.x: Mrs. Amal should have had the cast split down to the skin at once and her fingers rechecked, with orthopedic review if they did not improve.
a.w: A tight cast can cut off blood flow and cause compartment syndrome. Cold, numb, very painful fingers are warning signs.

a.o: Dr. Nada told her to keep the arm raised.
a.x: Raising the arm makes no difference.
a.w: Raising the arm reduces swelling.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked how quickly the fingers turned pink.
a.w: Slow return of color shows poor blood flow.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about Mrs. Amal's other medicines.
a.w: Medicines affect painkiller choice and swelling.

t: Shoulder put back without a nerve check
s:
Mr. Kareem, 25, dislocated his left shoulder playing basketball. It had popped out forwards, and his arm was held away from his body. An X-ray confirmed an anterior dislocation with no fracture.

Dr. Fady gave him gas and air and IV morphine and put the shoulder back with gentle traction. Mr. Kareem felt immediate relief, and a repeat X-ray showed it was back in place.

He put the arm in a sling and arranged a physiotherapy referral and a fracture clinic review in a week.

Mr. Kareem plays for a university team and asked when he could go back to playing. He said his outer shoulder felt numb, like a patch had been anesthetized.

Dr. Fady did not check the feeling over the outer shoulder or the movement of his deltoid muscle, before or after putting it back.
h: Dr. Fady did not check the feeling over the outer shoulder or the movement of his deltoid muscle, before or after putting it back

a.o: Dr. Fady didn't check Mr. Kareem's axillary nerve before or after the reduction.
a.x: Mr. Kareem should have had the feeling over his outer shoulder and his deltoid checked and recorded before and after.
a.w: The axillary nerve is often injured in shoulder dislocations. A numb patch over the outer shoulder shows the damage.

a.o: Dr. Fady did a repeat X-ray.
a.w: It confirms the shoulder is back in place.

a.o: Dr. Fady arranged physiotherapy.
a.w: Physio helps prevent another dislocation.

a.o: Dr. Fady put the arm in a sling.
a.w: A sling rests the shoulder for comfort.

t: Achilles tear called an ankle sprain
s:
Mr. Raafat, 42, felt a sudden "kick" at the back of his left heel while playing squash, and heard a pop. He looked round to see who had kicked him, but no one was there. He could walk but limped badly.

Dr. Inas found swelling at the back of his heel and a gap she could feel just above it. When she squeezed his calf with him kneeling on a chair, his foot did not move.

She X-rayed his ankle, which showed no fracture. He could still move his foot up and down a little.

Mr. Raafat is a lawyer and had an important court case the next week. He takes ciprofloxacin, started five days ago for a urine infection.

Dr. Inas diagnosed an ankle sprain, gave him a bandage and crutches and advised rest.
h: Dr. Inas diagnosed an ankle sprain, gave him a bandage and crutches and advised rest

a.o: Dr. Inas called Mr. Raafat's Achilles tear an ankle sprain.
a.x: Mr. Raafat should have had his foot put in a pointed-toe boot and an urgent orthopedic or fracture clinic review.
a.w: A pop, a felt gap and a foot that doesn't move when the calf is squeezed mean an Achilles tendon rupture.

a.o: Dr. Inas did the calf squeeze test.
a.w: No foot movement shows a tendon tear.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about ciprofloxacin.
a.w: Ciprofloxacin can weaken tendons.

a.o: Dr. Inas X-rayed the ankle.
a.w: An X-ray rules out a bone injury.

t: Back pain after breast cancer given exercises
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 58, came in with back pain in the middle of her back for six weeks. It was worse at night and when lying down, and paracetamol did not help. She had breast cancer treated five years ago.

Dr. Ghada found her spine tender in the middle of her back. Her leg strength, feeling and reflexes were normal. She had lost 3 kg.

She checked her blood count and calcium. Her calcium was mildly raised.

Mrs. Hanem had moved house recently and thought she had hurt her back carrying boxes. She was keen to start yoga with her daughter.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed a back strain and referred her for physiotherapy and exercises.
h: Dr. Ghada diagnosed a back strain and referred her for physiotherapy and exercises

a.o: Dr. Ghada called Mrs. Hanem's night back pain a strain.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem should have had an urgent MRI of the spine and referral to oncology.
a.w: Back pain at night after breast cancer, with tenderness, weight loss and a high calcium, can be cancer spread to the spine.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked her calcium.
a.w: Bone cancer can raise calcium.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked leg strength.
a.w: Weakness can mean spinal cord pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about weight loss.
a.w: Weight loss is a red flag.

t: Hip replacement without clot prevention
s:
Mrs. Samia, 70, had a planned hip replacement this morning. She was comfortable and the wound was dry. She has a BMI of 34 and takes HRT. She had a clot in her leg ten years ago.

Dr. Hala checked her blood count and kidney tests, which were fine. She asked the physiotherapist to get her up the next morning.

She prescribed regular paracetamol and a little oxycodone for pain.

Mrs. Samia asked whether she would need injections at home, because she hated needles.

She lives with her husband in a house with stairs and had a raised toilet seat fitted before surgery. Her pre-operative blood pressure and heart tracing were normal. The anesthetist had used a spinal anesthetic, and her legs were now waking up.

Dr. Hala did not prescribe any clot prevention, writing "early mobilization".
h: Dr. Hala did not prescribe any clot prevention, writing "early mobilization"

a.o: Dr. Hala gave Mrs. Samia no clot prevention after hip replacement.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have had low molecular weight heparin or a tablet blood thinner for about 28 to 35 days, with stockings.
a.w: Hip replacement is one of the highest-risk operations for clots, and her past clot, weight and HRT add to it.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked the physiotherapist to get Mrs. Samia up the next day.
a.x: She should stay in bed for a week.
a.w: Early walking helps recovery and lowers clot risk.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked Mrs. Samia's kidney tests.
a.x: Kidneys were off topic after a hip operation.
a.w: Kidney function affects blood thinner choice and dose.

a.o: Dr. Hala prescribed regular paracetamol.
a.x: Paracetamol is too weak after surgery.
a.w: Regular paracetamol cuts the need for opioids.

t: Night bone pain in a teenager called growing pains
s:
Karim, 15, came in with pain above his left knee for two months. It was worse at night and woke him up. In the last two weeks he had noticed a firm swelling there. He plays basketball and thought he had knocked it.

Dr. Ihab found a hard, slightly tender lump above the knee on the inner side, fixed to the bone. The knee itself moved fully, with no fluid.

He checked his temperature, which was normal, and his weight, which had dropped by 2 kg. He asked about other joint pains, which Karim did not have.

Karim's mother said her son had grown 8 cm in the past year and that his older brother had "growing pains" too. Karim wanted to play in a tournament next month.

Dr. Ihab diagnosed growing pains, advised ibuprofen at night and rest from basketball, and booked a review in three months.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed growing pains, advised ibuprofen at night and rest from basketball, and booked a review in three months

a.o: Dr. Ihab called Karim's night pain and bony lump growing pains.
a.x: Karim should have had an urgent X-ray of the knee and referral to a bone tumor team if it was abnormal.
a.w: Night pain in one bone with a hard lump in a teenager can be a bone cancer such as osteosarcoma. Growing pains affect both legs and never cause a lump.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Karim's weight.
a.w: Weight loss is a red flag.

a.o: Dr. Ihab felt whether the lump was fixed to the bone.
a.w: A lump fixed to bone suggests a bone tumor.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about other joint pains.
a.w: Pain in many joints points to other causes, like arthritis.

t: Hand cut without a tendon check
s:
Mr. Tamer, 28, cut the palm side of his right index finger on a broken glass while washing up. The cut was 2 cm long, just over the middle crease of the finger. It had bled a lot but now stopped. He is a guitarist.

Dr. Fady cleaned the wound and checked for glass with an X-ray, which showed none. He checked his tetanus, which was up to date.

He checked the feeling on both sides of the fingertip, which was normal, and the blood supply, which was good.

Mr. Tamer said the finger felt a little weak when he tried to grip his phone. He had a gig in a week.

Dr. Fady closed the cut with stitches and sent him home, without testing whether he could bend the tip and middle joints of the finger on their own.
h: Dr. Fady closed the cut with stitches and sent him home, without testing whether he could bend the tip and middle joints of the finger on their own

a.o: Dr. Fady stitched Mr. Tamer's finger cut without checking the flexor tendons.
a.x: Mr. Tamer should have had each flexor tendon tested on its own, with referral to the hand surgeons if weak or painful.
a.w: A cut over the finger crease can cut a tendon. Missed tendon cuts are hard to fix later, and a guitarist needs full finger movement.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked the feeling on both sides of the fingertip.
a.w: Finger nerves run on both sides and are often cut too.

a.o: Dr. Fady X-rayed for glass.
a.w: Glass shows on X-ray and must be removed.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Tamer's tetanus.
a.w: Cuts can cause tetanus.

t: Breathless after a thigh fracture blamed on anxiety
s:
Mr. Hany, 22, broke his thigh bone in a car crash yesterday and is waiting for surgery in traction. Tonight he became breathless and confused. His oxygen was 88% on air, his pulse 128 and his temperature 38.1°C. Small red spots had appeared on his chest and in his armpits.

Dr. Ayman listened to his chest, which had a few crackles. He gave oxygen and checked his blood gas, which showed low oxygen.

He checked his blood count, which showed low platelets, and his sugar, which was normal.

Mr. Hany's mother said he had always been anxious in hospitals. He kept trying to pull off his oxygen mask.

Dr. Ayman wrote "anxiety and pain", gave him lorazepam to calm him, and planned to review him on the morning round.
h: Dr. Ayman wrote "anxiety and pain", gave him lorazepam to calm him, and planned to review him on the morning round

a.o: Dr. Ayman blamed Mr. Hany's breathlessness and confusion on anxiety.
a.x: Mr. Hany should have had urgent high-flow oxygen, ICU review and early fixation of the fracture.
a.w: Low oxygen, confusion and a rash in the armpits after a thigh fracture point to fat embolism syndrome, which can be fatal.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked his blood gas.
a.w: The gas shows how low the oxygen is.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked his platelets.
a.w: Low platelets are part of fat embolism.

a.o: Dr. Ayman listened to his chest.
a.w: Crackles show lung involvement.

t: Older man's neck not scanned after a fall
s:
Mr. Raouf, 78, tripped on a step and fell forwards, hitting his forehead on the pavement. He had a cut on his forehead and pain in his neck. He could move his arms and legs. He has arthritis in his neck.

Dr. Nada checked his strength and feeling, which were normal. He was tender in the middle of the back of his neck.

She cleaned and closed the cut on his forehead. She checked his blood thinner status; he takes none.

Mr. Raouf wanted to go home to his wife, who has dementia and was alone. He turned his head slowly to show he was fine.

Dr. Nada sent him home with painkillers, without imaging his neck, writing "moving all limbs".
h: Dr. Nada sent him home with painkillers, without imaging his neck, writing "moving all limbs"

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Raouf home without imaging his neck.
a.x: Mr. Raouf should have had a CT scan of his neck before moving it, with a collar until cleared.
a.w: Age over 65 with neck pain after a head injury means a high risk of a neck fracture. Stiff, arthritic necks break easily.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked his strength and feeling.
a.w: A normal exam is important but doesn't rule out a fracture.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about blood thinners.
a.w: Blood thinners raise bleeding risk.

a.o: Dr. Nada closed the cut.
a.w: Closing the cut prevents infection.

t: Spine fracture without bone protection
s:
Mrs. Nabila, 71, came in with sudden pain in the middle of her back after lifting a bag of rice two weeks ago. An X-ray showed a squashed bone in her spine. She has had no cancer or weight loss, and her blood tests, including calcium and myeloma tests, were normal.

Dr. Ghada gave her regular paracetamol and a small dose of codeine with a laxative, and advised gentle walking. She referred her to physiotherapy for back exercises.

She asked about falls, and Mrs. Nabila had fallen once last year. She checked her vitamin D, which was low, and started calcium and vitamin D.

Mrs. Nabila went through the menopause at 44 and took steroid tablets for asthma flares several times last year. Her mother broke her hip at 75.

Dr. Ghada said the bone would heal by itself, and did not arrange a bone density scan or start bone-protecting treatment.
h: did not arrange a bone density scan or start bone-protecting treatment

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave Mrs. Nabila no bone protection after a fragility spine fracture.
a.x: Mrs. Nabila should have started a bisphosphonate such as alendronic acid, with a bone density scan if needed.
a.w: A spine fracture from a small strain means osteoporosis. Without treatment, the chance of another fracture, including the hip, is high.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Nabila's myeloma tests.
a.w: Myeloma can also cause squashed spine bones.

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave a laxative with codeine.
a.w: Codeine causes constipation, especially in older people.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about Mrs. Nabila's steroid tablets.
