a.w: Repeated steroid courses weaken bones.

t: Limping child with fever sent home
s:
Yasmin, 5, came in with a limp and pain in her right hip since yesterday. She would not put weight on the leg. She had a fever of 38.9°C. She had a cold a week ago.

Dr. Dina found her hip held bent and turned out, and any movement hurt. Her blood tests showed a white count of 16 and a CRP of 90.

She gave her ibuprofen and paracetamol, and the fever settled a little. An ultrasound showed fluid in the hip joint.

Yasmin's mother said Yasmin had been playing on the trampoline. Her father asked whether it was a pulled muscle.

Dr. Dina diagnosed an irritable hip after a virus and sent her home with ibuprofen and rest.
h: Dr. Dina diagnosed an irritable hip after a virus and sent her home with ibuprofen and rest

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Yasmin home with a possible septic hip.
a.x: Yasmin should have had the hip fluid drained urgently for testing and IV antibiotics.
a.w: Fever, refusing to walk, a high white count and CRP and fluid in the joint point to septic arthritis, which can destroy the hip within days.

a.o: Dr. Dina did an ultrasound.
a.w: Ultrasound shows fluid in the hip.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked blood tests.
a.w: Blood tests help tell infection from irritable hip.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked about the trampoline.
a.w: An injury could explain a limp.

t: Hot swollen diabetic foot called cellulitis
s:
Mr. Hamed, 58, has had type 2 diabetes for 20 years with numb feet. His right foot had become hot, red and swollen over two weeks. It was not painful. He had twisted it slightly stepping off a curb. He had no fever.

Dr. Ihab found the foot warm, with the arch flattened. There were no cuts or ulcers. The skin temperature was clearly higher than the other foot.

He checked his blood tests, which showed a normal white count and CRP. His sugar was high.

Mr. Hamed works as a postman and walks all day. He said the foot did not hurt, so he kept working.

Dr. Ihab diagnosed cellulitis and gave him antibiotics, telling him to keep walking.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed cellulitis and gave him antibiotics, telling him to keep walking

a.o: Dr. Ihab called Mr. Hamed's hot, painless foot cellulitis.
a.x: Mr. Hamed should have had an urgent X-ray, a total contact cast to take weight off the foot and referral to the foot team.
a.w: A hot, swollen, painless foot in diabetes with numb feet is Charcot foot until proven otherwise. Walking on it can collapse the foot.

a.o: Dr. Ihab looked for ulcers.
a.w: Ulcers can let in infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab compared the foot temperatures.
a.w: A hot foot is a key sign of Charcot.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked the CRP.
a.w: A normal CRP makes infection less likely.

t: Dislocated ankle with tented skin left for X-ray
s:
Mrs. Rana, 45, slipped on ice outside her office and twisted her left ankle badly. Her foot was turned out at an odd angle. The skin on the inside of her ankle was stretched white over a bone, and her foot was pale and cool.

Dr. Fady gave her gas and air and IV morphine. He felt for the pulse in her foot, which was faint, and checked the feeling, which was a little reduced on top of the foot.

He took photos of the foot for the orthopedic team and kept her nil by mouth. He asked about her last meal and her allergies.

Mrs. Rana works as a bank manager and was frightened. She asked whether she would need an operation and how long she would be off work. The X-ray department had a 40-minute queue.

Dr. Fady sent her for an X-ray first, so he could see the fracture before trying to straighten the ankle.
h: Dr. Fady sent her for an X-ray first, so he could see the fracture before trying to straighten the ankle

a.o: Dr. Fady made Mrs. Rana wait for an X-ray before straightening her dislocated ankle.
a.x: Mrs. Rana should have had the ankle pulled back into line at once under pain relief, then a splint and an X-ray.
a.w: White, tented skin and a faint pulse mean the skin and blood supply are dying. Straightening cannot wait for an X-ray.

a.o: Dr. Fady felt for Mrs. Rana's foot pulse.
a.x: The pulse was off topic in a fracture.
a.w: A faint pulse shows the blood supply is at risk.

a.o: Dr. Fady kept Mrs. Rana nil by mouth.
a.w: She may need surgery under anesthetic.

a.o: Dr. Fady photographed the foot.
a.w: Photos stop repeated exposure of the injury.

t: Knee dislocation without a blood vessel check
s:
Mr. Atef, 30, was hit by a car while crossing the road. His right knee was dislocated, but it went back into place by itself when the paramedics moved him. Now the knee was very swollen and wobbly in every direction. His foot felt cool and numb.

Dr. Nada felt for the foot pulses, which were faint compared with the other foot. She did not measure the blood pressure at the ankle.

She X-rayed the knee, which showed no fracture, and put the leg in a splint. She checked the nerve on the outside of the knee, and he could not lift his foot well.

Mr. Atef plays football at weekends and was worried about playing again. His wife asked whether he could go home that night.

Dr. Nada referred him to the fracture clinic for the next day, without a CT angiogram or a vascular surgery review.
h: Dr. Nada referred him to the fracture clinic for the next day, without a CT angiogram or a vascular surgery review

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Atef to fracture clinic without checking his knee artery.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have had ankle-brachial pressures, a CT angiogram and an urgent vascular surgery review.
a.w: A knee dislocation often tears the artery behind the knee, even if it pops back. A missed artery injury can cost the leg within hours.

a.o: Dr. Nada X-rayed Mr. Atef's knee.
a.w: An X-ray rules out fractures.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked whether Mr. Atef could lift his foot.
a.w: The nerve on the outside of the knee is often damaged too.

a.o: Dr. Nada compared the foot pulses on both sides.
a.w: Comparing sides shows a weaker pulse.

t: Bronchiolitis baby sent home feeding poorly
s:
Baby Hamza, 3 months old, came in with a runny nose for three days and now fast breathing and a wet cough. His mother said he was taking less than half his usual milk and had only two wet nappies today. He was born at 34 weeks.

Dr. Dina found him breathing 64 times a minute, with the skin pulling in under his ribs. His oxygen was 89% on air. His temperature was 37.8°C and his chest had fine crackles all over.

She suctioned his nose gently, which helped him feed a little better, and explained to his mother that this was bronchiolitis, a virus that usually peaks on day three to five.

His mother has two other young children at home and her husband works nights. She asked whether antibiotics or an inhaler would help.

Dr. Dina said there was no treatment for the virus, and sent Hamza home with nasal saline drops and advice to come back if he got worse.
h: sent Hamza home with nasal saline drops and advice to come back if he got worse

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Baby Hamza home with low oxygen and poor feeding.
a.x: Baby Hamza should have been admitted for oxygen, help with feeding through a tube if needed, and close monitoring.
a.w: Oxygen below 90 to 92%, feeding under half, fast breathing and prematurity mean moderate to severe bronchiolitis. Babies can tire and stop breathing.

a.o: Dr. Dina did not give Baby Hamza antibiotics.
a.w: Bronchiolitis is a virus, and antibiotics do not help.

a.o: Dr. Dina suctioned Baby Hamza's nose.
a.w: Clearing the nose helps babies breathe and feed.

a.o: Dr. Dina noted that Baby Hamza was born early.
a.w: Premature babies get sicker with bronchiolitis.

t: Drooling child laid flat to look at the throat
s:
Mariam, 4, came in with a high fever and a sore throat that started a few hours ago. She was sitting forward, drooling and refusing to swallow. Her voice was muffled. She had not had all her vaccines because the family had moved countries.

Dr. Nada noticed a soft, high-pitched noise when she breathed in. Her oxygen was 95% and her temperature 39.6°C.

She called the senior anesthetist and the ENT surgeon, and kept Mariam on her mother's lap.

Mariam's mother was frightened and asked why her daughter would not swallow her own spit.

Before the team arrived, Dr. Nada laid Mariam flat on the trolley and used a tongue depressor to look at her throat.
h: Dr. Nada laid Mariam flat on the trolley and used a tongue depressor to look at her throat

a.o: Dr. Nada laid Mariam flat and looked in her throat with a tongue depressor.
a.x: Mariam should have been kept calm and upright on her mother's lap, with no throat exam until the airway team was ready in theater.
a.w: Drooling, fever and a muffled voice in an unvaccinated child suggest epiglottitis. Upsetting the child or laying her flat can block the airway completely.

a.o: Dr. Nada called the anesthetist and ENT surgeon.
a.w: A swollen epiglottis may need an expert to secure the airway.

a.o: Dr. Nada kept Mariam on her mother's lap.
a.x: The child should be on the trolley.
a.w: Calm and upright keeps the airway open.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about vaccines.
a.w: The Hib vaccine prevents epiglottitis.

t: Croup sent home without steroids
s:
Ali, 2, came in at 2 a.m. with a barking cough like a seal and a hoarse voice. He had a mild cold for two days. When he cried, he made a harsh noise breathing in, but at rest he was quiet.

Dr. Fady found his oxygen 97% and his chest with mild pulling in under the ribs when crying. He was alert and drinking.

He told his mother to keep Ali calm and upright, and explained that croup is caused by a virus and is usually worse at night.

Ali's mother said cold air outside had seemed to help on the way in. She asked whether steam from a hot shower would help.

Dr. Fady sent him home with paracetamol and no steroid, saying "it's only mild croup".
h: Dr. Fady sent him home with paracetamol and no steroid, saying "it's only mild croup"

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Ali no steroid for croup.
a.x: Ali should have had a single dose of oral dexamethasone before going home.
a.w: One dose of dexamethasone helps even mild croup, shortening the illness and reducing return visits.

a.o: Dr. Fady told Ali's mother to keep him calm.
a.w: Crying makes the airway narrowing worse.

a.o: Dr. Fady explained croup is worse at night.
a.w: Knowing this helps parents.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Ali's oxygen.
a.w: Low oxygen shows severe croup.

t: Five days of fever called a virus
s:
Yusuf, 3, has had a high fever for six days that does not settle with paracetamol. He has red eyes without discharge, cracked red lips, and a red rash on his body. His hands and feet are swollen and red. He has a swollen gland on one side of his neck.

Dr. Rana checked his throat, which was red, and his ears, which were normal. His blood tests showed a high CRP and platelets of 520.

She gave him ibuprofen and fluids, and checked his urine, which showed a few white cells.

Yusuf's mother said he had been very irritable and would not let anyone touch him. She asked whether it was measles, because there had been cases at his nursery.

Dr. Rana diagnosed a viral illness and sent him home to rest, with a review if the fever lasted another week.
h: Dr. Rana diagnosed a viral illness and sent him home to rest, with a review if the fever lasted another week

a.o: Dr. Rana called Yusuf's illness a virus.
a.x: Yusuf should have been admitted for IV immunoglobulin and aspirin, with a heart scan.
a.w: Five days of fever, red eyes, cracked lips, rash, swollen hands and a neck gland mean Kawasaki disease. Without treatment within 10 days, 1 in 4 children get damage to the heart arteries.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Yusuf's platelets.
a.w: High platelets are common in Kawasaki disease.

a.o: Dr. Rana thought about measles.
a.w: Measles can look similar and must be considered.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Yusuf's urine.
a.w: A urine infection can cause fever in children.

t: Red jelly stool called gastroenteritis
s:
Baby Adam, 9 months old, came in with sudden screaming attacks every 15 minutes, when he drew his legs up and went pale. Between attacks he was sleepy and floppy. He had vomited three times and passed a stool that looked like red currant jelly.

Dr. Dina felt a sausage-shaped lump in his belly on the right side. His temperature was normal and his pulse 160.

She put in a drip and gave him fluids. She checked his sugar, which was normal.

His mother said he had a cold last week. She wanted to know if it was something he ate.

Dr. Dina diagnosed gastroenteritis, gave oral rehydration solution and planned to see him again in the morning.
h: Dr. Dina diagnosed gastroenteritis, gave oral rehydration solution and planned to see him again in the morning

a.o: Dr. Dina called Baby Adam's intussusception gastroenteritis.
a.x: Baby Adam should have had an urgent ultrasound and a surgical review, with air enema to unfold the bowel.
a.w: Screaming attacks, red jelly stool and a sausage-shaped lump mean the bowel has telescoped into itself. Delay can kill the bowel.

a.o: Dr. Dina felt Baby Adam's belly.
a.w: A sausage-shaped lump is a key sign.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Baby Adam's sugar.
a.w: Sick babies can have low sugar.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked about the cold.
a.w: A recent virus can trigger intussusception.

t: Projectile vomiting called reflux
s:
Baby Omar, 5 weeks old, has been vomiting after every feed for a week. The vomit shoots across the room and is milky, never green. He is hungry right after vomiting and wants to feed again. He has lost weight since last week.

Dr. Ghada watched him feed and felt a small, olive-sized lump in the upper middle of his belly. She saw waves moving across his belly from left to right.

She checked his nappies, which were fewer and drier than usual. His soft spot was slightly sunken.

Omar is the first son in the family. His father had an operation for vomiting as a baby.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed reflux, advised smaller, more frequent feeds and prescribed a thickener.
h: Dr. Ghada diagnosed reflux, advised smaller, more frequent feeds and prescribed a thickener

a.o: Dr. Ghada called Baby Omar's projectile vomiting reflux.
a.x: Baby Omar should have been sent to hospital for blood tests, an ultrasound and surgery.
a.w: Projectile vomiting, an olive lump and visible waves mean pyloric stenosis. It causes dehydration and salt imbalance and needs an operation.

a.o: Dr. Ghada watched Baby Omar feed.
a.w: A test feed shows the waves and the lump.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked his nappies.
a.w: Fewer wet nappies show dehydration.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about the father's baby operation.
a.w: Pyloric stenosis runs in families.

t: Child in DKA given a large fluid bolus
s:
Lina, 9, was admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. She had been thirsty and passing a lot of urine for a month and had lost weight. Her sugar was 32, her pH 7.08 and her ketones 6.2. She weighed 26 kg. She was alert, with a blood pressure of 102/64.

Dr. Ayman put in two drips and sent blood for salts, kidney tests and a blood gas. He started a heart monitor.

He planned an insulin drip at 0.05 units/kg/hour, starting an hour after fluids began, and asked for hourly checks of her sugar, ketones and neurological state.

Lina's mother was frightened and asked whether her daughter had diabetes for life. Lina was sleepy but answered questions.

To rehydrate her quickly, he gave 20 mL/kg of saline over 15 minutes, followed by another 20 mL/kg.
h: he gave 20 mL/kg of saline over 15 minutes, followed by another 20 mL/kg

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave Lina two large fast fluid boluses in DKA.
a.x: Lina should have had a single 10 mL/kg bolus over an hour only if needed, then slow fluid replacement over 48 hours.
a.w: Fast fluids in children with DKA raise the risk of cerebral edema, swelling of the brain, which can be fatal.

a.o: Dr. Ayman waited an hour before starting insulin.
a.w: Starting insulin after fluids lowers the risk of brain swelling.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked for hourly neurological checks.
a.w: Headache or drowsiness can be early signs of brain swelling.

a.o: Dr. Ayman started a heart monitor.
a.w: Potassium changes can cause heart rhythm problems.

t: First febrile fit given long-term epilepsy medicine
s:
Malak, 2, had a fit at home lasting two minutes, with her arms and legs jerking. She had a fever of 39.3°C and a cold. After the fit she was sleepy for half an hour, then back to normal.

Dr. Inas found her alert, with a red throat and ears. Her neck was not stiff, and she had no rash.

She explained to her parents that febrile fits are common and usually harmless, and gave them advice about keeping her safe during a fit.

Malak's father had febrile fits as a child. Her parents were very frightened and asked whether she had epilepsy.

Dr. Inas started sodium valproate every day to prevent more fits, and told them Malak would probably have epilepsy.
h: Dr. Inas started sodium valproate every day to prevent more fits, and told them Malak would probably have epilepsy

a.o: Dr. Inas started daily valproate after Malak's simple febrile fit.
a.x: Malak should have had reassurance, treatment of the fever's cause and safety advice, with no long-term medicine.
a.w: Simple febrile fits are common and harmless. They rarely lead to epilepsy, and daily medicine brings side effects without benefit.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked Malak's neck.
a.w: A stiff neck can mean meningitis.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about the father's fits.
a.w: Febrile fits run in families.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave advice on fit safety.
a.w: Parents need to know what to do.

t: Aspirin for chickenpox fever
s:
Sami, 7, has chickenpox, with itchy spots all over and a fever of 38.7°C for two days. He was eating less but drinking well. His spots were crusting on his chest but new ones were appearing on his legs.

Dr. Ihab checked his chest, which was clear, and looked at the spots, which showed no signs of infection.

He advised calamine lotion for the itch, short nails to prevent scratching, and keeping him off school until all the spots had crusted.

Sami's mother said ibuprofen was out of stock at the pharmacy. She asked what else she could give, as paracetamol alone was not enough.

Dr. Ihab told her to give children's aspirin with the paracetamol for the fever.
h: Dr. Ihab told her to give children's aspirin with the paracetamol for the fever

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised aspirin for Sami's chickenpox fever.
a.x: Sami should have had paracetamol only, with no aspirin and no ibuprofen in chickenpox.
a.w: Aspirin in children with viral illness can cause Reye's syndrome, with liver and brain damage. Ibuprofen in chickenpox raises the risk of severe skin infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab kept Sami off school until the spots crusted.
a.x: He could go back to school at once.
a.w: Chickenpox is catching until all spots have crusted.

a.o: Dr. Ihab looked for infected spots.
a.w: Infected spots can lead to serious skin infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised short nails.
a.w: Scratching causes scars and infection.

t: Jaundice on the first day called normal
s:
Baby Lina was born last night by normal delivery at term. This morning, at 18 hours old, the midwife noticed her skin and eyes were yellow. Her mother is blood group O positive. Lina was feeding well on breast milk.

Dr. Rana examined her and found yellow skin down to her belly. She was alert and pink, with no bruises.

She asked about the mother's other children, and her first child needed light treatment for jaundice.

Lina's mother was tired and wanted to go home that afternoon. Her husband asked whether sunlight would help.

Dr. Rana said newborn jaundice is common and normal, and planned to check her again on day three.
h: Dr. Rana said newborn jaundice is common and normal, and planned to check her again on day three

a.o: Dr. Rana called Baby Lina's jaundice at 18 hours normal.
a.x: Baby Lina should have had an urgent blood test for bilirubin, blood group and a Coombs test, with light treatment if needed.
a.w: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is never normal. It is often from blood group problems and can rise fast, damaging the brain.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about the first child.
a.w: Past jaundice needing treatment raises the risk again.

a.o: Dr. Rana looked for bruises.
a.w: Bruising can raise bilirubin.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Lina's feeding.
a.w: Poor feeding makes jaundice worse.

t: Moderate asthma attack without steroids
s:
Hana, 8, has asthma and came in with wheezing and breathlessness for a day after a cold. She could speak in sentences, and her oxygen was 94%. Her peak flow was 60% of her best.

Dr. Fady gave her ten puffs of salbutamol through a spacer. Her wheeze improved and her peak flow rose to 75%.

He checked her inhaler technique, which was poor, and showed her how to use the spacer. He asked about smoking at home, and her father smokes.

Hana's mother said she often forgot her brown preventer inhaler. She asked whether Hana could go to school the next day.

Dr. Fady sent her home with salbutamol as needed, without giving oral steroids.
h: Dr. Fady sent her home with salbutamol as needed, without giving oral steroids

a.o: Dr. Fady sent Hana home after a moderate asthma attack without oral steroids.
a.x: Hana should have had a three-day course of prednisolone, with a review of her preventer.
a.w: Steroids reduce airway swelling and lower the risk of the attack returning or getting worse.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked her inhaler technique.
a.w: Poor technique means the medicine doesn't reach the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about smoking at home.
a.w: Smoke triggers asthma.

a.o: Dr. Fady used a spacer.
a.x: A spacer is unnecessary in an attack.
a.w: A spacer works as well as a nebulizer.

t: Anaphylaxis treated with an antihistamine only
s:
Omar, 10, ate a cake at a birthday party and within ten minutes his lips swelled and he had hives all over. He started wheezing and said his throat felt tight. He has a peanut allergy but had no auto-injector with him. His oxygen was 92% and his blood pressure 84/50.

Dr. Nada laid him flat with his legs raised and gave high-flow oxygen. She put in a drip and gave a fluid bolus.

She called for senior help and asked the nurse to start a timer and watch his breathing closely.

Omar's mother said they had forgotten the auto-injector at home. She was crying and asked whether he would be all right.

Dr. Nada gave IV chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone, and planned adrenaline "if he gets worse".
h: Dr. Nada gave IV chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone, and planned adrenaline "if he gets worse"

a.o: Dr. Nada held back adrenaline in Omar's anaphylaxis.
a.x: Omar should have had IM adrenaline into the thigh straight away, repeated after five minutes if needed.
a.w: Wheeze, throat tightness and low blood pressure after a known allergen mean anaphylaxis. Adrenaline is the only drug that treats it; antihistamines and steroids are too slow.

a.o: Dr. Nada laid Omar flat with his legs raised.
a.x: He should have been sat up.
a.w: Lying flat helps low blood pressure, unless breathing is very hard.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave a fluid bolus.
a.w: Low blood pressure in anaphylaxis needs fluids.

a.o: Dr. Nada called for senior help.
a.w: Anaphylaxis can get worse quickly.

t: Testicle pain sent for a morning scan
s:
Ahmed, 14, woke up at 5 a.m. with sudden severe pain in his left testicle. He vomited twice. He had no injury. The pain had been going for two hours.

Dr. Fady found the left testicle swollen, very tender and sitting higher than the right. Lifting it did not ease the pain.

He checked his urine, which was clear, and gave him morphine.

Ahmed was embarrassed to be examined. His father asked whether it could be an infection.

Ahmed plays in the school football team and had a match that afternoon. He had a similar short pain a month ago that went away by itself after twenty minutes. The ultrasound department was closed until 8 a.m., and the surgeon on call was in the hospital.

Dr. Fady booked an ultrasound for the morning and admitted him for pain relief.
h: Dr. Fady booked an ultrasound for the morning and admitted him for pain relief

a.o: Dr. Fady left Ahmed's suspected torsion for a morning scan.
a.x: Ahmed should have gone straight to theater for urgent surgery, without waiting for a scan.
a.w: Sudden testicle pain in a teenager with a high-riding testicle is torsion until proven otherwise. The testicle can die after six hours.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his urine.
a.w: Infection can cause similar pain.

a.o: Dr. Fady lifted the testicle.
a.w: Relief on lifting suggests infection, not torsion.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave morphine.
a.w: Pain relief is needed.

t: Toddler with diarrhea given loperamide
s:
Yara, 2, has had watery diarrhea and vomiting for two days. Her brother had the same last week. She is drinking but less than usual and had fewer wet nappies today. She was alert and playful.

Dr. Ghada checked her for dehydration: her mouth was moist, her eyes were not sunken, and her skin bounced back.

She advised oral rehydration solution little and often, and to keep breastfeeding.

Yara's mother had a nursery appointment and asked for something to stop the diarrhea.

Yara has no other illnesses and her vaccines are up to date, including rotavirus. Her stools had no blood or mucus. She had no fever today. Her mother works as a cashier and had already missed two days of work.

Dr. Ghada prescribed loperamide syrup to slow the diarrhea.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed loperamide syrup to slow the diarrhea

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave loperamide to Yara for gastroenteritis.
a.x: Yara should have had oral rehydration only, without anti-diarrhea drugs.
a.w: Loperamide is not for children under 12 with gastroenteritis. It can cause bowel paralysis and drowsiness.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked for dehydration.
a.w: Dehydration guides treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised breastfeeding.
a.w: Breastfeeding helps recovery.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about her brother.
a.w: A shared illness suggests a virus.

t: Swallowed button battery told it will pass
s:
Laila, 3, swallowed a coin-shaped battery from a TV remote an hour ago. Her mother saw her do it. Laila was drooling a little and refusing to eat.

Dr. Inas X-rayed her chest and saw a round object in the gullet, with a double ring at the edge.

She checked her breathing, which was normal, and her oxygen, which was 98%.

Laila's mother asked whether it would pass in her poo like a coin.

Laila had no other illnesses and had eaten breakfast two hours earlier. Her mother had brought the remote, which was missing its battery cover. The camera team was busy with another case and said they could see her later in the day.

Dr. Inas said it would likely pass and sent her home, asking the mother to check her stools.
h: Dr. Inas said it would likely pass and sent her home, asking the mother to check her stools

a.o: Dr. Inas sent Laila home with a button battery stuck in her gullet.
a.x: Laila should have had the battery removed with an urgent camera test within two hours.
a.w: A button battery in the gullet burns through the wall within hours and can cause death from bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Inas did an X-ray.
a.w: The X-ray shows the double ring of a battery.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked her breathing.
a.w: A stuck object can block the airway.

a.o: Dr. Inas noticed the drooling.
a.w: Drooling shows the gullet is blocked.

t: Toddler drinking a liter of milk given iron
s:
Adam, 2, is pale and tired. His blood test showed iron deficiency anemia, with a hemoglobin of 88. He drinks about a liter of cow's milk a day from a bottle and eats little else.

Dr. Ihab checked his growth, which was normal, and his stool, which had no blood.

He started iron drops and asked for a repeat blood count in a month.

Adam's mother said he refuses food but loves his milk. She asked whether the drops would stain his teeth.

Adam is a happy boy who is talking well. His older sister eats a mixed diet and is well. The family eats meat twice a week. His mother works part-time, and his grandmother looks after him and gives him a bottle whenever he cries.

Dr. Ihab told her to carry on with the milk because "milk is healthy".
h: Dr. Ihab told her to carry on with the milk because "milk is healthy"

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Adam's mother to keep giving a liter of milk.
a.x: Adam should have had his milk cut to about 400 mL a day, from a cup, with more iron-rich foods.
a.w: Too much cow's milk causes iron deficiency. It fills the child up and blocks iron absorption.

a.o: Dr. Ihab started iron drops.
a.w: Iron treats the anemia.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Adam's growth chart.
a.x: Growth was off topic in anemia.
a.w: Poor growth would point to other causes, like coeliac disease.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Adam's stool for blood.
a.w: Hidden gut bleeding can cause anemia.

t: Purple leg rash without urine or blood pressure follow-up
s:
Mona, 6, has a raised purple rash on the backs of her legs and her bottom for three days. Her knees and ankles are sore, and she had tummy aches. She had a sore throat two weeks ago. She has no fever and is otherwise well.

Dr. Ghada found the rash did not fade under a glass, but it was raised and only on the legs and bottom. Her blood count, including platelets, and her clotting tests were normal.

She checked her urine, which showed a little blood, and her blood pressure, which was normal. She advised paracetamol for the joint pain and rest.

Mona's mother was relieved the blood tests were normal. She said they were going to her grandmother's village for the summer, far from any clinic. She asked whether the rash would leave scars.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed Henoch-Schonlein purpura and said it would settle by itself, with no follow-up needed.
h: Dr. Ghada diagnosed Henoch-Schonlein purpura and said it would settle by itself, with no follow-up needed

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave Mona no follow-up for HSP with blood in her urine.
a.x: Mona should have had her urine and blood pressure checked regularly for at least six months, with a plan for checks while away.
a.w: HSP can damage the kidneys weeks or months later. Blood in the urine at the start raises that risk.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mona's platelets.
a.w: A normal platelet count separates HSP from other causes of purple spots.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mona's blood pressure.
a.x: Blood pressure was off topic in a rash.
a.w: High blood pressure can be the first sign of kidney damage.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about the sore throat.
a.x: The sore throat was off topic.
a.w: HSP often follows a throat infection.

t: Wheeze on one side treated as asthma
s:
Karim, 3, has had a cough and a wheeze for a week. It started suddenly while he was eating nuts at a family party, when he choked and coughed for a few minutes. He has never wheezed before. He had no fever.

Dr. Ihab listened to his chest and heard a wheeze only on the right side, with less air going in there. His oxygen was 95%.

He gave him a salbutamol inhaler through a spacer in the clinic, but the wheeze did not change.

Karim's mother said her own brother has asthma. She asked whether Karim would need an inhaler forever.

Dr. Ihab diagnosed asthma, prescribed a salbutamol inhaler and booked a review in a month.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed asthma, prescribed a salbutamol inhaler and booked a review in a month

a.o: Dr. Ihab called Karim's one-sided wheeze asthma.
a.x: Karim should have been referred urgently to hospital for a chest X-ray and a camera test to remove an inhaled object.
a.w: A sudden choking episode with nuts, then a wheeze on one side that doesn't respond to salbutamol, points to an inhaled foreign body. It can cause pneumonia and lung damage.

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave a trial of salbutamol.
a.w: No response points away from asthma.

a.o: Dr. Ihab listened to both sides.
a.w: A one-sided wheeze is a red flag.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about the party.
a.w: A choking episode is a key clue.

t: Codeine after a child's tonsillectomy
s:
Yousef, 6, had his tonsils removed this morning for sleep apnea. He snored loudly and stopped breathing at night. He was sore but drinking. His oxygen was 96% on air.

Dr. Ayman gave him regular paracetamol and ibuprofen and encouraged him to eat soft food. He checked the throat for bleeding, and there was none.

He asked the nurses to check his oxygen overnight, given his sleep apnea.

Yousef's mother said he was crying with pain and asked for something stronger. She said codeine had worked for her own pain.

Yousef weighs 19 kg and has no allergies. He is due to start a new school next week and was upset about missing the first days. The ward was busy, and the night nurse would be looking after six children.

Dr. Ayman added codeine syrup every six hours as needed.
h: Dr. Ayman added codeine syrup every six hours as needed

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave codeine to Yousef after tonsillectomy for sleep apnea.
a.x: Yousef should have had paracetamol and ibuprofen, with a carefully dosed opioid like morphine only if needed and monitored.
a.w: Some children turn codeine into morphine very fast. After tonsillectomy for sleep apnea, this has caused deaths from stopped breathing. Codeine is banned under 12.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave ibuprofen after tonsillectomy.
a.w: Ibuprofen is safe and helpful after tonsillectomy.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked for oxygen checks overnight.
a.w: Sleep apnea raises breathing risk after surgery.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked the throat for bleeding.
a.w: Bleeding is a risk after tonsillectomy.

t: Baby of a diabetic mother not checked for low sugar
s:
Baby Nour was born at 38 weeks to Mrs. Huda, who has type 1 diabetes on insulin. Nour weighed 4.4 kg. She was jittery and floppy at two hours old, and was not feeding well.

Dr. Rana examined her and found her heart, lungs and hips normal. Her temperature was 36.3°C, so she asked for skin-to-skin contact and a hat.

She checked the mother's sugar, which was high in labor, and asked the midwife to help with breastfeeding.

Mrs. Huda was tired and worried her diabetes had harmed her baby. Her husband asked whether Nour would get diabetes too.

Dr. Rana said jitteriness is common in big babies and did not check Nour's blood sugar.
h: Dr. Rana said jitteriness is common in big babies and did not check Nour's blood sugar

a.o: Dr. Rana didn't check Baby Nour's blood sugar.
a.x: Baby Nour should have had her sugar checked at once and fed early, with IV glucose if low.
a.w: Babies of diabetic mothers make too much insulin and often have low sugar. Jitteriness and floppiness are signs, and low sugar can damage the brain.

a.o: Dr. Rana warmed Baby Nour.
a.w: Cold babies use up their sugar faster.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked the mother's sugar in labor.
a.w: High sugar in labor makes low sugar in the baby more likely.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked for help with breastfeeding.
a.w: Early feeding helps keep sugar up.

t: Child vomiting after a head bump sent home
s:
Sami, 7, fell off a climbing frame at school and hit the back of his head on the ground two hours ago. He cried at once and did not pass out. Since then he has vomited three times and says his head hurts. He is a little sleepy but answers questions.

Dr. Fady found a boggy swelling on the back of his head. His Glasgow Coma Score was 15, his pupils were equal and his arms and legs moved normally.

He gave him paracetamol and an anti-sickness medicine, and asked the nurse to check him every half hour.

Sami's teacher brought him in, and his mother arrived later from work. She said he had not eaten since breakfast and thought he was just hungry and upset.

Dr. Fady said children often vomit after a bump and sent him home with head injury advice, without a CT scan.
h: Dr. Fady said children often vomit after a bump and sent him home with head injury advice, without a CT scan

a.o: Dr. Fady sent Sami home without a CT scan after a head injury with three vomits.
a.x: Sami should have had a CT scan of the head within an hour.
a.w: Three or more vomits after a head injury in a child is a warning sign of a bleed inside the skull.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Sami's pupils.
a.w: Unequal pupils can mean pressure on the brain.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked for half-hourly checks.
a.w: A falling conscious level is an early warning sign.

a.o: Dr. Fady felt the swelling on Sami's head.
a.w: A boggy swelling can sit over a skull fracture.

t: Insulin stopped in a vomiting child
s:
Lina, 11, has type 1 diabetes and uses a basal-bolus insulin plan. She has had a stomach bug since last night, vomiting four times and not eating. Her sugar this morning was 16 and her ketones 1.8. She was drinking sips of water.

Dr. Ghada found her mouth a little dry and her breathing normal. She was alert, with no belly pain.

She gave her mother advice on sugar-free fluids little and often, and checking sugar and ketones every two hours.

Lina's mother said she was scared of giving insulin when Lina was not eating, in case her sugar went too low. Lina said she felt sick and tired.

Dr. Ghada told her to stop all insulin until Lina could eat again.
h: Dr. Ghada told her to stop all insulin until Lina could eat again

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped all of Lina's insulin while she was ill.
a.x: Lina should have kept her long-acting insulin, with extra quick-acting insulin for high sugar and ketones, following sick-day rules.
a.w: Without insulin, ketones build up fast and cause diabetic ketoacidosis, even when not eating.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised checks every two hours.
a.w: Frequent checks catch rising ketones.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Lina's breathing.
a.w: Deep breathing is a sign of ketoacidosis.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised fluids little and often.
a.w: Fluids help flush out ketones.

t: Blind finger sweep in a choking toddler
s:
Yusuf, 18 months, was eating grapes at home when he started choking. His mother brought him straight in. He was coughing hard and crying, and his color was pink. He could breathe between coughs.

Dr. Nada encouraged him to keep coughing and kept him upright on his mother's lap. She asked the nurse to call for senior help and prepare suction.

She looked in his mouth but could not see anything.

Yusuf's mother was panicking and asked the doctor to "get it out".

Yusuf had no other illnesses and had been playing happily before lunch. His older sister had cut the grapes in half, but some were whole. His breathing was noisy, and his oxygen was 96%.

Dr. Nada put her finger into the back of his throat and swept around blindly to find the grape.
h: Dr. Nada put her finger into the back of his throat and swept around blindly to find the grape

a.o: Dr. Nada did a blind finger sweep in Yusuf's throat.
a.x: Yusuf should have been encouraged to keep coughing while watched closely, with back blows only if his cough became weak.
a.w: A blind finger sweep can push the object deeper and block the airway completely.

a.o: Dr. Nada encouraged him to keep coughing.
a.x: She should have stopped the coughing.
a.w: A strong cough is the best way to clear an object.

a.o: Dr. Nada called for senior help.
a.w: A choking child can get worse quickly.

a.o: Dr. Nada looked in his mouth.
a.w: A visible object can be removed safely.

t: ADHD medicine without growth or blood pressure checks
s:
Ahmed, 9, has ADHD and started methylphenidate six months ago. His concentration at school has improved a lot. He eats less at lunch and takes longer to fall asleep.

Dr. Rana talked with Ahmed and his mother about school, which was going much better. She asked about his mood, which was fine.

She advised giving the medicine after breakfast and a bigger meal in the evening.

Ahmed's mother said he had become a fussy eater and seemed thinner. She asked whether the medicine was stunting his growth.

Ahmed's teacher had written a letter praising his work and behavior. He plays the drums and wants to join the school band. His father had a heart murmur as a child, but no heart problems since.

Dr. Rana renewed the prescription for six months without measuring his height, weight, pulse or blood pressure.
h: Dr. Rana renewed the prescription for six months without measuring his height, weight, pulse or blood pressure

a.o: Dr. Rana renewed Ahmed's methylphenidate without growth or heart checks.
a.x: Ahmed should have had his height, weight, pulse and blood pressure measured and plotted.
a.w: Stimulants can slow growth, reduce appetite and raise heart rate and blood pressure.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about Ahmed's mood.
a.w: Stimulants can affect mood.

a.o: Dr. Rana advised giving it after breakfast.
a.w: Giving it after food helps appetite.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about school.
a.w: School shows whether the medicine works.

t: Undescended testis left until school age
s:
Baby Omar, 9 months old, came for a check. His right testicle has never been felt in the scrotum since birth. His left testicle is normal. He was born at term.

Dr. Ihab examined him in a warm room and could not feel the right testicle in the scrotum or groin.

He checked his growth and development, which were normal.

Omar's mother said her husband had the same problem and had an operation as a boy.

Omar was feeding well on solids and had started crawling. He had had all his vaccines on time. His mother works as a teacher and wanted to plan any treatment around the school holidays. His older brother is healthy.

Dr. Ihab told her it might still come down and booked a review at age 5.
h: Dr. Ihab told her it might still come down and booked a review at age 5

a.o: Dr. Ihab left Baby Omar's undescended testicle until age 5.
a.x: Baby Omar should have been referred to a children's surgeon to have the testicle brought down between 6 and 12 months.
a.w: A testicle that has not come down by 6 months rarely comes down. Early surgery protects fertility and lowers cancer risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab examined Omar in a warm room.
a.w: Cold makes the testicle pull up out of view.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about the father's operation.
a.w: Undescended testes run in families.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Omar's crawling and growth.
a.x: Development was unrelated to the testicle.
a.w: Development is part of every baby check.

t: Ibuprofen added to lithium
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 48, has bipolar disorder, well controlled on lithium for ten years. Her last lithium level, three months ago, was 0.7, and her kidney and thyroid tests were normal. She came in with a painful knee after a fall at the market.

Dr. Ghada examined the knee and found it bruised and a little swollen, with full movement and no sign of a fracture. She advised ice, rest and a knee support.

She asked about her mood, which was steady, and checked that she was taking her lithium every night, which she was.

Mrs. Nadia works as a primary school teacher and stands most of the day. She said paracetamol had not touched the pain, and that a friend had told her ibuprofen worked wonders.

Dr. Ghada prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for two weeks, with no plan to check her lithium level.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for two weeks, with no plan to check her lithium level

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave Mrs. Nadia ibuprofen on lithium with no level check.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have avoided NSAIDs, using paracetamol, a gel or a short course of codeine instead, or had her lithium level checked within a week.
a.w: NSAIDs reduce how much lithium the kidneys clear. Levels can rise to toxic, causing tremor, confusion, fits and kidney damage.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked that Mrs. Nadia took her lithium.
a.w: Missed or extra doses change lithium levels.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about Mrs. Nadia's mood.
a.x: Mood was off topic for a knee.
a.w: Any visit is a chance to check bipolar is stable.

a.o: Dr. Ghada suggested a knee support.
a.w: A support eases pain after a minor injury.

t: High fever and stiffness on an antipsychotic called infection
s:
Mr. Waleed, 32, was started on haloperidol injections five days ago for a psychotic relapse. Today he had a fever of 40.1°C and a pulse of 128, and he was sweating heavily. His muscles were rigid like lead pipes, and he was confused. His blood pressure swung from 160/100 to 110/70.

Dr. Ayman checked his CK, which was 18,000, and his kidney function, which was worsening. His white count was 15.

He gave him IV fluids and cooling with fans and ice packs. He took blood cultures and a urine sample.

Mr. Waleed's brother said he had been well apart from his mental illness, and had not been sick or coughing before this. The nurses said he had needed several extra injections of haloperidol for agitation.

Dr. Ayman diagnosed sepsis, started IV antibiotics and continued the haloperidol for his agitation.
h: Dr. Ayman diagnosed sepsis, started IV antibiotics and continued the haloperidol for his agitation

a.o: Dr. Ayman kept giving haloperidol to Mr. Waleed with neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
a.x: Mr. Waleed should have had all antipsychotics stopped at once, with ICU review, cooling, fluids and possibly dantrolene or bromocriptine.
a.w: High fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, swinging blood pressure and a very high CK after starting an antipsychotic mean NMS, which can kill.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked the CK.
a.w: A very high CK shows muscle breakdown in NMS.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave IV fluids.
a.w: Fluids protect the kidneys from muscle breakdown.

a.o: Dr. Ayman took blood cultures.
a.w: Infection must still be ruled out.

t: Tramadol added to an antidepressant
s:
Mrs. Rasha, 45, takes sertraline 150 mg for depression. Two days ago her GP added tramadol for back pain. Today she came in agitated and sweating, with a fever of 38.6°C, a pulse of 122 and diarrhea. Her legs were twitching and jerking, and her reflexes were very brisk.

Dr. Nada checked her pupils, which were large, and her sugar and salts, which were normal. She had no neck stiffness and no rash.

She gave her IV fluids, kept her in a cool, quiet room and put her on a heart monitor.

Mrs. Rasha's husband said she had been taking extra tramadol because the pain was bad. She had also taken a cough syrup with dextromethorphan for a cold.

Dr. Nada diagnosed a viral infection, gave paracetamol and told her to keep taking her usual medicines, including the tramadol.
h: Dr. Nada diagnosed a viral infection, gave paracetamol and told her to keep taking her usual medicines, including the tramadol

a.o: Dr. Nada called Mrs. Rasha's serotonin syndrome a virus and kept the tramadol.
a.x: Mrs. Rasha should have had the sertraline, tramadol and cough syrup stopped, with benzodiazepines for agitation and cyproheptadine if severe.
a.w: Agitation, fever, sweating, twitching, brisk reflexes and large pupils after adding tramadol to an SSRI mean serotonin syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about cough syrup.
a.w: Dextromethorphan also raises serotonin.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked her reflexes.
a.w: Brisk reflexes and jerks are key signs.

a.o: Dr. Nada put her on a monitor.
a.w: Serotonin syndrome can cause rhythm problems.

t: Antidepressant started in a teenager without follow-up
s:
Yara, 16, has had low mood for four months. She has stopped seeing friends, sleeps badly and has dropped out of her dance class. She said she sometimes wishes she would not wake up, but has no plan. Talking therapy for eight weeks had not helped.

Dr. Mervat, a child psychiatrist, assessed her and diagnosed moderate to severe depression. She talked with Yara and her mother about options.

She started fluoxetine 10 mg, the right first choice for teenagers, and explained it would take a few weeks to work. She gave them a crisis line number.

Yara's mother works long shifts and said she could not easily get time off. Yara asked to keep her therapy going.

Dr. Mervat booked her next review in three months.
h: Dr. Mervat booked her next review in three months

a.o: Dr. Mervat left Yara for three months after starting an antidepressant.
a.x: Yara should have been reviewed within one to two weeks, by phone if needed, and regularly after that.
a.w: In young people, antidepressants can raise suicidal thoughts in the first weeks. Close follow-up catches this early.

a.o: Dr. Mervat chose fluoxetine.
a.w: Fluoxetine is the first-choice antidepressant for under 18s.

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave them a crisis line number.
a.w: Families need to know where to get help.

a.o: Dr. Mervat kept Yara's therapy going.
a.w: Medicine works best with therapy.

t: Sore throat on clozapine without a blood count
s:
Mr. Kamal, 40, has schizophrenia and has taken clozapine for two years with good results. He came to clinic with a sore throat and a fever of 38.3°C for two days. He felt weak and had mouth ulcers.

Dr. Fady checked his throat, which was red with white patches, and his chest, which was clear. His pulse was 104.

He asked about his clozapine and his smoking, as smoking changes clozapine levels. He had recently stopped smoking.

Mr. Kamal's mother said he was drooling more at night and had been constipated. His last routine blood count was a month ago and normal.

Dr. Fady prescribed penicillin for tonsillitis, without an urgent blood count.
h: Dr. Fady prescribed penicillin for tonsillitis, without an urgent blood count

a.o: Dr. Fady treated Mr. Kamal's sore throat without an urgent blood count.
a.x: Mr. Kamal should have had an urgent full blood count that day, with clozapine stopped if his white cells were low.
a.w: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, a loss of white cells. A sore throat and fever can be the first sign of a deadly infection.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about smoking.
a.w: Stopping smoking raises clozapine levels.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about constipation.
a.w: Clozapine can cause dangerous constipation.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his chest.
a.w: Pneumonia can come with low white cells.

t: Paracetamol overdose sent home because she looked well
s:
Miss Nour, 19, took 30 paracetamol tablets of 500 mg six hours ago after an argument with her boyfriend. She weighs 55 kg. She came in with her friend and felt a little sick but was otherwise well. Her blood tests at four hours were not done because she arrived late.

Dr. Inas checked her pulse and blood pressure, which were normal, and her belly, which was soft. She sent a paracetamol level, liver tests and INR.

She asked about other tablets or alcohol, and Miss Nour said she had drunk two glasses of wine. She asked about her mood and her safety.

Miss Nour said she regretted it and wanted to go home. Her friend offered to stay with her overnight. The paracetamol level would take two hours.

Dr. Inas said she looked well and that 15 g was "not a big amount", and sent her home with her friend before the results came back.
h: Dr. Inas said she looked well and that 15 g was "not a big amount", and sent her home with her friend before the results came back

a.o: Dr. Inas sent Miss Nour home after a paracetamol overdose before the results.
a.x: Miss Nour should have stayed for the paracetamol level, with acetylcysteine started if it was above the treatment line, and a mental health assessment before leaving.
a.w: Paracetamol overdose causes no early symptoms. 15 g in a 55 kg woman is about 270 mg/kg, a dangerous dose that can kill through liver failure.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about alcohol.
a.w: Alcohol and other drugs change the risk.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked the INR.
a.w: A raised INR shows liver damage.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about her mood and safety.
a.x: That was not the doctor's job.
a.w: Every overdose needs a risk assessment.

t: Anorexia with a very slow heart sent home
s:
Miss Lina, 17, has anorexia nervosa. Her mother brought her in because she fainted at school. Her BMI was 13.8, and she had lost 5 kg in a month. Her pulse was 38 at rest and her blood pressure 82/50. Her hands were cold and blue.

Dr. Rana checked her salts, which showed low potassium and phosphate, and a heart tracing, which showed a slow rhythm with a long QT.

She talked with Lina kindly and asked about exercise and vomiting; Lina was running every day and sometimes made herself sick.

Lina said she felt fine and was scared of being forced to eat. Her mother was desperate and asked what to do.

Dr. Rana referred her to the eating disorder clinic for an appointment next month and sent her home.
h: Dr. Rana referred her to the eating disorder clinic for an appointment next month and sent her home

a.o: Dr. Rana sent Miss Lina home with a pulse of 38 and low salts.
a.x: Miss Lina should have been admitted for heart monitoring, careful refeeding with salt replacement and specialist eating disorder care.
a.w: A pulse under 40, low blood pressure, low potassium and a long QT in anorexia mean a high risk of sudden death.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about vomiting.
a.w: Vomiting lowers potassium.

a.o: Dr. Rana did a heart tracing.
a.w: A long QT raises the risk of a dangerous rhythm.

a.o: Dr. Rana talked with Lina kindly.
a.w: Kindness builds trust in eating disorder care.

t: Olanzapine without weight or sugar checks
s:
Mr. Sami, 28, has schizophrenia and has taken olanzapine for a year. His voices have gone and he has started a part-time job. He says he is always hungry and his clothes no longer fit.

Dr. Mervat asked about his mood and side effects. He said he felt sleepy in the mornings.

She talked about his job and his hobbies, and encouraged him to keep up his medicine.

Mr. Sami's mother said he drinks a lot of sugary drinks and has gained a lot of weight. His father has type 2 diabetes.

He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and does not exercise. His last blood tests were taken before he started olanzapine.

Dr. Mervat renewed his olanzapine without checking his weight, blood pressure, sugar or cholesterol.
h: Dr. Mervat renewed his olanzapine without checking his weight, blood pressure, sugar or cholesterol

a.o: Dr. Mervat renewed Mr. Sami's olanzapine without metabolic checks.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have had his weight, waist, blood pressure, HbA1c and cholesterol checked, with diet and exercise help.
a.w: Olanzapine causes weight gain, diabetes and high cholesterol, raising heart disease risk. A family history of diabetes adds to it.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about sleepiness.
a.w: Sleepiness is a common side effect.

a.o: Dr. Mervat encouraged him to keep taking it.
a.w: Stopping suddenly risks relapse.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about his job.
a.w: Work shows recovery.

t: Sleeping tablets renewed for years
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 74, has taken zopiclone every night for six years for poor sleep after her husband died. She came in for a new prescription. She had a fall last month in the night when going to the toilet.

Dr. Ihab asked about her sleep, which she said was still poor. She naps in the afternoon and drinks tea in the evening.

He checked her blood pressure and her balance, which was a little unsteady.

Mrs. Hanem said she was afraid she could not sleep at all without the tablets. Her daughter worried she seemed drowsy in the mornings.

She lives alone and takes amlodipine and a water tablet. She gets up twice a night to pass urine.

Dr. Ihab renewed the zopiclone for another six months.
h: Dr. Ihab renewed the zopiclone for another six months

a.o: Dr. Ihab renewed Mrs. Hanem's long-term sleeping tablets.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem should have been offered a slow, supported reduction of zopiclone, with sleep advice such as cutting evening tea and naps.
a.w: Sleeping tablets in older people cause falls, fractures and confusion, and stop working after a few weeks.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her balance.
a.w: Unsteadiness raises fall risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about evening tea.
a.w: Caffeine can stop sleep.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about naps.
a.w: Daytime naps make night sleep worse.

t: Antidepressant alone in bipolar depression
s:
Mr. Tarek, 35, has bipolar disorder, with two past manic episodes needing hospital. He is not on any medicine because he stopped lithium a year ago. He has been low for two months, sleeping a lot and not working.

Dr. Fady asked about his mood and safety; he had no plans to harm himself.

He asked about alcohol and drugs, and Mr. Tarek drinks a little at weekends.

Mr. Tarek said he wanted something to lift his mood quickly, because he had a new job offer. His wife was worried about him becoming "high" again.

His last manic episode began after a course of an antidepressant from another doctor. He has no thyroid problems.

Dr. Fady started sertraline 50 mg alone and booked a review in six weeks.
h: Dr. Fady started sertraline 50 mg alone and booked a review in six weeks

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mr. Tarek an antidepressant alone for bipolar depression.
a.x: Mr. Tarek should have had a mood stabilizer or an antipsychotic such as quetiapine, with close follow-up.
a.w: Antidepressants alone in bipolar disorder can trigger mania or rapid mood swings.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about his safety.
a.w: Depression carries a risk of suicide.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about alcohol.
a.w: Alcohol worsens mood.

a.o: Dr. Fady listened to his wife's worry.
a.w: Family often spot mania first.

t: Paroxetine stopped overnight
s:
Mrs. Samar, 39, has taken paroxetine 40 mg for anxiety and depression for three years. She feels well and wants to stop because she is planning a pregnancy next year. Her mood has been stable, and she has a good job and a supportive husband.

Dr. Ghada praised her progress and asked about her mood, sleep and anxiety, which were all good. She checked that she had no thoughts of self-harm.

She talked about pregnancy planning and started folic acid, and suggested she keep up the talking therapy skills she had learned.

Mrs. Samar said she had missed a dose once and felt dizzy, with "electric shocks" in her head the next day. She wanted to be off the tablets quickly.

Dr. Ghada told her she could stop the paroxetine straight away, since she felt well.
h: Dr. Ghada told her she could stop the paroxetine straight away, since she felt well

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped Mrs. Samar's paroxetine overnight.
a.x: Mrs. Samar should have reduced the dose slowly over weeks to months, with checks along the way.
a.w: Stopping paroxetine suddenly causes withdrawal: dizziness, electric-shock feelings, anxiety and low mood. Her missed-dose reaction showed the risk.

a.o: Dr. Ghada started folic acid.
a.w: Folic acid before pregnancy prevents spine defects.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about self-harm.
a.x: That question was unnecessary in a well patient.
a.w: Risk should be checked when changing treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ghada encouraged her to use her therapy skills.
a.x: Therapy skills fade and are useless.
a.w: Skills learned in therapy help prevent relapse.

t: Heroin overdose discharged after naloxone
s:
Mr. Hany, 30, was found unconscious in a public toilet with a needle in his arm. His breathing was slow and his pupils pinpoint. The paramedics gave him naloxone, and he woke up and pulled off the mask.

Dr. Fady checked his breathing, which was now 14 a minute, and his oxygen, which was 96%. He checked his sugar and looked for injuries, finding none.

He offered him help from the drug service and gave him a naloxone kit to take home, with training for his friend.

Mr. Hany was angry that the naloxone had made him feel sick and shaky. He said he wanted to leave at once to find his girlfriend.

Dr. Fady let him go 20 minutes after the naloxone, writing "breathing normally".
h: Dr. Fady let him go 20 minutes after the naloxone, writing "breathing normally"

a.o: Dr. Fady let Mr. Hany leave 20 minutes after naloxone.
a.x: Mr. Hany should have been watched for at least two hours, with repeat naloxone if he became drowsy, and talked into staying.
a.w: Naloxone wears off faster than heroin. He can stop breathing again after he leaves.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave him a naloxone kit.
a.w: A kit lets friends save his life next time.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his sugar.
a.w: Low sugar can also cause unconsciousness.

a.o: Dr. Fady offered help from the drug service.
a.w: Offering help is the start of recovery.

t: First psychosis without a physical work-up
s:
Mr. Sherif, 23, was brought by his parents because for three weeks he had been hearing voices and believed the neighbors were spying on him. He had stopped going to university. He had no past mental illness.

Dr. Mervat talked with him calmly and asked about his safety and the safety of others. He had no plans to harm anyone.

She asked about cannabis and other drugs, and he said he smoked cannabis daily.

His mother said he had headaches and had a fit last week. His father was worried about the shame in the family.

Dr. Mervat diagnosed schizophrenia and started an antipsychotic, without blood tests, a drug screen or a brain scan.
h: Dr. Mervat diagnosed schizophrenia and started an antipsychotic, without blood tests, a drug screen or a brain scan

a.o: Dr. Mervat started an antipsychotic for Mr. Sherif without any physical tests.
a.x: Mr. Sherif should have had blood tests, a drug screen and, given his headaches and fit, a brain scan.
a.w: A first psychosis can be caused by drugs, infection, thyroid problems, or a brain tumor. A fit makes a physical cause more likely.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about cannabis.
a.w: Cannabis can trigger psychosis.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about safety.
a.w: Risk to self and others must be checked.

a.o: Dr. Mervat talked with him calmly.
a.w: Calm talk helps people with psychosis feel safe.

t: Teenager after self-harm sent home alone
s:
Rania, 15, came in with cuts on her forearm that she made with a razor blade. The cuts were shallow and were closed with strips. She came in with a friend; her parents did not know.

Dr. Inas cleaned the cuts and checked her tetanus. She asked about other self-harm, and Rania said she had cut herself many times before.

She asked about her mood, and Rania said she felt hopeless. She said her uncle had been "touching her" at home.

Rania begged the doctor not to tell anyone, especially her parents.

Dr. Inas promised to keep it secret and sent her home, without a mental health review or a safeguarding referral.
h: Dr. Inas promised to keep it secret and sent her home, without a mental health review or a safeguarding referral

a.o: Dr. Inas sent Rania home and kept the abuse secret.
a.x: Rania should have had a child mental health assessment, and a safeguarding referral should have been made, with her told kindly why.
a.w: A child who discloses sexual abuse must be protected, even without consent. Self-harm with hopelessness needs a specialist review.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked her tetanus.
a.w: Cuts can cause tetanus.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about past self-harm.
a.w: Past self-harm raises the risk.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about her mood.
a.w: Low mood raises suicide risk.

t: Lithium level checked at the wrong time
s:
Mr. Raafat, 50, has bipolar disorder and takes lithium 800 mg every night at 10 p.m. He came for his routine three-monthly lithium blood test at 4 p.m., after a morning of errands. He said he had been feeling well and working full time as a taxi driver.

Dr. Fady sent his lithium level, kidney tests and thyroid tests. His kidney function was stable and his thyroid normal.

He asked about tremor, thirst and diarrhea, and Mr. Raafat had a mild hand tremor that had been there for years.

The lithium level came back at 0.35, below his usual 0.7. Mr. Raafat said he never missed doses, and his wife, who keeps his pill box, agreed. He was in a hurry to get back to work.

Dr. Fady increased his lithium to 1,000 mg a night, based on that result, and booked the next level in three months.
h: Dr. Fady increased his lithium to 1,000 mg a night, based on that result

a.o: Dr. Fady raised Mr. Raafat's lithium dose on a level taken 18 hours after his dose.
a.x: Mr. Raafat should have had his level repeated 12 hours after the evening dose before any change, and a level a week after any change.
a.w: Lithium levels are only valid 12 hours after the last dose. A late sample looks falsely low, and raising the dose can make him toxic.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Raafat's thyroid.
a.w: Lithium can cause an underactive thyroid.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked Mr. Raafat about tremor and diarrhea.
a.w: Worse tremor or diarrhea can be signs of high lithium.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked whether Mr. Raafat missed doses.
a.w: Missed doses would explain a truly low level.

t: Haloperidol for hallucinations in Lewy body dementia
s:
Mr. Kamal, 78, has dementia with Lewy bodies. His memory and alertness change a lot from day to day, and he has mild Parkinson-like stiffness. He was admitted after a fall. At night he saw children and animals in his room that were not there, and became frightened.

Dr. Mai checked for infection, pain and constipation, and found none. His salts and sugar were normal. She reviewed his medicines and stopped an old bladder tablet that can cause confusion.

She asked the nurses to keep a night light on and to have his wife stay with him if possible. His wife said he usually calms down when she holds his hand and plays old songs.

Mr. Kamal already takes rivastigmine, which had helped his alertness at home. The night staff asked for something to stop him shouting.

Dr. Mai prescribed haloperidol 2 mg at night "to settle the hallucinations".
h: Dr. Mai prescribed haloperidol 2 mg at night "to settle the hallucinations"

a.o: Dr. Mai gave haloperidol to Mr. Kamal with Lewy body dementia.
a.x: Mr. Kamal should have had calming care, with antipsychotics avoided; if really needed, a very low dose of quetiapine under specialist advice.
a.w: People with Lewy body dementia can react severely to antipsychotics like haloperidol, with sudden stiffness, falls, confusion and even death.

a.o: Dr. Mai stopped the bladder tablet.
a.w: Anticholinergic bladder tablets worsen confusion.

a.o: Dr. Mai asked his wife to stay.
a.w: Familiar faces calm people with dementia.

a.o: Dr. Mai kept the rivastigmine going.
a.w: Rivastigmine can help hallucinations in Lewy body dementia.

t: Depressed man not asked about suicide
s:
Mr. Samy, 55, came in with poor sleep and tiredness for two months. He lost his job four months ago and his wife left him last month. He has been drinking more in the evenings. He said he felt like a burden to his children.

Dr. Ihab asked about his appetite, which was poor, and his weight, which had dropped. He checked his blood tests, which were normal.

He diagnosed depression and explained it kindly, and offered talking therapy and an antidepressant.

Mr. Samy said he had been giving away his things and had written letters to his children. He has a hunting rifle at home.

Dr. Ihab started sertraline and booked a review in four weeks, without asking about suicide.
h: Dr. Ihab started sertraline and booked a review in four weeks, without asking about suicide

a.o: Dr. Ihab didn't ask Mr. Samy about suicide.
a.x: Mr. Samy should have been asked directly about suicidal thoughts and plans, and referred the same day to the crisis team, with the rifle made safe.
a.w: Giving away things, writing letters, feeling a burden, job loss, separation, drinking and a gun are strong warning signs of suicide.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about weight.
a.w: Weight loss is a sign of depression.

a.o: Dr. Ihab offered talking therapy.
a.w: Therapy helps depression.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked blood tests.
a.w: Thyroid and other problems can cause tiredness.

t: Alcohol withdrawal sent home without treatment
s:
Mr. Medhat, 52, drinks a bottle of vodka a day. He stopped suddenly two days ago because he ran out of money. He came in shaking, sweating and anxious, with a pulse of 112. He had a fit when he stopped drinking last year.

Dr. Nada checked his sugar, which was normal, and his salts, which showed low magnesium. She gave him IV thiamine.

She asked about his drinking and offered him help from the alcohol team, which he accepted.

Mr. Medhat said he wanted to go home to his cat. He lives alone and has no family nearby.

Dr. Nada gave him advice about drinking water and sent him home without a benzodiazepine.
h: Dr. Nada gave him advice about drinking water and sent him home without a benzodiazepine

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Medhat home in alcohol withdrawal without treatment.
a.x: Mr. Medhat should have been admitted for chlordiazepoxide on a withdrawal scale, thiamine and magnesium.
a.w: Withdrawal after heavy drinking, with a past fit and living alone, can lead to fits and delirium tremens, which can kill.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave IV thiamine.
a.w: Thiamine protects the brain in heavy drinkers.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked his magnesium.
a.w: Low magnesium raises the risk of fits.

a.o: Dr. Nada offered help from the alcohol team.
a.w: Help with drinking is the long-term answer.

t: Methadone dose doubled on admission
s:
Mr. Ali, 38, takes methadone 60 mg a day from a community clinic for heroin addiction. He was admitted with a leg infection. He said his usual dose was "120 mg" and that he was in withdrawal.

Dr. Ayman checked his pupils, which were normal, and his pulse, which was normal. He was not sweating or yawning.

He started IV antibiotics and asked the drug team to see him.

The community clinic was closed for the weekend. Mr. Ali was angry and demanded his methadone.

He works as a mechanic and had been stable on treatment for two years. He also takes diazepam that a friend gives him. His girlfriend said she did not know his dose.

Dr. Ayman prescribed 120 mg of methadone that evening, as Mr. Ali said.
h: Dr. Ayman prescribed 120 mg of methadone that evening, as Mr. Ali said

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave Mr. Ali 120 mg of methadone without checking his dose.
a.x: Mr. Ali's dose should have been confirmed with the clinic or pharmacy, with a small dose given until then based on signs of withdrawal.
a.w: Methadone builds up slowly. Giving double the real dose can cause fatal breathing problems overnight.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked his pupils.
a.w: Large pupils are a sign of withdrawal.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked the drug team to see him.
a.w: The drug team helps manage his treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ayman started IV antibiotics.
a.w: The leg infection needs treatment.

t: Tricyclic after a heart attack
s:
Mr. Hesham, 62, had a heart attack two months ago. Since then he has felt low, tearful and has lost interest in life. He sleeps badly and has stopped going to his cardiac rehab.

Dr. Mervat diagnosed depression and asked about suicide, which he had not thought about.

She encouraged him to return to cardiac rehab and offered talking therapy.

Mr. Hesham said he had read that old-style antidepressants help with sleep. His wife said he had a heart rhythm problem since the heart attack.

He takes aspirin, ticagrelor, bisoprolol and a statin. His heart tracing showed a long QT. He is a retired engineer and used to love fishing.

Dr. Mervat started amitriptyline 75 mg at night to help his mood and sleep.
h: Dr. Mervat started amitriptyline 75 mg at night to help his mood and sleep

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave amitriptyline to Mr. Hesham after a heart attack.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have had sertraline, which is safe after a heart attack, with therapy and rehab.
a.w: Tricyclic antidepressants can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems, especially after a recent heart attack.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about suicide.
a.w: Depression carries a risk of suicide.

a.o: Dr. Mervat encouraged cardiac rehab.
a.w: Rehab helps both heart and mood.

a.o: Dr. Mervat offered talking therapy.
a.w: Therapy helps depression.

t: Breastfeeding mother told to stop for sertraline
s:
Mrs. Hala, 30, had her second baby eight weeks ago. She has felt low, tearful and unable to enjoy anything for a month. She sleeps badly even when the baby sleeps and feels she is a bad mother. She has no thoughts of harming herself or the baby.

Dr. Ghada listened carefully and diagnosed postnatal depression. She asked about support at home, and Mrs. Hala's mother visits every day.

She offered talking therapy and referred her to the perinatal mental health team. She asked the health visitor to visit more often.

Mrs. Hala is breastfeeding and loves it; it is the one time she feels close to her baby. She agreed to try an antidepressant if it was safe.

Dr. Ghada started sertraline 50 mg and told her she must stop breastfeeding while on it.
h: Dr. Ghada started sertraline 50 mg and told her she must stop breastfeeding while on it

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mrs. Hala to stop breastfeeding for sertraline.
a.x: Mrs. Hala should have been told she can keep breastfeeding, as sertraline is one of the safest antidepressants in breastfeeding.
a.w: Very little sertraline passes into milk. Stopping breastfeeding can worsen her mood and take away something that helps her bond.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about thoughts of harming the baby.
a.w: Asking about harm is vital in postnatal depression.

a.o: Dr. Ghada referred her to the perinatal team.
a.w: Perinatal teams know how to treat mothers and babies together.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked the health visitor to visit more.
a.w: Health visitors support mother and baby at home.

t: Naltrexone started while still on methadone
s:
Mr. Sami, 34, has been on methadone 70 mg a day for a year after heroin addiction. He has a new job and wants to come off methadone completely. His last dose was this morning. He asked about a "blocker" medicine he had read about.

Dr. Fady praised his progress and checked his urine drug test, which was positive only for methadone.

He talked about the risks of relapse and overdose after stopping, and gave him a naloxone kit.

Mr. Sami said he was keen to start the blocker today so he could tell his new boss he was "clean". He lives with his supportive sister.

Dr. Fady gave him a first dose of naltrexone in clinic that afternoon.
h: Dr. Fady gave him a first dose of naltrexone in clinic that afternoon

a.o: Dr. Fady gave naltrexone to Mr. Sami the same day as his methadone.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have had his methadone slowly reduced and stopped, then waited at least 7 to 10 days opioid-free before naltrexone.
a.w: Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors at once and throws someone on methadone into severe sudden withdrawal.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave him a naloxone kit.
a.w: The overdose risk is high after stopping.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his urine drug test.
a.w: The test shows which opioids are in his body.

a.o: Dr. Fady warned about relapse.
a.w: Relapse is common and dangerous.

t: Lorazepam for delirium in an older man
s:
Mr. Hassan, 84, was admitted with a chest infection. On the second night he became confused, restless and pulled out his drip. He did not know where he was. He has no history of alcohol use or dementia.

Dr. Mai checked his oxygen, which was 93%, and his sugar and salts, which were normal. She looked for a full bladder and constipation, finding constipation, and gave a laxative.

She asked the nurses to keep a clock and his glasses near him, and to call his son.

His son said his father had been sharp and lived alone until this week. He asked whether his father was "losing his mind".

Dr. Mai gave lorazepam 1 mg to calm him so he could sleep.
h: Dr. Mai gave lorazepam 1 mg to calm him so he could sleep

a.o: Dr. Mai gave lorazepam for Mr. Hassan's delirium.
a.x: Mr. Hassan should have had his infection treated and calming care, with benzodiazepines avoided; a tiny dose of haloperidol only if he was a danger.
a.w: Benzodiazepines make delirium worse in older people and raise the risk of falls, except in alcohol withdrawal.

a.o: Dr. Mai treated his constipation.
a.w: Constipation can cause delirium.

a.o: Dr. Mai asked for Mr. Hassan's glasses and a clock.
a.x: Glasses and clocks don't help confusion.
a.w: Orientation aids help delirium.

a.o: Dr. Mai checked Mr. Hassan's oxygen.
a.x: Oxygen was off topic in confusion.
a.w: Low oxygen can cause confusion.

t: Donepezil in a man with a slow heart
s:
Mr. Raouf, 79, has Alzheimer's disease that has slowly worsened over a year. His wife says he forgets names and gets lost in the market. He faints sometimes when standing. His pulse is 46 and his heart tracing shows heart block.

Dr. Mervat did a memory test, which showed mild dementia, and checked his blood tests, which were normal.

She asked about his mood, which was fine, and his driving; he had stopped.

His wife asked whether there was a tablet that could help his memory.

He takes bisoprolol for blood pressure, which slows the heart too. He is a retired engineer who loves chess but can no longer follow a game. His daughter lives nearby and helps with his tablets.

Dr. Mervat started donepezil, without checking his heart rhythm with a cardiologist.
h: Dr. Mervat started donepezil, without checking his heart rhythm with a cardiologist

a.o: Dr. Mervat started donepezil in Mr. Raouf with a slow heart and heart block.
a.x: Mr. Raouf should have been seen by a cardiologist first, as donepezil can slow the heart further.
a.w: Donepezil can cause slow heart rates, faints and falls, which are dangerous with heart block.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about driving.
a.w: Dementia affects driving safety.

a.o: Dr. Mervat did a memory test.
a.w: The test confirms dementia.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked his blood tests.
a.w: Thyroid and B12 problems can affect memory.

t: Bulimia with low potassium not checked
s:
Miss Salma, 20, came in asking for help with her eating. She binges and makes herself sick several times a day. She has done this for a year. Her weight is normal. She feels tired and her heart sometimes races.

Dr. Ghada listened without judging and thanked her for being brave. She checked her teeth, which showed worn enamel, and her hands, which had calluses on the knuckles.

She referred her to the eating disorder service for therapy and gave her a support line.

Miss Salma is a nursing student and was ashamed. She said she also uses laxatives.

Dr. Ghada said her weight was normal, so blood tests were not needed.
h: Dr. Ghada said her weight was normal, so blood tests were not needed

a.o: Dr. Ghada skipped blood tests for Miss Salma, who vomits and uses laxatives.
a.x: Miss Salma should have had her potassium, salts and a heart tracing checked.
a.w: Vomiting and laxatives lower potassium, which can cause fatal heart rhythms even when weight is normal.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked her teeth.
a.w: Stomach acid wears away the enamel.

a.o: Dr. Ghada thanked her.
a.w: Kindness helps people seek help.

a.o: Dr. Ghada referred her for therapy.
a.w: Therapy treats bulimia.

t: High-flow oxygen in COPD
s:
Mr. Atef, 70, has severe COPD and came in breathless with a chest infection. He has needed a breathing machine once before. His oxygen was 84% on air. His first blood gas showed a raised carbon dioxide of 7.1 with a normal pH. He was alert.

Dr. Nada gave him nebulized salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone and antibiotics. She asked for a chest X-ray, which showed a patch on the left.

She checked his alert card, which said "CO2 retainer, target sats 88 to 92%". She asked the physiotherapist to help him clear his phlegm.

Mr. Atef's wife said he gets drowsy when he has too much oxygen. He was frightened and gasping.

Dr. Nada put him on a non-rebreather mask at 15 liters a minute "to get his oxygen up fast", and planned to repeat the gas in two hours.
h: Dr. Nada put him on a non-rebreather mask at 15 liters a minute "to get his oxygen up fast"

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Atef high-flow oxygen with COPD and a raised CO2.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have had controlled oxygen through a Venturi mask, aiming for 88 to 92%, with a repeat gas in 30 to 60 minutes.
a.w: Too much oxygen in COPD with CO2 retention can raise CO2 further, causing drowsiness, acidosis and breathing failure.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave him oral prednisolone.
a.w: Steroids speed recovery from a COPD flare.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked his alert card.
a.w: The card gives his safe oxygen target.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked the physiotherapist to help.
a.w: Clearing phlegm helps breathing.

t: Propranolol for exam nerves in an asthmatic
s:
