Miss Rana, 22, is a medical student with exams next month. She gets a racing heart, shaky hands and sweating before exams. She has asthma and uses a brown preventer inhaler twice a day and salbutamol about once a week.

Dr. Ihab listened carefully and checked her pulse and blood pressure, which were normal. He checked her thyroid tests, which were normal.

He talked with her about breathing exercises, sleep and cutting down on coffee, and offered a referral for talking therapy for exam anxiety.

Miss Rana said a friend took "beta blockers" for exams and found them great. She asked whether she could have some too.

Dr. Ihab prescribed propranolol 40 mg to take before each exam.
h: Dr. Ihab prescribed propranolol 40 mg to take before each exam

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave propranolol to Miss Rana, who has asthma.
a.x: Miss Rana should have had therapy and practical help for anxiety, with no beta blocker.
a.w: Non-selective beta blockers like propranolol can cause severe, even fatal, asthma attacks.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her thyroid.
a.w: An overactive thyroid can cause a racing heart and shakes.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised less coffee.
a.w: Caffeine worsens anxiety symptoms.

a.o: Dr. Ihab offered talking therapy.
a.w: Therapy treats exam anxiety.

t: High chance of clot ruled out with a blood test
s:
Mrs. Samia, 45, came in with sudden breathlessness and sharp chest pain on breathing in, for six hours. She had a knee operation two weeks ago. Her right calf was swollen and tender. Her pulse was 112 and her oxygen 93%.

Dr. Fady worked out her Wells score for a lung clot, which was 7.5, a high chance. He checked her heart tracing, which showed a fast rhythm.

He sent a D-dimer and gave her oxygen. Her chest X-ray was normal.

Mrs. Samia works as a nurse and wanted to go home to her children. The D-dimer came back normal.

Dr. Fady said the normal D-dimer ruled out a clot and sent her home.
h: Dr. Fady said the normal D-dimer ruled out a clot and sent her home

a.o: Dr. Fady used a normal D-dimer to rule out a clot in Mrs. Samia with a high Wells score.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have had a CT pulmonary angiogram, with a blood thinner started while waiting.
a.w: A D-dimer only rules out a clot when the chance is low. With a high score, a scan is needed whatever the D-dimer.

a.o: Dr. Fady worked out the Wells score.
a.w: The score guides which tests to do.

a.o: Dr. Fady did a chest X-ray.
a.w: The X-ray looks for other causes.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about the knee operation.
a.w: Recent surgery raises clot risk.

t: Collapsed lung and a flight next week
s:
Mr. Karim, 22, is tall and thin and smokes. He came in with sudden sharp chest pain on the right and breathlessness after a game of basketball. An X-ray showed a collapsed lung on the right with a 3 cm rim of air.

Dr. Inas checked his oxygen, which was 94%, and his blood pressure, which was normal. She put a needle into the chest and drew off air, and a repeat X-ray showed the lung had come up.

She advised him to stop smoking and gave him a leaflet about the condition. She booked him into the chest clinic in two weeks.

Mr. Karim said he had a flight to his cousin's wedding next week. He was very excited about it.

Dr. Inas told him he could fly next week because the lung had re-expanded.
h: Dr. Inas told him he could fly next week because the lung had re-expanded

a.o: Dr. Inas told Mr. Karim he could fly a week after a collapsed lung.
a.x: Mr. Karim should have been told not to fly until a clinic X-ray shows the lung has fully healed, and then to wait at least another week.
a.w: Air pressure changes in flight can collapse the lung again, far from help.

a.o: Dr. Inas advised him to stop smoking.
a.w: Smoking greatly raises the chance of another collapse.

a.o: Dr. Inas drew off air with a needle.
a.x: A chest drain is always needed.
a.w: A needle can treat a first collapsed lung.

a.o: Dr. Inas booked a chest clinic review.
a.w: The clinic checks the lung has healed.

t: Coughing blood with a normal X-ray
s:
Mr. Hassan, 62, has smoked 30 a day for 40 years. He came in because he coughed up streaks of blood three times this month. He has a cough every morning, which he puts down to smoking. He has lost 4 kg.

Dr. Ghada listened to his chest, which was clear, and felt his neck, which had no lumps. She sent him for a chest X-ray, which was normal.

She advised him to stop smoking and offered a stop-smoking course.

Mr. Hassan worked in a shipyard for many years. He said he was relieved the X-ray was normal.

Dr. Ghada said the normal X-ray ruled out cancer and booked a review in six months.
h: Dr. Ghada said the normal X-ray ruled out cancer and booked a review in six months

a.o: Dr. Ghada used a normal X-ray to rule out cancer in Mr. Hassan.
a.x: Mr. Hassan should have been referred urgently for a CT scan and chest clinic review.
a.w: A chest X-ray can miss lung cancer. Coughing blood in a heavy smoker over 40, with weight loss, needs urgent tests.

a.o: Dr. Ghada felt his neck.
a.w: Lumps in the neck can be spread from cancer.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about his work.
a.w: Shipyard work means asbestos exposure.

a.o: Dr. Ghada offered a stop-smoking course.
a.w: Stopping smoking lowers cancer risk.

t: Infected pleural fluid left without a drain
s:
Mr. Fathi, 58, was admitted with pneumonia five days ago. He was improving on IV antibiotics, but now his fever came back and he was breathless again. An ultrasound showed a large fluid collection with strands in it at the base of his right lung.

Dr. Ayman put a needle into the fluid and drew off a sample. It was cloudy, with a pH of 6.9 and a low sugar. He sent it for culture.

He checked his blood count and CRP, which had both risen again. He changed the antibiotics to a broader one.

Mr. Fathi has diabetes and drinks heavily at weekends. His wife asked why he was getting worse after getting better.

Dr. Ayman continued the new antibiotics and planned to repeat the ultrasound in a week, without putting in a chest drain.
h: Dr. Ayman continued the new antibiotics and planned to repeat the ultrasound in a week, without putting in a chest drain

a.o: Dr. Ayman left Mr. Fathi's infected pleural fluid without a drain.
a.x: Mr. Fathi should have had a chest drain put in under ultrasound guidance that day, with chest team review.
a.w: Cloudy fluid with a pH below 7.2 means an empyema. Antibiotics alone can't clear pus, and it can scar the lung.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked the fluid pH.
a.w: A low pH shows the fluid is infected.

a.o: Dr. Ayman sent the fluid for culture.
a.w: Culture guides antibiotics.

a.o: Dr. Ayman used ultrasound.
a.w: Ultrasound shows where the fluid is.

t: Breathless on amiodarone told it was his heart
s:
Mr. Tamer, 68, has taken amiodarone for atrial fibrillation for three years. For two months he has had a dry cough and growing breathlessness on walking. He has no chest pain or ankle swelling.

Dr. Fady listened to his chest and heard fine crackles at both bases. His heart scan last month showed his heart was pumping normally.

He checked his thyroid tests, which were mildly underactive, and his liver tests, which were a little raised.

Mr. Tamer said he used to walk his dog for an hour but now stops after ten minutes. He has never smoked.

Dr. Fady said the breathlessness was from his heart, added furosemide and continued the amiodarone.
h: Dr. Fady said the breathlessness was from his heart, added furosemide and continued the amiodarone

a.o: Dr. Fady blamed Mr. Tamer's breathlessness on his heart and kept the amiodarone.
a.x: Mr. Tamer should have had a chest X-ray, a CT scan and lung function tests, with the amiodarone stopped if lung damage was found.
a.w: Amiodarone can cause lung scarring. A dry cough, crackles and a normal heart scan point to amiodarone lung toxicity.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Tamer's thyroid.
a.w: Amiodarone affects the thyroid.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his liver tests.
a.w: Amiodarone can harm the liver.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his heart scan.
a.w: A normal heart scan points away from heart failure.

t: Lorry driver with sleep apnea told to keep driving
s:
Mr. Sabri, 50, drives a lorry long distances. His wife says he snores loudly and stops breathing at night. He falls asleep watching TV and once nodded off at traffic lights. His BMI is 36 and his neck is thick.

Dr. Ihab checked his blood pressure, which was 158/96, and his sugar, which was high.

He referred him for a sleep study and advised weight loss and cutting down on alcohol.

Mr. Sabri said his job was his only income. He asked whether he could keep driving while he waited for the sleep study.

The sleep study had a waiting list of three months. He drinks four beers most evenings to help him sleep and takes no other medicines.

Dr. Ihab said he could keep driving until the results came back.
h: Dr. Ihab said he could keep driving until the results came back

a.o: Dr. Ihab let Mr. Sabri keep driving his lorry with likely sleep apnea and daytime sleepiness.
a.x: Mr. Sabri should have been told to stop driving and to tell the licensing authority until his sleep apnea is treated.
a.w: Sleepiness at the wheel from sleep apnea causes serious crashes. Lorry drivers carry extra risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked his blood pressure.
a.w: Sleep apnea raises blood pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised weight loss.
a.w: Weight loss improves sleep apnea.

a.o: Dr. Ihab referred him for a sleep study.
a.w: The study confirms the diagnosis.

t: Long-acting reliever without a steroid inhaler in asthma
s:
Miss Yasmin, 26, has asthma. She uses her blue salbutamol inhaler most days and wakes at night coughing twice a week. She stopped her brown steroid inhaler because she worried about "steroids".

Dr. Ghada checked her inhaler technique, which was good, and her peak flow, which was 75% of her best.

She asked about triggers, and Miss Yasmin has a cat and lives in a damp flat.

Miss Yasmin asked for "a stronger inhaler that lasts longer" so she would not need the blue one so often.

She works as a nursery teacher and had missed three days of work this month. She had one hospital visit for asthma last winter.

Dr. Ghada prescribed a long-acting salmeterol inhaler on its own, twice a day.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed a long-acting salmeterol inhaler on its own, twice a day

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave Miss Yasmin a long-acting reliever without a steroid inhaler.
a.x: Miss Yasmin should have restarted an inhaled steroid, or been given a combined steroid and long-acting inhaler.
a.w: Long-acting relievers alone in asthma raise the risk of severe and fatal attacks.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked her technique.
a.w: Poor technique means the medicine does not work.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about triggers.
a.w: Cats and damp can worsen asthma.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked her peak flow.
a.w: Peak flow shows how well asthma is controlled.

t: Home oxygen for a man who still smokes
s:
Mr. Hamdy, 72, has severe COPD. His oxygen at rest is 86% when well, and he gets breathless walking across the room. He still smokes 15 cigarettes a day and cooks on a gas stove.

Dr. Fady checked his blood gas, which showed low oxygen. He checked his inhalers and his technique, which was good.

He offered pulmonary rehab and stop-smoking help, which Mr. Hamdy said he would think about.

Mr. Hamdy lives with his wife, who also smokes. He said he would never give up cigarettes.

Their flat is on the fourth floor with no lift. Their grandchildren visit every weekend and play in the living room.

Dr. Fady arranged home oxygen for 16 hours a day, without discussing the fire risk.
h: Dr. Fady arranged home oxygen for 16 hours a day, without discussing the fire risk

a.o: Dr. Fady gave home oxygen to Mr. Hamdy, who still smokes.
a.x: Mr. Hamdy should not have had home oxygen while he still smokes, and should have had a fire risk check and stop-smoking help.
a.w: Smoking near oxygen causes burns, house fires and deaths.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his blood gas.
a.w: The gas shows if oxygen is needed.

a.o: Dr. Fady offered pulmonary rehab.
a.w: Rehab improves breathlessness.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his inhaler technique.
a.w: Poor technique wastes medicine.

t: COPD diagnosed without breathing tests
s:
Mr. Raouf, 55, has smoked 20 a day since he was 18. He came in with a cough most mornings and breathlessness on stairs for a year. He gets two or three chest infections every winter. He has no weight loss.

Dr. Ihab listened to his chest and heard a mild wheeze. His oxygen was 96%. A chest X-ray showed slightly overinflated lungs but no other changes.

He advised him strongly to stop smoking and offered a stop-smoking course and nicotine patches, which Mr. Raouf accepted.

Mr. Raouf works as a taxi driver and said he did not have time for more tests. His brother has asthma and uses inhalers.

Dr. Ihab diagnosed COPD from the history and X-ray and started inhalers, without spirometry.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed COPD from the history and X-ray and started inhalers, without spirometry

a.o: Dr. Ihab diagnosed COPD in Mr. Raouf without spirometry.
a.x: Mr. Raouf should have had spirometry before and after a reliever to confirm COPD and rule out asthma.
a.w: COPD can only be confirmed with spirometry. Asthma, heart failure and other illnesses can look the same and need different treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ihab offered nicotine patches.
a.x: Patches are as bad as smoking.
a.w: Patches double the chance of quitting.

a.o: Dr. Ihab did a chest X-ray.
a.w: An X-ray looks for cancer and other causes.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about weight loss.
a.w: Weight loss in a smoker is a warning sign.

t: Baby with coughing fits and pauses sent home
s:
Baby Mariam, 6 weeks old, has had a cough for ten days that comes in fits. During the fits she goes red, then blue, and sometimes stops breathing for a few seconds. Between fits she seems well. She was born at term.

Dr. Dina watched a coughing fit, which ended with a gasp and vomiting. Her oxygen dropped to 85% during the fit and came back to 98% after. Her chest was clear between fits.

She asked about vaccines, and Mariam was too young for her first ones. Her mother had not had the whooping cough vaccine in pregnancy.

Mariam's 8-year-old brother has had a bad cough for a month. Her mother asked whether it was just a cold.

Dr. Dina sent her home with advice to come back if the fits got worse.
h: Dr. Dina sent her home with advice to come back if the fits got worse

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Baby Mariam home with likely whooping cough and breathing pauses.
a.x: Baby Mariam should have been admitted for monitoring, oxygen and a macrolide antibiotic, with the family treated and public health told.
a.w: Whooping cough in babies under 2 months can cause apneas and death. Blue spells and pauses need hospital care.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked about the mother's vaccine.
a.x: The mother's vaccine was off topic.
a.w: The pregnancy vaccine protects newborns.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked about the brother's cough.
a.w: Older children often spread whooping cough.

a.o: Dr. Dina watched a coughing fit.
a.w: Seeing a fit helps make the diagnosis.

t: Shipyard worker's chest pain called muscular
s:
Mr. Kamel, 70, worked fitting pipes in a shipyard for 30 years. For three months he has had a dull ache on the right side of his chest and breathlessness. He has lost 6 kg. He stopped smoking 20 years ago.

Dr. Mervat found reduced breath sounds and dullness at the right base. A chest X-ray showed fluid around the right lung and thickening of the lining.

She checked his blood tests, which were normal apart from a mild anemia.

Mr. Kamel said many of his old colleagues had died of "lung problems". His wife worried about him.

Dr. Mervat said the ache was muscular from age, prescribed painkillers and did not drain the fluid or arrange a CT.
h: Dr. Mervat said the ache was muscular from age, prescribed painkillers and did not drain the fluid or arrange a CT

a.o: Dr. Mervat called Mr. Kamel's chest pain muscular.
a.x: Mr. Kamel should have had a fluid sample, a CT scan and a chest clinic referral for possible mesothelioma.
a.w: Chest pain, weight loss, fluid and a thickened lining after asbestos work point to mesothelioma.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about his work.
a.w: Asbestos causes lung disease.

a.o: Dr. Mervat did a chest X-ray.
a.w: It shows the fluid.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked his blood.
a.w: Anemia can be a sign of cancer.

t: Thrush from a steroid inhaler without rinse advice
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 44, has asthma and started a higher-dose steroid inhaler two months ago. Her asthma is much better. She now has a sore mouth with white patches and a hoarse voice.

Dr. Ghada looked in her mouth and saw white patches that came off easily, leaving red spots.

She checked her inhaler technique and saw she did not use a spacer.

Mrs. Nadia is a singer in a choir and was upset about her voice.

She has no diabetes and takes no antibiotics. She had not had thrush before. She was worried the steroid inhaler was dangerous and wanted to stop it, but Dr. Ghada explained it was keeping her asthma under control.

Dr. Ghada prescribed antifungal drops, without advice on rinsing or using a spacer.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed antifungal drops, without advice on rinsing or using a spacer

a.o: Dr. Ghada treated Mrs. Nadia's thrush without prevention advice.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have been told to rinse her mouth after each use and use a spacer.
a.w: Rinsing and a spacer reduce the steroid left in the mouth, preventing thrush and a hoarse voice.

a.o: Dr. Ghada looked in her mouth.
a.w: The look confirms thrush.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked her technique.
a.w: Poor technique leaves more steroid in the mouth.

a.o: Dr. Ghada prescribed antifungal drops.
a.w: Antifungals clear thrush.

t: Theophylline with ciprofloxacin
s:
Mr. Sami, 66, has COPD and takes theophylline tablets. He was admitted with a urine infection, and the team started ciprofloxacin. On day three he felt sick, vomited and had a racing heart.

Dr. Ayman checked his heart tracing, which showed a fast rhythm. His potassium was low.

He gave him anti-sickness medicine and potassium.

Mr. Sami's son asked whether the infection had spread to his heart.

He also takes salbutamol and a steroid inhaler, and he still smokes a few cigarettes a day, though he had stopped since admission. He had no fever now, and his urine was clearing. The ward pharmacist was on leave that week.

Dr. Ayman continued both the theophylline and the ciprofloxacin, without checking a theophylline level.
h: Dr. Ayman continued both the theophylline and the ciprofloxacin, without checking a theophylline level

a.o: Dr. Ayman kept Mr. Sami on theophylline with ciprofloxacin and no level check.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have had a theophylline level checked, the theophylline held and a different antibiotic chosen.
a.w: Ciprofloxacin raises theophylline levels. Toxicity causes vomiting, fast heart rhythms, low potassium and fits.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked his potassium.
a.w: Theophylline toxicity lowers potassium.

a.o: Dr. Ayman did a heart tracing.
a.w: Toxicity causes heart rhythm problems.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave anti-sickness medicine.
a.w: Vomiting is a common symptom.

t: Bubbling chest drain clamped
s:
Mr. Tarek, 30, has a chest drain for a collapsed right lung after a fall from a ladder. The drain bottle is still bubbling with each breath. He was comfortable this morning, with an oxygen level of 96%.

Dr. Hala checked the drain site, which was clean, and the X-ray, which showed the lung partly up. She checked his pain relief and asked the physiotherapist to help with deep breathing.

She made sure the drain bottle was kept below the level of his chest and the water seal was correct.

Mr. Tarek wanted to walk to the hospital shop and asked whether the drain could be disconnected for a while. The nurse was worried about him tripping over the tube.

Dr. Hala clamped the drain so he could walk around without the bottle.
h: Dr. Hala clamped the drain so he could walk around without the bottle

a.o: Dr. Hala clamped Mr. Tarek's bubbling chest drain.
a.x: Mr. Tarek's drain should have stayed open, with him walking carrying the bottle below his chest.
a.w: A bubbling drain means air is still leaking. Clamping it can cause a tension pneumothorax, which can kill.

a.o: Dr. Hala kept the bottle below the chest.
a.w: A raised bottle can siphon fluid back into the chest.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked the X-ray.
a.w: The X-ray shows if the lung is up.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked the physiotherapist to help.
a.w: Deep breathing helps the lung re-expand.

t: Large lung clot with low blood pressure not thrombolysed
s:
Mrs. Amira, 52, collapsed at home. She had been breathless for two days after a long flight. Her blood pressure was 78/40, her pulse 130 and her oxygen 85% on high-flow oxygen. A bedside heart scan showed a very swollen right side of the heart.

Dr. Nada started heparin and gave fluids carefully. She called intensive care.

A CT scan confirmed large clots in both lung arteries.

Mrs. Amira had no recent surgery, bleeding or stroke. Her husband asked whether she would survive.

She takes the combined pill and has no other illnesses. Her troponin was raised. The ward had a bed free, while the intensive care unit was nearly full.

Dr. Nada continued heparin and admitted her to the ward, without giving clot-busting treatment.
h: Dr. Nada continued heparin and admitted her to the ward, without giving clot-busting treatment

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mrs. Amira heparin alone for a massive lung clot with low blood pressure.
a.x: Mrs. Amira should have had clot-busting treatment, such as alteplase, at once, with ICU care.
a.w: A clot that drops the blood pressure is a massive PE. Without clot-busting treatment, the risk of death is very high.

a.o: Dr. Nada called intensive care.
a.w: A massive PE needs intensive care.

a.o: Dr. Nada did a bedside heart scan.
a.w: A swollen right heart supports a massive PE.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about bleeding history.
a.w: Bleeding risk matters before clot-busting treatment.

t: Young man with emphysema not tested for a gene
s:
Mr. Sherif, 38, has emphysema on his CT scan, mostly at the bottom of his lungs. He smoked only lightly for five years in his twenties. His liver tests are mildly raised. His uncle died of lung disease at 45.

Dr. Fady checked his lung function tests, which showed COPD. He started inhalers and offered pulmonary rehab.

He advised him never to smoke again and to avoid dust and fumes at work.

Mr. Sherif has two children and works as a carpenter. He asked why he had lung disease so young.

His brother, 34, has a cough but has never been checked.

Dr. Fady said it was from smoking and did not test for alpha-1 antitrypsin.
h: Dr. Fady said it was from smoking and did not test for alpha-1 antitrypsin

a.o: Dr. Fady blamed smoking for Mr. Sherif's early emphysema without testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin.
a.x: Mr. Sherif should have had an alpha-1 antitrypsin level and gene test, with family testing if positive.
a.w: Emphysema under 45, at the lung bases, with liver changes and a family history, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised avoiding dust.
a.w: Dust worsens lung disease.

a.o: Dr. Fady offered pulmonary rehab.
a.w: Rehab improves breathing.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked lung function.
a.w: They confirm COPD.

t: Swollen face in lung cancer given an antihistamine
s:
Mr. Hamed, 64, has lung cancer on the right side, found last month. For a week his face, neck and arms have become swollen, worse in the mornings. The veins on his chest are swollen. He is breathless when lying flat.

Dr. Inas found his face red and puffy, with swollen veins across his chest and neck. His oxygen was 93%. He had no rash or itch.

She asked him to sit up, gave oxygen and checked his blood tests.

Mr. Hamed's wife thought he was allergic to his new pillow. He had no hives or wheeze.

Dr. Inas diagnosed an allergic reaction, gave an antihistamine and sent him home.
h: Dr. Inas diagnosed an allergic reaction, gave an antihistamine and sent him home

a.o: Dr. Inas called Mr. Hamed's swelling an allergy.
a.x: Mr. Hamed should have had urgent imaging and specialist care for superior vena cava obstruction, with steroids and possibly a stent.
a.w: Face, neck and arm swelling with swollen chest veins in lung cancer means the big vein to the heart is blocked.

a.o: Dr. Inas sat him up.
a.w: Sitting up eases breathing and swelling.

a.o: Dr. Inas looked for a rash.
a.w: No rash or itch makes allergy unlikely.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave oxygen.
a.w: His oxygen was low.

t: Sarcoidosis with high calcium given vitamin D
s:
Mrs. Samar, 40, has sarcoidosis in her lungs and skin. Her calcium was 2.9, high, and she had kidney stones last year. She feels tired and thirsty.

Dr. Mervat checked her kidney function, which was a little reduced, and her chest X-ray, which showed swollen glands in the chest.

She advised her to drink more water and avoid too much sun.

Mrs. Samar said her friend told her vitamin D helps tiredness. Her vitamin D level was low.

She works as an office manager and has two teenage sons. She takes no other medicines. Her eyes had been checked last month and were healthy. She said she felt foggy and forgetful, and her husband said she had become irritable.

Dr. Mervat prescribed high-dose vitamin D tablets to "fix the low vitamin D".
h: Dr. Mervat prescribed high-dose vitamin D tablets to "fix the low vitamin D"

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave vitamin D to Mrs. Samar with sarcoidosis and high calcium.
a.x: Mrs. Samar should have avoided vitamin D, with her high calcium treated, possibly with steroids.
a.w: In sarcoidosis, the granulomas turn vitamin D into its active form. Extra vitamin D pushes calcium even higher.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised drinking more water.
a.w: Water helps prevent kidney stones.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised avoiding too much sun.
a.w: Sunlight raises vitamin D and calcium.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked her kidney function.
a.w: High calcium can harm the kidneys.

t: Silent chest sent to the ward
s:
Miss Dina, 24, has asthma and came in after two days of worsening breathlessness. She could only say single words. Her peak flow was 30% of her best, her oxygen 91% and her pulse 128. Her chest was nearly silent, with very little wheeze.

Dr. Nada gave back-to-back salbutamol and ipratropium nebulizers and oral prednisolone. She started IV magnesium.

She checked a blood gas, which showed a normal carbon dioxide level of 5.6, and asked for a chest X-ray to look for a collapsed lung.

Miss Dina had been in intensive care once before with asthma. Her mother said she ran out of her preventer inhaler last month.

After an hour, she was a little better, and Dr. Nada sent her to the general ward, without calling a senior or intensive care.
h: Dr. Nada sent her to the general ward, without calling a senior or intensive care

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Miss Dina to the ward with life-threatening asthma and no senior or ICU review.
a.x: Miss Dina should have had senior and intensive care review at once, staying in a place where she could be closely watched.
a.w: A silent chest, oxygen under 92% and a "normal" CO2 in a tired asthmatic mean life-threatening asthma. She can stop breathing suddenly.

a.o: Dr. Nada started IV magnesium.
a.w: Magnesium helps severe asthma.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked for a chest X-ray.
a.w: A collapsed lung can complicate asthma.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked about past ICU stays.
a.w: Past ICU stays raise the risk of a fatal attack.

t: Three liters drained from the chest at once
s:
Mr. Fikry, 66, has a large fluid collection around his left lung from a cancer. He was very breathless. Dr. Ayman put a drain into the chest under ultrasound to drain the fluid.

He checked his blood thinner, which he had stopped, and his platelets, which were normal. He used local anesthetic and drained the fluid into a bag.

He sent the fluid for tests and checked his oxygen, which improved from 89% to 95%.

Mr. Fikry felt much better and asked for all the fluid to be removed at once. His wife was relieved.

Dr. Ayman let 3 liters drain out in 30 minutes, then left the drain open.
h: Dr. Ayman let 3 liters drain out in 30 minutes, then left the drain open

a.o: Dr. Ayman drained 3 liters from Mr. Fikry's chest in 30 minutes.
a.x: The drain should have been clamped after about 1.5 liters, with the rest drained slowly over hours.
a.w: Draining a large effusion too fast can cause re-expansion pulmonary edema, filling the lung with fluid.

a.o: Dr. Ayman used ultrasound.
a.w: Ultrasound makes drain insertion safer.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked his platelets.
a.w: Low platelets raise bleeding risk.

a.o: Dr. Ayman sent the fluid for tests.
a.w: Tests show the cause.

t: Coughing man with TB put on an open ward
s:
Mr. Sami, 45, came from a country where TB is common. He has had a cough for two months, night sweats and weight loss. His chest X-ray showed a cavity at the top of the right lung.

Dr. Fouad sent three sputum samples and an HIV test. He checked his liver tests before treatment.

He asked about family and work contacts.

Mr. Sami was tired and wanted to rest. The side rooms were all full.

He works in a restaurant kitchen and shares a flat with four other men. One of the patients in the open bay was on chemotherapy. The infection control nurse had gone home for the day.

Dr. Fouad admitted him to an open ward bay with five other patients, without a mask or isolation.
h: Dr. Fouad admitted him to an open ward bay with five other patients, without a mask or isolation

a.o: Dr. Fouad put Mr. Sami, with likely TB, in an open ward.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have been placed in a side room, ideally a negative pressure room, until his sputum showed no TB.
a.w: TB with a cavity spreads through the air and can infect other patients and staff.

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent an HIV test.
a.w: HIV and TB often go together.

a.o: Dr. Fouad checked his liver tests.
a.w: TB drugs can harm the liver.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked about contacts.
a.w: Contacts need screening.

t: Flu in a pregnant woman without antivirals
s:
Mrs. Rana, 30, is 28 weeks pregnant. She came in with a sudden fever of 39°C, aching muscles, headache and dry cough since yesterday. Flu is spreading in the area.

Dr. Ghada listened to her chest, which was clear, and checked her oxygen, which was 97%.

She advised rest, fluids and paracetamol.

Mrs. Rana works as a teacher and had not had her flu vaccine this year.

This is her first pregnancy and the baby had been moving well. She has mild asthma and uses an inhaler now and then. Two children in her class had been off sick with flu last week. Her husband had the same illness a few days earlier and was still in bed.

Dr. Ghada told her it was a virus that would pass, without offering oseltamivir.
h: Dr. Ghada told her it was a virus that would pass, without offering oseltamivir

a.o: Dr. Ghada didn't give Mrs. Rana antivirals for flu in pregnancy.
a.x: Mrs. Rana should have had oseltamivir within 48 hours of symptoms.
a.w: Pregnant women are at high risk of severe flu and pneumonia. Antivirals lower the risk.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked her oxygen.
a.w: Low oxygen shows severe illness.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised paracetamol.
a.w: Paracetamol is safe in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about the vaccine.
a.w: The vaccine protects pregnant women.

t: Lung nodule on a scan not followed up
s:
Mr. Hesham, 61, had a CT scan for kidney stones. The report also mentioned a 9 mm nodule in the right lung, with advice to follow up. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day.

Dr. Fady treated his kidney stones and checked his kidney function.

He advised him to drink more water and avoid salty food.

Mr. Hesham was pleased the stone had passed. He asked whether he needed more tests.

He works as a taxi driver and has a cough most mornings, which he puts down to smoking. His father died of lung cancer at 66. The kidney stone report was long, and the line about the lung was near the end. He had no weight loss and felt well.

Dr. Fady discharged him without acting on the lung nodule.
h: Dr. Fady discharged him without acting on the lung nodule

a.o: Dr. Fady ignored Mr. Hesham's lung nodule.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have been referred to the chest team for follow-up of the nodule.
a.w: A 9 mm lung nodule in a smoker can be an early lung cancer, which is curable if caught early.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Hesham's kidney function.
a.x: Kidney tests were unnecessary for a stone.
a.w: A blocking stone can harm the kidney.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised more water.
a.w: Water prevents stones.

a.o: Dr. Fady treated Mr. Hesham's kidney stone.
a.x: The stone would pass by itself.
a.w: Painful stones need pain relief and a check that they pass.

t: Allopurinol stopped during a gout attack
s:
Mr. Hany, 56, has had gout for years and has taken allopurinol 300 mg daily for a year. His uric acid has come down well. He came in with a hot, swollen right ankle that started last night after a wedding feast.

Dr. Ghada examined the ankle, which was red and very tender, with no break in the skin. He had no fever. His kidney function was normal.

She prescribed colchicine 500 micrograms two to three times a day and advised rest, ice and plenty of water.

Mr. Hany works as a chef and was frustrated because he thought the allopurinol was supposed to stop attacks. He had read online that it can make attacks worse. He asked whether he should stop it.

Dr. Ghada told him to stop the allopurinol until the attack settled, then restart it.
h: Dr. Ghada told him to stop the allopurinol until the attack settled, then restart it

a.o: Dr. Ghada stopped Mr. Hany's allopurinol during the attack.
a.x: Mr. Hany should have kept taking allopurinol at the same dose and treated the attack with colchicine.
a.w: Stopping and restarting allopurinol changes uric acid levels and can trigger more attacks. It should continue through a flare.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked kidney function.
a.w: Colchicine doses depend on the kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised plenty of water.
a.w: Water helps the kidneys clear uric acid.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked about the feast.
a.w: Rich food and alcohol can trigger gout.

t: Allopurinol added to azathioprine
s:
Mr. Sherif, 48, has had a kidney transplant and takes azathioprine 100 mg daily and prednisolone. He has had three gout attacks this year. His uric acid is high and his kidney function is stable.

Dr. Mervat checked his blood count, which was normal, and his liver tests, which were fine.

She advised him to cut down on beer and red meat, and to drink plenty of water.

Mr. Sherif said the gout was stopping him from working as a delivery driver. He wanted a tablet to prevent it. He takes no other medicines.

Dr. Mervat started allopurinol 100 mg daily, without changing his azathioprine or checking his blood count soon after.
h: Dr. Mervat started allopurinol 100 mg daily, without changing his azathioprine or checking his blood count soon after

a.o: Dr. Mervat added allopurinol to Mr. Sherif's azathioprine without changing the dose.
a.x: Mr. Sherif should have had a different gout drug, such as febuxostat after specialist advice, or his azathioprine cut to a quarter with close blood checks.
a.w: Allopurinol stops the breakdown of azathioprine, causing a dangerous drop in blood cells.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked his blood count.
a.w: Azathioprine can lower the blood count.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised cutting down on beer.
a.w: Beer raises uric acid.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked his liver tests.
a.w: Azathioprine can harm the liver.

t: Methotrexate without folic acid or blood tests
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 52, has rheumatoid arthritis affecting her hands and wrists. She has morning stiffness for two hours. Her CRP is high and her rheumatoid factor positive.

Dr. Fady examined her hands and found swollen knuckles. He checked her chest X-ray and her hepatitis tests, which were normal.

He explained that methotrexate is a weekly tablet and that she should avoid alcohol.

Mrs. Nawal works as a seamstress and could no longer hold her needles. She was keen to start treatment quickly. She lives far from the clinic.

Her kidney and liver tests were normal at the start.

Dr. Fady started methotrexate 15 mg weekly, without folic acid or any plan for blood tests.
h: Dr. Fady started methotrexate 15 mg weekly, without folic acid or any plan for blood tests

a.o: Dr. Fady started methotrexate without folic acid or blood monitoring.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have had folic acid once a week on a different day, and blood tests every two weeks at first.
a.w: Methotrexate can lower the blood count and harm the liver. Folic acid cuts side effects, and blood tests catch problems early.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked her chest X-ray.
a.w: Methotrexate can affect the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised avoiding alcohol.
a.w: Alcohol adds to liver damage.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked hepatitis tests.
a.w: Hepatitis raises liver risk.

t: Steroids stopped suddenly in polymyalgia
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 72, has polymyalgia rheumatica and has taken prednisolone for eight months. She started on 15 mg and is now on 7.5 mg. Her shoulder and hip pain is much better and her ESR is normal.

Dr. Ihab checked her blood pressure and sugar, which had risen a little on the steroids. He checked that she was on calcium and vitamin D.

He asked about headaches and jaw pain, which she did not have.

Mrs. Fawzia said she hated the steroids because they made her face round. She wanted to stop them as soon as possible. She has not had a bone scan.

Dr. Ihab told her to stop the prednisolone that day, as she was better.
h: Dr. Ihab told her to stop the prednisolone that day, as she was better

a.o: Dr. Ihab stopped Mrs. Fawzia's long-term steroids suddenly.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have reduced her prednisolone slowly, by 1 mg every month or so.
a.w: After months of steroids, the body stops making its own. Stopping suddenly can cause an Addisonian crisis and a flare of polymyalgia.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about headaches.
a.w: Giant cell arteritis can come with polymyalgia.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her sugar.
a.w: Steroids raise sugar.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked calcium and vitamin D.
a.w: Steroids weaken bones.

t: Lupus with protein in the urine left for months
s:
Miss Yasmin, 26, has lupus with joint pains and a rash. She came for her review. Her ankles were swollen and her urine was frothy. Her blood pressure was 148/94, higher than usual.

Dr. Mervat checked her urine, which showed 3+ protein and blood. Her creatinine had risen a little.

She checked her complement levels, which were low, and her double-stranded DNA antibodies, which were high.

Miss Yasmin is a law student with exams soon. She said she felt fine and did not want a hospital stay. She takes hydroxychloroquine.

Her mother also has lupus.

Dr. Mervat booked a review in three months, without referring her to the kidney team.
h: Dr. Mervat booked a review in three months, without referring her to the kidney team

a.o: Dr. Mervat left Miss Yasmin's likely lupus nephritis for three months.
a.x: Miss Yasmin should have been referred urgently to the kidney team for a biopsy and treatment.
a.w: Protein and blood in the urine, high blood pressure and active lupus point to lupus nephritis, which can cause kidney failure.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked her complement levels.
a.w: Low complement shows active lupus.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked her urine.
a.w: Urine shows kidney involvement.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked her blood pressure.
a.w: High blood pressure can be a sign of kidney disease.

t: Scleroderma kidney crisis without an ACE inhibitor
s:
Mrs. Samar, 45, has scleroderma with tight skin on her hands, face and arms, diagnosed a year ago. She was started on high-dose prednisolone last month by another doctor. Now she has a severe headache, blurred vision and blood pressure of 210/120. Her creatinine has doubled in a week.

Dr. Ayman checked her blood film, which showed broken red cells, and her platelets, which were low. Her urine showed a little protein.

He asked the nurses to check her blood pressure every 15 minutes and called the kidney team.

Mrs. Samar's husband said she had been very well until the steroids. She has Raynaud's and her fingertips have small ulcers.

Dr. Ayman started IV labetalol to lower her blood pressure, without an ACE inhibitor, and continued the steroids.
h: Dr. Ayman started IV labetalol to lower her blood pressure, without an ACE inhibitor, and continued the steroids

a.o: Dr. Ayman treated Mrs. Samar's scleroderma kidney crisis without an ACE inhibitor.
a.x: Mrs. Samar should have had an ACE inhibitor such as captopril, raised steadily, and her steroids reduced.
a.w: Scleroderma renal crisis needs ACE inhibitors, which save kidneys and lives. High-dose steroids can trigger it.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked her blood film.
a.w: Broken red cells show damage to small vessels.

a.o: Dr. Ayman called the kidney team.
a.w: She may need dialysis.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked for frequent blood pressure checks.
a.w: Blood pressure must be lowered carefully.

t: Reactive arthritis without a sexual health check
s:
Mr. Karim, 25, came in with a swollen, painful left knee and right ankle for a week. He also had sore red eyes and burning on passing urine two weeks ago, which got better by itself. He had a new partner a month ago.

Dr. Ihab examined him and found both joints swollen and warm. He checked his blood tests, which showed a raised CRP.

He asked about diarrhea, which Mr. Karim did not have, and about back pain, which he had a little.

Mr. Karim plays football and was worried about missing a match. He was embarrassed about the urine symptoms.

Dr. Ihab diagnosed reactive arthritis and prescribed naproxen, without testing for sexually transmitted infections.
h: Dr. Ihab diagnosed reactive arthritis and prescribed naproxen, without testing for sexually transmitted infections

a.o: Dr. Ihab treated Mr. Karim's reactive arthritis without a sexual health check.
a.x: Mr. Karim should have been tested for chlamydia and gonorrhea, with treatment for him and his partner if positive.
a.w: Reactive arthritis after urine symptoms is often caused by chlamydia. Untreated, it can spread and harm his partner.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about diarrhea.
a.w: Gut infections can also trigger reactive arthritis.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked about back pain.
a.w: Reactive arthritis can affect the spine.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked his CRP.
a.w: A raised CRP shows inflammation.

t: Biologic started without TB screening
s:
Mr. Fathi, 50, has rheumatoid arthritis that has not responded to methotrexate. The team decided to start adalimumab, an anti-TNF injection. He grew up in a village where TB was common, and his father had TB.

Dr. Fady checked his blood count, liver tests and hepatitis tests, which were normal.

He advised him to avoid live vaccines and to report any fever.

Mr. Fathi was keen to start because his hands were very painful. He works as a farmer.

He has a mild cough every winter, which he blames on dust from the fields. He has diabetes, controlled with tablets. His wife had TB treatment years ago, which she finished.

Dr. Fady started adalimumab, without a TB test or chest X-ray.
h: Dr. Fady started adalimumab, without a TB test or chest X-ray

a.o: Dr. Fady started adalimumab without TB screening.
a.x: Mr. Fathi should have had a TB blood test and a chest X-ray, with preventive treatment if positive.
a.w: Anti-TNF drugs can wake up hidden TB, which can spread through the body and kill.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Fathi's hepatitis tests.
a.w: Anti-TNF drugs can wake up hepatitis B.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised avoiding live vaccines.
a.w: Live vaccines can cause infection on biologics.

a.o: Dr. Fady told Mr. Fathi to report any fever.
a.w: Serious infections are a major risk on biologics.

t: Nosebleeds and coughing blood called a cold
s:
Mr. Raouf, 55, has had a blocked, crusty nose and nosebleeds for two months. Recently he has coughed up blood and his joints ache. He has lost 4 kg. His urine dipstick showed blood and protein.

Dr. Ghada looked in his nose and saw crusts and bleeding. His blood pressure was 152/96.

She sent blood tests, which showed a raised creatinine and CRP.

Mr. Raouf works as a bus driver and thought he had a bad cold. He takes no regular medicines.

His ears had also felt blocked. He had no fever. His chest X-ray from last year was normal.

Dr. Ghada prescribed a nasal spray and antibiotics and booked a review in a month.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed a nasal spray and antibiotics and booked a review in a month

a.o: Dr. Ghada called Mr. Raouf's illness a cold.
a.x: Mr. Raouf should have been referred urgently for an ANCA test, chest imaging and kidney team review.
a.w: Nose crusting, coughing blood, joint pain and blood in the urine with rising creatinine point to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which can destroy the kidneys within weeks.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked his urine.
a.w: Blood and protein show kidney involvement.

a.o: Dr. Ghada looked in his nose.
a.w: Nasal crusting is a sign of vasculitis.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked his blood pressure.
a.w: Kidney disease raises blood pressure.

t: Propranolol for a woman with Raynaud's
s:
Miss Hala, 32, has Raynaud's, where her fingers turn white then blue in the cold. She also has migraines twice a month. She came asking for a tablet to prevent the migraines.

Dr. Ihab checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and examined her fingers, which had no ulcers.

He advised her to keep her hands warm with gloves and to stop smoking.

Miss Hala works in a supermarket freezer section. She said her fingers had been worse this winter.

Her migraines come with flashing lights and she takes the progestogen-only pill. Triptans help her attacks. She has no asthma. Her mother also has Raynaud's.

Dr. Ihab prescribed propranolol to prevent her migraines.
h: Dr. Ihab prescribed propranolol to prevent her migraines

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave propranolol to Miss Hala, who has Raynaud's.
a.x: Miss Hala should have had a different migraine preventer, such as amitriptyline or topiramate.
a.w: Beta blockers narrow the small blood vessels and make Raynaud's worse.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised gloves.
a.w: Warmth prevents attacks.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised stopping smoking.
a.w: Smoking narrows blood vessels.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her fingers.
a.w: Ulcers show severe Raynaud's.

t: Knee arthritis told to rest and avoid exercise
s:
Mrs. Nabila, 63, has had aching knees for two years, worse after walking and at the end of the day. Her knees are stiff for ten minutes in the morning. Her X-ray showed narrowing of the joint space on both sides. Her BMI is 32.

Dr. Ghada examined her knees, which creaked but were not hot or swollen. She checked her kidney function, which was normal.

She prescribed paracetamol and an anti-inflammatory gel to rub on the knees, and talked about weight loss.

Mrs. Nabila used to walk to the market every day but has stopped because of the pain. She lives with her husband and enjoys gardening. She asked whether walking was wearing out her knees.

Dr. Ghada told her to rest her knees and avoid exercise to stop them wearing out.
h: Dr. Ghada told her to rest her knees and avoid exercise to stop them wearing out

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mrs. Nabila to rest and avoid exercise for knee arthritis.
a.x: Mrs. Nabila should have been encouraged to stay active, with strengthening exercises and physiotherapy.
a.w: Exercise is a core treatment for osteoarthritis. It strengthens the muscles that protect the knee and eases pain. Rest makes it worse.

a.o: Dr. Ghada prescribed a gel.
a.w: Anti-inflammatory gels help knee pain with fewer side effects.

a.o: Dr. Ghada talked about weight loss.
a.w: Weight loss eases knee pain.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked her kidney function.
a.w: Kidney function affects painkiller choice.

t: Strong opioids for fibromyalgia
s:
Mrs. Rasha, 42, has had widespread pain all over her body for two years, with poor sleep and tiredness. Her blood tests, including thyroid and inflammation markers, were normal. She was diagnosed with fibromyalgia.

Dr. Fady explained the condition and that the pain is real but not caused by damage. He advised graded exercise like swimming and better sleep habits.

He referred her for talking therapy and started amitriptyline at a low dose at night.

Mrs. Rasha works as a teacher and was desperate for relief. She said codeine had not helped and asked for something stronger.

She has two teenage children.

Dr. Fady started oxycodone twice a day "to break the pain cycle".
h: Dr. Fady started oxycodone twice a day "to break the pain cycle"

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Rasha oxycodone for fibromyalgia.
a.x: Mrs. Rasha should have continued exercise, therapy and amitriptyline, with no strong opioids.
a.w: Opioids don't help fibromyalgia, can make pain worse, and lead to dependence.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised graded exercise.
a.w: Gentle exercise helps fibromyalgia.

a.o: Dr. Fady referred her for therapy.
a.w: Therapy helps people cope with chronic pain.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked her thyroid.
a.w: An underactive thyroid can cause aches.

t: Long-term steroids without bone protection
s:
Mr. Kamel, 68, has a lung disease that needs prednisolone 20 mg daily. He has taken it for six months and will need it for at least another year. He is otherwise well.

Dr. Mervat checked his blood pressure, which was a little high, and his sugar, which was borderline.

She advised him to carry a steroid card and never stop the steroids suddenly.

Mr. Kamel said he had broken his wrist last year when he tripped. He walks with a stick.

He had his vitamin D checked last year, which was low, but never started a supplement. His mother broke her hip in her seventies. He lives alone in a house with stairs.

Dr. Mervat continued the prednisolone, without bone protection or a bone scan.
h: Dr. Mervat continued the prednisolone, without bone protection or a bone scan

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave Mr. Kamel no bone protection on long-term steroids.
a.x: Mr. Kamel should have started a bisphosphonate, with calcium and vitamin D.
a.w: Steroids for three months or more weaken bones. Over 65 or with a past fracture, bone protection should start at once.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked his sugar.
a.w: Steroids can cause diabetes.

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave him a steroid card.
a.w: The card warns doctors in an emergency.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked about the wrist fracture.
a.w: A past fracture shows weak bones.

t: Child with arthritis without eye screening
s:
Laila, 4, has juvenile idiopathic arthritis in her right knee and left ankle. She was diagnosed three months ago. Her ANA blood test was positive. She is on naproxen and doing well, with less swelling.

Dr. Rana examined her joints and found mild swelling. She checked her growth, which was normal.

She referred her to the physiotherapist and gave advice on keeping active.

Laila's mother said Laila's eyes looked fine and she had no complaints. Laila loves drawing and painting.

She is in nursery and her teacher said she runs around like the other children. Her vaccines are up to date. Her father has psoriasis.

Dr. Rana booked a review in six months, without arranging eye screening.
h: Dr. Rana booked a review in six months, without arranging eye screening

a.o: Dr. Rana didn't arrange eye screening for Laila with JIA.
a.x: Laila should have had slit-lamp eye checks every three months, as she is young, has few joints involved and is ANA positive.
a.w: Children with JIA can get silent uveitis with no red eye or pain, which can cause blindness.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked her growth.
a.w: Arthritis can affect growth.

a.o: Dr. Rana referred her to physio.
a.w: Physio keeps joints moving.

a.o: Dr. Rana gave advice on staying active.
a.w: Staying active keeps joints healthy.

t: Colchicine every hour until diarrhea
s:
Mr. Sami, 60, has gout and came in with a red, swollen big toe since this morning. He has kidney disease with an eGFR of 40 and takes atorvastatin.

Dr. Ihab examined the toe and found it hot and swollen. He checked his kidney function.

He advised rest, ice and elevation.

Mr. Sami said the pain was the worst he had ever had and wanted the strongest treatment.

He also takes clarithromycin, started yesterday for a chest infection. He works as a security guard and stands all night. He has had two attacks this year and is not on allopurinol.

Dr. Ihab told him to take colchicine 500 micrograms every hour until the pain stopped or he got diarrhea.
h: Dr. Ihab told him to take colchicine 500 micrograms every hour until the pain stopped or he got diarrhea

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mr. Sami to take colchicine every hour.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have had a short course of prednisolone instead, since colchicine at any dose is risky with clarithromycin and weak kidneys.
a.w: The old "hourly" plan causes colchicine poisoning, with diarrhea, organ failure and death. Weak kidneys, a statin and clarithromycin all raise the level.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised elevation.
a.w: Raising the foot eases swelling.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked his kidney function.
a.w: Kidneys affect the colchicine dose.

a.o: Dr. Ihab advised ice.
a.w: Ice eases gout pain.

t: Muscle weakness and rash without a cancer search
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 58, has had weakness in her thighs and shoulders for two months. She struggles to climb stairs and lift her arms to brush her hair. She has a purple rash on her eyelids and red patches over her knuckles. Her CK is 4,500.

Dr. Mervat examined her and found weakness in the muscles near the trunk, with normal reflexes. She diagnosed dermatomyositis.

She started high-dose prednisolone and asked the physiotherapist to see her. She checked her swallowing, which was a little slow.

Mrs. Hanem had lost 6 kg without trying. She had stopped going for her breast screening two years ago. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day.

Dr. Mervat booked a review in a month, without any tests to look for an underlying cancer.
h: Dr. Mervat booked a review in a month, without any tests to look for an underlying cancer

a.o: Dr. Mervat didn't look for cancer in Mrs. Hanem with new dermatomyositis.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem should have had a CT of the chest, belly and pelvis, a mammogram and other cancer screening.
a.w: Dermatomyositis in adults is often linked to a hidden cancer, especially with weight loss.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked her swallowing.
a.w: Weak throat muscles can cause choking and pneumonia.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked the physiotherapist to see her.
a.w: Physio keeps muscles working.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked the CK.
a.w: A high CK shows muscle damage.

t: Rheumatoid neck not checked before surgery
s:
Mrs. Samia, 66, has had severe rheumatoid arthritis for 25 years, with badly deformed hands. She is due for a hip replacement under general anesthetic tomorrow. She has had neck pain and tingling in her hands when she bends her head forward.

Dr. Hala checked her airway, heart and lungs. Her mouth opening was a little limited.

She checked her blood count and kidney tests, and planned to hold her methotrexate around surgery as advised by the rheumatologist.

Mrs. Samia said she had been dropping things recently. She takes prednisolone 5 mg daily.

She lives with her daughter.

Dr. Hala planned a standard intubation, without neck X-rays or a plan to protect the neck.
h: Dr. Hala planned a standard intubation, without neck X-rays or a plan to protect the neck

a.o: Dr. Hala didn't check Mrs. Samia's neck before intubation.
a.x: Mrs. Samia should have had neck X-rays in flexion and extension, with a plan to keep the neck still during intubation, or a spinal anesthetic.
a.w: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis can loosen the top of the neck. Bending it during intubation can damage the spinal cord.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked her mouth opening.
a.w: A small mouth opening makes intubation hard.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked about her steroids.
a.w: Long-term steroids may need extra cover during surgery.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked her blood count.
a.w: Anemia is common in rheumatoid arthritis.

t: Yellow fever vaccine on a biologic
s:
Mr. Waleed, 40, has psoriatic arthritis and takes etanercept injections every week. His joints are well controlled. He came to clinic asking about vaccines for a work trip to West Africa next month.

Dr. Fady checked his blood tests, which were normal. He gave him advice on malaria tablets and insect bites.

He arranged hepatitis A and typhoid injection vaccines, which are not live.

Mr. Waleed said the travel clinic told him he needed a yellow fever vaccine to enter the country. He asked whether he could have it.

He has two children and his wife is pregnant.

Dr. Fady said it was fine and arranged the yellow fever vaccine for next week.
h: Dr. Fady said it was fine and arranged the yellow fever vaccine for next week

a.o: Dr. Fady approved a yellow fever vaccine for Mr. Waleed on etanercept.
a.x: Mr. Waleed should not have had the yellow fever vaccine; he needed a medical exemption letter and specialist travel advice.
a.w: Yellow fever vaccine is live. On a biologic, it can cause a severe, even fatal, infection.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave malaria advice.
a.w: West Africa has malaria.

a.o: Dr. Fady arranged the typhoid injection.
a.w: The injection is safe on biologics.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked his blood tests.
a.w: Biologics can affect blood counts.

t: Leflunomide stopped for pregnancy without a washout
s:
Mrs. Nour, 31, has rheumatoid arthritis well controlled on leflunomide for three years. She and her husband want to start trying for a baby now. She is not pregnant and uses condoms.

Dr. Mervat checked her joints, which were quiet, and her blood tests, which were normal.

She talked about switching to a pregnancy-safe treatment like hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine, and started folic acid.

Mrs. Nour is a pharmacist and asked how long the leflunomide stays in the body. She was keen to try for a baby next month.

Her mother had two miscarriages.

Dr. Mervat stopped the leflunomide and told her she could try for a baby from next month, without a washout.
h: Dr. Mervat stopped the leflunomide and told her she could try for a baby from next month, without a washout

a.o: Dr. Mervat let Mrs. Nour try for a baby a month after stopping leflunomide without a washout.
a.x: Mrs. Nour should have had a washout with colestyramine and blood levels checked before trying to conceive.
a.w: Leflunomide can stay in the body for up to two years and may harm a baby. A washout clears it in weeks.

a.o: Dr. Mervat started folic acid.
a.w: Folic acid before pregnancy prevents spine defects.

a.o: Dr. Mervat discussed safer drugs.
a.w: Hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are safe in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked her joints.
a.w: Joints show if the arthritis is active.

t: Antiphospholipid syndrome switched to apixaban
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 38, has antiphospholipid syndrome. She had a stroke at 34 and a clot in her leg. All three of her antibody tests are strongly positive. She takes warfarin and has had no clots since.

Dr. Fady checked her INR records, which were mostly in range.

He checked her kidney function, which was normal, and asked about bleeding, which she had none.

Mrs. Asmaa said she was fed up with INR checks every two weeks and wanted a newer blood thinner. Her friend takes apixaban and loves it.

She works as a lawyer and travels for court cases.

Dr. Fady switched her from warfarin to apixaban 5 mg twice a day.
h: Dr. Fady switched her from warfarin to apixaban 5 mg twice a day

a.o: Dr. Fady switched Mrs. Asmaa from warfarin to apixaban.
a.x: Mrs. Asmaa should have stayed on warfarin, with help like a home INR machine.
a.w: In antiphospholipid syndrome with past artery clots and triple positive tests, newer blood thinners lead to more strokes and clots than warfarin.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked her INR records.
a.w: Records show how stable her treatment is.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about bleeding.
a.w: Bleeding is the main risk of blood thinners.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked her kidney function.
a.w: Kidneys affect blood thinner choice.

t: Consent from the wrong person
s:
It was almost five in the afternoon when Mr. Tarek rushed into the ER carrying his nephew Omar, a skinny nine-year-old with a towel pressed to his left arm. Omar had crashed his bicycle into broken glass outside the bakery. By the time they arrived the bleeding had stopped, but the towel was soaked and Omar was pale and crying.

Nurse Salma checked him quickly. His heart was racing at 112, but his blood pressure was fine and he was talking clearly, so she put him in the yellow area. Omar weighed 28 kg, had no allergies his uncle knew of, and had his last tetanus shot at six.

Dr. Hany unwrapped the towel and found a clean 5 cm cut on the inside of the forearm. Omar could move every finger. "We'll need stitches," Dr. Hany said. Mr. Tarek nodded. "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him." Dr. Hany washed the wound, numbed it with lidocaine and closed it with six neat stitches. He gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol for the pain and sent him home with his uncle and a wound-care leaflet.
h: "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him."

a.o: Dr. Hany stitched Omar's arm after only his uncle agreed, when his parents were a phone call away.
a.x: Dr. Hany should have phoned Omar's parents for consent before stitching.
a.w: An uncle is not Omar's legal guardian. The bleeding had stopped, so this was not an emergency and there was time to reach a parent.

a.o: Nurse Salma sent Omar to the yellow area, when a child cut by glass with a racing heart should be seen first.
a.x: Omar should have gone straight to the red area.
a.w: Yellow was right: the bleeding had stopped, his blood pressure was normal and he was talking. A fast heart in a scared, crying child is not shock.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol, far too much for a 28 kg boy.
a.x: Omar should have had 280 mg of paracetamol.
a.w: 420 mg is 15 mg/kg for a 28 kg child, a normal dose.

a.o: Omar went home without a tetanus shot after falling on dirty glass.
a.x: Omar should have had a tetanus booster before leaving.
a.w: His last tetanus shot was three years ago. A dirty wound needs a booster only if the last one was more than 5 years ago.
